Option B does not create an imbalance because discount allowed is correctly posted to the debit side of that account, and option C involves omitting a whole account whose absence is self-contained and does not unsettle the balance between the two sides.

For a bakery, cost of goods sold includes opening stock, raw material purchases, and direct labour, then closing stock is deducted: N800 + N2,450 + N675 − N940 = N2,985. Bakery staff wages are a direct production cost and must be added in, because without labour the flour cannot be converted into finished goods. Administrative staff salaries (N225) and carriage outwards (N50) are period expenses, not production costs, so they are excluded from this calculation. Option A (N3,925) is wrong because it forgets to deduct closing stock, while option B (N3,250) omits the wages entirely and also does not deduct closing stock.

Gross cost of 10 bags is 10 x N500 = N5,000. Trade discount of 5% equals N250 and is simply deducted from the invoice before recording; it never appears in the accounting books as a separate entry. Cash discount of 12% is applied to the original gross price: 12% x N5,000 = N600, and this is the figure recorded as discount received in the company's ledger. Option B (N570) is wrong because it applies the 12% to the post-trade-discount price of N4,750 instead of the original price, and option C (N850) incorrectly treats both discount percentages as additive and applies the total 17% to N5,000.

The sales ledger control account represents the total amount owed to the business by its credit customers (debtors), and this balance sits on the debit side. A provision for bad debts reduces the value of those debtors, so it is entered on the credit side of the sales ledger control account, just as any reduction to an asset is recorded as a credit. Options B and D are wrong because the purchases ledger control account tracks what the business owes to suppliers, which has no connection to bad debt provisions. Option C is wrong because a debit entry to the sales ledger control account would increase debtors rather than reduce them, which is the opposite of what a provision does.

Accounts payable are amounts a business owes to its suppliers for goods or services purchased on credit, making them obligations that must be settled in the future. Under the accounting equation, Assets = Liabilities + Capital, these obligations belong on the liabilities side because they represent claims by outside parties against the business. Options A and C are wrong because equities and capital both refer to the owner's own stake or interest in the business, not debts owed to third parties. Option B is wrong because assets are resources owned or controlled by the business, whereas accounts payable is something the business owes to others, not something it owns.

In an imprest system, the petty cashier receives just enough money at the start of each period to restore the float to the fixed amount (₦500). At the end of period 1, the cashier had ₦50 left (₦500 received minus ₦450 spent), so ₦450 was advanced at the start of period 2. After paying ₦350 for writing materials, the cashier's closing balance for period 2 is ₦50 + ₦450 - ₦350 = ₦150. To restore the float back to ₦500, the cashier must receive ₦500 - ₦150 = ₦350, making B correct. Option A (₦150) is the remaining balance, not the reimbursement, while D (₦500) would only apply if the cashier had spent everything.

Subscriptions accrued means members owe subscription fees to the club or organization but have not yet paid them. Because this money is owed to the organization, it represents an amount receivable, which is classified as a current asset on the balance sheet, just like trade debtors. It is not a liability because the organization is owed money, not owing it. Fixed cost is an income statement concept, not a balance sheet classification, so A is wrong. Long-term liability and current liability both describe money the organization owes to others, which is the opposite situation here.

At the start of period 1, the petty cashier received ₦500. Total payments made were ₦200 (stamps) plus ₦250 (newspapers), giving ₦450 spent in total. The balance remaining with the petty cashier is ₦500 - ₦450 = ₦50, making C the correct answer. Option A (₦450) is the total amount spent, not the balance. Option B (₦300) and D (₦200) have no basis in the given figures.

Cash accounting records transactions only when cash physically changes hands, so it does not recognize amounts owed or owing. Accrual accounting goes further by recording revenue when it is earned (creating debtors — people who owe the business) and expenses when they are incurred (creating creditors — people the business owes), even before cash moves. This is why D (debtors and creditors) is correct. Options that include cash (A, B, C) are wrong because the key difference between accrual and cash accounting is precisely that accrual accounting handles non-cash items like debtors and creditors.

Net working capital measures short-term financial health and is calculated as current assets minus current liabilities. Using the given figures: ₦2,000 - ₦1,200 = ₦800, so B is correct. Fixed assets (₦4,000), drawings (₦200), and the long-term loan (₦2,000) are not included in net working capital because they are not current items. Option A (₦1,800) is wrong — that comes from incorrectly subtracting drawings instead of current liabilities. Option D (₦600) appears to subtract an extra ₦200, likely confusing drawings with a current liability.

Bookkeeping's core function is maintaining a systematic, permanent record of every financial transaction as it occurs. This historical nature makes option A wrong — bookkeeping is retrospective, not futuristic. Option D is also incorrect because double entry is actually a fundamental procedure in bookkeeping, where every debit has a corresponding credit. Option B fails because bookkeeping records transactions mechanically; responsibility for wrong postings lies with the bookkeeper, not the system itself.

When the head office dispatches goods to a branch, the head office current account in the head office ledger is debited to record the outflow of goods from head office resources. This entry reflects that the head office has committed stock to the branch and maintains the reciprocal relationship between both sets of accounts. Crediting the head office current account would wrongly imply head office received value rather than gave it. Entries to the branch current account belong in the branch books, not in the head office ledger for this transaction.

A direct payment occurs when a third party deposits funds straight into the company's bank account; the bank records it immediately, but the company has not yet entered it in the cashbook, so the bank statement shows a higher balance. This credit exists on the bank statement but is absent from the cashbook, causing the overstatement. Commission paid and direct withdrawals reduce the bank balance, so they would understate the bank statement rather than overstate it. Interest received could also overstate the bank statement, but direct payment by third parties is the major structural cause identified here.

Because the vehicles were purchased for cash, money left the business immediately, so the corresponding credit must appear in the cash book to reduce the cash balance. Day books — sales day book, purchase day book, and sales subsidiary book — are only used to record credit transactions, not cash purchases. A cash purchase bypasses all subsidiary day books entirely and goes straight into the cash book. The vehicle account gets the debit to recognise the new asset, while the cash book takes the credit.

Under the straight-line method, annual depreciation equals cost minus residual value divided by useful life; using the revised scrap value of ₦15,000 gives (₦35,000 − ₦15,000) ÷ 5 = ₦4,000 per year. The question specifically asks you to apply the current scrap value of ₦15,000, not the original estimate of ₦9,000. Option A of ₦7,000 and option B of ₦11,000 result from incorrect figures or wrong arithmetic. Option D of ₦24,000 is the total depreciable amount before dividing by the number of years, a common error when students forget the final step.

Net profit in a partnership equals the sum of all items distributed through the appropriation account. Adding interest on capital (750+550=1,300), salaries (800+600=1,400), and shares of profit (3,300+3,300=6,600) gives 1,300+1,400+6,600=9,300. Option A (6,600) counts only the profit shares. Options C and D are arithmetic errors that ignore one or more components of the distribution.

Note: The answer key marks D, but the standard accounting answer is B — the appropriation account is the major distinguishing feature of partnership final accounts. A sole trader has no appropriation account because there is no need to divide profit among partners using salaries, interest on capital, and profit shares. Drawings accounts and capital accounts exist in both sole trader and partnership records, and creditors appear in any business that buys on credit, so they do not distinguish one from the other.

Overhead costs in cost accounting are grouped into four broad categories: production (factory-related costs like factory rent), selling (costs of promoting and obtaining sales), distribution (costs of delivering goods to customers), and administration (general management costs like office salaries). Material is a direct cost, not an overhead, so options B, C, and D are wrong for including it or omitting one of the four true overhead classifications.

Departmental accounts show the profit or loss of each department separately, so management can immediately identify which department is most profitable and make informed decisions about resource allocation. Option C is tempting but healthy rivalry is an indirect benefit that is hard to measure from accounts. Options A and B relate to overall business finance and funding sources, which departmental accounts do not directly reveal since they focus on trading results, not capital structure.

Advertising is a selling expense because its purpose is to promote products and generate sales revenue, which is the direct function of the sales department. Charging it to the sales department ensures the cost is matched against the revenue it produces. The production department handles manufacturing costs, the purchases department handles procurement, and the administrative department handles general management — none of these is responsible for driving product sales through promotion.

When a debenture is issued above its nominal (face) value, the extra amount paid over that face value is called a premium. For example, a N100 debenture sold for N110 is issued at a premium of N10. A margin refers to the difference between selling price and cost in trading, while mark-up is the percentage added to cost price to arrive at selling price — neither describes debenture issuance above par. Cost price simply means what something originally cost, which is unrelated to the concept here.

The sales ledger records all credit sales made to customers, meaning it tracks amounts owed to the business by debtors. The sales ledger control account therefore summarises the total debtors control account balances. The creditors control account belongs to the purchases ledger, not the sales ledger. While day books provide source data, the control account value specifically represents the total of individual debtor balances, not all day books combined.

A standing order is an instruction given by an account holder (customer) to their bank to pay a fixed amount to another party at regular intervals automatically. The key point is that the customer initiates and controls it — the bank simply executes the instruction. A direct debit, by contrast, is initiated by the payee through the bank. The bank never issues standing orders to customers, and customers cannot instruct fellow customers in this formal banking context.

In a trial balance, income accounts (such as sales and rent received) carry credit balances, and liabilities (such as loans and creditors) also carry credit balances — so both appear on the credit side. Assets and expenses appear on the debit side. Option B (credited and debited respectively) wrongly places liabilities on the debit side, and option C reverses both incorrectly. Saying both are debited contradicts the fundamental double-entry rule where liabilities and income increase on credit.

Under the Nigerian Constitution (Section 86), the President of the Federal Republic has the power to appoint the Auditor-General for the Federation, subject to confirmation by the Senate. This appointment is an executive function, so it does not belong to the National Assembly as a body. The Civil Service Commission handles appointments of civil servants, and the Judicial Service Commission handles judicial appointments — neither has jurisdiction over the Auditor-General.

Prime cost (direct materials + direct labour) plus indirect manufacturing costs gives total manufacturing cost. Adding opening work-in-progress and deducting closing work-in-progress converts this into cost of goods manufactured — the cost of items fully completed during the period. Cost of goods available for sale would require adding opening finished goods stock, while cost of goods sold goes a step further by deducting closing finished goods. Materials put into production only accounts for raw materials, not all costs.

Kemi takes 1/5, leaving 4/5 for Kola and Sunday to share equally (their original ratio was 1:1). Each of them gets half of 4/5, which is 2/5. The new ratio is therefore Kola 2/5, Sunday 2/5, Kemi 1/5, which adds up to 1 (the whole profit). Options A and C are wrong because they don't preserve the equal sharing between Kola and Sunday. Option B incorrectly gives Kemi the largest share.

Conservatism (also called prudence) is the accounting convention that requires accountants to anticipate potential losses immediately but recognise profits only when they are certain. This deliberately understates results to avoid misleading users with overly optimistic figures. The monetary and historical cost conventions relate to how transactions are measured and recorded, not to the direction of valuation bias. The cost convention simply requires assets to be recorded at original purchase price.

A Partnership Deed is the legal document that governs the internal management, profit-sharing, capital contributions, and financial affairs of a partnership business. A Memorandum of Association governs a limited company's relationship with the outside world, not a partnership. Bye-laws and financial regulations are terms associated with incorporated companies or public bodies, not partnerships. When no deed exists, the Partnership Act provisions apply by default.

Let M's space = x; then L = 2x and O = x/2. Total space = 2x + x + x/2 = 7x/2. M's fraction of total space = x ÷ (7x/2) = 2/7. M's rent = 2/7 × ₦70,000 = ₦20,000. L would receive 4/7 × ₦70,000 = ₦40,000, and O receives 1/7 × ₦70,000 = ₦10,000. Options A and C are amounts for L and O respectively, while D is too small.

Sales ledger control account is a summary account that records all transactions with customers who buy goods on credit, meaning it tracks amounts owed to the business — these are debtors. Creditors are suppliers the business owes money to, and they appear in the purchases ledger control account. Investors and shareholders relate to ownership of the business, not credit sales. So debtors is the only correct answer here.

Under inflationary conditions, prices are rising, so FIFO (First In, First Out) is most suitable because it issues older, cheaper stock first and leaves newer, more expensive stock in closing inventory, resulting in a higher closing stock value and a more realistic balance sheet. LIFO issues the most recent (expensive) stock first, which reduces profit and closing stock value during inflation — not ideal for realistic reporting. Simple average and weighted average smooth out prices but do not reflect current market values as accurately as FIFO during sustained inflation.

Receiving dividends at a predetermined rate is a right of preference shareholders, not ordinary shareholders — preference shares carry a fixed dividend rate regardless of profit levels. Ordinary shareholders receive variable dividends that depend on how much profit the company decides to distribute. Ordinary shareholders do have the rights to vote at AGMs, elect the board of directors, and participate in rights issues. This question tests the distinction between ordinary and preference share rights.

In government accounting, capital and revenue expenditures are tracked under specific fund categories including personal advances, technical funds, and public funds. Personal advances cover staff-related outlays, technical funds handle specialized project spending, and public funds cover general government expenditure. Options A, C, and D either mix in incorrect fund types or omit core categories used in Nigerian government accounting practice.

In non-profit organisations such as clubs and societies, when total income exceeds total expenditure, the surplus is transferred to the accumulated fund, which serves the same purpose as retained earnings in a profit-making business. It is not transferred to the profit and loss account because non-profits do not prepare that account — they prepare an income and expenditure account instead. The surplus is not a current asset or current liability; it belongs to the capital section of the balance sheet via the accumulated fund.

Factory overhead costs are indirect costs incurred within the factory during production. The qualifying items here are: depreciation of plant and machinery (1,600), factory rent (650), indirect wages (695), general indirect expenses (726), lubricants (1,235), and factory power (350), giving a total of 5,256 naira. Carriage inwards (829) is added to the cost of purchases in the trading account, not classified as factory overhead. Bank charges (612) are administrative expenses, and carriage outwards (2,900) is a selling and distribution expense — neither belongs in factory overhead.

Expenses are shared between departments in the ratio 60:40. Department A's electricity is 60% of the total 2,000 naira which equals 1,200 naira, and depreciation is 60% of 1,000 naira which equals 600 naira. Subtracting all three expenses from Department A's gross profit gives: 6,000 minus 1,800 (salaries) minus 1,200 (electricity) minus 600 (depreciation) equals 2,400 naira net profit. Many students mistakenly use the total net profit or forget to apply the 60% ratio to electricity, leading to wrong answers like 2,000 or 3,000.

Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering finished goods to customers, so it rises and falls directly with the volume of sales made by each department. Apportioning it by turnover (sales revenue) is therefore the fairest method because departments with higher sales are responsible for more delivery costs. Carriage inwards relates to purchasing goods and would be apportioned based on purchases, not turnover. Discount received and returns outwards are not selling expenses and are not apportioned by turnover.

Total depreciation for both departments is 1,000 naira, apportioned 60% to Department A and 40% to Department B. Department B's share is 40% of 1,000 naira, which equals 400 naira. Option A (500) and option D (600) are incorrect because they do not reflect the 40% share for Department B. Option B (300) would represent 30%, which has no basis in the given apportionment ratio.

The materiality concept allows accountants to treat insignificant items in the most convenient way rather than following strict accounting rules. Stationery used over a long period technically qualifies as an asset, but because its cost is too small to be material to the financial statements, it is simply written off as an expense. The entity concept separates the business from its owner, the accrual concept matches income and expenses to the period they occur, and the realization concept deals with when revenue is recognized — none of these explain treating a small asset as an expense.

Accrual accounting records income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of whether cash has actually been received or paid. This follows the matching principle, which ensures revenues and related expenses appear in the same accounting period. Cash accounting (option B) only records transactions when cash physically changes hands, so it would miss income earned but not yet collected. Fund accounting (option C) is used by non-profit and government entities to track restricted funds, while commitment accounting (option D) records obligations before they become actual payments.

Fixed assets are long-term tangible assets used in business operations over many years and not intended for quick conversion to cash. Premises (iii) and land (iv) both qualify because a business uses them continuously to generate income over a long period. Cash at bank (i) and cash in hand (ii) are current assets because they are already in liquid form. Creditors (v) and loan from friends or bank (vi) are liabilities, meaning they represent amounts owed by the business, so they cannot be assets at all.

Current assets are assets that are either already in cash form or can be converted to cash within one accounting year. Cash at bank (i) and cash in hand (ii) are the most liquid of all assets, already existing as money, which makes them classic current assets. Premises (iii) and land (iv) are fixed assets because they are held for long-term use, not for quick conversion. Creditors (v) is a liability representing what the business owes others, so it does not belong under assets at all.

In a trial balance, accounts with credit balances — liabilities, capital, and income — appear on the credit side, while assets and expenses appear on the debit side. Bank overdraft (₦2,000) is a liability because it represents money owed to the bank, so it sits on the credit side. Cash (₦2,000) is an asset and furniture (₦4,000) is a fixed asset, so both appear on the debit side. Only the bank overdraft of ₦2,000 forms the credit total, making option C correct.

Note to students: this question contains a marking error — the published answer (C) contradicts standard accounting principles. Under LIFO during a period of rising prices, the most recently purchased and most expensive items are treated as sold first, which increases the Cost of Goods Sold. Higher cost of goods sold reduces gross profit, not increases it, and lower profit means less income tax is paid. Option A (higher cost of goods sold) is what standard accounting theory and WAEC/JAMB syllabuses teach; option C (higher gross profit) is incorrect. Options B and D are also wrong because closing stock is lower under LIFO in rising prices, and lower profit leads to lower, not higher, tax.

Share premium is the amount received above the nominal value of a share. Each share has a nominal value of N1 but was issued at N1.50, so the premium per share is 50k. Multiplied across all 750,000 issued shares, total share premium is 750,000 x 0.50 = N375,000. Share premium account is always credited because it represents income or gain to the company, not an expense. Options A and C give the wrong figure of N187,500, while option B incorrectly says the account is debited.

When a company makes a call on shares, the journal entry is to debit the Call Account and credit the Share Capital Account, recording the amount now due from shareholders. The second final call is 25k per share on 750,000 shares, giving 750,000 x 0.25 = N187,500. So the Second Final Call Account is debited and 12% Preference Share Capital Account is credited with N187,500, making option B correct. Option C has the wrong amount of N375,000, option A names the wrong class of share capital, and option D incorrectly uses Bank Account as the credit entry rather than the share capital account.

Issued share capital refers to the shares that a company has formally offered and allotted to shareholders, having been authorised by those shareholders to do so through the company's proper procedures. This is different from authorised share capital, which is only the maximum a company is permitted to issue, and not all of it need be issued. Option A is wrong because shares are not simply divided among directors. Option C confuses issued capital with fully subscribed capital, and option D confuses share certificates, which are just proof of ownership, with the definition of issued capital.

Departmental accounts are prepared to evaluate how much each department contributes to the overall profit or loss of the business, helping management make informed decisions about resource allocation and performance. This is the core purpose of departmental accounting. Options A, B, and C describe operational details like materials sold, insurance, or staff numbers, but none of these are financial performance measurements that departmental accounts are designed to reveal.

To register a company in Nigeria with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), all three documents must be submitted: the Memorandum of Association (which states the company's name, objectives, and authorized capital), the Articles of Association (which governs internal management rules), and the incorporation forms or documents required by the Companies and Allied Matters Act. All three are legally required before a certificate of incorporation can be issued, making option A correct. Options B, C, and D are wrong because leaving out any one document means the registration process cannot be completed.

Double-entry bookkeeping requires every debit to have a corresponding credit. When a personal account (such as a debtor) appears on the debit side of the cashbook, it means cash was received from that person, so the matching entry is to credit that personal account in the ledger — option B. Crediting a real account (option A and C) applies to asset accounts like machinery or buildings, not personal accounts. Debiting the ledger (option D) would create a second debit, violating the double-entry principle.

Nigerian law formally recognizes two professional accounting bodies: the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN) and the Association of National Accountants of Nigeria (ANAN), making option C correct. The other options contain names of bodies that either do not exist in Nigeria or are not legally recognized as statutory professional accounting bodies under Nigerian law. ICAN focuses on chartered accountants while ANAN serves national accountants, and both operate under separate Nigerian Acts of Parliament.

Straight-line depreciation spreads an asset's loss in value evenly over its useful life, calculated as (Cost minus Scrap Value) divided by Useful Life — option A. Scrap value is subtracted from cost because that amount will be recovered when the asset is disposed of, so only the net loss is depreciated. Options B, C, and D incorrectly include sales figures in the formula, which have nothing to do with how an asset loses value over time.

Prime cost represents the basic direct costs of production — direct materials plus direct labour (which includes direct wages), so option A is correct. Option B adds production overhead and selling expenses, which go beyond prime cost into total production cost and period costs. Option C lists only indirect expenses (administrative, selling, distribution), none of which are direct costs. Option D mixes direct materials with work overhead, but overhead is an indirect cost and does not form part of prime cost.

Owner's equity refers specifically to the paid-up share capital contributed by shareholders, which is ₦200,000 — option B. Share premium (₦15,000) represents the excess paid above nominal value and is classified as a capital reserve, while the profit and loss balance (₦60,000) is a revenue reserve; both are separate from owner's equity in this context. Option A of ₦275,000 results from adding all three components together, which represents total shareholders' funds rather than owner's equity alone. Option C of ₦755,000 is the total of the balance sheet, and option D does not follow from any standard calculation of the given figures.

Quick ratio excludes stock because it measures only assets that can be converted to cash almost immediately. Quick assets here are net debtors (87,000) plus cash (60,000) plus bank (100,000), giving 247,000. Dividing by current liabilities of 260,000 (creditors 200,000 plus other current liabilities 60,000) gives 0.95:1. Options A and D arise from using wrong current liability figures, while B is close to the current ratio which incorrectly includes stock in the numerator.

Recurrent expenditure covers day-to-day running costs of a business within one accounting year, such as salaries, rent, and utilities. Because the accounting period is twelve months, any expense that repeats or is consumed within that single year qualifies as recurrent. Capital expenditure, by contrast, benefits the business over several years. Options A, B, and C all describe periods longer than one accounting year, which would instead describe capital or long-term spending.

A source document, such as an invoice or receipt, is the original record created at the point of a transaction and shows the price at which goods were sold or bought. It is therefore used to verify the selling price of goods. Amounts owed by debtors or to creditors are confirmed through the ledger accounts and statements of account, not source documents directly. The actual cost of an asset is confirmed through the asset register and purchase documentation, but the selling price verification is the primary function of a source document in trade transactions.

When revenue of 15,000 is wrongly posted as an expense, it causes a double error: revenue is understated by 15,000 and expenses are overstated by 15,000, reducing profit by 30,000 in total. To correct this, 30,000 must be added back to revenue (reversing both effects). The 4,000 expense recorded as revenue is a separate error that requires a deduction, not an addition, so it does not form part of the revenue to be added. Option D of 15,000 only accounts for half the correction and misses the overstated expense component.

When purchase consideration is lower than the net assets acquired, the buyer has paid less than the fair value of what was received, creating negative goodwill. This surplus goes to capital reserve because it arises from a capital transaction, not from normal trading activity. Revenue reserve, by contrast, is built from retained trading profits. Net loss and net income are irrelevant here because no trading has taken place — the gain comes purely from the favourable terms of the acquisition.

When revenue of ₦15,000 was wrongly recorded as expense, profit was reduced twice — once by missing the revenue and once by adding a false expense — so profit is understated by ₦30,000. When expense of ₦4,000 was wrongly recorded as revenue, profit was overstated by ₦8,000 (false revenue added, real expense missed). Adjusted profit = ₦180,000 + ₦30,000 − ₦8,000 = ₦202,000. Options B and C only make one adjustment each instead of two, and D barely adjusts at all.

The purchase ledger control account normally carries a credit balance because it represents what the business owes suppliers. To close the account, the balance c/d is entered on the debit side to make both sides equal, making it a debit item. Balance b/d (option A) and purchases (option D) are credit entries because they increase creditor balances. A dishonoured cheque (option B) would reverse a payment and go back on the credit side, restoring the liability.

A partner's loan to the firm is a business liability, and the interest paid on it is a business expense, so it must be debited in the Profit and Loss account to reduce net profit. Option C is wrong because crediting P&L would mean recording it as income, not expense. Option A is wrong because the partner's current account handles salary, drawings, and profit share — not loan interest. Option D is wrong because the current account is not where loan-related charges are recorded.

Double entry requires every transaction to be recorded as both a debit and a credit of equal value, so total debits must always equal total credits across all accounts. When a trial balance is extracted and both sides agree, this confirms mathematical accuracy in the recording process. It does not guarantee a positive bank balance (option A) or correct cash book balance (option C), nor does it automatically increase assets and liabilities (option B) — those depend on the nature of transactions.

Working capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. Current assets are stock (₦3,600,000) + cash at hand (₦800,000) + cash in bank (₦2,400,000) + debtors (₦580,000) = ₦7,380,000. Current liabilities are trade creditors (₦920,000) + bank overdraft (₦200,000) + tax liabilities (₦600,000) + salary owed (₦180,000) = ₦1,900,000. Working capital = ₦7,380,000 − ₦1,900,000 = ₦5,480,000. Option D (₦7,380,000) is just total current assets with no deduction, and options B and C result from incorrect grouping of items.

When stationery is bought for cash, the double entry rule requires that you debit the account receiving value and credit the account giving value. Stationery (an expense account) receives value, so it is debited; Cash gives value, so it is credited. Option A incorrectly reverses the accounts. Option C credits purchases, which is wrong because this is not a trading transaction. Option B uses the purchases account, which is reserved for goods bought for resale, not stationery.

Conservatism (also called prudence) is the accounting principle that requires caution when making estimates — recognize losses as soon as they are probable but only record profits when they are certain. Materiality relates to whether information is significant enough to affect decisions. Objectivity requires that accounting records be based on verifiable evidence. Consistency means applying the same accounting methods from one period to another.

The matching concept requires that revenues earned and expenses incurred in the same period be reported together in that period's financial statements, regardless of when cash is received or paid. This ensures the profit reported truly reflects the period's performance. Consistency convention refers to using the same accounting methods across periods. Adjusting for revenue and passing of entries are not standard accounting concepts and do not describe this principle.

Any cost that is necessary to bring a fixed asset to its intended location and working condition — including labour for installation — is capitalized, meaning it is added to the cost of the asset on the balance sheet. This follows the cost principle of fixed asset accounting. Treating it as wages and salaries or a general business cost would incorrectly reduce profit for the period without properly reflecting the asset's full value. Option C is close in meaning but option A is the precise accounting treatment.

Investors and creditors primarily use accounting information to assess a company's ability to generate cash in the future, since future cash flows determine whether dividends can be paid and debts can be repaid. Tax payments are determined by tax authorities, not directly predicted by investors from financial statements. Merger candidates and staff remuneration are management and strategic decisions beyond what financial reporting is primarily designed to inform.

A freezer is a fixed asset — capital expenditure — so it must be debited to a fixed asset account, not office expenses. Office expenses is a revenue account, and mixing capital items with revenue items is an error of principle. The double entry credit to bank is correct, but the debit went to the wrong class of account entirely. Error of commission means right type of account but wrong specific account; reversal means debit and credit are swapped; compensating error means two errors cancel each other out.

Double entry works by identifying who receives value and who gives value in every transaction. The receiver is always debited and the giver is always credited. For example, when cash is paid into bank, bank receives (debit bank) and cash gives (credit cash). Option A is wrong because increasing accounts can be credits (liabilities increase on credit side). Options C and D are too narrow — they only cover specific account types, not the universal rule.

In a three-column cashbook, the discount columns are memorandum columns only — they record information but are not part of the double entry within the cashbook itself. The actual double entry for discounts is completed when the column totals are periodically posted to the discount allowed or discount received accounts in the ledger. Balancing the column would imply it forms part of cashbook double entry, which it does not. Discounts are not cash movements, so option B is wrong, and they have no role in bank reconciliation.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier receives cash at the start (establishment), which is recorded as a debit to petty cash account. Each time the float is restored to its original amount, another debit entry is made to petty cash. When money is actually spent on petty expenses, it is the individual expense accounts that are debited, not the petty cash account — petty cash is credited for those payments. Option A is wrong because spending reduces petty cash (credit side), and option C is wrong because decreasing the float size reduces the petty cash account.

Unpresented cheques are cheques the business has already recorded as payments in its cashbook, but which have not yet been presented to the bank for clearing. The bank statement still shows the higher balance because the bank has not yet paid out these amounts. To reconcile, unpresented cheques are deducted from the bank statement balance to arrive at the cashbook balance. Bank charges are already on the bank statement so they adjust the cashbook, not the bank statement; uncredited lodgements are added to, not deducted from, the bank statement balance.

When a bad debt is written off, it is treated as an expense. If the debtor later pays, the business has gained money it no longer expected, so the recovered amount is recorded as income in the profit and loss account to reverse the earlier loss. It cannot be income in a balance sheet because the balance sheet shows financial position, not income. It is not an additional cash entry in the P&L, nor is it an expense — receiving money back is never an expense.

Use the accounts receivable formula: Opening AR + Credit Sales − Collections = Closing AR. Substituting: N8,000 + Credit Sales − N36,000 = N15,000, so Credit Sales = N15,000 − N8,000 + N36,000 = N43,000. Option C (N36,000) confuses collections with sales. Option B (N29,000) incorrectly subtracts the opening balance instead of adding it back. The increase in receivables from N8,000 to N15,000 means more was sold than collected, confirming sales must exceed N36,000.

Net profit is calculated by taking gross profit, deducting all operating and administrative expenses, and then adding any other income such as rent received or commission earned. Option A only describes the trading account step that gives gross profit, not net profit. Option B is wrong because administrative expenses are deducted from gross profit, not added to it. Option C is incomplete — adding only commission without removing all expenses does not produce net profit.

Direct labour refers to workers who are physically and directly involved in making a product, so factory workers qualify because their effort is traceable to specific units of output. An accountant, managing director, and cashier all perform support or administrative functions that benefit the whole business, not a specific product, so their salaries are classified as indirect labour or overhead. Only costs that can be directly traced to production are called direct costs.

A receipts and payments account records every cash receipt and payment made during the year, regardless of whether it belongs to the current, past, or future period — it is purely cash-based. The income and expenditure account follows the accruals concept, recording only income earned and expenses incurred in the current accounting year. Both accounts can be T-accounts and both are maintained by non-profit organisations, so options A, C, and D do not correctly identify the key difference between them.

Purchases journal records all credit purchases from suppliers, and it is from this book of original entry that the creditors control account (purchases ledger control account) receives its postings. Each individual purchase on credit is first recorded in the purchases journal, then posted in total to the creditors control account. Supplier invoices are source documents, not books of prime entry, so posting does not come directly from them. Cash disbursements journal relates to payments going out, which would reduce creditor balances. The subsidiary debtors ledger belongs to debtors, not creditors.

A partnership has multiple owners, so after calculating net profit, the appropriation account is used to divide that profit among partners according to agreed terms — salaries, interest on capital, and profit-sharing ratios. A sole trader has no such division because there is only one owner who takes all the profit. Drawings and capital accounts exist in both sole trader and partnership accounts, so they are not distinguishing features. Creditors accounts appear in both types of business as well.

In partnership accounting, goodwill is raised and recorded in the books specifically when a new partner is admitted, because the incoming partner compensates existing partners for the reputation and value they built before joining. This requires goodwill to be formally recognised and entered in the ledger. Option A describes purchased goodwill, which applies more to limited companies acquiring other businesses, not the typical partnership scenario tested here. Options C and D describe situations that may trigger revaluation but are not the primary basis for raising goodwill as stated in standard JAMB partnership accounting.

Non-profit organisations prepare an income and expenditure account instead of a profit and loss account, and any surplus or profit generated from a trading activity (like a tuck shop or canteen) is transferred into this account as a form of income. The receipt and payment account is simply a summary of all cash received and paid out, and does not classify items as income or expenditure. The balance sheet shows assets and liabilities at a point in time, not income flows. The statement of affairs is used to determine opening capital, not to record trading profits.

When a company receives payment for shares issued, cash or bank increases, so Bank or Cash account is debited. The company's obligation to shareholders increases equity, so Share Capital account and Share Premium account (if shares are issued above par value) are credited. Option B incorrectly credits bank and debits share capital, which would mean cash left the business. Options C and D use incorrect account names and wrong entry directions that do not reflect how share transactions are recorded in double-entry bookkeeping.

Admitting a new partner legally dissolves the existing partnership because the original agreement was between specific individuals, and adding a new member changes the fundamental composition of that contract. A completely new partnership is then formed. Changing the head office (A) is merely an administrative decision that does not affect the legal standing of the partnership. Purchasing fixed assets (C) is a normal business transaction, while the retirement of a manager who is not a partner (D) has no legal effect on the partnership agreement since only partners determine its existence.

Issued capital is calculated using the nominal (face) value of shares, not the subscription price. The nominal value per share is N50 million divided by 100 million shares, which equals N0.50. Multiplying 80 million issued shares by N0.50 gives N40 million. Option B (N48 million) is the trap — it uses the 60 kobo subscription price instead of the nominal value. Option D (N80 million) incorrectly uses the number of shares offered as naira without proper calculation.

The Articles of Association is the internal rulebook of a company, governing matters such as share transfer procedures, conduct of meetings, directors' powers, and dividend payment. The Memorandum of Association (A) is an external document that defines the company's relationship with the outside world, covering its name, objectives, and registered office. A prospectus (C) is used to invite the public to invest in a company's shares. Company law (D) is government legislation, not a document produced by a company.

Nominal (face) value is found by dividing total authorized share capital by total number of shares: N50 million divided by 100 million shares equals N0.50 per share. Option C (N0.60) is the issue price or subscription price at which shares were offered, which is different from nominal value. Options A (N2) and B (N0.80) do not correspond to any figure derivable from the given data, making them clearly incorrect.

Recurrent expenditure covers spending on goods and services that are used up within the current accounting period, such as salaries, electricity, rent, and stationery. Capital expenditure (B) is incorrect because it relates to acquiring long-term assets that provide benefits beyond one accounting period. Fixed expenditure (A) describes costs that remain constant regardless of output level, which is a different classification. Annual expenditure (C) is not a recognised accounting category for this type of spending.

When government imposes a special tax levy specifically to meet interest payments on debt, those receipts are recorded in a Tax Assessment Fund because the levy is directly tied to assessed tax obligations for that purpose. Debt Service Fund (option B) is used for accumulating resources to repay principal and interest on general long-term debt, not specifically for special tax levies. Capital Project Fund handles proceeds for acquiring fixed assets, while Special Revenue Fund records proceeds from specific revenue sources restricted for designated spending, neither of which fits a special tax levy for interest obligations.

Accounting ratios are most valuable because they transform raw financial figures into meaningful comparisons that help managers, investors, and creditors make informed business decisions such as whether to invest, extend credit, or cut costs. Option A is incorrect because ease of calculation is a feature, not an advantage in terms of usefulness. Option C is wrong because ratios are analytical tools developed by accountants, not legal requirements. Option D is incorrect because detecting errors and fraud is the role of auditing, not ratio analysis.

As businesses grew larger, owners could no longer personally supervise all operations, so they employed professional managers, creating an urgent need for systematic accounting records to report performance back to owners, this separation of ownership and management drove accounting development most directly. Option A is weak because nation-states existed long before modern accounting developed. Option B is incorrect because mineral resource discovery is more about economic growth than accounting need. Option D describes monetary policy development, which is a related but separate discipline from accounting.

In government budgeting, the term vote refers to the specific amount of money approved and allocated for each individual line item or department in the national or state budget, representing parliament's authorisation to spend. A deposit is money received and held temporarily, not a budget allocation term. A loan implies borrowing with repayment obligation, while a grant is money given to an entity without repayment, neither describes the approved spending figure for a budget item.

Under the cash basis of accounting, revenue is only recognised and recorded in the books when actual cash is received, regardless of when it was earned or when it became due. Option A (due) and option B (earned) both describe the accrual basis, where revenue is recorded when it is owed or earned even before cash changes hands. Option C (paid) relates to expenses under cash basis, not revenue, since payments go out while receipts come in.

Accounting exists to serve both internal users like managers and external users like investors, creditors, and government agencies, so option C correctly captures the full scope of an effective accounting system. Option A describes marketing or research functions, not accounting. Option B describes customer service activities. Option D lists some stakeholders but misses the core purpose of providing structured internal and external financial reports.

Source documents are original papers that provide first-hand evidence of a business transaction before any recording takes place; sales invoices and debit notes both qualify because they are issued at the point of a transaction. Journals and ledgers in option A are books of account where transactions are recorded, not original evidence. The cash book in options B and C is itself a book of prime entry, not a source document. Only option D lists two genuine source documents.

The accrual concept requires that revenue be recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves, so profit under this concept is simply revenue minus expenses for a period. The prudence and conservatism concepts in options B and C both refer to recognising potential losses early while not anticipating profits, which is about caution, not the profit definition. The materiality concept in option D relates to whether information is significant enough to influence decisions, not to how profit is calculated.

When an owner pays capital into the business bank account, the bank account (an asset) increases and is therefore debited, while the capital account (owner's equity) increases and is therefore credited, making option B correct. Option A reverses both entries, debiting capital and crediting cash, which is wrong because assets rise on the debit side. Option C records only one side of the double entry, violating the dual aspect principle. Option D uses incorrect account names that do not reflect the nature of the transaction.

The general journal is used for transactions that do not belong in any specialised subsidiary book; an inter-branch transfer of cash is non-routine and has no dedicated book, so it fits best in the general journal. Payment of rent by cheque belongs in the cash book. Purchase of stock with cash is recorded in the cash book or purchases journal. Purchase of an asset on credit, while sometimes journalised, is a more standard credit transaction, whereas the inter-branch transfer in option D is the clearest case for general journal use.

The imprest system replenishes the petty cash float by cheque for exactly the amount spent, making cheque drawing easy (Statement I). It also limits the petty cashier's responsibility to only the fixed float amount (Statement III), and this restriction naturally reduces potential losses (Statement IV). Statement II is excluded because 'a cheque on the use of cash' is not a recognised advantage of the imprest system — the control comes from limiting the float, not from using cheques as a control mechanism. Options A, B, and D all incorrectly include Statement II.

A trial balance extracts all debit and credit balances from the ledger and checks that they are equal, confirming that every debit entry has a matching credit entry and that arithmetic is correct throughout the ledger. It does not classify accounts — the ledger does that — and it does not directly identify balance sheet items, which requires preparing financial statements separately. Proving an accountant's competence is not an accounting function at all. The trial balance is strictly an arithmetic check, not a guarantee that all transactions were recorded to the right accounts.

A ledger can be maintained by any type of business — sole traders, partnerships, limited liability companies, and non-profit organisations — because it is a universal principal book of accounts, making option D correct. Option A is wrong because the ledger is not a book of original entry; journals and daybooks record transactions first, then they are posted to the ledger. Option B is false because the ledger is not restricted to shareholders during liquidation. Option C is wrong because the ledger does not remove the need for a balance sheet; financial statements are still prepared from ledger balances.

Paying N20 to John should have been recorded as Debit John N20 (reducing the amount owed to him) and Credit Cash N20 (cash going out). Instead, the wrong entry recorded Debit Cash N20 and Credit John N20 — both sides are reversed. The correcting journal entry that eliminates this error is Debit John N20 and Credit Cash N20 (option C), because the wrong entry is the exact mirror image of the correct one, so a single N20 correcting entry restores both accounts to their proper positions. Option A (N40) is not needed here since only one erroneous double entry was made, not two separate mistakes requiring independent reversal and re-entry.

Bola owed N1,000 but sent a cheque for N1,500, meaning he overpaid by N500 — UTC now owes Bola that excess, so UTC issues a credit note to formally acknowledge the credit balance on Bola's account. A credit note reduces what the customer owes or records an amount owed back to the customer. A debit note is used in the opposite situation, when the buyer owes more money — for example, after an undercharge is discovered. A waybill accompanies goods during delivery, and a journal voucher is an internal accounting document; neither is used to communicate a credit balance to a customer.

Adjustments are made in the profit and loss account because accounting follows the accrual concept, which requires matching income earned and expenses incurred to the correct period, regardless of when cash is received or paid. Without adjustments for items like accruals, prepayments, and depreciation, the profit figure would be misleading. Option D is wrong because recording only cash paid and received describes cash basis accounting, not proper accrual accounting. Option A confuses prepayments with the general purpose of adjustments, and C is wrong because provisions are just one specific type of adjustment, not the overall reason.

Sales ledger is another name for the debtors ledger, which records all customers who have bought goods on credit and still owe money to the business. The sales ledger control account summarises all individual debtor balances into one total figure. Creditors belong in the purchases ledger control account, not the sales ledger. Investors and shareholders are capital providers whose records appear in different sections of the accounts entirely.

Adama's bank statement shows an overdraft of N600, but the N1,080 deposit made on 29th March has not yet been credited by the bank. To find the correct cash book balance, add the uncredited deposit to the bank statement balance: N1,080 minus N600 overdraft gives N480 credit, meaning there is actually money in the account. Option A is wrong because adding both figures gives an incorrect debit balance; N600 Dr simply ignores the deposit altogether. The correct adjusted balance is N480 Cr, confirming the account is in funds once the deposit is properly recorded.

When a business keeps incomplete records, there is no full set of books to work from, so the accountant must first establish what the business owned and owed at the beginning of the period by preparing a statement of affairs. This opening statement of affairs reveals the opening capital, which becomes the foundation for reconstructing all other figures. Computing sales, purchases, or opening stock are steps that come later in the process, after the opening capital is known. Without knowing the starting capital, there is no reliable baseline to calculate profit or loss.

Since the retailer adds one-quarter to cost as markup, the selling price equals five-quarters of cost, making cost 4/5 (80%) of sales. Cost of goods sold is therefore 80% of N23,000, which equals N18,400. Dividing cost of goods sold by the stock turnover rate of 5 gives average stock at cost: N18,400 divided by 5 equals N3,680. The expenses figure of 10% of sales is not needed for this calculation as it relates to net profit, not stock valuation.

In the Purchase Ledger Control Account, both sides must balance: the debit side records payments to suppliers (N437,000) plus discounts received (N18,600) plus the closing balance (N72,600), totalling N528,200. Credit purchases are found by subtracting the opening balance from this total: N528,200 − N45,600 = N482,600. Option A (N509,600) results from adding the opening balance instead of subtracting it, while option C (N428,600) ignores the closing balance adjustment. Option D (N418,400) arises from swapping the opening and closing balances in the equation.

Production cost is calculated as prime cost plus factory overhead, adjusted for work in progress: N220,000 + N32,000 + N25,000 (opening WIP) − N19,000 (closing WIP) = N258,000. Opening WIP is added because those partly finished goods are completed during the period, while closing WIP is deducted because those goods are not yet finished and should not be included in this period's production cost. Administrative expenses of N21,000 are a period cost that appears below gross profit in the income statement, not inside the production cost schedule; option A (N296,000) wrongly includes them. Option B (N277,000) ignores the WIP adjustments entirely, and option D (N246,000) deducts WIP without adding factory overhead.

Factory cost, also called cost of production, combines prime cost — which is the total of direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses — with factory overhead, which covers indirect manufacturing costs such as factory rent, indirect labour, and depreciation of plant and machinery. Office overhead relates to the administration of the business as a whole and does not arise inside the factory, so option B is incorrect. Option C is wrong because raw materials alone represent only part of prime cost, and 'fixed cost' is a cost-behaviour classification rather than a distinct cost component. Option D incorrectly brings administrative overhead into the factory cost, when it belongs in selling and administration expenses.

Because the retailer adds one-quarter to the cost price, selling price equals five-quarters of cost, which means gross profit is one-fifth (20%) of sales. After deducting expenses of 10% of sales, the net profit margin is 10% of total annual sales, giving a net profit of N3,200. Option A (N5,750) is wrong because it applies the 25% markup rate directly to the sales figure, confusing markup on cost with gross margin on sales. Option D (N2,300) represents the value of expenses deducted rather than the net profit remaining, while option B (N5,650) does not correspond to any correct step in the calculation.

Under the accruals basis, income is recognised when earned and expenditure when incurred, regardless of when cash moves, so the correct statement for measuring a non-profit organisation's performance is the income and expenditure account, which shows whether a surplus or deficit was made during the period. A receipts and payments account (option D) records only actual cash received and paid out, which is a cash-basis statement and does not match income to the period it relates to. An appropriation account (option A) distributes profit among partners or shareholders in a profit-making entity and has no relevance to non-profit organisations. A balance sheet (option B) shows the financial position at a single point in time but cannot indicate how well the organisation performed over the period.

Subscriptions in arrears are amounts owed to the club by members who have not yet paid their dues for the period. Since this income has been earned, it is recognised in the Income and Expenditure account, and because the club is owed this money it is a receivable shown as a current asset in the balance sheet. Options A and C wrongly classify arrears as a liability — liabilities represent money the club owes others, not money owed to it. Option D is wrong because it combines an incorrect I&E treatment with an incorrect balance sheet classification.

The manufacturing account formula is: Opening WIP + Prime Cost + Manufacturing Overhead − Closing WIP = Finished Goods Transferred. Rent paid in advance (N5,000) is a prepayment, not a cost of the current period, so it must be deducted from manufacturing overhead, giving adjusted overhead of N132,000 − N5,000 = N127,000. Substituting: Opening WIP + N999,000 + N127,000 − N75,000 = N1,116,000, so Opening WIP = N65,000. Options A and B result from failing to adjust for the prepaid rent, while option C uses an entirely incorrect figure.

Interest on drawings is a charge levied on a partner who withdraws money from the business, reducing the amount the business owes that partner and benefiting all partners collectively. It is therefore debited to the drawing partner's current account (reducing their balance) and credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account (increasing distributable profit). Option B incorrectly reverses these entries. Options C and D are wrong because this transaction belongs in the P&L Appropriation Account, not the ordinary Profit and Loss Account.

Unlike a limited company, partners in a partnership bear unlimited personal liability for all business debts, meaning creditors can pursue their private assets if the business cannot pay. Option A is wrong because a partnership does not have perpetual or indefinite life — it dissolves automatically when a partner dies, retires, or is added. Option C is incorrect because transferring a partnership interest requires unanimous consent of all partners, making it far from easy. Option D is false because partnerships are comparatively simple to form, requiring far fewer legal formalities than companies.

The N1,200 paid for year 1992 was received during the 1993 financial year, but it relates to a period that has already closed. In 1992's accounts, this subscription was already recognised as income (recorded as a subscription in arrears, a current asset in 1992's balance sheet), so when the club actually receives it in 1993 it cannot be treated as income again. It must therefore be shown as a current liability in the 1993 balance sheet, representing funds received that were already accounted for in a prior period. Option A applies to subscriptions still owed but not yet received, and options C and D are entirely inappropriate categories for a subscription receipt.

Partners' current accounts are the correct destination for profit share allocations because current accounts are designed to record ongoing transactions between the partnership and each partner, including profit distributions, salaries, and drawings. Capital accounts remain fixed at the agreed initial investment and are not adjusted for routine profit shares. Crediting the appropriation account would be wrong because the appropriation account is where profit is distributed from, so it gets debited as each partner's share is removed. Debiting the drawing account reduces a partner's balance and is only used when a partner withdraws cash or goods, not when profit is being credited to them.

Halidu's salary of N3,000 must first be deducted from the total profit of N12,000, leaving N9,000 to be shared between the partners in their capital ratio. The capital ratio is N30,000 to N20,000, which simplifies to 3:2, making a total of five equal parts. Halidu's share of the remaining profit is three-fifths of N9,000, which equals N5,400. Options A and D result from applying the ratio to the full N12,000 without first deducting the salary, and option B uses an incorrect proportional split of the distributable profit.

When a partnership revalues an asset upward on admitting a new partner, the increase in value represents an unrealized gain belonging to the existing partners and is recorded by debiting the asset revaluation account. This debit entry of N40,000 captures the profit to be shared among old partners in their profit-sharing ratio before the new member joins. Option C would apply when an asset decreases in value, as that loss is credited to the revaluation account. Option A is incorrect because crediting the land and building account would reduce the asset's book value rather than increase it. Option D is reserved for distributing ordinary trading profits and is not used for revaluation adjustments.

After removing the 100,000 dishonored applications, there are 500,000 valid applications competing for 400,000 available shares, giving a pro-rata allotment ratio of 4 to 5. A subscriber who applied for 5,000 shares is therefore allotted 4,000 shares, leaving 1,000 shares unallotted. The refund due is calculated on the 1,000 unallotted shares at the N1.00 nominal value per share, giving N1,000. Option B of N1,200 incorrectly applies the full N1.20 issue price to all unallotted shares rather than the nominal value. Options C and D represent the value of allotted shares and total application money paid respectively, not a refund figure.

The quick ratio, also called the acid-test ratio, measures a firm's ability to meet short-term obligations using only its most liquid assets such as cash, receivables, and short-term investments, deliberately excluding inventory that may be slow to convert. This makes it the standard measure of a firm's immediate liquidity position. The turnover ratio measures how efficiently a business converts assets into sales revenue, which is an efficiency indicator and not a liquidity measure. The debt ratio compares total debt to total assets to assess solvency and financial leverage, not short-term payment ability. Dividend yield measures the return shareholders receive relative to share price, which is a profitability and investment performance metric.

In a limited partnership, limited liability partners already had some liability protection, but it was conditional — they could lose it the moment they participated in active management of the business. Converting to a limited liability company allows these partners to fully enjoy limited liability protection without that restriction, since all members of an LLC are protected regardless of their role in management. General partners (option A) actually gain the most from conversion since they previously had unlimited liability, but the question asks who is specifically afforded the chance to enjoy the protection properly. Creditors and debtors are external parties whose legal positions are not changed by how the owners structure their own liability.

Departmental accounts are maintained to measure the contribution of each department, meaning its individual profit or net performance after accounting for both revenues and costs. Knowing only sales (option D) tells management nothing about whether a department is actually profitable, and knowing only expenses (option C) gives an equally incomplete picture. The profit of the entire organisation (option A) is the combined result of all departments together, not what departmental accounts individually reveal. The purpose is to compare departments so that management can reward high-performing units and address underperforming ones.

With a 22% markup on cost, the cost of goods is calculated as: N549,000 divided by 1.22, which equals exactly N450,000, giving a gross profit of N99,000. Deducting branch expenses of N34,400 from N99,000 yields a net branch profit of N64,600 (option B), which is the result standard markup accounting produces with these figures. Option D (N514,600) is the error of subtracting only expenses from sales while completely ignoring the cost of goods sold. Students should note that markup is always expressed as a percentage of cost, so dividing by 1.22 (not multiplying) is the correct method to find the cost from the selling price.

The acid test ratio, also called the quick ratio, measures how quickly a company can pay its immediate debts using only its most liquid assets — cash and receivables — excluding inventory which takes time to sell. This makes it a stricter and more reliable measure of short-term debt-paying ability than the current ratio (option A), which includes inventory. The turnover ratio (option B) measures how efficiently assets generate sales revenue, not the ability to repay debts. Return on investment (option D) measures profitability, a separate concept from liquidity.

Statutory allocation (I) is the share of Federation Account revenue distributed to each state by the federal government, making it a core source of state income in Nigeria. Personal income tax (IV), collected as PAYE from workers in a state, is also a state-level revenue retained by state governments under Nigerian tax law. Petroleum profit tax (III) is a federal tax exclusively collected by the FIRS on behalf of the federal government, so states have no direct claim on it — this rules out options B and D. Fines from customary courts (II) may seem like a state revenue since customary courts are under state authority, but for JAMB purposes the principal constitutional sources of state revenue are statutory allocation and income tax, making option C correct.

Capital expenditure refers to money spent on long-term assets that provide benefits over many years. From the list, hospital building (N200,000) and hospital beds and mattresses (N40,000) are capital expenditures because they are durable assets, giving a total of N240,000. Drugs are consumables spent within a short period, making them revenue expenditure. Salaries and administrative expenses are also revenue expenditures because they are recurring costs that do not create lasting assets. Options A and B wrongly include revenue items like drugs and salaries.

In branch accounting, the head office opens a Branch Current Account in its own books to record all resources sent to the branch, so this account carries a debit balance, representing what the branch owes or has received. The branch, on the other hand, opens a Head Office Current Account in its own books to record its obligation to the head office, giving it a credit balance since it represents a liability. These two accounts are mirror images of each other and should cancel out during consolidation. Options A and B are wrong because neither account always has the same type of balance on both sides. Option C reverses the correct positions of the two balances.

Accounting exists primarily to produce financial information that helps managers, investors, creditors, and other stakeholders make informed decisions. Without useful decision-making information, accounting would have no practical value regardless of its other benefits. Option B is too general and does not explain the specific purpose of accounting. Option C describes a personal career benefit, not the core purpose of the discipline. Option D is too narrow because accounting provides far more than just gross profit figures.

Government accounting operates within a framework of laws, budgets, and regulations that determine how public funds can be collected and spent, so compliance with all legal provisions is the primary obligation. Unlike private businesses, governments do not always need revenue to exceed expenditure, as they may intentionally run deficits for economic reasons, making Option A incorrect. Option C is not a standard accounting requirement, as capital and revenue figures do not need to be equal. Option D describes an incorrect relationship, since capital project funds and recurrent expenditure serve entirely different purposes under government finance rules.

Creditors, such as banks and suppliers who extend credit, primarily want to know whether a company has enough liquid assets to meet its short-term obligations, so they focus on liquidity. Before granting credit or loans, they analyse current ratios, cash flow, and working capital to judge repayment ability. Option A describes the goal of a company's own sales team, not external creditors. Option B represents the role of management or regulatory bodies, not creditors. Option C is the purpose of shareholders and potential investors, who seek returns on equity rather than debt repayment assurance.

Source documents are the original papers produced when a business transaction takes place, such as receipts, invoices, and delivery notes. They serve as evidence and the starting point for all accounting entries. Purchase documents is too narrow a term since it covers only buying transactions. Journals are books where transactions are recorded after source documents are received, not the documents themselves. Invoices are just one type of source document, not the general category.

This is the Business Entity Concept, one of the fundamental accounting principles, which holds that the business is a separate legal entity from its owner. This means only business transactions are recorded in the business books, not the owner's personal affairs. Treating them as the same person would mix personal and business finances, violating this principle. They are not partners because a partnership is a legal arrangement between two or more distinct people, not an owner and their own business.

When a buyer returns goods, the seller issues a credit note to acknowledge receipt of those goods and to reduce the amount the buyer owes. It represents a reduction in the seller's revenue and the buyer's debt. A debit note is the opposite — it is sent by the buyer to the seller to formally notify them of the return before the credit note is issued. An invoice records a sale, while a voucher is used internally to authorize payments.

Books of original entry, also called journals or day books, are where business transactions are first recorded in chronological order as they occur. They capture the details of every transaction before the information is posted to the ledger accounts. They are not used for adjusting accounts, which is done in the ledger at period end. Their purpose is recording, not reminding or informing the bookkeeper about financial position.

When a liability is paid, cash or bank balance (an asset) decreases because money is going out, and simultaneously the liability being settled also decreases since the debt no longer exists. This keeps the accounting equation balanced: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Options A and B are wrong because paying a liability never increases assets. Option C is wrong because paying off a debt reduces, not increases, the liability.

When digits in a figure are rearranged or swapped in position — like writing N624 as N264 — this is a transposition error, which is the defining feature of option A. The digits 6 and 2 have simply changed places, making the figure look different but still using the same digits. Commission error means recording a wrong amount entirely, while omission means failing to record a transaction at all. Principle error involves posting to the wrong class of account, which is unrelated to digit rearrangement.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier begins with a fixed float, uses it to pay expenses, and then receives a reimbursement from the bank equal to exactly what was spent, restoring the float to its original amount. Option C correctly shows expenses are paid first before the bank tops up the float. Option B wrongly suggests cash comes from the bank before expenses are paid, which defeats the whole purpose of the system. Option D uses the phrase 'cash in bank' rather than 'cash from bank,' misrepresenting the direction of the reimbursement.

Posting is the process of transferring entries from the journal (the book of original entry) into the appropriate ledger accounts, making D correct. Option A describes journalizing, which is recording transactions in the journal — the step that comes before posting. Option B describes extracting a trial balance, a completely separate process. Option C describes the work of tracing figures to detect errors, which is an audit activity, not posting.

The rent of N50,000 covers 2 years (24 months) from 30/5/93. To find the monthly charge: N50,000 ÷ 24 = N2,083.33. From 30/5/93 to 31/12/93 is 7 months, so the portion attributable to that period is 7 × N2,083.33 = N14,583. This is the amount that relates to the time already elapsed within the accounting year up to 31 December 1993. Options B and C would result from miscounting the months or dividing the total incorrectly, while D (N37,415) does not correspond to any correct calculation of the period.

When a cheque appears on the credit side of the cash book (meaning the business has recorded it as paid out) but has not yet appeared on the bank statement, it means the payee has not yet presented it to the bank for payment — these are unpresented cheques. Uncredited cheques are the opposite: they appear on the debit side of the cash book but the bank has not yet credited the account. A dishonoured cheque is one the bank has returned unpaid, which would actually appear on the bank statement. Direct remittances are lodgements made straight to the bank, not outgoing payments.

The stated profit of N120,000 contains two classification errors that must be reversed. Revenue of N12,000 was wrongly treated as an expense, which reduced profit by N12,000, so adding it back corrects this. Expense of N4,000 was wrongly treated as revenue, which inflated profit by N4,000, so it must be deducted. Corrected profit: N120,000 + N12,000 - N4,000 = N128,000. Option C (N136,000) applies double-entry corrections to both sides of each error, option D (N144,000) adds both amounts without deducting anything, and option A (N104,000) deducts both amounts instead of making the proper two-way correction.

Trade discount is always deducted from list price first, before cash discount is considered. Applying 25% trade discount to N800 gives an invoice price of N800 x 75% = N600; this is the amount the buyer owes. The terms 2/10, n/30 mean a 2% cash discount is earned if payment is made within 10 days, so the discount is 2% x N600 = N12. Cash received is therefore N600 - N12 = N588. Option C (N600) ignores the cash discount entirely, while option A (N576) incorrectly applies the 2% cash discount to the original list price of N800 instead of the trade-discounted price.

When two years of rent is paid in full and debited entirely to the rent account, the portion extending beyond 31 December 1993 has not yet been incurred and must be set aside. The year-end adjustment transfers the unexpired portion to the balance sheet by debiting rent account (to recognise the amount being expensed in the current period) and crediting prepayment account (to isolate the deferred amount that carries forward to future periods).
