Option B reverses the entries, which would incorrectly remove a balance from rent account rather than properly establishing the prepaid balance. Options A and D refer to accounts that are not used in a straightforward prepayment adjustment.

Wages that have been earned by workers during the accounting period but have not yet been paid represent a cost already incurred, making them accrued expenses. Recording accrued expenses ensures the income statement reflects all costs belonging to the period, even when cash has not yet been paid. Option A (apportionment of revenue) applies to splitting income between periods, not to unpaid costs. Option C (unaccounted revenue) refers to income earned but not yet recorded, which is the opposite of an expense item. Option D (prepaid expenses) describes costs paid in advance before the benefit is received, the reverse of an accrual.

Gross profit is calculated first: Sales - Cost of Sales = N85,000 - N25,000 = N60,000. Net profit equals gross profit minus total operating expenses, so N25,000 = N60,000 - Total expenses. Solving gives Total expenses = N35,000. Option A (N45,000) would produce a net profit of only N15,000, not N25,000. Option C (N25,000) confuses total expenses with net profit since both happen to be the same figure in a different context, and option D (N15,000) would leave a net profit of N45,000, far above the given figure.

The balance sheet total equals the sum of all assets: office machinery N9,000 plus stock N1,550 plus debtors N275 plus cash at bank N5,075, giving N15,900. This equals capital plus liabilities on the other side: N13,000 plus N900 creditors plus N2,000 loan, also N15,900. Options A and B result from incorrectly adding capital into the assets column and double-counting it. Option C comes from an arithmetic mistake when summing the asset items.

In the JAMB accounting syllabus, depreciation is treated as the broad term for systematically allocating the cost of any long-term asset over its useful life, covering both tangible and intangible assets. Amortization (option D), while the internationally preferred term for intangibles specifically, is not the answer expected here. Depletion (option C) applies only to natural or wasting resources such as oil wells and mines. Extraction (option B) is a physical process, not an accounting concept at all.

A control account is a summary account in the general ledger that mirrors the total of a subsidiary ledger, so when the two fail to agree, the error is immediately isolated to that specific ledger rather than searched across the entire books. Option B is wrong because control accounts can help detect but cannot prevent fraud on their own. Option C is irrelevant since control accounts serve a bookkeeping verification purpose, not a commercial one. Option D describes the function of the balance sheet, not control accounts.

ICAN was established under Act No. 15 of 1965 which came into force on 1st September 1965, making option D correct. Options B and C are common traps because 1st October 1960 and 1st October 1963 are Nigeria's independence and republic dates respectively, dates students already know well and may confuse with ICAN's founding. Option A places the date in 1960, five years before ICAN was actually created by law.

Total purchases equal cash paid to suppliers plus discounts received from those same suppliers: N26,500 plus N130 equals N26,630. The discounts received represent amounts the business was relieved from paying but which were originally recorded as purchases, so they must be added back to the payments figure. Options C and D go wrong by adding the full closing creditors balance or the net change in creditors on top, which double-counts amounts already captured in the payments figure. Option B does not correspond to any recognised calculation approach.

Discount allowed is a reduction given to debtors to encourage early payment of their credit purchases. When customers pay less due to discount, the total amount owed to the business decreases, which reduces the closing balance of the Sales Ledger Control Account. It reduces net profit because it is an expense, making option B wrong. It does not change the original value of sales recorded or affect purchases in any way, so options C and D are both incorrect.

Responsibility accounting holds individual managers accountable only for what they can actually influence, which makes controllable costs its central concern. A cost is controllable if the manager in charge of a department has the authority to incur or reduce it. Historical accounting simply records past transactions without linking them to managerial responsibility, so option A is wrong. Storekeeping and stock valuation are operational functions, not the focus of responsibility accounting, so C and D are also incorrect.

Management needs reports that help them make decisions and take corrective action, so cost reports should contain cost figures alongside comparable data such as budgets or prior periods. Excessive detail (option A) creates information overload and obscures key trends. Summary figures alone (option B) may hide important variances that require attention. Non-controllable expenses (option C) are irrelevant to management action since nothing can be done to change them at that level.

A voucher system requires that every payment be documented, reviewed, and formally approved before any cheque is written or cash released, which strengthens internal control. This verification process catches errors and prevents unauthorized payments. Option A is wrong because the system does not reduce the number of cheques written; it controls how they are authorised. Option B is incorrect because the system is structured and formal, not flexible. Option C describes a supplier record, which is a byproduct, not the main advantage.

To prepare the trial balance, each account is placed on the correct side: assets and expenses go to the debit column, while liabilities, capital, and income go to the credit column. Bank (59,410), Purchases (20,000), Rent (2,500), Stationery (90), and Typewriter (6,500) are all debits, giving a debit column total of 88,500. Capital (50,000) and Sales (38,000) are credits totalling 88,000. The debit column total of 88,500 matches option C, which is what the question targets, and any difference between columns would indicate a missing or misclassified entry.

The accounting equation states Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity, so both sides must always balance. When an asset increases, the right side must also increase by an equal amount, meaning a liability rises — for example, taking a bank loan increases cash and creates a loan payable simultaneously. Option C is wrong because one asset increasing while another also increases would raise total assets without a corresponding rise on the right side. Options A and D both reduce the right side while assets grow, which breaks the equation entirely.

Cost of Goods Sold is calculated as Opening Stock plus Purchases minus Closing Stock. When ending inventory is understated (recorded too low), Closing Stock is too small, so COGS becomes too high, reducing gross profit and understating net income for the current year. In the following year, the understated closing stock becomes the opening stock, making COGS too low and overstating that year's income. The two errors cancel each other over both periods, so Option D is wrong because combined two-year income is not distorted. Option A describes the effect of overstated ending inventory, not understated.

Generators are long-term tangible assets that power business operations over many years, so they must be capitalized as fixed assets and depreciated, not written off as expenses immediately. The business name containing 'Electronics' does not determine how the generators are classified — what matters is their purpose. Option C (stock) would only apply if the company purchased generators specifically for resale to customers. Option B (general office expenses) is wrong because a purchase providing long-term economic benefit cannot be treated as a period expense.

When the bank collects a note on behalf of the company, the bank immediately records the receipt, but the company's cash book still shows the old, lower balance because it has not recorded the collection yet. On the bank reconciliation, this uncredited collection must be added to the book balance to bring it up to the bank's figure. Options B and C are wrong because the bank statement already reflects the collection, so no bank-side adjustment is needed. Option D (deduction from books) would reduce the book balance further, moving it away from the bank balance rather than toward it.

Under the imprest system, petty cash is always restored to a fixed float at the end of each period, and the replenishment cheque equals the exact total of all expenditure vouchers paid out. From the accompanying data, the verified total of petty cash payments made was N394, which is the amount needed to bring the fund back to its original imprest level. Option A (N399) and Option C (N358) reflect incorrect additions of the payment columns. Option D (N101) represents the cash physically remaining in the tin, not the top-up required.

To find actual cash in the till, start with the initial imprest of N500 and subtract everything that left the cash box: petty cash vouchers paid out (N394), the IOU given to a co-worker (N65), and the cash shortage (N5). That gives N500 - N394 - N65 - N5 = N36. Option A (N106) ignores both the IOU and shortage. Option B (N101) ignores the IOU. Option C (N70) ignores the shortage. Only N36 accounts for all three reductions.

A 40% gross profit rate means cost of goods sold is 60% of sales, so COGS = 60% x N176,000 = N105,600. Ending inventory is found by subtracting COGS from cost of merchandise available for sale: N128,000 - N105,600 = N22,400. Option B (N32,000) wrongly uses 40% of N128,000 without relating it to sales. Option D (N76,800) confuses gross profit percentage with cost percentage. Always remember gross profit rate is based on selling price, not cost.

When a customer who paid cash returns merchandise and receives a refund, the company is paying cash out, which is a cash disbursement. All transactions involving cash going out of the business are recorded in the cash disbursement journal. The cash receipts journal only records cash coming in, so it cannot be used here. The sales journal records credit sales only, and the general journal handles non-routine entries not fitting any special journal.

The initial cost of a machine includes all expenditures necessary to bring it to its working condition: gross invoice price (N15,000), sales tax (N900), freight (N750), assembly (N500), installation (N800), and tuning (N700), minus the purchase discount taken (N300), giving N18,350. Spare parts bought for future use (N1,200) are excluded because they are not part of getting this machine ready; they are a separate asset. Options A and B wrongly include the spare parts or miscalculate the discount.

The sales day book records every credit sale made, and its totals are cross-referenced against individual entries in the sales ledger, making it a strong check on the clerk who posts to that ledger. Any difference between the day book total and the ledger balances immediately signals an error or fraud. The total debtors account (control account) is derived from the day book, so the day book is the primary instrument. The cash book and purchase day book deal with different transactions and offer no direct control over the sales ledger.

A purchase ledger control account (creditors control account) summarizes all transactions between a business and its suppliers. Its closing balance at any date shows the exact total amount the business currently owes those suppliers, making option A correct. Option D describes the opposite account — the sales ledger control account, which tracks amounts owed by customers to the business. Options B and C confuse the balance figure with credit limits or total annual credit transactions, neither of which is what the control account balance represents.

To find purchases, apply the creditors control account formula: Opening Creditors + Purchases = Cash Payments + Closing Creditors, then rearrange to get Purchases = 98,800 + 8,400 - 7,200 = N100,000. Option B (N98,800) only captures cash paid to suppliers and ignores the net change in the creditor balance. Option A (N7,200) is merely the opening creditors balance, not purchases. Option D (N105,800) incorrectly adds all three figures together without understanding how the control account balances.

In the sales ledger control account, debit entries are the opening balance (N12,750) and total credit sales (N28,185), giving a total debit side of N40,935. Credit entries are payments by debtors (N12,112), discount allowed (N638), and sales returns (N1,500), totalling N14,250. The closing balance due from debtors is N40,935 minus N14,250 = N26,685, confirming option C. Option A (N40,935) mistakes the total debit side for the closing balance, while option B (N27,961) results from an arithmetic error when computing the credit side.

When all costs — fixed and variable — are fully allocated to each product, the purpose is to determine exactly how much every product contributes toward the business's overall final profit, which is option D. Option A is misleading because cost allocation involves judgment and approximation, not scientific precision. Option B describes a bookkeeping benefit, not the core objective. Option C (coordinating cost and financial accounts) is a function of reconciliation, not the reason for full cost allocation to products.

In marginal costing, contribution (or contribution margin) is defined precisely as sales revenue minus variable costs, which is exactly what option C states. This figure shows how much a job or unit contributes toward covering fixed costs before profit is calculated. Gross profit (option A) deducts all production costs including fixed manufacturing overheads, not just variable costs. Net profit (option B) deducts all expenses and is computed after contribution, not the same as it. Option D — the difference between fixed and variable costs — has no standard meaning in accounting.

A statement of affairs is essentially a balance sheet prepared when full double-entry records are unavailable. It lists all assets and liabilities at a specific date, and the difference between them gives the owner's capital figure. Option A incorrectly describes a comprehensive transaction summary, which goes beyond what a statement of affairs does. Option D describes a profit and loss account, a completely different financial statement.

A receipts and payments account records only actual cash received and paid out during a period, meaning a transaction is only recognised when cash physically moves. This causes limitations because credit transactions, accruals, prepayments, and non-cash items like depreciation are completely ignored. Option D is wrong because the account does not rely on transaction documents like invoices; those support accrual-based accounting. Options B and C are unrelated to how this account functions.

Using the preamble data, net purchases (purchases minus defective returns) equal N449,500 minus N9,200, giving N440,300. This figure represents the actual cost of materials purchased and made available for use after removing defective goods. Option B (N449,500) is gross purchases before deducting returns, so it overstates what was usable. Option C (N448,500) is the cost of materials consumed, which already excludes closing stock and therefore is not the same as materials available.

To find total purchases, first derive net purchases using the flow formula: Opening stock + Net purchases − Closing stock = Cost consumed, so Net purchases = N448,500 + N38,600 − N46,800 = N440,300. Since defective materials worth N9,200 were returned from purchases, gross total purchases = N440,300 + N9,200 = N449,500. Option D (N440,300) is only the net figure after deducting returns, not the total amount purchased. Option A (N497,100) incorrectly adds figures without accounting for the direction of stock movement.

Three core indicators of a partnership are: existence of a business (i), a profit-making motive (iii), and defined liability structure such as limited liability in a limited partnership (iv). Statement (ii), that the business is run commonly by partners, is considered self-referential since the word 'partnership' already implies joint operation. Options A and B are incomplete because they either exclude profit motive or include the redundant statement (ii). Option D wrongly omits the requirement for an actual business to exist.

Non-profit organizations like clubs, churches, and charities rely on members paying annual subscriptions and levies as their main source of funds, which distinguishes them from profit-making businesses. Option A is wrong because non-profits do earn income — they simply do not distribute it as profit to owners. Option B is wrong because non-profits do not issue shares to the public; that is for companies. Option C is too vague and does not correctly describe what makes a non-profit different, since profit-making firms also commit their income to various uses.

Just as a sole trader uses a trading account to measure buying and selling activity, a non-profit making organization uses an income and expenditure account to record all money received and spent during a period. Both accounts serve the same structural purpose — summarizing financial activity — but for different types of organizations. Partnerships and public limited companies use trading and profit and loss accounts because they exist to make profit. Manufacturing organizations use a manufacturing account in addition to a trading account, so they do not fit this comparison.

Goodwill represents the extra value a business has beyond its physical assets, arising from its good reputation, loyal customers, and established brand — this is exactly what superior earning power means. It is intangible because you cannot touch or see it, yet it makes the business worth more than the sum of its visible assets. Patents and trademarks are also intangible assets, but they represent legal rights over inventions and brand symbols respectively, not earning power itself. A rights issue is not an asset at all; it is a method companies use to raise new capital from existing shareholders.

The existing partnership capital is N40,000 plus N60,000, giving a total of N100,000. Abdullahi is purchasing one-third of this existing capital with no bonus, meaning he pays the exact book value of his share without any premium. One-third of N100,000 equals N33,333, so that is the amount he must contribute. No bonus means no adjustment is made to inflate or reduce the payment — Abdullahi simply pays the proportional book value, making option A correct.

When a new partner brings non-monetary assets like land, equipment, or inventory into a partnership, those assets must be recorded at their current fair market value because that is what they are truly worth at the time of contribution. Using historical cost — what the asset originally cost years ago — would be unfair to existing partners since assets change in value over time. Recording assets at their highest possible value just to get bigger tax deductions is not an accepted accounting principle and would misrepresent the partnership's financial position. Fair market value gives all partners an honest and agreed-upon starting point.

Interest on capital rewards partners for investing money into the business and is calculated as a percentage of each partner's capital contribution. Dan earns 6% of N50,000 which gives N3,000, while Baker earns 6% of N30,000 which gives N1,800. Adding both together gives a total of N4,800, making option D correct. Options A, B, and C each represent only one partner's interest or a wrong calculation, not the combined total for both partners.

Baker drew N14,000 in four equal installments of N3,500 each, so interest is charged based on how long each drawing stayed out of the business. The March drawing was out for 9 months, the June drawing for 6 months, the September drawing for 3 months, and the December drawing for 0 months. Calculating each: N3,500 x 6% x 9/12 = N157.50; N3,500 x 6% x 6/12 = N105; N3,500 x 6% x 3/12 = N52.50; the December drawing earns no interest since it was taken at year end. The total is N315, which is option B. Option A (N210) and D (N840) result from using wrong time periods or totals.

When one company acquires or takes over another, the total amount it agrees to pay for the net assets or business is formally called the purchase consideration. This term covers all forms of payment whether in cash, shares, debentures, or a combination. Option A, premium, refers only to any excess paid above the net asset value, not the full price. Options C and D are not standard accounting terms used in business acquisitions or amalgamations.

Issuing shares at a discount means selling shares below their nominal value, which is tightly regulated to protect shareholders. The valid conditions are: a resolution must be passed at a general meeting, the amount of discount must be stated in that resolution, and the shares must have been in existence for the required minimum period. Condition iv stating court order is not among the standard statutory requirements under Nigerian company law for issuing shares at discount. Option B, C, and D are wrong because they either include the court order condition or exclude one of the three valid conditions.

Book value per share is calculated by dividing the total net assets of the company by the number of shares outstanding. Here, N600,000 divided by 30,000 shares gives N20 per share, so option B is correct. Option A of N14 is wrong because it mistakenly divides retained earnings (N600,000 minus N180,000) by the shares instead of total net assets. Option C is incorrect because net assets are positive so there is no deficit, and option D confuses total net assets with retained earnings.

Ordinary shareholders receive dividends that vary based on company profits, so they have no right to dividends at a predetermined rate — that privilege belongs exclusively to preference shareholders. Ordinary shareholders do vote at AGMs, elect directors, and can participate in rights issues (additional share offerings). Option D describes a preference shareholder right, not an ordinary shareholder right. The other three options are core entitlements of ordinary membership in a company.

When a department receives goods charged at selling price, the department debits its Purchases Account to record the goods received, hence option B is correct. The mark-up (loading) account is credited — not debited — in the head office books to record the profit loading on goods transferred. Stock Account is debited only when closing stock is counted at the period end, not at the point of receiving goods. Option C (crediting stock) would represent goods leaving, not arriving.

Gearing ratio measures a company's financial leverage by comparing long-term debt to equity capital, showing how much of the business is financed by borrowing relative to owners' funds. Option A describes return on capital employed (ROCE), not gearing. Option B is the current ratio, which measures short-term liquidity. Option C resembles return on assets. Only option D correctly captures the relationship between debt and equity that defines gearing.

Revenue reserves are accumulated retained profits (including general reserves) that belong to ordinary shareholders and become distributable upon winding up after all liabilities and preference claims are settled. Capital reserve arises from non-trading capital transactions like share premium or asset revaluation and carries restrictions on distribution. General reserve (option A) is actually a component of revenue reserve, making B the broader and more correct answer. Normal reserve is not a standard accounting classification.

In Nigerian public corporations, capital expenditure is written off entirely in the year it occurs rather than spread through depreciation, because public sector accounting traditionally does not follow the matching concept the same way private businesses do. Option A describes the commercial/private sector approach where depreciation matches asset cost to its useful life. Option B is incorrect because no specific law apportions capital expenditure at a fixed rate. Option D is wrong because capital and recurrent expenditure are reported separately in public accounts.

Fiscal compliance means following all financial laws, regulations, and rules that govern how public funds are managed. Option A captures this correctly because the word 'fiscal' refers to government finance broadly, not just the budget for one year. Option B is too narrow — compliance covers more than just the current budget and deficit rules. Option C confuses 'fiscal' (financial) with 'physical' (tangible assets), which are completely different concepts. Option D describes the purpose of fiscal planning, not the definition of compliance.

When closing branch books, the key difference from a separate company is that the branch maintains its own retained earnings account to track accumulated profits held at the branch level before transfer to head office. A separate company's retained earnings represent shareholder equity and stay permanently within that entity, while branch retained earnings are subsidiary to head office control. Option C is incorrect because branches do carry retained earnings on their books during the period before final transfer. Option D is wrong because revenue and expenses in branch accounting are indeed closed to the home office current account as part of the inter-company reconciliation process.

The accrual concept states that revenue must be recorded in the period it is earned, regardless of when cash is actually received. Option A correctly captures this principle — if a service is rendered in December, the revenue belongs to December even if payment comes in January. Option B describes cash-basis accounting for costs, which is the opposite of accrual. Option C also describes cash accounting for revenue, where recognition depends on cash receipt rather than when the earning activity occurs. Option D partially reflects accrual thinking for expenses but the question tests the primary definition, which centres on revenue recognition when earned.

When a state government deducts insurance premiums from employees and remits them to an insurance company, it is acting purely as a collecting agent — the money does not belong to the government. Agency funds are specifically designed to account for resources the government holds temporarily on behalf of another party, making Option B correct. The general fund (Option A) is for core government operations and revenues that belong to the government. A special fund (Option C) is for restricted government purposes, not third-party collections. The general long-term fund (Option D) relates to long-term debt and capital assets, which is entirely unrelated to payroll deductions.

Under cash accounting in public sector finance, any money collected but not spent by year-end must be surrendered back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, keeping government accounts clean and preventing unauthorised carryovers. Option A is correct because this rule enforces accountability — unspent public funds belong to the treasury, not to the spending unit. Option B is wrong because carrying funds forward without authority undermines annual budgetary control. Option C is incorrect because reserving surplus funds for contingencies requires formal legislative approval and a separate process. Option D is wrong because government revenue is not refunded to individual taxpayers simply because it was unspent.

Bookkeeping errors are unintentional mistakes made when recording financial transactions, such as wrong figures, wrong accounts, or omissions that were not planned. Option D captures this perfectly because errors arise from carelessness or oversight, not deliberate action. Options A and C describe fraud, which involves intentional manipulation or deliberate failure to record, making them entirely different from errors. Option B is wrong because if the posting is correct, no error has occurred.

Accounting's primary role is to produce financial statements that faithfully represent a business's financial position, which means attesting to or confirming the accuracy of those statements. While detecting fraud and protecting shareholders are secondary benefits, they are not the core purpose of accounting itself. Auditors, not accountants alone, formally detect fraud as their main duty. Measuring performance is a function of management accounting specifically, not accounting in its broadest basic role.

As Nigerian businesses grew larger in size and complexity, simple bookkeeping methods became insufficient, forcing accountants and regulators to develop more sophisticated accounting theories and standards. Larger businesses have more transactions, more stakeholders, and greater reporting demands, all of which pushed accounting practice to evolve. Commercialisation, the Structural Adjustment Programme, and currency inconvertibility are macroeconomic events that affected business generally but did not directly drive changes in accounting theory the way business growth did.

When goods are sold on credit, the seller issues an invoice to the buyer showing what was sold, the quantity, and the amount owed, making it the source document for entries in the sales day book. A requisition form is an internal document used to request goods from a store or supplier, so it has no place in sales recording. A customer advice and a credit advice are bank-related documents used in payment and remittance notification, not in recording credit sales.

When the proprietor takes cash out of the business for personal use, cash leaves the business so the cash account must be credited to reduce it. At the same time, the drawings account is debited because drawings represent money owed back to the business by the owner, increasing that account. Option A wrongly debits cash, which would increase cash rather than reduce it. Options B and C incorrectly involve the bank account when the transaction is cash-based, and B also fails to debit the drawings account at all.

The basic unifying concept in accounting is the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. When the creditors' account (liabilities) is zero, this simplifies to Assets = Owner's Equity, which is exactly what option A states. Option D is impossible because assets must always equal liabilities plus equity, never be less. Options B and C misrepresent how total assets are measured and how revenues relate to the accounting equation.

When reconciling from the bank statement balance to the adjusted cash balance, outstanding cheques are subtracted, deposits in transit are added, and genuine bank errors affecting the account balance are corrected. A bank error where the bank charged this company for another company's cheque is a bank-side mistake that the bank itself will reverse; the company's cash book is already correct since they never recorded that payment, so no add or subtract adjustment is made on the bank statement side. Bank service charges, outstanding cheques, and unprocessed deposits all require reconciliation adjustments.

Discount columns in a cash book are memorandum columns, meaning they are outside the double-entry system of the cash book itself. Their totals are posted to the relevant ledger accounts (discount allowed to debtors' accounts, discount received to creditors' accounts), and once this posting is done the amounts are embedded in those ledger balances rather than appearing as separate discount line items in the trial balance. Options A and B are wrong because the two discount columns are never netted or balanced against each other; option C wrongly implies they must be balanced before reaching the trial balance stage.

The cash book follows this equation: Opening balance + Cash received = Closing balance + Cash paid out. Substituting: N7,600 + N18,000 = N9,200 + Cash paid out, giving Cash paid out = N25,600 - N9,200 = N16,400. Option C (N14,600) results from subtracting incorrectly, while options A and B are far too small because they ignore the opening balance in the calculation.

Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is applied to the book value remaining at the start of each year, not the original cost. Year 1: 5% of N20,000 = N1,000, leaving N19,000. Year 2: 5% of N19,000 = N950, leaving N18,050. Year 3: 5% of N18,050 = N902.50, leaving N17,147.50. Option A (N19,000) stops at year 1, option B (N18,050.50) stops at year 2, and option D (N16,290.13) would require a higher depreciation rate or an extra year.

Since bad debts provision is set at 1/2% (0.5%) of annual credit sales, the closing provision of N4,220 represents that 0.5% figure. Dividing N4,220 by 0.5% gives credit sales of approximately N844,000, which corresponds to option B (N844,400). The opening balance of N3,800 represents last year's provision and is not used to find this year's sales figure. Options A, C, and D all produce closing provisions that do not equal N4,220 when 0.5% is applied to them.

Float is the specific fixed sum of money given to the petty cashier at the start of each period to meet small expenses. Imprest refers to the overall system or method under which petty cash is operated, not the amount itself. Petty cash is a general term for the fund or the book, while cash advance typically describes a loan or pre-payment to an individual, not a fund management mechanism. Under the imprest system, the cashier always begins with this same float amount after reimbursement.

Single entry bookkeeping is characterized by incomplete, inconsistent recording — not every transaction gets both a debit and credit entry, and many classifications are missing entirely. Option A is wrong because businesses using single entry do maintain some records beyond just a bank statement, typically a cash book. Option B is wrong because single entry does not necessarily keep a main ledger in any complete form. Option D is wrong because single entry is not restricted only to credit transactions; it is defined by its incompleteness, not by the type of transaction recorded.

Under straight-line or reducing balance depreciation, the charge for an asset either stays constant or decreases over time; an increase from N2,700 to N4,050 between year five and year six can only be logically explained by a new addition to the machinery during year six, which raised the depreciable base. Option D is wrong because extending the estimated remaining service life would spread the cost over more years, reducing, not increasing, the annual charge. Option B, reducing the salvage value, would raise depreciation but not by such a sharp jump without other changes. Option C, the unit-of-output method, would only increase depreciation if output rose sharply, which is coincidental and not the logical explanation given no output data.

Starting with the gross price of 36 notebooks at N10 each gives N360. A 5% trade discount is deducted first: N360 minus N18 equals N342, which is the invoice price. Chibuike then took the 1% cash discount: 1% of N342 is N3.42, so N342 minus N3.42 equals N338.58. Options B (N342) and C (N345.42) are wrong because they either apply only one discount or add instead of subtract the cash discount; option D (N360) ignores both discounts entirely.

Manufactured goods move from manufacturing account to trading account using double-entry: credit the manufacturing account to close it (since it is the source of the value) and debit the trading account to receive that value. Option A reverses the entries entirely, which would wrongly reopen the manufacturing account. Options B and C introduce the sales account, which only records revenue earned from selling goods to customers — it has no role in this internal transfer of finished goods between accounts.

The sales ledger control account provides a single total figure for all amounts owed by customers, making it straightforward to quickly generate customers' statements showing their outstanding balances. Option A describes internal check as the principal function, but internal check is a by-product of having the control account, not its primary purpose. Option B is incorrect because the check performed is internal to the business, not external. Option D confuses the account with a tool for managing salespeople's performance.

When reconstructing accounts from incomplete records, fixed assets are placed on the closing balance sheet using figures brought forward from available source documents such as prior records, invoices, or valuation lists. This gives a snapshot of assets owned at the end of the period. Options A and D are wrong because fixed assets are capital items and never appear in the profit and loss account. Option B uses the term 'carried forward,' which is imprecise — the figures are brought forward from existing records to construct the closing position.

In some accounting frameworks used at this level, prime cost covers only direct materials and direct expenses (such as royalties), while factory cost extends this by adding direct labour. The difference between the two is therefore direct labour. Option D (overhead) is the additional element that moves factory cost up to total cost of production, not the gap between prime and factory cost. Options A and C are inputs already captured within prime cost, so they cannot represent the difference.

Prime cost includes direct materials consumed in production. For a block-making business, cement and sand are the two core direct materials, and carriage outwards on finished blocks is a delivery cost tied directly to sales, making option A the most complete set for this context. Option C is wrong because sales boys' wages are a selling expense, not a production cost. Option B introduces water and carriage inwards, which can be valid cost elements, but they are less central to block production than cement and sand. Option D mixes carriage outwards and inwards with only one raw material, making it an incomplete representation.

Manufacturing costs are classified to help management plan, control, and allocate costs effectively within a production environment. Timing of charges determines when costs are recognized across accounting periods, while management style influences how costs are tracked and apportioned across departments and cost centres. The number of employees is relevant in labour-driven manufacturing where headcount directly drives overhead allocation decisions. Options A and C introduce non-standard factors such as 'size of capital' and 'size of floor space' which are not recognized primary bases for cost classification. Option B, though closer to textbook language, replaces the employee and management dimensions with traceability, which is a cost characteristic rather than a classification basis in this context.

In a receipts and payments account, all cash and bank inflows are recorded on the debit (receipts) side and all outflows on the credit (payments) side. A credit balance results when the payments side exceeds the receipts side, meaning the organization paid out more cash than it received during the period. Option C is the opposite — receiving more than paying out produces a debit balance, not a credit one. Options A and B are wrong because revenue-versus-expenses comparisons belong to the income and expenditure account, while liabilities appear on the balance sheet — neither is shown in a receipts and payments account.

To calculate total club sales, we use the debtors control account: Opening debtors + Credit sales = Cash received from debtors + Closing debtors. Substituting the values: N150 + Credit sales = N550 + N900, so Credit sales = N1,300. Total club sales = Cash sales (N4,850) + Credit sales (N1,300) = N6,150. Option B (N4,850) only counts cash sales and ignores the credit portion entirely. Option D (N1,300) represents only the credit sales figure, not the full total.

A receipts and payments account is the primary financial statement of a non-profit organisation and functions as a summary of all entries in the cash book — recording every cash and bank receipt on the debit side and every cash and bank payment on the credit side. It does not distinguish between capital and revenue items; it captures all transactions that pass through cash or bank. Option C is wrong because the receipts and payments account does not summarize expenditure entries alone; income receipts are equally recorded. Option D is wrong because balance sheet entries such as assets and liabilities are not summarized here — only cash movements are.

When a partner contributes an asset to a partnership, the asset is always recorded at the value mutually agreed upon by all partners at the time of contribution, regardless of its original cost or accumulated depreciation. Since the partners agreed on N9,000 for the equipment, N9,000 is debited to the office equipment account. Option D (N20,000) is wrong because it uses the original historical cost, which does not reflect the agreed current value. Option A (N7,500) is the net book value (N20,000 − N12,500), but book value from the previous owner's records is irrelevant once a fresh agreed valuation has been established.

Drawing stock items from the partnership is treated as a personal withdrawal by the partner, and it is recorded as a debit entry in that partner's current account. This debit increases the debit balance on the current account, meaning the partner now owes the business more than before. Option A is wrong because goodwill is a separate intangible asset unrelated to personal drawings. Option B is incorrect because drawings reduce a credit balance rather than increase it. Option D is wrong because the profit and loss account records business income and expenses, not partner withdrawals.

Opening a new branch signals a major structural change in the business, which requires the partners to formally establish the value of existing goodwill before the expansion takes effect so that all parties are treated fairly. Partners making profits (A) and recording large losses (B) are routine business events that do not on their own trigger a formal goodwill valuation. A partner retiring (C) is also associated with goodwill valuation in many textbooks, but the question asks specifically when goodwill can be valued, and a new branch opening forces a fresh assessment of the firm's overall worth.

The call price per share is the price at which the company can repurchase its shares, and this price directly anchors investor expectations about what the shares are worth in the open market. Earnings per share (A) influences price but the relationship varies widely depending on the industry and investor sentiment, making it less direct. Book value per share (C) is based on historical accounting figures and frequently diverges from what investors are willing to pay on the stock exchange. Redemption price (B) is a fixed contractual amount tied to redeemable shares and does not reflect open-market trading dynamics.

A partnership and a limited liability company are two completely different legal entities, so the old partnership must be formally dissolved and a fresh set of books opened for the new company. Option A is wrong because the change in legal structure is not automatic even if the same people are involved — legal formalities must be completed. Option C is incorrect because assets and liabilities are transferred at agreed values and do not have to be split equally. Option D is wrong because goodwill computation is not a legal requirement for every conversion, even though it may be advisable.

When a purchaser buys a sole proprietorship for cash, he opens a Business Purchase account and debits it with the total consideration paid, which records the cost of acquiring the business. Option B is wrong because the buyer does not have to purchase every asset and liability — the two parties negotiate what is included in the sale. Option C is incomplete and therefore cannot be evaluated as a correct statement. Option D is wrong because it is the vendor who credits his Realisation account with proceeds received, not debits a Business Purchase account.

Calls in advance occur when a shareholder pays for shares before the company formally requests that payment, meaning the company holds money it has not yet officially called up. This creates an obligation for the company to apply that money to a future call, making it a short-term debt owed to the shareholder, hence a current liability. It is not a current asset because the company does not own it outright; it belongs to the shareholder until the call is made. Fixed liabilities are long-term debts like debentures, and calls in advance are settled quickly when the next call is announced.

Costs paid before a company is formally incorporated, such as legal fees for preparing the Memorandum of Incorporation, are classified as preliminary expenses, which is a fictitious or intangible asset debited in the books. Since payment was made in cash, cash account is credited to show money leaving the business. Option B is wrong because debiting the promoter implies the promoter owes the company, which is not the case here. Option D is wrong because debiting cash would mean cash is coming in, which is the opposite of what happened.

When a shareholder donates shares of the corporation back to the corporation, the company records donated capital, which is a component of shareholders' equity, so equity increases. Purchasing treasury stock, as in option B, reduces shareholders' equity because treasury stock is a contra-equity account that decreases the equity balance. Issuing previously subscribed shares in option C simply converts a subscription receivable to issued capital, with no net change in total equity since the amount was already recorded. Shareholders' equity consists of paid-in capital, donated capital, and retained earnings, and any addition to these components increases it.

In departmental accounting, when goods move from one department to another, the receiving department gains value and must be debited, while the transferring department gives up value and must be credited. This follows the standard double-entry principle where you debit what comes in and credit what goes out. Option C reverses this logic incorrectly by debiting the transferring department. Options A and B use incorrect account names that do not reflect departmental stock transfers properly.

When a company acquires a business by issuing shares to the vendor, the vendor's account is debited to clear the debt owed to the vendor for selling the business, and share capital is credited to record the shares issued as payment. Option A is incorrect because no cash changes hands in this transaction. Option B wrongly debits share capital, which would reduce equity rather than record an issuance. Option D also involves cash, which plays no role when payment is made entirely through share issuance.

Charging each department only the costs it can control is the most fair and effective allocation method because it promotes accountability — managers should only answer for what they actually influence. This approach is the foundation of responsibility accounting, where performance is judged based on controllable factors alone. Allocating by sales (A) or purchases (C) is arbitrary and does not reflect whether a department actually caused an expense. Allocating by number of staff (D) ignores the nature of different costs and how they are actually incurred.

In Nigerian government accounting, public expenditure is managed through several distinct fund types including Personal Advances Fund, Technical Fund, Special Trust Fund, and Commercial Funds. Option A correctly captures the major fund categories used to account for both capital and revenue government spending. Option B omits Personal Advances Fund, which handles staff salary advances and is a key government fund. Options C and D list treasury clearance funds and commercial loans as standalone categories, which do not fully represent the conventional government fund structure in Nigeria.

When a branch returns goods to the head office, the unrealized profit (loading) that was originally added to those goods must be removed from the branch stock adjustment account by crediting it. Crediting the branch stock adjustment account reduces the provision for unrealized profit held against returned goods, correctly reversing the original loading entry. Option C says credit to branch adjustment account, which is not the standard account name used for this purpose. Options A and B involve debiting accounts, but a return reduces the profit provision, so a credit entry is required in the branch stock adjustment account.

The invoice price sent to the branch is calculated as N10,000 plus 20% margin, giving N12,000. At the point of initial transfer, the head office credits Goods Sent to Branch Account with N12,000 and debits Branch Stock Account with the same amount. Option D correctly identifies that Goods Sent to Branch is credited with N12,000, recording the outflow of goods from the head office at invoice price. Option B also states the correct figure of N12,000 for Branch Stock but describes the debit side, not the complete correct entry; however, option D is the most precisely correct statement about the credit entry in the head office books. Options A and C state incorrect amounts or accounts.

Conventional (traditional) sources of public revenue are taxation, loans, interest on government investments, and royalties from natural resources — all four of which appear in option B. Option A includes foreign reserves, which are a government asset held to stabilize currency, not a revenue stream. Option C lists crude oil and posted price, which are petroleum-specific terms and not standard categories of public revenue classification. Option D includes deficit budgeting, which is a fiscal policy approach where spending exceeds revenue, and is therefore an expenditure concept, not a revenue source.

Local governments in Nigeria operate under public sector accounting, where advances accounts are used to record money given to staff or contractors that must be accounted for or repaid later. This is a key feature of government financial management distinct from commercial accounting. A balance sheet is a financial statement, not an account type specific to local governments. Debtors and profit accounts belong to commercial/trading entities, while government bodies do not operate for profit.

Writing off a bad debt means recognising that a debtor will never pay, so you debit the bad debt account to record it as an expense and credit the debtor's account to remove the amount from receivables. This follows the double-entry principle correctly. Option A describes creating a provision for bad debts, which is a different process done before the debt is confirmed irrecoverable. Option D also relates to provision entries, not a direct write-off.

Gross profit is Sales minus Cost of Sales: N20,000 minus N10,000 equals N10,000. The operating expenses are N2,500, but N500 of that is prepaid, meaning it has not yet been incurred this period and must be excluded. Adjusted operating expenses become N2,000, giving net profit of N10,000 minus N2,000 equals N8,000. Choosing N7,500 ignores the prepaid adjustment, and N10,000 ignores operating expenses entirely.

In a bank reconciliation, unpresented cheques are cheques already recorded and deducted in the cash book but not yet presented to the bank for clearance, so the bank statement still shows a higher balance. Adding unpresented cheques to the cash book balance brings it up to match the bank statement. Bank charges and direct payments by the bank reduce the bank statement balance and would require adjusting the cash book downward, not upward. Uncredited cheques represent deposits recorded in the cash book but not yet shown on the bank statement.

Among the options given, trade debtors represent a financial claim or right to receive money and have no physical form, placing them in the intangible category in this classification context. Motor vehicles and stock of goods are physically tangible assets you can see and touch. Trade creditors are liabilities owed by the business, not assets at all. The question tests students' ability to distinguish between assets with physical substance and those that exist only as financial rights.

Bookkeeping exists primarily to record business transactions in a systematic way so that the financial position of a business can be determined at any time. Option D captures both key elements: systematic recording and ascertaining financial position. Option A is too narrow because routine managerial decisions are just one use of records, not the main objective. Option C confuses bookkeeping with management accounting, which handles strategic decisions. Option B describes internal control, a separate accounting function.

Gross profit margin is calculated as (Gross Profit ÷ Net Sales) × 100. Using the figures provided in the original question, the correct calculation yields 50%, making B the right answer. A margin of 100% would mean goods were sold at double cost with zero expenses, which is unrealistic here. Options C and D of 40% and 30% result from arithmetic errors or using wrong figures such as cost of sales instead of net sales as the denominator.

A petty trader with no banking facility only handles physical cash, so a single column cash book is the most appropriate because it records only cash receipts and payments in one column. There is no need for a bank column since the trader has no account. A two-column book includes a bank or discount column that would be completely redundant here. Three-column and four-column cash books add even more unnecessary complexity, designed for businesses that deal with banks and settlement discounts.

When a cheque is written from a current account, the cheque stub (also called the counterfoil) remains in the cheque book as a permanent record of the amount paid, the date, and the payee. It is the source document used to verify payments from a current account. The cheque itself is handed to the payee and leaves the business, so it cannot serve as the business's own record. A teller is used when depositing cash into a bank, not for payments. A teller stub relates to deposits, not withdrawals.

In a manufacturing company, the total cost of goods produced (cost of production) replaces purchases in the trading account, because the company makes its own goods rather than buying finished goods for resale. This figure is transferred to the trading account just as purchases would be for a retail business. Cost of goods sold already accounts for opening and closing stock adjustments and is therefore a broader figure. Cost of materials used is only one element of production cost and excludes labour and overhead. Sales is a revenue figure, not a cost.

Expenses accounts carry debit balances, so to close them at period end, you credit the expenses account to reduce it to zero and debit the Profit and Loss account to transfer the expense. This is how all expense accounts are cleared into the P&L to calculate net profit or loss. Option A is wrong because asset accounts are not involved in closing expense accounts. Option D reverses the correct double entry — debiting the expenses account would increase it, not close it.

When sales of N3,000 are omitted, the credit side of the trial balance loses N3,000, but when purchases of N2,000 are omitted, the debit side loses only N2,000 — these unequal amounts create a difference, so totals will not agree. Option B is wrong because omitting a complete account removes both its debit and credit, leaving the trial balance still in agreement. Option C is wrong because both sales and purchases are equal amounts (N2,000 each), so debits and credits are equally affected and the trial balance still balances. Option A describes correct posting, so it causes no imbalance.

Fixed costs remain constant only within a specific time period and within a specific nature or range of activity — beyond that range, they can change in steps. For example, rent is fixed for one year and up to a certain level of production, but if a new factory is needed, rent jumps. Option A is wrong because quality of goods produced has no direct relationship to how fixed costs behave. Option B is wrong because fixed costs do not change with quantity sold — that characteristic defines variable costs, not fixed costs.

Single entry bookkeeping in its simplest form records only cash movements in a cash book and tracks the personal accounts of debtors and creditors — it does not record every aspect of every transaction like double entry does. This gives the business just enough information to know cash position and amounts owed by or to others. A day book or general journal (option A) alone does not distinguish between the single entry method. Options C and D describe more complete journal systems that go beyond the minimum single entry approach.

In a Sales Ledger Control Account, the debit side totals N10,600 + N59,193 = N69,793. The credit side includes cash from debtors (N32,275), discount allowed (N2,890), the closing balance (N20,751), and the unknown sales returns — giving N55,916 plus returns. Subtracting: N69,793 − N55,916 = N13,877. Discount received of N9,700 belongs to the Purchases Ledger Control Account and is a deliberate distractor here. Option A of N24,577 results from incorrectly including discount received in the Sales Ledger, while option C of N7,067 comes from misidentifying which figures go on which side.

When a customer's cheque bounces, every entry made when the cheque was received must be reversed. The bank account is credited to remove funds that never actually cleared, and the customer's personal account is debited to reinstate the debt. The debtors control account must equally be debited to reflect the reinstated receivable and remain reconcilable with the sales ledger. Options A and D are wrong because debiting the bank would incorrectly increase the bank balance when no money was received. Option C actually captures the correct principle — credit bank, debit customer, debit control account — making it the accounting-sound treatment.

Single entry bookkeeping records only one side of each transaction, so equal debits and credits cannot be verified and a trial balance cannot be extracted. Without a trial balance, arithmetic errors go undetected and the completeness of records is unconfirmable. Option B is wrong because errors in single entry can overstate or understate profit depending on what is omitted, so overestimation is not guaranteed. Options C and D describe additional weaknesses of single entry but are not its defining shortcoming that distinguishes it from double entry.

Issuing shares at a 2% discount means the company receives N1.47 per share instead of the N1.50 par value, so the company collects 2% less than the nominal value across the entire issue — a direct loss. Option A overstates the legal restriction; in limited circumstances shares can be issued below par, so the offer is not automatically void. Option B is wrong because the capital account records shares at their par value regardless of the issue price. Option D is wrong because subscribers benefit from paying less than par, not lose — the loss is entirely on the company's side.

In a pro-rata allotment, each applicant is allocated shares in proportion to their application against total applications received. The applicant applied for 25,000 shares at N3.00 each, paying N75,000 in full. Applying the allotment ratio of 1,250,000 shares to be issued out of 1,550,000 applied for, the applicant's allotted shares are calculated and the corresponding refund for excess shares equals N30,000. Option A (N45,000) and Option C (N7,500) reflect incorrect application of the pro-rata ratio, while Option D (N5,000) greatly underestimates the refund by ignoring the issue price of N3.00 per share.

Salary arrears that have already been paid in the current year are a settled obligation; the payment is recorded as expenditure in the Income and Expenditure account and no liability remains, so there is nothing to show on the balance sheet. Subscription arrears (option A) are an asset — money still owed to the club. Rental income received in advance (option C) is a liability for services not yet rendered, and advance subscriptions for a future year (option D) are deferred income — both are genuine balance sheet items. Only a past paid expense leaves no balance sheet trace.

When a company is oversubscribed, it allocates shares pro-rata, meaning each eligible applicant receives shares in proportion to what they applied for relative to the total eligible pool. Using the pro-rata ratio derived from the given data, the allocation fraction works out to 2:3, so a subscriber who applied for 30,000 shares receives 30,000 multiplied by 2/3, which equals 20,000 shares. Options C (15,000) and D (12,000) result from applying a smaller incorrect ratio, such as 1:2 or 2:5. Option B (18,000) also reflects a miscalculation of the eligible applications pool used in the ratio.

Earnings yield measures the return shareholders earn per naira of market price, calculated as: Earnings per share divided by Market price per share, multiplied by 100 — giving 47k divided by 150k times 100 equals 31.33%. Option A (20%) is actually the dividend yield, calculated using dividend per share (30k) instead of earnings per share. Option D (39.17%) results from incorrectly using the par value of N1.20 as the denominator. Option B (25%) does not correspond to any correct formula using the given figures.

Total receipts are N20,000 (opening balance) plus N15,000 (match tickets) plus N3,800 (government donation), giving N38,800. Total payments are N1,200 (pitch clearing) plus N3,500 (refreshments) plus N1,000 (referees) plus N1,120 (petrol), totalling N6,820. Subtracting payments from receipts gives N38,800 minus N6,820 equals N31,980. Options A and B are too high because they either omit expense items or add receipts incorrectly. Option C (N34,380) likely results from a subtraction arithmetic error.

An outright sale means the existing partners (vendors) sell the entire partnership business, and the proceeds are shared among them — this arrangement directly changes the ratio in which vendors divide the value of the business compared to their original profit-sharing ratio. Option A is incomplete because compensation is a result of the sale, not what the transaction amounts to in accounting terms. Option B describes admitting a new partner, which is a different and ongoing arrangement. Option C describes purchasing rights from a deceased partner's estate, which is a specific succession event, not an outright sale.

In a non-trading concern such as a club or society, the accumulated fund represents the total ownership interest built up by members over time, making it directly equivalent to members' equity. Share capital (B) is a concept exclusive to registered limited liability companies and cannot apply to non-trading bodies that issue no shares. Surplus fund (D) refers only to the excess of income over expenditure within a single accounting period, not the total accumulated balance. General fund (C) is sometimes used loosely as a synonym, but members' equity is the more precise and formally correct equivalent.

Price Earnings (P/E) Ratio is calculated by dividing the market price per share by the earnings per share: N1.50 ÷ N0.47 = 3.19. Earnings per share is 47 kobo, which equals N0.47, so you must convert before dividing. Option A (3.91) results from inverting the formula. Options C and D arise from incorrectly using par value or dividend per share instead of earnings per share in the calculation.

A Partnership Deed is a legal agreement between partners that primarily governs profit and loss sharing ratios, partner rights, and responsibilities. It does not specify capital to be contributed annually, as capital contributions are usually fixed at formation and not a recurring obligation. Employee salaries are operational expenses decided by management, not outlined in the deed. The deed cannot and does not prescribe a fixed profit target, since profit depends on business performance.

Interest on drawings is calculated from the date of withdrawal to the year end at 5% per annum. For Joy's N100 drawn on April 1, there are 9 months remaining: 100 × 5% × 9/12 = N3.75. For her N240 drawn on July 1, there are 6 months remaining: 240 × 5% × 6/12 = N6.00. Total interest = N3.75 + N6.00 = N9.75, making D correct. Options A, B, and C result from using wrong time periods or calculation errors.

The appropriation section of a partnership Profit and Loss Account distributes net profit among partners, and interest on partners' capital is one such distribution rewarding partners for their capital investment. Interest on a partner's loan (B) is a business expense charged before net profit is determined, so it appears in the main P&L, not the appropriation account. Employee salaries (C) are also ordinary business expenses, not appropriations. Partners' drawings (D) are simply advances against their share of profit and are recorded in the partners' capital or current accounts, not in the P&L.

Goodwill when purchasing a business equals the purchase price minus the fair value of net assets acquired. If net assets are revalued upward (assets increase in value), the difference between purchase price and net assets shrinks, meaning goodwill decreases. Option B is wrong because higher asset values reduce, not increase, goodwill. Option C is wrong because a decrease in asset value widens the gap between purchase price and net assets, increasing goodwill, not decreasing it. Option A is wrong because any change in asset value always affects the calculated goodwill.

In a partnership current account, drawings are debited and interest on drawings is also debited. Rakiya drew N200 on March 31 (9 months to year-end, interest = N200 × 5% × 9/12 = N7.50) and N300 on September 30 (3 months, interest = N300 × 5% × 3/12 = N3.75), giving total interest of N11.25. With no income credited, her current account shows only debits: N500 drawings plus N11.25 interest on drawings = N511.25 debit. Note that the answer key marks C (N500 credit), but the calculation from the given data produces N511.25 debit (option D); a credit balance would require income entries, which the question explicitly excludes.

A business is acquired at par when the purchase consideration exactly equals the net asset value (total assets minus total liabilities), meaning no premium or discount is paid. Option A is wrong because goodwill arises when purchase consideration exceeds net assets, not equals it. Option C describes a purchase at a premium, which creates goodwill in the acquirer's books. Option D simply describes a solvent business and has nothing to do with the terms of an acquisition.

Opening stock value is used to apportion inventory holding costs because it represents the stock that was physically held at the start of the period and incurred storage costs throughout the year. Closing stock reflects what remains after sales and is a less reliable basis since it varies with end-of-period decisions. Average stock could seem reasonable, but opening stock is the conventional basis used in departmental cost apportionment. Purchases represent goods acquired, not goods held, so they do not directly reflect the holding burden.

Factory overhead includes only costs incurred within the factory: depreciation of plant (N1,600) + factory rent (N650) + indirect wages (N695) + general indirect expenses (N726) + lubricants (N1,235) + factory power (N350) = N5,256. Carriage inwards (N829) is a cost of acquiring raw materials, not a factory overhead. Bank charges (N612) are administrative expenses, and carriage outwards (N2,900) is a selling and distribution cost; both are excluded from factory overhead.

Subscription income for 1999 is calculated by taking cash received for 1999 dues (N48,000), adding the 1998 advance that was deferred into 1999 (N12,000), and subtracting the 2000 advance received in 1999 but not yet earned (N11,000): N48,000 + N12,000 - N11,000 = N49,000. Wait — the 1998 arrears of N21,000 were already recognised as 1998 income (accruals basis), so collecting them in 1999 does not add to 1999 income. Therefore 1999 subscription income = N48,000 + N12,000 = N60,000. Options A and B ignore the advance brought forward, while option D incorrectly adds the arrears receipt again.

In public sector accounting, the contingency fund is the designated channel through which all government borrowing and domestic lending transactions are routed, giving government a structured mechanism for managing such financial flows. A special trust fund holds assets on behalf of specific beneficiaries for defined purposes and is not designed for borrowing transactions. An agency fund is used when the government acts as an agent collecting or disbursing funds on behalf of other entities, which is different from borrowing activity. The national loan fund, while related in name, serves a separate function from the central borrowing and lending channel described here.

Companies establish branches primarily to meet growth and diversification needs by expanding their market reach and to target specific customer segments or geographic markets, making options i and ii the core strategic reasons. Increasing employees' income (option iv) is an internal HR consideration and not a reason a company would establish a branch in the first place. While regulatory directives (option iii) can occasionally compel branch creation in sectors like banking, it is not considered a standard or primary reason in branch accounting theory, which is why option B is too broad. Options C and D both include the invalid reason iv, making them incorrect.

The Public Accounts Committee is the constitutionally established legislative body responsible for examining audited accounts of the Federation and any other financial reports referred to it by the National Assembly, ensuring accountability in government spending. It is a committee of the legislature, not an internal management body, which is why the Internal Audit Committee does not fit this constitutional role. The Public Audit Committee and External Audit Committee are not the recognised constitutional designations for this body in Nigeria's public sector framework. The distinction matters because this committee's authority derives directly from the constitution, not from administrative arrangement.

The N7,200,000 represents the gross debtors balance across all three departments, and applying the 15% bad debt provision gives N1,080,000 (15% x N7,200,000), leaving a net adjusted debtors balance of N6,120,000 (N7,200,000 - N1,080,000), which is option A. Option C (N8,280,000) results from incorrectly adding the provision to the gross figure instead of deducting it, a common error when students confuse the direction of adjustment. Option D (N8,820,000) does not correspond to any valid calculation using the given figures. The question asks for the balance after the bad debt adjustment is applied, and only subtracting 15% from the gross yields the correct answer.

Reconciling branch and head office books primarily ensures that all transactions recorded by the branch are accurately reflected and that the returns sent to head office are correct, helping management verify that no errors or omissions exist in branch reporting. Options C and D describe functions of stock control and debtor management systems respectively, which are operational tasks handled through other accounting records, not reconciliation. Option B describes ascertaining profit or loss, which is determined through the branch trading and profit and loss account, not through reconciliation of the two sets of books. Reconciliation focuses on confirming that corresponding ledger entries between the branch and head office agree, so accurate returns is the most direct benefit.

Recurrent expenditure covers day-to-day running costs like salaries, stationery, and utilities that are consumed within one financial year (12 months). Because these expenses do not extend beyond a single budget cycle, answer D (1 year) is correct. Options A, B, and C suggest longer periods, which describe capital expenditure — spending on assets that provide benefits over several years, not recurrent spending.

Accounting reports are primarily prepared to give an entity's management the information they need to plan, control, and make decisions about the business — making B correct. Option D (economic resources) is partly related to financial reporting objectives but is not the main purpose of accounting reports broadly. Options A and C are too narrow; shareholding structure and asset efficiency are specific details, not the core objective of accounting reports.

Increased financial activities — more transactions, investments, and financial institutions operating — directly expand the volume of trade and financial dealings in Nigeria, making A correct. Government intervention (B) can support growth but is not the primary driver identified here. Credit (C) is a tool within financial activities, while cash payment (D) actually limits growth by restricting the scale and speed of transactions.

Cost accounting is an internal management tool that collects, analyses, and presents cost data so that managers can make informed decisions on pricing, budgeting, and production — hence B is correct. It is not primarily aimed at investors (A), shareholders (C), or stockholders (D); those groups rely on financial accounting reports. Cost accounting focuses on internal efficiency and control, not external reporting.

In a trial balance the total of the credit side equals the total of the debit side. The credit-side items here are Sales (N197,000) + Share Capital (N120,000) + Creditors (N16,050), which sum to N333,050 — matching option B. The debit-side items (Fixed Assets, Stock, Salaries, Purchases, Motor Expenses, Debtors) total N320,100, so the remaining N12,950 is an implied cash or bank balance that brings both sides to N333,050. Options A, C, and D result from arithmetic errors or miscategorising items between debit and credit columns.

Using the accounting equation, total assets equal liabilities plus equity: N12,045 + N26,896 = N38,941. Since other assets are N36,800, cash at hand is the difference: N38,941 - N36,800 = N2,141. Option A (N2,241) and B (N2,214) result from arithmetic errors in addition. Option D (N2,114) miscomputes the final subtraction.

This is a trial balance problem where debits must equal credits. Debit items are fixed assets, stock, purchases, salaries, motor expenses, and debtors, totalling N320,100; credit items are sales, share capital, and creditors, totalling N333,050. Cash fills the gap on the debit side: N333,050 - N320,100 = N12,950. Options A, B, and C arise from incorrectly classifying items or making addition errors when summing either column.

The cash book relationship is: opening balance plus cash received minus cash paid equals closing balance. Rearranging gives: cash paid = opening balance + cash received - closing balance = N15,200 + N36,000 - N18,400 = N32,800. Option C (N29,200) comes from subtracting closing balance from receipts alone without adding the opening balance. Options A and B result from incorrect arrangements of the formula.

Total cost before discounts is 10 x N500 = N5,000. Trade discount of 5% equals N250 and reduces the purchase price to N4,750, but trade discounts are never recorded in the books. The cash discount of 12% is the one recorded as discount received; applied to the N5,000 invoice value in JAMB's approach, it gives 12% x N5,000 = N600. Option B (N570) incorrectly applies the 12% to the post-trade-discount price of N4,750, while option A is only the trade discount amount which is not recorded.

Checking journal accuracy means verifying that transactions were correctly captured and recorded, which is done by comparing ledger account entries against the original journal entries to confirm every posting is complete and correct. Option A describes how you verify a trial balance, not a journal. Option B describes the posting process itself, not a check on its accuracy. Option C is incomplete because checking only one column cannot confirm correctness without the corresponding column.

Bank reconciliation formula: Cash book balance + Unpresented cheques - Uncredited cheques = Bank statement balance. So: 4,315 + 1,688 - Uncredited = 4,791, giving Uncredited cheques = 6,003 - 4,791 = N1,212. Unpresented cheques are issued but not yet cleared by the bank, while uncredited cheques are deposits made but not yet recorded by the bank. Option A (N1,223) and C (N1,202) result from arithmetic errors, and D (N1,115) uses an incorrect formula arrangement.

Discounting means the holder of a bill of exchange transfers it to a bank before maturity in exchange for immediate cash, with the bank deducting interest (the discount) from the face value. The bank then collects the full amount when the bill matures. Surrendering implies giving up rights without compensation, cashing implies full face value payment on demand, and accepting is when the drawee agrees to pay the bill — which happens at the creation stage, not when transferred to a bank.

Under the imprest system, total petty cash payments equal the imprest amount minus the closing balance: 1,250 - 235 = N1,015. Since stationery expenses were N655, other general expenses = 1,015 - 655 = N360. Options B (N355), C (N350), and D (N305) all result from either miscalculating total expenditure or incorrectly subtracting the stationery figure from a wrong total.

To find opening fixed assets at cost, use the fixed assets account: Opening balance + Additions - Disposals = Closing balance, so Opening = Closing + 900,000 - 100,000. The provision for depreciation account confirms the year's charge: 350,000 + Annual charge - 150,000 = 300,000, giving an annual charge of N100,000. Working back from the closing position yields an opening fixed asset value of N3,900,000. Options A and B are too low, and D overshoots because it ignores the net effect of the disposal.

In accounting, buildings are classified as capital (fixed) assets, so proceeds from their sale are treated as capital receipts regardless of the seller's industry. For a property developing company, the completed building represents a capital asset on its balance sheet, and its disposal generates a capital receipt. Revenue receipts arise from the company's regular trading income such as service fees or rents, not asset disposals. Windfall and miscellaneous receipts are informal terms not used as formal accounting classifications for asset sale proceeds.
