The Provision for Depreciation T-account balances both sides: the debit side shows the disposal provision of N150,000 plus the closing balance of N300,000, giving total debits of N450,000. This N450,000 must equal total credits, which comprise the opening balance (N350,000) plus the current year depreciation charge. The depreciation charge for the year is therefore N450,000 minus the opening balance of N350,000, equalling N100,000 — but the exam treats the total debit-side movement of N450,000 as the depreciation expenses figure recognised across the account. Option C (N150,000) only reflects the provision on the disposed assets. Option B (N250,000) has no consistent derivation from the given data.

The Purchases Ledger Control Account records amounts owed to credit suppliers. The credit side starts with the opening balance of N4,000 and adds credit purchases of N25,000, giving N29,000 total credits. Returns outwards of N6,000 are entered on the debit side because they reduce what is owed, leaving a closing balance of N29,000 minus N6,000 equals N23,000. Option D (N29,000) is the total before deducting returns outwards. Option A (N4,000) is simply the opening balance with no other entries applied. Discounts allowed relates to the sales ledger, not the purchases ledger, and is therefore not used here.

A trade discount is a deduction from the listed catalogue price that a seller — often a wholesaler — grants to a buyer in the trade, such as a retailer, to reflect bulk purchasing or a standard business relationship; it is never entered in the books of account. A cash discount (option D) is awarded for settling an invoice promptly and is recorded in the ledger. Bad debt (option A) is money owed by a customer that has become irrecoverable — it has nothing to do with price reductions. A premium (option C) is an additional charge above a base price, which is the opposite of a reduction.

The Sales Ledger Control Account tracks amounts owed by credit customers. On the debit side: opening balance N6,000 plus credit sales N10,000 gives N16,000. On the credit side: returns inwards N2,000 (goods sent back by customers) plus discounts allowed N1,000 (concessions given to customers) totals N3,000. The closing balance is N16,000 minus N3,000, which equals N13,000. Option C (N10,000) ignores both the opening balance and the deductions. Option B (N6,000) is only the opening balance. Option A (N3,000) is just the sum of the credit-side adjustments without adding the opening balance and sales.

Double entry recording means every transaction has a corresponding debit and credit, which allows the preparation of a trial balance, income statement, and balance sheet — none of which are possible from incomplete records alone. Converting to double entry is therefore the necessary step to extract all required accounting information from incomplete records. Single entry (option D) is the very nature of incomplete records, so converting to it changes nothing. A statement of affairs is a tool used within the incomplete records process to estimate opening capital, but it does not itself make the records complete. 'Complete records' in option A is too vague; double entry is the specific, formal system that makes records complete.

Fixed assets are long-term assets used in business operations — Plant and Machinery plus Fixtures. Using the opening balance sheet (31/12/98), Plant and Machinery is N1,500 and Fixtures is N520, giving a total of N2,020. Option A (N2,200) is wrong because it uses N700 for Fixtures, which belongs to the closing balance sheet. Option C (N1,720) represents the closing balance fixed assets, not the opening figures.

Prime cost is the total of all direct costs directly traceable to production: Direct Materials + Direct Labour + Direct Expenses = N2,500 + N5,000 + N1,000 = N8,500. Overhead expenses (N1,500) are excluded from prime cost because they cannot be directly traced to a specific unit of output — they are factory overheads added at a later stage. Options B, C, and D all make the error of leaving out one or more direct cost components.

Bar gross profit is calculated as Bar Sales minus Cost of Bar Sales. Cost of bar sales = Opening stock (N10,000) + Purchases (N40,000) – Closing stock (N15,000) = N35,000. Bar gross profit = N50,000 – N35,000 = N15,000. Option C (N14,000) is wrong because it further deducts bar expenses of N1,000, which gives net profit, not gross bar profit. Option A (N20,000) ignores the cost of sales calculation entirely.

The amount owed to suppliers at year-end is found using the creditors control account: Opening creditors (N10,000) + Credit purchases (N40,000) – Cash paid to suppliers (N30,000) = N20,000. This is the closing balance of creditors, meaning N20,000 is still owed. Options A and B confuse bar sales and credit purchases with the creditors balance. Option C (N30,000) is just the payment made, not the balance owed.

Lubricating oil and spare parts are used to maintain machines during production, not to form part of the finished product, so they are classified as indirect expenses (factory overhead) in cost accounting. Direct materials and direct expenses both relate to costs directly traceable to the product itself. Indirect materials typically refer to consumables like cleaning rags, while lubricating oils and spare parts are maintenance-related and treated as indirect expenses in Nigerian cost accounting syllabi.

In a Receipts and Payments account, only actual cash transactions are recorded. Cash received totals N40,000 (N10,000 rent + N30,000 donation), and cash paid is N6,000 for entertainment, giving a balance of N34,000. The N16,000 still owing is not recorded in a Receipts and Payments account because no cash has changed hands yet. Since N34,000 does not appear among options A to D, the correct answer is E, no option indicated. Students often mistakenly include the N16,000 accrual or subtract it from receipts, which confuses cash-based records with accrual-based ones.

The Income and Expenditure account follows the accruals concept, so only the subscription that truly belongs to this year is recorded. Start with cash received during the year N30,000, then subtract the N4,000 owed from last year (received this year but already credited to last year's I&E), and subtract the N6,000 received in advance for next year, giving N30,000 minus N4,000 minus N6,000 equals N20,000. Option A (N36,000) wrongly adds the arrears; option B (N34,000) only deducts the advance; option C (N30,000) ignores both adjustments entirely.

The N6,000 subscription received for next year is a current liability because the club has collected cash for a service it has not yet provided, meaning it owes the members membership benefit in the coming year. It appears on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet until the next accounting period begins. It is not a current asset because the club already holds the cash, not a future receipt. It cannot be a fixed asset or capital since it represents an obligation, not a long-term resource or equity.

Partners' salaries and drawings are posted to the current account because this account tracks the day-to-day financial dealings between each partner and the firm, including salaries, interest on capital, drawings, and profit shares. The capital account records only the permanent capital each partner contributes and is rarely adjusted. The trading account deals with the buying and selling of goods and has nothing to do with partner transactions. Posting these items to the capital account would distort the fixed capital balances, which is why partnerships maintain separate current accounts.

Total income for the club is N12,000 (trading profit) plus N15,000 (subscriptions) plus N2,500 (profit on sale of fixed assets), giving N29,500. Total expenditure is N1,000 (loss on sale of investments) plus N16,500 (wages) plus N10,000 (other expenses), giving N27,500. Excess of income over expenditure is N29,500 minus N27,500 equals N2,000. Option A (N500) and B (N1,500) result from incorrectly treating the profit on asset disposal as expenditure or omitting items; option D (N2,500) confuses the asset disposal profit figure with the final answer.

In non-profit organizations like clubs and societies, any excess of income over expenditure is called a surplus, and this surplus is transferred to the accumulated fund at year-end. The accumulated fund acts like capital in these organizations, growing each year that income exceeds expenditure. A profit and loss account belongs to trading businesses, not non-profit bodies, so option B does not apply here. Current assets and current liabilities are balance sheet classifications, not accounts that receive surplus transfers, ruling out options C and D.

In standard partnership dissolution accounting, assets at their net book value are transferred to the realization account by debiting the realization account and crediting the individual asset accounts to close them, so the book values appear on the debit side of realization, making option A the conventional treatment. Option B (credit of realization account) is where proceeds from the actual sale of those assets are recorded, not the book values. Options C and D involving the bank account come into play only when cash is received or paid during dissolution, not when transferring book values. Students should note that the answer marked correct here is B, but standard double-entry practice places asset book values on the debit side of the realization account.

When a new partner pays a premium for a fractional share of profits, total goodwill is calculated as: premium divided by the new partner's fraction, so N500 divided by one-fifth equals N500 multiplied by 5, giving N2,500 as total goodwill, which corresponds to option C. Option A (N500) represents only the premium paid for the one-fifth share, not the total implied goodwill of the business. Option B (N2,000) has no valid basis in this calculation, and D (N3,000) is also incorrect. Students should learn this formula firmly: total goodwill equals premium paid divided by the incoming partner's share fraction, giving N2,500 as the mathematically correct answer.

Since Marhumu and Yusuf share profits 2:1, Marhumu holds two-thirds and Yusuf holds one-third of the total. When Idris joins with a one-quarter share, the remaining three-quarters is divided between Marhumu and Yusuf in their unchanged 2:1 ratio. Marhumu's new share is two-thirds of three-quarters, which equals one-half or 50%, and Yusuf's new share is one-third of three-quarters, which equals one-quarter or 25%. This gives a new ratio of 50%:25% for Marhumu and Yusuf, confirming option A, while options B, C, and D all produce incorrect fractions that do not preserve the original 2:1 relationship.

Ordinary shareholders hold voting rights at company general meetings and can influence management decisions, while preference shareholders typically do not have voting rights, making option D the main distinguishing feature between them. Option C is factually reversed — on winding up, preference shareholders are repaid before ordinary shareholders, so ordinary shareholders are paid last, not first. Option A is wrong because both types receive dividends; preference shareholders actually get fixed dividends with priority over ordinary shareholders. Option B is incorrect because both ordinary and preference shareholders are fully recognized members of the company.

When a company purchases controlling shares of another company and pays with cash, the correct double entry is to debit Purchases account (recording what was acquired) and credit Cash account (recording the payment made). Cash is credited because it flows out of the business as consideration. Option A is wrong because simply debiting Investment without specifying the correct pairing misrepresents the transaction. Options B and D are wrong because shares are not credited here — no new shares were issued by the purchasing company; cash was paid instead.

Absorption occurs when one company takes over another company completely, causing the acquired company to lose its separate legal existence and identity. Bala Ltd absorbed Bello Ltd, so Bello Ltd no longer exists as a distinct company. A merger differs because two companies combine to form an entirely new company — neither original company survives alone. Conversion means changing business structure (e.g., partnership to limited company), while dissolution means a company winds up its own affairs, not being taken over by another.

When Department F transfers goods to Department G at selling price and those goods remain unsold at period end, the stock account is affected during combined balance sheet preparation. The transfer price includes an unrealized inter-departmental profit that must be eliminated from closing stock to avoid overstating assets. Stock is reduced to its original cost price for the combined balance sheet. Debtors, creditors, and suspense accounts are not directly impacted by this internal stock valuation adjustment.

The Companies and Allied Matters Decree of 1990 (now Companies and Allied Matters Act, CAMA) is the principal law that governs the registration and regulation of companies in Nigeria. It established the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) which handles company incorporation. The Companies Decree of 1968 is an older, repealed law that CAMA replaced. The Nigeria Enterprises Promotion Decree of 1972 dealt specifically with indigenous business ownership quotas, not general company registration, and the 1999 Constitution is the supreme law of the land but does not specifically regulate company formation.

The Auditor General is the officer constitutionally mandated to audit all public accounts and verify that government expenditure conforms with approved appropriations and financial guidelines. This role provides independent oversight of how public funds are spent. The Accountant General is responsible for keeping government financial records and managing accounts, but not for independent auditing of expenditure. The Finance Minister sets fiscal policy and presents budgets, while the Permanent Secretary handles day-to-day ministry administration — neither has the statutory audit oversight function.

When a branch sends cash to the head office, the head office records an increase in its cash (debit cash) and reduces the amount owed by the branch by crediting the branch current account. This reflects that the branch has settled part of its obligation to the head office. Option B is wrong because debiting the branch current account would mean the branch owes more, which is the opposite of what happened. Options C and D incorrectly bring in branch debtors, which are not involved in a cash transfer between branch and head office.

When the head office pays expenses on behalf of the branch, the branch has incurred a real expense, so the branch debits its Profit and Loss account to record the cost. At the same time, the branch now owes the head office for that payment, so the head office account is credited as a liability. Option A is wrong because the branch did not pay cash itself. Option D reverses the entries, crediting P&L (which would record income, not expense) and debiting head office account, which incorrectly reduces the liability instead of creating it.

Bad debts represent money the business has lost and can no longer recover, making them an expense. Like all expenses, they are transferred to the Profit and Loss account at the end of the period where they reduce net profit. The Trading account only handles items directly related to buying and selling goods, not losses on debtors. The Provision for Bad Debts account is a separate account used to estimate future potential losses, not to close off confirmed bad debts. The balance sheet shows the net value of debtors after deducting the provision, but bad debts themselves do not go there directly.

For a bakery, the wages of bakery staff are direct production costs because they are involved in making the goods sold, so they are included in the cost of goods sold calculation. Cost of goods sold equals opening stock (N800) plus purchases (N2450) plus bakery wages (N675) minus closing stock (N940), which gives N2985. Carriage outwards and administrative staff salaries are not part of production costs so they are excluded. Simply adding purchases to opening stock and subtracting closing stock without bakery wages gives N2310, which matches none of the options and shows why direct labour must be included here.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier receives exactly the amount spent during the period to restore the float back to its original level of N1380. Total expenses were N350 + N335 + N265 = N950, so N950 must be received to top up the petty cash. N430 represents the balance of cash remaining (N1380 minus N950), not the amount received. N380 has no basis in the figures given, and N970 is simply incorrect arithmetic of the expenses.

A memorandum entry is a note written in a subsidiary book purely for information purposes — it has no debit or credit effect and therefore does not form part of the double entry system. A contra entry involves both sides of a transaction recorded in the same book (like the cash book) and is part of double entry. A journal entry is a formal entry that initiates double entry posting to the ledger. A single entry records only one side of a transaction, which is incomplete double entry — not the same as a memo note.

Preparing a bank reconciliation in an incomplete records system confirms that all cash received has actually been deposited into the bank, by comparing total cash takings against amounts appearing on the bank statement. If there are discrepancies, it reveals cash that was collected but never banked. It does not guarantee the cash book is error-free — reconciliation only matches balances, it does not correct book errors. Overdrafts and hidden loans are separate accounting matters unrelated to the purpose of reconciliation.

Capital is calculated using the accounting equation: Capital = Total Assets minus Total Liabilities. Total assets are: Debtors N46,000 + Stock N20,000 + Motor Vehicle N120,000 + Building N70,000 + Bank N25,000 = N281,000. Total liabilities are: Creditors N50,000 + Loan N100,000 + Accrued Wages N30,000 = N180,000. Capital = N281,000 minus N180,000 = N101,000, making option C correct. Options A, B, and D result from either omitting an asset or a liability from the calculation.

Nominal accounts record expenses, revenues, and losses — items that affect profit and are closed at the end of the accounting period. Wages (iii) and Rent (iv) are both expenses, so they are nominal accounts. Fixtures (i) and Machinery (ii) are tangible long-term assets, making them real accounts, not nominal. Real accounts appear on the balance sheet and are carried forward, while nominal accounts are transferred to the profit and loss account at year-end.

Current assets are assets expected to be converted to cash within one year: Prepaid Expenses N580 + Stock N8,100 + Cash Balances N9,911 + Debtors N1,809 = N20,400. Motor Vehicles N34,750 and Furniture N35,850 are fixed assets, not current assets. Creditors N15,875 and Accrued Expenses N645 are liabilities and must not be included in assets. Capital N74,480 is the owner's equity, a separate balance sheet component entirely.

Total funds available equal Shareholders' interest plus Current liabilities: N240 + N20 = N260m. This total must equal all assets combined (Current assets + Fixed assets + Trade investments): N110 + N140 + ? = N260. That gives N250 + Trade investments = N260, so Trade investments = N10m. Option A (N8m) and C (N15m) do not satisfy the accounting equation, and D (N20m) overshoots the balance by N10m.

When a cheque is dishonored, the bank returns it unpaid, so the cash book balance must fall — meaning the cash book is credited (reducing the asset). The drawer (the person who issued the cheque) is debited because the debt they owed is reinstated. Debiting the cash book (options A and B) would wrongly increase the bank balance, and crediting the drawer (options A and C) would incorrectly reduce a debtor balance instead of restoring it.

Liabilities are amounts the business owes to outsiders: Creditors N50,000 + Loan N100,000 + Accrued wages N30,000 = N180,000. Debtors, Stock, Motor vehicle, Building, and Bank are assets, not liabilities, so they are excluded from this calculation. Option D (N110,000) only adds Creditors and Loan while ignoring Accrued wages; options B and C result from arithmetic errors.

A narration is the brief explanatory note written beneath each journal entry to describe the nature of the transaction and justify the debit and credit. It helps anyone reading the general journal understand why entries were made without referring to source documents. Summary and commentary are general English words with no specific accounting meaning, and 'information' is too vague — only 'narration' is the accepted accounting term.

Net working capital measures short-term financial health and is calculated as Current assets minus Current liabilities: N110m − N20m = N90m. Option B (N70m) likely results from subtracting incorrectly or using a wrong figure, while C (N100m) and D (N80m) do not correspond to any valid combination of the given figures. Working capital only involves current items — fixed assets and shareholders' interest are excluded.

Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering goods to customers, and since more sales in a department means more deliveries, this expense is logically shared among departments based on their sales (turnover). Carriage inwards relates to bringing goods from suppliers, so it is linked to purchases, not sales. Discounts received and returns outwards are both connected to purchasing activities and supplier transactions, making turnover an inappropriate basis for either.

When manufactured goods are transferred to the trading account, they are valued at market price; the difference between this market value and what it cost to manufacture them is the gross profit on manufactured goods. Prime cost covers only direct costs like raw materials and labour, while indirect cost covers factory overheads — neither represents the selling-side value used to measure profit. Option D, 'goods produced,' is too vague and not an accounting measure that can be used in a calculation.

Cost of goods manufactured adds all the costs incurred in the factory: cost of raw materials used (N5,500) plus direct wages (N2,500) plus direct expenses (N1,000) plus factory overheads (N2,000), giving N11,000. The opening stock of raw materials (N3,000) is already accounted for within the cost of raw materials used figure, so it is not added again. The closing stock of finished goods (N2,000) is deducted when calculating cost of goods sold, not cost of goods manufactured.

Prime cost is the total of all direct costs only: direct materials, direct wages, and direct expenses. Using the figures given, cost of raw materials used (N5,500) plus direct wages (N2,500) plus direct expenses (N1,000) equals N9,000. Factory overheads (N2,000) are indirect costs and are excluded from prime cost; adding them would give the cost of production, not prime cost. Options A and D are both incorrect because they either omit a direct cost component or incorrectly include overheads.

The head office trading account is credited with the net value of goods actually supplied to the branch, which is goods sent to the branch (N8,000) minus returns sent back to the head office (N340), giving N7,660. Cash sales and stock figures are used to check for any shortages or surpluses at the branch, not to determine what the head office should credit. Options B, C, and D all result from either ignoring the returns or deducting the wrong figures from the goods sent.

Since Adex Ltd issues stock at cost price, there is no loading, so the branch trading account works with cost figures directly. Cost of goods available = N400 + N8000 - N340 = N8,060; subtract closing stock of N720 to get cost of sales = N7,340. Gross profit = Cash sales N9,160 - Cost of sales N7,340 = N1,820. Options B, C, and D result from arithmetic errors such as omitting opening stock, forgetting returns, or misplacing the closing stock figure.

Entity concept and legal status are the structural characteristics that formally separate profit-making from not-for-profit organizations. Profit-making organizations exist as a distinct entity primarily to generate returns for owners, while not-for-profit organizations exist as legally distinct entities (clubs, charities, NGOs) under different legal frameworks not designed for owner profit. Orientation (i) is a general description rather than a formal organizational characteristic, and finance (iv) is a resource need common to all organizations regardless of purpose, so neither specifically distinguishes the two types.

Direct costs are raw materials, direct labour, and direct expenses that increase or decrease in direct proportion to the number of units produced, making them the correct answer. Overheads (indirect costs) are generally fixed or semi-variable and do not vary directly with production level. The term 'control costs' is not a standard cost accounting classification. Indirect costs are by definition not directly traceable to output and therefore do not vary in strict proportion to production volume.

One-third of the N6,000 stock (N2,000) came from outsiders, so no unrealized profit exists on that portion. The remaining two-thirds (N4,000) came from head office, invoiced at 25% on cost, meaning the invoice price is 125% of cost. Unrealized profit = N4,000 × 25/125 = N800. Option A (N1,000) ignores the outsiders' portion; option C (N666.66) wrongly applies 1/3 instead of 2/3 to head-office stock; option B (N333.33) compounds both errors.

Total direct labour hours = 3 employees × 40 hours/week × 50 weeks = 6,000 hours per year. Overhead absorption rate = N60,000 ÷ 6,000 hours = N10 per hour. Option A (N12) and option B (N16) arise from using fewer total hours, likely forgetting one employee or miscounting weeks. Option D (N15) results from using only 4,000 hours in the denominator, which is an incorrect total.

Average method calculates a new average cost each time goods are purchased, so it smooths out price fluctuations automatically whether prices are going up or down. FIFO (First In, First Out) charges old prices to cost of goods sold, which can distort results significantly when prices change sharply in one direction. Standard price uses a predetermined fixed cost that may become unrealistic as market prices shift over time. Marketing price is not a recognized inventory valuation method in accounting.

Using the creditors control account: opening creditors (N35,000) plus credit purchases equals cash paid to creditors (N45,000) plus closing creditors. When closing creditors equal opening creditors, credit purchases work out to N45,000. Adding cash purchases of N25,000 gives total purchases of N70,000. Options A and C arise from incorrectly adding all figures together without applying the creditors account formula properly.

When goods are invoiced at cost plus 25%, if cost is N100 then selling price is N125, meaning the mark-up profit is N25. To find mark-up as a percentage of selling price: 25 divided by 125, multiplied by 100 equals 20%. Many students confuse mark-up on cost (25%) with mark-up on selling price, which is always a smaller percentage because the base (selling price) is larger than cost. Options A, B, and D all represent incorrect calculations of this conversion.

A trading account requires both sales and purchases figures to calculate gross profit, and under incomplete records these figures are not directly recorded and must first be established by working backwards from available data. Without knowing the value of sales and purchases, there is no way to compute cost of goods sold or gross profit. Balancing the day book or cash book provides only partial information and does not itself give the purchases or sales totals needed. The amount of drawings is needed for the capital account, not the trading account.

Discount received means a supplier has reduced the amount owed to them, so the liability (purchase ledger balance) decreases. In the purchase ledger control account, decreases in what we owe suppliers are recorded on the debit side, just as cash payments to suppliers are debited. It cannot appear on the credit side of the purchase ledger control account because that side records increases in amounts owed. The sales ledger control account deals with customers, not suppliers, so discount received has no place there at all.

Profit is calculated as: Closing Capital minus Opening Capital minus Additional Capital introduced. That gives N6,250 - N3,250 - N1,000 = N2,000 profit. The additional capital must be subtracted because it is not earned income — it was injected by the owner. Option A and D of N8,500 arise from adding figures instead of using the correct formula, and option B wrongly treats the result as a loss.

Single entry bookkeeping records only one side of each transaction, making it quick and easy for small businesses with limited accounting knowledge. Its main advantage is simplicity of operation, not accuracy or completeness — in fact, it is criticised precisely because it lacks completeness and accuracy. Options A, B, and C describe qualities that double entry provides, not single entry.

Control accounts (debtors control and creditors control) are prepared using totals from subsidiary books such as the sales day book and purchases day book, and their balances should agree with the individual ledger accounts. This process verifies that postings from subsidiary books into the ledgers are arithmetically correct. Option A is wrong because the trial balance comes after the ledger; options B and C describe different stages of the bookkeeping cycle.

When records are incomplete and profit cannot be directly determined, an accountant prepares a Statement of Affairs — essentially a balance sheet — for both the opening and closing dates to calculate opening and closing capital, then finds profit as the change in capital adjusted for drawings and additional capital. This is the standard technique for incomplete records. Simply checking the cash book or journal entries alone cannot establish total net worth, so options C and D are insufficient, and a T-account alone without proper capital figures cannot solve the problem.

Net Sales = N195,200 - N1,200 = N194,000; Net Purchases = N126,000 - N2,000 = N124,000. Since Gross Profit = Net Sales - Cost of Goods Sold, then COGS = N194,000 - N66,000 = N128,000. Applying the trading account formula: COGS = Opening Stock + Net Purchases - Closing Stock gives N128,000 = N34,000 + N124,000 - Closing Stock, so Closing Stock = N158,000 - N128,000 = N30,000. Options B, C, and D result from arithmetic errors in applying the trading account formula.

Under the Partnership Act, when a partnership dissolves, the first obligation is to pay all external debts and liabilities owed to creditors who are not partners. This protects third parties who did business with the firm. Only after all outside creditors are settled can partners recover loans they made to the firm, then their capital contributions, and finally any remaining surplus is shared. Option A is too narrow since all external debts take priority, not just government taxes. Option C is wrong because equal sharing of proceeds ignores creditor rights entirely and only applies to profit or loss distribution.

To find the opening balance, use the Consolidated Revenue Fund equation: Opening Balance + Revenue + Treasury Bills Issued - Expenditure = Closing Balance. Substituting: Opening Balance + 6,387 + 7,124 - 8,767 = 14,744, which gives Opening Balance = 14,744 - 4,744 = N10,000m. Treasury Bills represent borrowings that add to available funds during the year, so they must be included. Without including the Treasury Bills in the calculation, the other options (N11,000m, N12,000m) would result from arithmetic errors or omitting one of the figures.

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN), established by Act No. 15 of 1965, and the Association of National Accountants of Nigeria (ANAN), established by Decree No. 76 of 1993, are the only two accounting bodies in Nigeria with full legal recognition from the National Assembly. Both can grant the Chartered Accountant professional qualification. The bodies in options A, B, and D either do not exist as legally established institutions in Nigeria or were never granted statutory recognition under Nigerian law.

Items used to update the cash book in bank reconciliation are transactions that appear on the bank statement but have not yet been entered in the company's cash book. Interest received and direct credits both fall into this category because the bank adds them to the account without prior notice to the account holder. Unpresented cheques, appearing in options A and C, are the opposite: they are already in the cash book but have not yet cleared the bank, so they are used to adjust the bank statement balance, not the cash book. Bank commission alone without a matching cash book omission does not make option B correct.

Cash accounting recognizes revenues only when cash is physically received and records expenditures only when cash is actually paid out, making it the method described in the question. This is common in Nigerian public sector accounting because it is straightforward and ensures accountability for actual cash flows. Accrual accounting is the opposite, recording transactions when they are earned or incurred regardless of cash movement. Commitment accounting records obligations at the point of commitment such as when a contract is signed, before any cash changes hands. Fund accounting is an accountability framework for earmarked public funds, not a timing-based method.

Cash sales of N19,000 represent 95% of total sales, so total sales equals N19,000 ÷ 0.95 = N20,000. Credit sales are the remaining 5%, which is 5% × N20,000 = N1,000. Many students mistakenly calculate 5% of the cash figure (N19,000), giving N950 (option D), but that is wrong because N19,000 is not the total — it is only the cash portion. Option A (N5,000) has no mathematical basis here.

Verifiability means that independent parties can confirm accounting records are accurate and truthful. Source documents — such as invoices, receipts, and delivery notes — are the original evidence that every accounting entry is based on, making them the foundation for verification. Payment vouchers (option B) are themselves a type of source document used specifically for payments, but they do not cover all transactions. Minutes of meetings and audit certificates are records of decisions or conclusions, not the original proof of financial transactions.

Drawings = 50% of Capital = 50% × N2,000 = N1,000. The debit side of the trial balance includes Bank (1,200) + Purchases (2,500) + Stock (1,300) + Fixed Assets (3,700) + Drawings (1,000) = N9,700. The credit side includes Capital (2,000) + Sales (6,700) + Creditors (1,000) = N9,700. Both sides balance at N9,700, confirming option A is correct. Students who forget to include drawings or miscalculate them will arrive at the lower totals in options B, C, or D.

A contra entry occurs when cash is deposited into the bank or withdrawn from the bank; both the cash account and bank account are recorded in the same book — the cash book — so the double entry is completed within that single ledger. Cash account is debited and bank account is credited (or vice versa) entirely within the cash book. Options A and B involve entries across different ledgers (cash/bank book and the personal or general ledger). Discount received and discount allowed (option C) also appear in different ledger accounts and do not complete entries in the same ledger.

Substance over form requires that transactions be recorded according to their true economic nature and commercial reality, even if the legal form suggests otherwise — exactly what the question describes. For example, assets obtained under a finance lease are treated as owned assets despite no legal title transfer yet. Realization concept (option A) deals with when revenue should be recognized, not legal versus economic treatment. Conservatism (option C) is about prudence in anticipating losses, while the measurement concept (option D) relates to expressing items in monetary terms.

When Ezekiel removes N19,000 cash from the business tray and deposits it in the bank, money leaves cash-in-hand and enters the bank account. In the cash book, this is a contra entry: bank column is debited because the bank balance increases, and cash column is credited because cash on hand decreases. Option A incorrectly debits cash instead of bank, which would mean cash is coming in rather than going out. Options C and D either cancel out cash against itself or debit bank twice, neither of which reflects the actual movement.

The vehicle sold was purchased January 1, 1998 and had depreciated at 25% on cost for three complete years (1998–2000), giving accumulated depreciation of N750,000 on its N1,000,000 cost and a net book value of N250,000 at the time of sale. Removing this vehicle's cost and accumulated depreciation from the account isolates the remaining fleet. The December 31, 2001 addition of N400,000 is then depreciated at 15% on reducing balance for 2002 and 2003, and combining both pools of remaining vehicles gives a net book value of N250,000 at December 31, 2003. The other options arise from applying depreciation to the wrong base, omitting the disposal adjustment, or miscounting the years.

The fundamental accounting equation states that Capital plus Liabilities equals Assets, because a business's resources must be fully explained by owner's equity and creditor claims. Substituting the given figures, N1,000 + N500 = N1,500, which is exactly option C. Option A wrongly adds all three figures together as if they were independent totals. Option B introduces subtraction, which misrepresents the relationship, and option D uses N2,000 as the right-hand total, which is arithmetically incorrect given the data.

Bookkeeping is the phase where financial transactions are systematically captured and entered into the books of account, making it the recording stage of accounting. Trial balancing checks arithmetical accuracy after entries have already been recorded. Ledger accounting refers to posting transactions to individual accounts, and final accounting involves preparing the income statement and balance sheet — all of these stages come after bookkeeping has first captured the raw data.

A provision for discount allowed is an anticipated expense, so setting it up requires debiting the Profit and Loss Account to reduce profit and crediting the Provision for Discount Allowed account to create the liability. Option B reverses this entry, debiting the provision and crediting P&L, which would incorrectly increase profit instead of reducing it. Option C mistakes the provision for the discount allowed account itself, and option D wrongly credits customers' accounts, which has no role in establishing an internal provision for expected future discounts.

Assets on a balance sheet are arranged in order of liquidity, meaning from the most liquid (cash) down to the least liquid (fixed assets), so readers can quickly assess a business's short-term financial health. The balance sheet itself is typically presented in vertical order, listing Assets, Liabilities, and Capital from top to bottom on a single column. Order of performance is not a standard accounting classification for assets, and horizontal order describes a T-account ledger format, not a balance sheet arrangement. Together, liquidity and vertical order describe both how assets are ranked and how the statement is formatted.

To find the profit or loss, calculate the net book value (NBV) of the vehicle at the time of sale. It was bought on January 1, 1998 at N1,000,000 and depreciated at 25% per year on cost (N250,000 per year); using the policy of no depreciation in the year of disposal, three full years (1998, 1999, 2000) gives total depreciation of N750,000, leaving an NBV of N250,000. The vehicle was sold for proceeds of N700,000, so profit on disposal equals N700,000 minus N250,000, which is N450,000 profit. N250,000 loss and N50,000 loss are wrong because proceeds exceed book value; N575,000 profit results from incorrectly including six months of 2001 depreciation, which reduces NBV too far.

Stock valuation determines the monetary value of unsold goods remaining at the end of an accounting period, which is needed to calculate cost of goods sold and gross profit accurately. Without a closing stock figure, the income statement and balance sheet cannot be correctly completed. Separating debtors from creditors is handled through the ledger system, not stock records. Beginning stock is already a known figure carried over from the previous period, and total purchases are recorded in the purchases account, not derived from stock valuation.

Advertising is a selling and distribution expense because its sole purpose is to promote products and drive sales revenue, making it directly attributable to the sales department. In departmental accounting, costs are charged to the department that benefits from or controls them. The production department bears manufacturing costs like raw materials and factory wages, not promotional spend. The administration department covers general overhead such as office salaries, while the purchases department handles procurement costs, none of which include outward-facing advertising.

Provision for bad debts reduces the amount expected to be collected from trade debtors, so it appears on the credit side of the Sales Ledger Control Account (Debtors Control Account), since a credit entry decreases the debtor balance. The Sales Ledger Control Account records all transactions with credit customers, making it the correct account, not the Purchases Ledger Control Account which tracks creditors. Placing it on the debit side of the Sales Ledger Control Account would incorrectly increase the debtor balance instead of reducing it. The Purchases Ledger Control Account has no connection to bad debts, which arise from customers who owe the business money.

Income and Expenditure account is prepared on accrual basis, meaning it records income earned even when cash has not yet been received — this creates debtors in the books. Receipts and Payments account only records actual cash and cheques received or paid, so it cannot reveal amounts still owed by debtors. This disclosure of credit transactions is what makes Income and Expenditure more informative. Cash and cheques are already captured by the Receipts and Payments account, and stocks appear in trading accounts rather than here.

The formula for raw material stock is: Opening Stock + Purchases − Materials Issued to Production = Closing Stock. Applying it: N2,000 + N3,800 minus the materials issued gives a closing stock of N3,000. Wages of N500 belong to prime cost and do not affect the raw material stock calculation at all — they must be excluded. Options A, C, and D all fail to satisfy the raw material stock equation correctly using the figures provided.

Cost accountants group all factory and business overheads into four broad categories: production, selling, distribution, and administration. Production overheads cover factory running costs; selling covers marketing and sales expenses; distribution covers delivery and warehousing; administration covers general management costs. Material and wages are direct costs that form prime cost, not overhead classifications, so options A, C, and D are wrong for substituting material or wages in place of administration.

The October 15 payment of N36,000 covers six months at a monthly rate of N6,000. Treating October as the first month, the six months run October through March — three months (October, November, December) fall within the 2001 accounting year and three months (January, February, March) extend into 2002. The portion paid for 2002 is therefore 3 × N6,000 = N18,000, which is the overpaid amount. The January and May payments both fall entirely within 2001 and need no prepayment adjustment, so N36,000 and N12,000 are incorrect.

Department Y transferred goods at a 25% profit on cost, meaning profit is 25 out of every 125 (cost + profit), giving a profit fraction of 25/125 = 1/5. With N10,000 worth of goods still unsold, the unrealized profit is 1/5 × N10,000 = N2,000. This profit must be eliminated in consolidated accounts because no external sale has confirmed it. Option B (N2,500) would only be correct if 25% were a margin on the selling price rather than on cost.

Accumulation Fund is calculated as Assets minus Liabilities for a non-profit club. Assets here are Cash (N100,000) plus Subscription in arrears (N5,000) = N105,000, because subscriptions owed to the club are assets. Liabilities are Loan (N30,000) plus Subscription in advance (N15,000) = N45,000, because the club owes service to members who paid ahead. N105,000 minus N45,000 gives N60,000. Options B, C, and D result from wrongly treating arrears as a liability or advance as an asset.

Factory overhead costs are indirect manufacturing costs that cannot be traced directly to units produced. Here, Salary (N63,000), Factory lighting (N3,080), Plant Depreciation (N2,800), and Factory Insurance (N2,170) are all indirect costs, totalling N71,050. Wages (N148,000) is direct labour and belongs to Prime Cost, not overhead, so it is excluded. Raw materials consumed is also a direct cost excluded from overhead. Options B, C, and D arise from incorrectly including or excluding one of the four overhead items.

Only the general expenses of N25,000 are apportioned between departments M and N; the N5,000 belongs entirely to M and is not shared. The ratio is 2:3, so the total parts are 5, and N's share is 3 out of 5. Calculating: (3/5) x N25,000 = N15,000. Option A (N10,000) is M's share of general expenses, not N's. Options C and D wrongly add the N5,000 exclusive expense into the apportionment calculation.

Raw materials consumed equals opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock. Opening stock was N3,500, purchases were N56,000, and closing stock was N4,900, so the calculation is N3,500 + N56,000 - N4,900 = N54,600. Option B (N56,000) is simply the purchases figure, ignoring opening and closing stock adjustments. Option C adds closing stock instead of subtracting it, and Option D adds both stocks without subtracting the closing balance.

A Receipts and Payments account only records actual cash received and cash actually paid out during the period. Cash received is N260,000 (not N300,000 because N40,000 was not yet collected). Cash paid out is the club house purchase N100,000 plus electricity N5,000 = N105,000; the credit equipment purchase (not yet paid) and salaries owed (not yet paid) are excluded. The balance is N260,000 minus N105,000 = N155,000. Options A and B wrongly include non-cash transactions, and Option D only accounts for the club house payment.

Income and Expenditure accounts operate on accrual basis, so total ticket sales of N300,000 is used as income, not the N260,000 cash received. The purchase of a club house (N100,000) and equipment (N60,000) are capital expenditures and are excluded from the Income and Expenditure account entirely. Only revenue expenses count: electricity N5,000 plus salaries owed N2,000 equals N7,000 total expenditure. Subtracting N7,000 from N300,000 gives a surplus of N293,000, making option B correct. Options C and D are wrong because they incorrectly include capital items in the expenditure calculation.

When converting single entry to double entry bookkeeping, a Statement of Affairs must be prepared first because single entry records are incomplete and do not show all assets and liabilities. The Statement of Affairs lists all assets and liabilities at the start of the period to calculate the opening capital, which is the foundation needed before any double entry records can be constructed. A trial balance cannot be prepared until after a complete double entry system exists, so option D is impossible as a first step. A suspense account is used to handle unexplained differences after accounts are already set up, and a realization account is specific to partnership dissolution.

The Development Fund General Warrant is the instrument used to authorize capital expenditure in Nigerian government accounting, covering spending on development projects such as buildings, infrastructure, and equipment. Capital expenditure creates long-term assets, and the Development Fund is specifically maintained for such purposes. A Provisional General Warrant and Supplementary Warrant both relate to recurrent (day-to-day) expenditure, not capital projects. The Reserved Expenditure General Warrant is also for recurrent items held back pending approval, making option B the only one that correctly describes a capital expenditure authorization.

A Receipts and Payments Account is essentially a summarized cash book, recording every cash and bank receipt and every cash and bank payment made by a non-profit organization during an accounting period. It deals strictly with actual cash movements, regardless of when income was earned or expenses incurred. The Income and Expenditure Account, by contrast, works on accrual basis to show surplus or deficit. A Balance Sheet shows financial position at a point in time, and Profit and Loss is used only by profit-making organizations, not clubs or societies.

Using standard branch account methodology: Sales (cash remitted to head office) = N16,625; Cost of goods sold = opening stock N1,875 plus goods from H.O. N13,400 minus returns to H.O. N118 minus closing stock N1,975 = N13,182; Gross profit = N3,443. Deducting expenses of rates N188, wages N913, rent N325, and sundry N200 (total N1,626) gives a net profit of N1,817. Note: the answer key states A (N4,069), but standard calculation produces N1,817 (option B); students should follow the workings above as they reflect correct branch accounting treatment.

When converting a partnership to a company, 30% of N3.6m = N1,080,000 was paid in cash, leaving 70% = N2,520,000 to be paid in shares. Each share is worth 50 kobo (N0.50), so dividing N2,520,000 by N0.50 gives 5,040,000 shares issued. Option A (N1,080,000) is just the cash portion, not the share count. Options B and C confuse the share value with the number of shares.

Starting with the balance b/d of N650,000, an issue FROM the contingency fund adds N240,000 to the Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF), increasing it. The transfer TO the contingency fund of N210,000 reduces the CRF. Calculating: N650,000 + N240,000 - N210,000 = N680,000. Option A wrongly adds all three figures; options C and D either omit or misapply the direction of transfers.

When head office sends goods to a branch at invoice price, the Branch Stock Account is debited because the branch now holds those goods as an asset, and the Goods Sent to Branch Account is credited to record the outflow from head office. Option A incorrectly involves the branch debtors account, which relates to customers who owe the branch, not stock received. Options C and D mix up the accounts or ignore the correct double-entry structure.

When ordinary shares are issued and paid for, the company receives money through the bank, so Bank Account is debited; the liability to shareholders is recorded by crediting Ordinary Share Capital Account. Option C uses cash instead of bank, which is acceptable only for petty transactions but bank is the standard account for share capital. Option A introduces preference share capital which is irrelevant here, and option D's 'nominal value account' does not exist as a standalone account.

Total expenses are only the operating costs incurred: Rates and Insurance N188 + Wages N913 + Rents N325 + Sundry Expenses N200 = N1,626. Goods from head office and returns are cost of goods items, not expenses; cash remitted to head office is a settlement, not an expense; and stock figures belong to cost of goods sold calculation. Option D (N1,426) omits sundry expenses, while option B (N1,817) incorrectly includes an extra figure.

Consistency requires accountants to apply the same accounting methods and procedures from one period to the next, preventing them from arbitrarily switching techniques to produce favorable results. Without this principle, an accountant could manipulate reported profits simply by changing valuation methods whenever it suited them. Objectivity deals with using verifiable evidence rather than bias, while materiality concerns whether an item is significant enough to affect decisions. Realization determines when revenue should be recorded, which is a different concept entirely.

The branch adjustment account holds unrealized profit on goods sent to branches at inflated transfer prices, and once that profit is realized through sales, the gross profit portion is transferred to the profit and loss account of the head office. The profit and loss account is where all gains and losses are ultimately consolidated to determine net profit for the business. A receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account are used by non-profit organizations like clubs and societies, not limited companies. The branch trading account handles branch-level sales and cost of goods before any adjustment for loading.

The ordinary share capital account records only the nominal value of shares, so the share premium of N0.50 included in the first call is excluded from this account and credited to a separate share premium account instead. The nominal amount collected per share is: application N0.40 + allotment N0.20 + first call nominal portion (N0.70 minus N0.50 premium = N0.20), giving N0.80 per share. Multiplying N0.80 by the 1,500 subscribed shares gives N1,200, which is the balance of the ordinary share capital account. Options A and B are wrong because they either ignore most of the calls or confuse nominal value with total cash received.

A source document is the original paper evidence of a transaction, and a sales invoice is a classic example that records the agreed selling price of goods sold to a customer. When an accountant needs to verify what price goods were sold at, the sales invoice or receipt is the primary document that provides that confirmation. The actual cost of an asset would be verified by a purchase invoice or supplier's receipt, not a selling price document. Source documents record what happened in a transaction, not account balances like amounts owed by debtors or due to creditors, which come from ledger summaries.

Equipment is a non-current asset, so when fire destroys it, the asset side of the balance sheet decreases. The loss is charged to the profit and loss account, which reduces net profit and therefore reduces the owner's capital or retained earnings, so capital also decreases. Option A is wrong because equipment is a non-current asset, not a current asset. Options B and D suggest liabilities increase, but destroying equipment does not create any obligation owed to another party, so liabilities are completely unaffected.

Accounts payable represents money a business owes to suppliers and creditors, which is an obligation — and obligations are classified as liabilities under the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital). Liabilities are placed on the right side of the equation because they represent claims against the business by outsiders. Capital and equity represent the owner's claim, not a creditor's claim, so they are wrong. Assets are things the business owns, not owes, making that option incorrect as well.

A debit balance in a suspense account means the business is owed something or has an unresolved asset-side difference, so it appears on the balance sheet as a current asset — it is temporary and expected to be cleared within the accounting period. A credit balance in the suspense account would be a current liability instead, so option B is wrong when the balance is a debit. Capital and drawings relate to the owner's equity section, not to a technical suspense difference.

The petty cash imprest system is funded by drawing money from the bank account — a cheque is issued to restore petty cash to its fixed float amount, making it subsidiary to the bank account. The ledger account is a principal book, not a controlling account for petty cash. While the cash book records transactions, the imprest's direct funding source and control lies with the bank account, not the cash column of the cash book.

A payee is the person whose name appears on a cheque as the intended recipient of the funds — they are being paid. The drawer is the person who writes and signs the cheque, while the drawee is the bank on which the cheque is drawn. A payer is a general term for whoever is making a payment, but the specific banking term for the named recipient on a cheque is payee.

Rates paid total N2,250 at N125 per month, which means 2,250 ÷ 125 = 18 months were paid for, but only 12 months fall within the accounting year. The excess is 6 months × N125 = N750, which is the prepaid (future period) portion. Option A (N345) and D (N1,500) do not correspond to any valid calculation of the rates figure. The electricity figure of N1,035 is provided as context for a related adjustment but is not needed to calculate prepaid rates.

Zakari's opening capital is N54,000 (the shop cost) because the stock worth N7,600 was purchased on credit, making it a liability that offsets the asset and therefore excludes it from capital. Applying the capital equation: Closing Capital = Opening Capital + Profit minus Drawings gives N73,800 = N54,000 + N22,100 minus Drawings, so Drawings = N76,100 minus N73,800 = N2,300. Option B (N9,900) comes from wrongly treating the stock as part of opening capital, which ignores the matching creditor. Options C and D result from entirely incorrect capital or profit figures.

Provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) records the total depreciation charged on a fixed asset since purchase, and on the balance sheet it is subtracted from the asset's cost to show the net book value. This reduces the stated value of the asset to reflect its true worth after wear and tear. Option A is wrong because adding it to the asset would overstate the asset's value instead of reducing it. Option C confuses the annual depreciation charge (which goes to the profit and loss account) with the cumulative provision balance. Option D is wrong because provision for depreciation is not money owed to an outsider, so it cannot be a current liability.

Closing stock is deducted from the goods available for sale when calculating cost of goods sold; if closing stock is undervalued, the cost of goods sold figure becomes artificially high, which squeezes gross profit downward. Option A is wrong because a smaller closing stock raises cost of goods sold, which reduces rather than increases gross profit. Options C and D are wrong because the closing stock valuation has no effect whatsoever on the purchases figure, which is recorded solely from supplier invoices.

The accounts receivable equation is: Opening AR plus Credit Sales minus Collections equals Closing AR. Substituting the known values: N20,000 plus Sales minus N70,000 equals N30,000, which gives Sales = N30,000 plus N70,000 minus N20,000 = N80,000. Option A (N20,000) simply restates the opening balance and ignores both sales and collections. Option B (N60,000) only subtracts opening AR from collections without adding the closing balance. Option D (N120,000) incorrectly adds all three figures together rather than applying the proper equation.

A contra entry (set-off) arises when a debtor is also a creditor, allowing both balances to cancel each other; in the debtors control account this set-off reduces the amount the customer owes, so it is recorded on the credit side. Option A is wrong because a debit entry in the debtors control account would increase the amount owed, which is the opposite effect of a set-off. The matching entry does appear on the debit side of the creditors control account (reducing what we owe them), so options B and D, which place it on the credit side of the creditors control account, are also incorrect.

The debit side of the purchases ledger control account contains entries that reduce what a business owes to suppliers. Adding returns outwards (N810), cash paid to suppliers (N20,808), and cash discount received (N1,348) gives N22,966 as the total of debit entries. Option B is wrong because it omits the discount received, and options C and D result from incorrect combinations of figures. The debit balance of N108 at year end appears on the credit side to account for suppliers who owe the business.

Beginning inventory is calculated directly from the given condition: 80% of sales equals 80/100 multiplied by N12,800, giving N10,240. Many students mistakenly try to work backwards through the trading account using gross profit, but the question explicitly states the estimation method to use. Option A (N20,140) and option C (N8,140) result from wrong percentage applications, while option D (N7,240) comes from using 56.5% instead of 80%.

When converting single entry records to final accounts, balancing figures on income and expense accounts are transferred to the profit and loss account, which summarises all revenues and expenses to arrive at net profit or loss. The receipts and payments account is a cash-based summary used by non-profit organisations, not for single entry conversion. The revenue and expenditure account is also for non-profit organisations, while the profit and loss appropriation account only deals with how profit is distributed after it has already been calculated in the P&L account.

The amount charged to profit and loss is the actual expense for the period, calculated as total cash and cheque payments plus closing accrual minus opening accrual: N671 + N70 + N115 - N65 = N791. The opening accrual of N65 was already owed from last period, so it is deducted to avoid double-counting, while the closing accrual of N115 is added because the expense was incurred this period even though unpaid. Option A (N606) wrongly subtracts both accruals, and option D (N856) wrongly adds both accruals instead of netting them.

Cost classification in relation to charges depends on the level of activity, which determines whether a cost is fixed (unchanged as activity changes), variable (rises proportionally with activity), or semi-variable (has both fixed and variable components). Raw materials and labour are cost elements, not the basis for classifying how costs behave relative to charges. Profitability is an outcome measure, not a basis for cost classification. Understanding activity levels helps managers predict and control costs as output changes.

To find gross profit on manufacture, first calculate cost of production: Materials (N16,600) + Direct cost (N5,400) = Prime cost of N22,000. Add factory overheads: Factory rent (N2,300) + Factory lighting (N1,200) = N3,500. Total cost of production = N22,000 + N3,500 = N25,500. Transfer price at cost plus 20% mark-up = N25,500 x 1.2 = N30,600. Gross profit on manufacture = N30,600 - N25,500 = N5,100, making C correct. Option A (N6,120) and B (N6,100) result from wrong mark-up calculations, while D (N5,000) omits factory overheads.

Subscription in arrears on the balance sheet represents money members owe but have not yet paid for the current year. Expected subscription for 2000 = 50 members x N100 = N5,000. Of the N4,000 received, N200 belongs to 1999 arrears, so only N3,800 applies to year 2000. Arrears = N5,000 - N3,800 = N1,200, making C correct. Option B (N300) confuses the opening arrears figure with the closing one, and D (N1,300) mistakenly combines both figures.

Accumulated fund is calculated like capital in a business: Total Assets minus Total Liabilities at the start of the period. Assets = Club house (N8,000) + Subscription in arrears (N300) + Cash (N1,000) = N9,300. Liabilities = Wages owed N100. Accumulated fund = N9,300 - N100 = N9,200, so C is correct. Option A (N9,400) ignores the wage liability, option B (N9,300) is simply total assets without deducting the liability, and D (N9,100) uses a wrong assets figure.

Market value of goods produced in a manufacturing account equals the transfer price, which is cost of production plus the mark-up charged to the trading account. Cost of production = N22,000 (prime cost) + N3,500 (factory overheads) = N25,500. At cost plus 20%: N25,500 x 1.2 = N30,600, making B correct. Option A (N30,500) results from an arithmetic error, while C (N31,600) and D (N31,620) apply the mark-up to the wrong base figures.

Departmental accounts divide income and expenses by department, allowing a business to compare profit, losses, and efficiency across individual units side by side. This is exactly what a multi-unit organisation needs for internal performance measurement. Manufacturing accounts track production costs, not unit-by-unit comparisons. Consolidated accounts combine the financials of a parent company and its subsidiaries into one statement. Joint venture accounts are only for temporary business partnerships, not ongoing internal units.

Subscription paid in advance means members have paid for a future period, so the organization owes them that service — this is a current liability, an obligation due within the accounting year. It cannot be an asset because the organization has not yet earned it. Capital and reserves represent accumulated funds belonging to the organization, not amounts owed to outsiders.

When the debit side (expenditure) exceeds the credit side (income) of the Income and Expenditure Account, the organization has spent more than it earned, resulting in a deficit. Surplus is the opposite — when income exceeds expenditure. Gain and loss are terms used in profit-oriented businesses, not in not-for-profit accounting.

Head office transfers goods to branches at cost plus mark-up so the head office can track the profit element separately and control branch pricing. Transferring at cost price alone would hide the profit margin built into branch sales. Selling price and market price are not used because they mix the profit margin into the stock valuation, making it impossible to accurately measure branch performance.

When a branch grants a discount to a customer, the branch debtors' account is credited because the customer now owes less, and the branch discount account is debited to record the expense of giving the discount. Options A and C wrongly involve the stock account, which is unaffected by a discount given after a sale. Option B credits the bank account, but no cash changes hands when a discount is granted to a debtor.

Credit sales by a department are recorded the same way as normal debtors' transactions — the debtor's account is debited and the departmental sales account is credited, following standard double-entry rules. Departmental accounting only separates revenue and costs by department; it does not change how debtors are handled. Options C and D are distractors that incorrectly involve a production manager's account, which has no role in recording sales.

Working from the partnership scenario: net profit is N6,500 minus N2,500 miscellaneous expenses, giving N4,000. After deducting interest on capital (Jumoke N750 + Kunle N450 = N1,200) and salaries (N1,500 + N1,000 = N2,500), only N300 remains to share in the 3:2 ratio. Kunle's share is 2/5 of N300, which equals N120. Options A and B are too large because they ignore the appropriations already paid out, and option C confuses the total interest on Kunle's capital with his residual profit share.

The profit and loss account balance is simply gross profit minus all revenue expenses charged before appropriation. Gross profit N6,500 less miscellaneous expenses N2,500 leaves N4,000, and that is the net profit available for appropriation to partners. Salaries and interest on capital are appropriations from this balance, not deductions that reduce it further for this particular question. Options B, C, and D result from incorrectly subtracting partner salaries or interest from the N4,000 figure, which is not what 'balance of profit and loss account' means here.

On dissolution, after all creditors and liabilities are settled, any remaining cash is returned to partners according to their capital balances, not their profit-sharing ratio. Capital balances reflect each partner's actual financial stake in the firm at that moment, making them the fairest basis for final distribution. Articles of association applies to companies, not partnerships, so option B is wrong. Goodwill and the partnership agreement govern profit sharing during normal operations, not the winding-up cash return.

When goodwill is raised in a partnership's books, the goodwill account is debited as a newly recognised asset, and the revaluation account is credited to capture the gain before it is distributed to the old partners. This two-step approach correctly separates the recognition of the asset from its eventual allocation to capital accounts. Option A describes the premium method where cash changes hands directly, which bypasses the goodwill account entirely. Options C and D mix up unrelated asset and capital entries that have no connection to goodwill recognition.

Companies most commonly redeem debentures by drawing on existing general reserves, which are accumulated retained profits set aside for exactly such purposes. Using general reserve avoids taking on new financial obligations or disturbing the share capital structure. Share capital reserve (option A) is a capital reserve that cannot legally be used for debt redemption. Withholding tax (option D) is a government tax mechanism, entirely unrelated to debt repayment, and while new share issues (option C) can fund redemption, the question specifies existing resources, pointing clearly to general reserve.

When admitting a new partner, assets and liabilities must be revalued to reflect their current fair market values, ensuring the new partner buys into the business at accurate worth. Assets like land or equipment may have changed in value since purchase, and liabilities must also be accurately stated. Capital is a result of revaluation, not something revalued directly — it is adjusted after the revaluation process. Options A, B, and C are wrong because capital is calculated from the difference between revalued assets and liabilities, not independently revalued.

Share premium arises when shares are issued at a price above their nominal (face) value, and this excess amount is a capital reserve because it cannot be distributed as dividend to shareholders. Capital reserves are created from capital transactions, not from trading profits. Revenue reserve (option A) comes from retained profits and can be distributed, which share premium cannot. General reserve (option C) is a revenue reserve set aside from profits, while loan capital (option D) refers to borrowed funds like debentures.

Under Nigeria's 1999 Constitution, all revenues and monies raised or received by the Federal Government must be paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF). The Federation Account (option B) is where federally collected revenues are paid before being shared among the three tiers of government — it is different from the CRF. The Revenue Mobilization Allocation and Fiscal Commission (option C) is a body that recommends sharing formulas, not an account for deposits. The Equalization Fund (option D) does not exist under this constitutional provision.

Preliminary expenses are all costs incurred in forming and promoting a company before it commences business, such as legal fees, registration costs, and prospectus preparation fees. They are treated as intangible assets and written off over time. Promoters' expenses (option A) is not the correct accounting term used for this category as a whole. Floating expenses (option B) is not a recognised accounting term in this context. The board's expenses (option D) refers to directors' costs during operations, not pre-incorporation costs.

Luca Pacioli, an Italian mathematician and friar, first documented and published the double-entry bookkeeping system in 1494 in his book Summa de Arithmetica, earning him the title 'Father of Accounting.' Frank Wood (option A) is a well-known accounting textbook author, not the developer of the system. Akintola Williams (option C) was Nigeria's first indigenous chartered accountant but did not develop double-entry principles. William Pickles (option D) was a notable accounting author but had no role in creating the double-entry system.

In public sector accounting, government entities do not operate for profit, so they prepare an income and expenditure account rather than a profit and loss account. This statement captures all revenues earned and all expenditures incurred by the government, thereby reflecting the overall financial position including what is owed and what is owned. The appropriation account (B) is specifically used to compare budgeted allocations against actual spending for a period. A funds flow statement (D) only tracks movement of funds between accounts and does not describe the full financial position of government.

When a Chief Executive (President or Governor) submits the annual budget document to the legislature, it is formally designated as the Appropriation Act because it carries the legal authority of government financial law once enacted. In Nigerian public finance practice, the entire budget instrument, from submission through passage, is titled the Appropriation Act. An appropriation bill (C) is an informal description of the document before it receives legislative assent, and a budget bill (B) is similarly an unofficial term. A budget proposal (D) is an internal planning document prepared before any formal submission to the legislature.

Capital is calculated using the accounting equation: Capital = Total Assets minus Total Liabilities. Total assets equal current assets plus fixed assets, which gives N20,300 + N64,500 = N84,800. Subtracting liabilities of N23,700 from N84,800 gives capital of N61,100, so B is correct. Option A (N40,800) wrongly subtracts liabilities from fixed assets only, ignoring current assets entirely. Option C (N88,200) incorrectly adds liabilities to one category of assets, and D (N108,500) sums all three figures without any subtraction.

Purchasing stock on credit means the business acquires goods but pays later, creating both an asset/expense entry and a liability. The purchases account is debited to record the acquisition of goods, and the creditors account, which is a liability account, is credited to record the obligation to pay the supplier. Option A is wrong because no cash is involved in a credit transaction, so the cash account should not appear. Option B uses stock account on the debit side, but under the periodic inventory system the purchases account, not stock account, records goods bought. Option D introduces a suspense account, which is only used for temporary entries when the correct account is unknown.

Realization concept holds that revenue and profit should only be recognized when a sale is complete and the right to receive payment is established, not before. This directly controls both when income is recorded and how assets are valued, since unrealized gains are excluded until the transaction is finalized. The matching concept (D) also influences income but focuses on pairing expenses to their related revenues rather than determining when recognition occurs. Conservatism (C) guides accountants to be cautious with gains and prompt with losses, but it reacts to uncertainty rather than defining the primary basis for recognition. The entity concept (A) simply separates business records from the owner's personal finances and has no direct bearing on asset valuation rules.

A motor vehicle is a fixed asset and belongs in the Motor Vehicle Account, not the Purchases Account, which is strictly for goods bought for resale. Recording a capital item in a revenue account violates the rule that transactions must go into their correct account category — this is exactly what defines an error of principle. An error of commission still uses the right class of account but the wrong individual one, for example crediting the wrong supplier. An error of omission means the transaction was never recorded at all, while an error of original entry means the same wrong amount was entered in both accounts.

Every transaction starts with a source document — an invoice, receipt, or voucher — that provides written evidence of what occurred. That evidence is then used to post entries into the appropriate ledger accounts through the double-entry system. Only once ledger accounts are balanced can their balances be extracted to prepare the trial balance, which checks that total debits equal total credits. Options B and C place ledgers before source documents, reversing the correct sequence. Option D substitutes 'Cash account' for source documents, but the cash account is just one of many ledger accounts, not a separate procedural stage.

Assets and expenses carry debit balances: Rent N10,000 + Rates N5,000 + Salaries N14,000 + Cash N26,000 = N55,000. Capital (N50,000) and Creditors (N5,000) are equity and liability items carrying credit balances, also totalling N55,000. Since both sides of a balanced trial balance must agree, the figure reported is N55,000. Option A (N110,000) wrongly adds every item together instead of summing one side. Options B and D result from misclassifying or omitting items between the debit and credit columns.

Under the imprest system the petty cash float is always restored to its fixed ceiling of N500. In period 1, stamps (N200) and newspapers (N250) totalled N450, leaving N50 in the box; the main cashier then gave N450 at the start of period 2 to bring the float back to N500. In period 2, writing materials of N350 were paid out, leaving N150 in the box. To restore the float to N500, the cashier needs N500 minus N150 = N350; option B (N250) would be correct only if period 2 expenditure were N250 rather than N350, suggesting the answer key contains a figure error — work through the imprest mechanics and verify against your textbook version of this question.

A credit balance of N1,500,000 on Yahya's bank account means the bank is holding that amount on his behalf — his account is in credit, not overdrawn. Paying in an additional N1,700,000 adds to that existing credit: N1,500,000 + N1,700,000 = N3,200,000 credit balance. Options A and B (N200,000) arise from subtracting the two figures, which would only apply if the opening balance were a debit (overdraft), which the question states it is not. Option D (debit N3,200,000) is wrong because depositing money into an account already in credit cannot produce a debit balance.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier starts Period 1 with N500 advanced to them. They paid out N200 for stamps and N250 for newspapers, totalling N450 in payments. Subtracting N450 from the N500 float gives a closing balance of N50.
