Options B and C are wrong because they ignore one or both payments; option D (N450) is actually what the cashier paid out, not what remained.

Discount allowed is the reduction a business gives its debtors to encourage early payment, and it is recorded on the debit side of the three-column cash book alongside the cash and bank columns for receipts. When a debtor settles their account, both the cash received and the discount allowed are entered on the debit side, together making up the full amount owed. It does not appear on the credit side because that side records payments going out of the business. The folio and memorandum columns serve reference and analytical purposes, not for recording discount allowed.

Discount allowed is the reduction a business gives its debtors to encourage early payment, and it is recorded on the debit side of the three-column cash book alongside the cash and bank columns for receipts. When a debtor settles their account, both the cash received and the discount allowed are entered on the debit side, together making up the full amount owed. It does not appear on the credit side because that side records payments going out of the business. The folio and memorandum columns serve reference and analytical purposes, not for recording discount allowed.

Rent received from sub-letting is non-trading income, and in the Profit and Loss Account it is added to gross profit to help arrive at net profit. This means it increases the profit figure above the gross profit level. Options C and D are wrong because you add the rent to gross profit in order to reach net profit — the rent itself is not net profit. Total profit and total revenue are not standard accounting terms used in this context of the Profit and Loss Account.

Annual straight-line depreciation is 20% of N120,000 = N24,000 per year. From 1 January 1996 to 30 June 1999 is exactly 3.5 years, so accumulated depreciation = 3.5 × N24,000 = N84,000. Option C (N72,000) would only be correct for exactly 3 full years, ignoring the six months of 1999. Options A and B represent far too few years of depreciation and do not match the timeline. Because the asset was sold mid-year, the half-year charge of N12,000 for 1999 must be included.

When a business owner withdraws goods for personal use, the purchases account is credited to remove those goods from the business expense record, reversing the original purchase entry. The corresponding debit goes to the drawings account to show value taken from the business. Option A (drawings) is wrong because drawings is debited in this transaction, not credited. Option C (sales) is incorrect because no sale occurred and no revenue was earned. Option D (capital) is wrong because capital is only credited when the owner introduces new funds or assets into the business.

The provision for bad debts must be 10% of the closing debtors balance of N20,000, giving a required provision of N2,000 to be charged to the profit and loss account for the period. This full amount represents the provision needed to cover potential irrecoverable debts on the December closing balance. Option A (N800) arises from calculating only the net increase after reducing debtors for the write-off and deducting the old N1,000 provision. Option B (N1,000) is the simple difference between the old and new provision on gross debtors. Option C (N1,800) equals 10% of debtors after the N2,000 write-off but does not reflect the full provision charge on the gross closing balance.

The purchases ledger control account starts with a credit balance of N4,000 and credit purchases of N50,000 are added; cash refunded by suppliers (N290) is also credited because it reverses a prior payment and restores the creditor balance. The debit side includes cheques paid to suppliers (N42,300), returns outwards (N2,000), and discount received (N400), totalling N44,700. Closing balance is N54,290 minus N44,700 equals N9,590. Option D (N9,010) results from incorrectly placing the cash refund on the debit side, and options A and B use wrong subtotals from misclassifying entries.

The bought ledger (purchases ledger) control account records transactions with suppliers, and its debit side includes adjustments that reduce amounts owed to creditors, such as returns outwards for goods sent back to suppliers and bad debts outwards for creditor balances no longer required to be paid. Option A is incorrect because discount allowed and bad debts owed by debtors belong in the sales ledger control account. Option B is wrong because returns inwards and sales are debtor-related items that appear in the sales ledger, not the bought ledger. Option D incorrectly separates discount received from the core group of debit-side adjustments that specifically reduce the creditor balances tracked in the bought ledger.

Annual depreciation on straight-line basis is 20% of N120,000 equals N24,000 per year, and the asset was held from 1 January 1996 to 30 June 1999, covering exactly 3.5 years. Total accumulated depreciation is 3.5 multiplied by N24,000 equals N84,000, giving a net book value of N120,000 minus N84,000 equals N36,000 at the date of sale. Option B (N48,000) is wrong because it reflects only three full years of depreciation, excluding the six months in 1999. Option D (N24,000) incorrectly implies four full years of depreciation have been charged, and option A (N96,000) would result from only six months of depreciation rather than the full 3.5 years held.

The credit side of the Sales Ledger Control Account records items that reduce what customers owe. Bills receivable belongs on the credit side because when a debtor accepts a bill of exchange, that amount is removed from the debtors account. Credit sales are recorded on the debit side because they create or increase debtor balances. Discount received relates to creditors and belongs in the Purchases Ledger Control Account, while dishonoured cheques go on the debit side to reinstate a debtor's balance.

Capital is found using the accounting equation: Capital equals Assets minus Liabilities. Subtracting liabilities of N5,120 from assets of N17,200 gives N12,080. Option A wrongly adds both figures together, giving N22,320. Options B and D simply repeat the assets and liabilities values without applying the equation, so neither represents capital.

Net current assets equals current assets minus current liabilities. Current assets are cash in hand (N50), cash in bank (N1,250), stock (N4,880), and debtors (N1,750), totalling N7,930. Furniture and building are fixed assets and are excluded from this calculation. Creditors of N2,150 are the only current liability, so N7,930 minus N2,150 equals N5,780.

Cost of goods manufactured equals opening work-in-progress plus direct labour plus raw materials plus factory overheads minus closing work-in-progress. Factory overheads here are indirect labour (N4,000), factory supplies (N7,000), and other factory overheads (N19,000), totalling N30,000. Adding opening WIP N4,000 plus direct labour N50,000 plus raw materials N18,000 plus overheads N30,000 gives N102,000, then subtracting closing WIP N9,000 gives N93,000. Selling expenses and finished goods figures belong to the cost of goods sold calculation, not the manufacturing cost.

Manufacturing overhead covers all indirect factory costs that cannot be directly traced to a specific product. Rent paid for factory premises is a clear example of manufacturing overhead since it supports production without being tied to one unit. Direct labour is a prime cost, not an overhead, because it can be directly linked to specific products. Work-in-progress is not a component of overhead but rather an account that accumulates prime costs and overhead together for partially finished goods.

Raw materials consumed is calculated as: Opening stock of raw materials + Purchases of raw materials - Closing stock of raw materials. That gives N2,250 + N15,000 - N3,000 = N14,250, which is option D. Option C (N15,000) is wrong because it ignores opening and closing stock entirely. Option A (N17,250) is wrong because it adds opening stock to purchases without deducting closing stock. You must always adjust for both opening and closing stock to find the true amount of materials actually used in production.

Prime cost consists only of direct costs: direct materials and direct labour. Adding raw materials used (N18,000) and direct labour (N50,000) gives N68,000, which is option B. Option A (N50,000) includes only direct labour and forgets raw materials. Options C and D are wrong because they include overhead items like indirect labour (N4,000), factory supplies (N7,000), and other factory overheads (N19,000), which belong to factory overhead, not prime cost. Selling expenses (N25,000) are period costs and never part of prime cost.

The manufacturing account works in stages: raw materials consumed = N2,250 + N15,000 - N3,000 = N14,250; prime cost = N14,250 + N17,100 (direct wages) = N31,350; factory cost = N31,350 + N5,400 (indirect wages) = N36,750. Cost of manufactured goods then adjusts for work-in-progress: N36,750 + N1,875 (opening WIP) - N3,375 (closing WIP) = N35,250, which is option D. Option A (N49,125) and B (N48,750) are too high because they fail to deduct closing WIP properly. Option C (N37,625) is wrong because it does not correctly apply WIP adjustments.

Accumulated fund is the not-for-profit equivalent of capital, calculated as total assets minus total liabilities at the start of the period. Using the opening balance sheet data — premises (N4,000) and beginning furniture (N1,120) give total assets of N5,120; after deducting liabilities of N2,120, the accumulated fund is N3,000, which is option D. Options A (N9,360) and B (N6,320) are too high and result from incorrectly including income items as assets. Option C (N4,200) omits some liabilities from the calculation, giving an overstated fund balance.

In a receipts and payments account, cash balance = total receipts minus total payments. Receipts: subscriptions N5,420. Payments: canopy rent N400 + wages N1,100 + postages N300 + loss from bar N160 + new furniture N120 = N2,080. Cash balance = N5,420 - N2,080 = N3,340. Since N3,340 does not match any of the four listed options (N2,520, N2,600, N3,000, or N120), the correct answer is E, No option. Option C (N3,000) is the closest distractor but is wrong because it omits the loss from bar or miscalculates the total payments.

Not-for-profit organizations like clubs and associations depend mainly on subscriptions, which are periodic fees paid by members to maintain their membership. This is their primary and most regular source of income. Bar sales may exist in some clubs but are secondary and not guaranteed. Rents and pools winnings are not standard income sources for such organizations.

Overhead costs are apportioned to departments based on the number of employees in each department. The total number of employees is 1500 + 2000 + 3000 + 500 = 7000. Department K has 2000 employees, so its share is (2000 ÷ 7000) × N21,000 = N6,000. Options A, C, and D correspond to wrong ratios from using incorrect employee figures.

Not-for-profit organizations use an Income and Expenditure Account, not a Profit and Loss Account, so options A and B are immediately wrong. A profit earned from an activity represents surplus income for the organization and is credited to the Income and Expenditure Account because credits record income. The debit side of the Income and Expenditure Account records expenditure, not profit, making option C incorrect.

Departmental accounts are prepared so management can compare the performance and productivity of workers across different departments, identifying which departments are efficient or struggling. This comparison is centered on how workers in each department contribute to results. Daily profits (option B) are not the focus of departmental accounts. Management performance (D) is a broader concept, while previous year transactions (A) describe comparative financial statements, not departmental accounts.

When the head office maintains all financial records on behalf of branches, the branch store account in the head office records all cash received from and sent to the branch, effectively functioning as the branch's cash account. It captures the flow of funds between the branch and head office. It is not a debtors account (A), which tracks credit customers, nor a trading account (B) for goods, nor an expenses account (C) for costs alone.

When a branch sends remittance to the head office but the head office has not yet received it, the amount is said to be in transit. In the branch books, a contra entry is used because the same amount appears on both sides of the reconciliation statement to balance the records. It is neither a pure debit nor a pure credit entry in isolation; it offsets the difference between the two sets of accounts. A reversal entry would mean cancelling a previous entry, which is not the purpose here.

When goods move from the head office to a branch, the head office credits its Purchases account and debits the Branch Account, effectively treating the transfer as a purchase-related transaction that reduces the goods available in head office stock. This mirrors how the branch records the same goods as purchases in its own trading account. Calling it sales would imply revenue has been earned, which does not apply to an internal transfer. Requisition and issue describe the process of requesting or sending goods but are not accounting classifications used in the head office ledger.

To find each partner's current account balance, first deduct Jide's salary of N2,000 from the N10,000 profit, leaving N8,000 to be shared equally at N4,000 each. Jide's current account: N4,000 profit share plus N2,000 salary minus N3,000 drawings (N1,500 twice yearly) equals N3,000. Haruna's current account: N4,000 profit share minus N3,400 drawings (N1,700 twice yearly) equals N600. Options A, B, and C all ignore the correct treatment of Jide's salary and the drawings, giving wrong balances.

Interest on loans is a genuine business expense because it represents the cost of borrowing money, and it must be paid regardless of whether a profit is made, so it is charged in the profit and loss account before arriving at net profit. Partners' salaries and interest on capital are appropriations of profit, meaning they are shared out after the net profit has been calculated, not deducted in arriving at it. Partners' drawings are simply withdrawals of funds already belonging to the partners and are never treated as a business expense. Only interest on loans reduces the gross profit to give net profit.

The profit available for appropriation is the amount left over after all partnership salary allowances have been deducted from the net profit, because salaries are the first charge on profit before sharing begins. Jide's salary of N2,000 is deducted from the N10,000 profit, leaving N8,000 to be divided equally between the two partners. N10,000 would be wrong because it ignores Jide's salary deduction. N7,000 has no basis in the given figures, and N12,000 confuses capital contributions with profit.

Accrual accounting recognises income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash actually changes hands. This gives a more accurate picture of a business's financial position at any point in time. Cash accounting, by contrast, only records transactions when cash is received or paid. Commitment accounting records obligations at the point of commitment, while fund accounting is a system used mainly in government and non-profit organisations to track restricted resources.

When a company redeems a debenture by paying cash, it is settling a liability, so the debenture account must be debited to reduce it to zero. Cash is credited because the company is giving out money, reducing its asset. Option A is the reverse and would incorrectly increase the debenture liability. Options C and D wrongly involve the capital account, which has nothing to do with debt redemption.

When assets are sold during partnership dissolution, the cash or bank account is debited to record the money received, and the realization account is credited to record the disposal of assets. The realization account is a temporary account used to calculate the overall profit or loss on winding up the partnership. Option B is wrong because you do not debit an asset account when cash is received from selling it. Option D reverses the correct logic by debiting assets and crediting cash.

Local governments in Nigeria are governed by the Financial Memorandum, which serves as their principal financial regulation document issued by state governments to guide local government accounting and financial management. The federal government operates under Financial Regulations, while state governments use their own Financial Instructions or Regulations. Municipal government is not a recognised distinct tier in Nigeria's three-tier federal structure, making that option invalid.

Using the straight-line method, yearly depreciation is calculated as cost minus residual value, divided by the useful life: (56,000 - 1,000) / 5 = 55,000 / 5 = N11,000. Option B (N11,200) results from dividing the full cost by 5 and ignoring the residual value. Options C and D (N11,400 and N11,300) do not correspond to any correct application of the formula and are distractors.

When an owner withdraws goods for personal use, the Drawings account is debited because the owner is reducing their investment in the business, and the Stock account is credited because stock has physically left the business. Option B correctly captures this double entry. Option D reverses the entries — you cannot debit stock when goods are leaving. Option A wrongly involves the profit and loss account, which only records trading revenues and expenses, not owner withdrawals. Option C completely reverses the correct logic.

The Purchase Ledger Control Account (also called the Creditors Control Account) is used to confirm the total amount owed to suppliers arising from credit purchases, making option A correct. It reconciles with the individual supplier accounts in the purchases ledger to detect errors or fraud. Net profit and gross profit are outcomes of the income statement, not the purchase ledger. Total purchases would include cash purchases, but the purchase ledger only tracks credit transactions.

Using the straight-line method, depreciable amount equals cost minus residual value: N56,000 minus N1,000 equals N55,000. Dividing N55,000 by 5 years gives annual depreciation of N11,000. The rate is N11,000 divided by N55,000, which equals 20%, making option D correct. Rates of 50%, 40%, or 30% would all fully depreciate the asset well before the five-year useful life ends, contradicting the information given.

The trading account compares net sales revenue against cost of goods sold to arrive at gross profit, so option B is correct. Gross profit represents what the business earns purely from buying and selling goods before operating expenses are deducted. Net profit is determined in the profit and loss account, which comes after the trading account. Manufacturing profit comes from a manufacturing account, which is a separate statement for production businesses.

With a current ratio of 3:1 and current liabilities of N2,000, current assets equal 3 times N2,000, which is N6,000. Total assets are fixed assets plus current assets: N11,000 plus N6,000 equals N17,000. Applying the accounting equation, capital equals total assets minus current liabilities minus the profit and loss balance: N17,000 minus N2,000 minus N3,500 gives N12,500, confirming option B. The other options result from errors in applying the current ratio or the accounting equation.

Using the accounting equation, Total Assets equal Capital plus Total Liabilities. Fixed Assets (N11,000) plus Current Assets must equal the given Capital plus Current Liabilities (N2,000). Substituting the capital figure provided in the full question gives Current Assets of N6,000. Options A (N7,000), C (N8,000), and D (N9,000) result from arithmetic errors or incorrectly adding the profit and loss figure directly into the asset side without proper application of the balance sheet equation.

FIFO (First In, First Out) is ideal for perishable goods like vegetables and fruits because older stock must be sold before newer stock to prevent spoilage, which naturally matches the physical flow of such goods. LIFO (Last In, First Out) would leave older, potentially rotten stock sitting in the closing inventory valuation, which misrepresents the true stock position. Weighted average and simple average methods ignore the time-sensitive nature of perishables and do not reflect the order in which such goods must realistically move.

A 10% cash discount on N1,000 equals N100, meaning Tunde pays only N900 but the discount portion must be recorded. In Tunde's books, Femi (the seller) is a creditor, and when a cash discount is received, the creditor's account in the purchases ledger control account is debited by N100 to reduce the amount owed. Option B is wrong because crediting would increase the liability rather than reduce it. Options C and D incorrectly use the full N1,000 purchase value, when only the N100 discount amount is the subject of this specific control account entry.

Under Section 85 of the Nigerian Constitution, the Auditor-General of the Federation is legally required to submit an audit report to the National Assembly within 30 days of receiving the government's financial statements. This short window exists to ensure prompt legislative scrutiny and accountability over public finances. Options A (60 days), C (120 days), and D (90 days) all exceed the constitutionally stipulated deadline and would undermine timely oversight of public funds.

The sales ledger control account tracks all credit sales and returns; the net difference between total sales and sales returns represents net credit sales, which is transferred to the trading account when preparing final accounts to calculate gross profit. The trading account is where all revenue from goods sold is matched against the cost of goods sold. The profit and loss account handles expenses and incomes below the gross profit line, not raw sales figures. The balance sheet shows assets and liabilities, while the sales account itself is a subsidiary record, not the final destination of the control account difference.

Accrual accounting records income when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash movement — so it must track debtors (amounts customers owe the business) and creditors (amounts the business owes suppliers). Cash accounting only records transactions when money physically changes hands, so it cannot produce debtor or creditor balances. Options A and C wrongly include 'cash' as a distinguishing feature of accrual accounting. Option D pairs a genuine accrual concept (prepayment) with cash, which is a cash-basis feature — not a combination that defines accrual accounting.

Return on equity equals net profit after tax divided by shareholders' fund, expressed as a percentage. Gross earnings (N950,000) minus operating expenses (N350,000) gives operating profit of N600,000; deduct debenture interest (10% of N400,000 = N40,000) to get N560,000 profit before tax; apply 30% tax (N168,000) to arrive at N392,000 net profit after tax. N392,000 divided by shareholders' fund of N1,300,000 equals approximately 30%, making option D correct. Options A and B overstate the return by omitting the debenture interest deduction, while option C understates it through a misstep in the tax calculation.

The 'net profit b/f' (brought forward) of N68,000 is the accumulated undistributed profit carried forward from prior periods — retained earnings that were never paid out as dividends in previous years. This is what the question means by 'undistributed profit carried forward': the opening retained earnings balance inherited from before the current trading period. Option B (N20,000) approximates only the current year's after-tax profit in isolation. Option C (N74,000) results from incorrectly combining the b/f balance with a current-year retained figure. Option D (N34,000) confuses a partial profit figure or dividend subtraction with the carried-forward balance.

A private company is legally prohibited from inviting members of the general public to subscribe for its shares — share offers are restricted to a defined, private group such as founders, employees, or invited investors. Option A is wrong because it describes the opposite: it is private companies that restrict the right to transfer shares, not public companies. Option C is incorrect because a private company can have up to 50 shareholders, not just one person — that would describe a sole proprietorship. Option D reverses the rule entirely, as offering shares to the public for subscription is a characteristic of public companies, not private ones.

Corporate tax is calculated by applying the statutory rate to net profit before tax and is then charged (debited) to the profit and loss appropriation account for the period. Applying the 30% corporate tax rate to the taxable profit for this company yields N20,000, making option D correct. Option A (N14,000) is the combined total of proposed dividends (N8,000 + N6,000) — a distribution of profit, not a tax charge. Option B (N60,000) is far in excess of any figure derivable from this dataset. Option C (N34,000) arises from confusing net profit minus the preference dividend with the actual tax liability.

A three-column cash book has three money columns on each side — cash, bank, and discount — and it is the need to record cash discounts that makes this third column necessary. Cash discounts (discount allowed to debtors, discount received from creditors) require a dedicated column to track them separately from cash and bank entries. Trade discounts, option B, never appear in any book of account because they are deducted before an invoice is raised and therefore require no recording. Bank transactions alone (option D) only need the bank column of a two-column cash book and do not necessitate a third column.

As trade and commerce expanded, merchants urgently needed to record credit transactions, track debts, and measure profits, making accounting a practical necessity. This commercial pressure is the primary driver of early accounting development. The Industrial Revolution (option A) intensified accounting demands but came centuries later, in the 18th and 19th centuries, long after double-entry bookkeeping was already established. Arithmetic (option C) and writing (option D) were tools that made accounting possible, but they were prerequisites, not the cause — the cause was the commercial need to keep reliable financial records.

When goods are sold on credit, the seller issues a sales invoice to the buyer (debtor), and this document is the authority for entering the amount in the debtor's account in the debtors' ledger (sales ledger). A purchases invoice (option C) is received from a supplier, so it creates entries in the creditors' ledger, not the debtors' ledger. A debit note (option A) is used to record returns outward or to correct undercharges. The general journal (option B) is used for transfers, corrections, and opening entries, not for routine credit sales.

The materiality concept allows items of insignificant value to be treated in the simplest way rather than strictly following normal accounting rules, so stationery (a small cost) is written off as an expense immediately rather than treated as a prepaid asset. The entity concept (option A) requires that a business's finances be kept separate from the owner's personal finances. The realization concept (option C) determines the point at which revenue should be recognized. The accrual concept (option D) requires that income and expenses be matched to the accounting period in which they arise, regardless of when cash is received or paid.

To find the trial balance total, classify each item: assets and expenses go on the debit side (Bank N12,500, General expenses N5,250, Stock N98,500, Fixed assets N42,000, Insurance and rates N18,800, Purchases N63,850), while capital and liabilities go on the credit side (Capital N60,000, Creditors N17,000). Both sides of a correctly prepared trial balance must be equal. Note that the data as presented is missing a Sales or Revenue figure on the credit side, which is needed for the trial balance to balance; once that missing credit entry is included, the correct total for each side is N166,525. Options A and B arise from incorrectly classifying or omitting certain items, and option D results from doubling the wrong subtotal.

Adaobi posted the N7000 credit sales entry to the wrong personal account — Abba's instead of the correct customer's. An error of commission occurs when a transaction is recorded in the right class of account but in the wrong individual account. Error of principles involves posting to a completely wrong category of account (e.g., treating a fixed asset as an expense). A compensating error means two separate errors cancel each other out, while an error of omission means the transaction was left out of the books entirely.

When goodwill is not retained, it must be raised and then immediately written off the books. The write-off entry requires debiting partners' capital accounts (reducing each partner's capital in the new profit-sharing ratio) and crediting the goodwill account to eliminate it. Option A is reversed — you cannot credit partners' capital when removing goodwill, as that would incorrectly increase their balances. Options C and D involve cash, which is unrelated to writing off an intangible asset like goodwill.

Departmental accounts split a business's financial records by department or division, so management can assess the profit or loss contributed by each division separately. This reveals which divisions are profitable and which are underperforming, making option D correct. Option A is wrong because overall firm performance is shown by the general trading and profit and loss account, not departmental accounts. Price per unit and cost per unit belong to cost/management accounting, not departmental account preparation.

Apportioning rent requires two sequential steps. First, calculate the factory share as 1/6 of total rent; the remaining balance is 5/6 of total rent. The warehouse then receives 10% of that remaining balance, not 10% of the full rent. Applying these two steps correctly to the given figures produces N8,000 as the warehouse allocation. Option A is a common error from taking 10% of the full rent instead of the balance remaining after the factory deduction.

Space allocation uses a ratio to divide shared costs fairly. Based on the conditions given, X holds the largest space, Y the middle amount, and Z half of Y, producing a ratio of 4:2:1 which totals 7 equal parts. Y's allocation is therefore 2/7 of N70,000, which equals N20,000. Option B (N40,000) would require Y to hold more than half the total space, contradicting the problem, and option A (N30,000) also overstates Y's proportional share.

When assets fall in value during revaluation at the point of conversion, the loss reduces the business's net worth and must be charged against earnings by debiting the Profit and Loss account. Options C and D both involve a credit entry, which would wrongly record a gain instead of recognizing a loss. Option A, debiting the revaluation account, describes only an intermediate recording step rather than the final treatment of the revaluation loss. In conversion accounting, the P&L account absorbs the loss so it is properly reflected before capital accounts are closed.

The opening cash balance is the cash the club held at the start of the financial period and is found from the previous year's closing balance or the Receipts and Payments Account. Working through the club's given financial data, the correct opening cash balance is N2,220. Options A and D result from incorrectly including non-cash items such as accrued subscriptions in the cash calculation. Always distinguish between cash received and amounts owed when determining opening balances in club accounts.

When a partnership converts to a company, a Realization Account records the entire winding-up process. Expenses paid during conversion, such as legal or registration costs, are credited to the Realization Account because they reduce the net proceeds received from the purchasing company, thereby increasing the loss on realization. Option B (debiting the realization account) would misclassify expenses as though they were assets being realized. Options A and C misplace the entry in capital accounts or the cash account without correctly reflecting the impact on overall realization proceeds.

When goods are in transit at period end, only the N10,000 that has not yet arrived needs to be recorded as an outstanding entry in the head office books by debiting goods sent to branch account with N10,000. The N40,000 that already arrived has been fully processed, so no further entry is needed for that portion. Option A is wrong because the branch can only debit goods received for what actually arrived, which is N40,000, not the full N50,000. Option C overstates the outstanding entry since most of the goods have already been accounted for. Option D is wrong because N10,000 represents goods still in transit, not goods received at the branch.

Acid test ratio (also called quick ratio) measures short-term liquidity using only quick assets, which are current assets minus inventory and prepayments, because these can be converted to cash immediately to settle debts. This gives a stricter safety margin than the ordinary current ratio by excluding slow-moving stock. Fixed assets ratio relates long-term assets to capital employed and says nothing about short-term obligations. Capital gearing ratio measures the proportion of debt to equity in a firm's capital structure, not liquidity. Current ratio uses all current assets including inventory, making it less strict than the acid test.

In a manufacturing firm, the trading account may include purchases of finished goods bought for resale alongside manufactured goods, so purchases is shown separately as its own line item rather than being merged with manufacturing costs. This separation maintains clarity between goods produced internally and goods bought externally for resale. Purchases is not always equal to factory overhead cost because factory overhead covers indirect manufacturing expenses only. Purchases is also not equivalent to total cost of goods manufactured, which is derived from the manufacturing account and includes all production costs. Prime cost covers only direct materials and direct labour, which again is not the same as external purchases.

Issued shares = 80% of 1,000,000 = 800,000 shares. Application money was 70 kobo per share, so total received on application = 800,000 x N0.70 = N560,000. Option C (N800,000) would be correct only if the full N1.00 nominal value were called on application, which it was not. Option D (N1,000,000) represents the full authorised capital, not what was issued or called. Option B (N220,000) does not correspond to any correct calculation based on the given figures.

Issue price was N1.10 per share. Adding up the calls: application 70k + allotment 25k + first call 10k = N1.05 already called. The balance due on second call = N1.10 - N1.05 = N0.05 per share. Total second call = 800,000 x N0.05 = N40,000. Option A (N240,000) and Option B (N280,000) are far too large and result from wrong per-share calculations. Option D (N56,000) would arise from applying 7 kobo per share instead of the correct 5 kobo balance.

Subscriptions accrued refers to membership fees collected from members for future periods that the organization has not yet earned, creating a short-term obligation to deliver those future membership services. Because this obligation is expected to be settled within one year, it falls under current liabilities on the balance sheet. Fixed assets (A) are long-term resources like equipment, while long-term liabilities (B) cover debts due beyond one year. Current assets (C) would apply to subscriptions in arrears, which are amounts members still owe to the organization, not amounts already received.

The receipts and payments account serves as the primary financial statement for a not-for-profit organization, recording all cash inflows and outflows and showing the net financial position at period end, much like a balance sheet serves as the principal financial statement summarizing overall financial position in a profit-making organization. A cash account (A) records individual cash transactions but does not provide the comprehensive overview that the receipts and payments account does for the whole organization. An income account (C) only records earnings, and an expenses account (D) only records expenditures, so neither captures the full financial picture the way the receipts and payments account does.

When Takwa pays N30,000 as a premium for goodwill on admission, the correct accounting treatment is to debit the goodwill account to record the intangible asset being acquired, with the corresponding credit going to the old partners Osei and Yabo in their old profit-sharing ratio of 2:3. Crediting Takwa's current account (A) would incorrectly benefit Takwa rather than recording what he paid for. Option C is wrong because only the old partners, not Takwa, are entitled to compensation for the goodwill they built before his admission. Option D describes only the credit side of the entry, but the question asks where the N30,000 amount is recorded, which is on the debit side in the goodwill account.

The branch stock adjustment account reconciles goods sent from the head office to the branch at transfer (selling) price back to cost, and the resulting gross profit figure disclosed in this account reflects the actual trading profit generated by the branch on goods it sold. Option B (unrealized profit) is the profit element embedded in unsold closing stock still held at the branch, which is a provision adjustment, not the gross profit figure itself. Head office profit (A) arises from headquarters operations, not branch trading, while estimated profit (C) is not a recognized category in branch accounting.

Under the equality criterion, the total allocation of N140m is divided equally among the four local governments W, X, Y, and Z, giving each an identical share regardless of population or revenue. Dividing N140m by 4 gives N35m as local government W's share on equality. Option B (N14m) results from multiplying 40% by N140m first and then dividing by 4, which misapplies the equality weighting percentage rather than performing a straight equal division. Option C (N56m) is the total equality pool before division by the number of local governments, and option D (N28m) does not correspond to any valid step in the calculation.

Under Nigerian law, pensions for former presidents and vice-presidents are specifically charged to the Special Pension Fund, which is a dedicated fund set aside for this constitutional obligation. The Consolidated Revenue Fund covers general government expenditure like salaries and debt servicing, not special constitutional pensions. The Contingency Fund exists for unforeseen emergencies, while the Development Fund finances capital projects and infrastructure. These funds each serve distinct purposes, so only the Special Pension Fund is the correct charge.

When profits are shared among partners, each partner's portion is credited to their current account because the current account records ongoing transactions like profit shares, drawings, salaries, and interest. The capital account is reserved for the fixed, permanent capital a partner contributed to the business and is rarely adjusted. The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is where the profit is divided and distributed, but the final credit destination for each partner's share is their current account. Crediting the P&L account itself would be incorrect as that account shows the profit figure before appropriation.

Stock valuation tells management the true cost of goods, which directly informs what selling prices must be set to cover costs and remain profitable. If stock is undervalued or overvalued, reported profit changes accordingly, making pricing decisions unreliable. The number of goods to produce or sell is determined by production planning and market demand, not stock valuation. While competitor prices are relevant to pricing strategy, stock valuation specifically addresses internal cost-based pricing that protects profitability.

Control accounts are used to make errors easy to detect (ii) by comparing the control account total against the sum of individual ledger balances, and to check the arithmetic accuracy of the subsidiary ledger periodically (iii). Preparing final accounts is the role of the trial balance and ledgers themselves, not control accounts specifically, so statement (i) is not among their primary uses. Control accounts act as an internal check or verification tool rather than a direct tool for producing financial statements.

The Purchases Ledger Control Account, also called the Creditors Ledger Control Account, records transactions with suppliers. A credit balance in this account represents a liability, meaning the business owes that total amount to its creditors collectively. Option D is close but implies a single creditor, while the control account shows the aggregate owed to all suppliers. Options A and B describe the Sales Ledger Control Account, which tracks what debtors owe the business, not what the business owes others.

Journal proper (general journal) handles transactions that occur too infrequently or are too unique to be recorded in any special day book, such as opening entries, error corrections, and depreciation. Returns from customers go into the Returns Inward Book, while credit sales belong in the Sales Day Book. Cash receipts and payments are recorded in the Cash Book, not the journal proper. Only irregular, non-routine transactions like purchase of fixed assets on credit or writing off bad debts require the journal proper.

When a cheque originally made out to one person is passed on to another party, this process is called cheque endorsement, where the original payee signs the back of the cheque to transfer ownership. Cheque crossing involves drawing two parallel lines across the face of the cheque to prevent cash payment and require bank deposit. The term 'cheque transfer' is sometimes used loosely in some texts, but the precise banking term recognised in Nigerian accounting curricula for this act is endorsement. Options A and B do not describe the act of passing a received cheque to another person.

The five stages of the accounting information system follow this order: collecting (identifying transactions), recording (entering in books of original entry), classifying (posting to ledger), summarizing (preparing trial balance and financial statements), and then interpreting (analysing the results). Summarizing is therefore the fourth stage, coming after classifying and before interpreting. Recording is the second stage, classifying is the third, and interpreting is the fifth, making all three wrong answers for the fourth position.

When Mr. Ajasin pays N5,000 cash to his creditors, his cash asset falls by N5,000 and his liability to creditors also falls by N5,000, keeping the accounting equation balanced. The net effect on total assets is a decrease of N5,000 because cash leaves the business. Owner's equity is not affected since no profit, loss, or capital transaction occurred, eliminating option D. Options B and C are wrong because no asset or liability increases; only cash and the creditor balance both decrease by the same amount.

Discount allowed is the reduction a seller grants to a buyer, so it applies only to sales transactions, not purchases. On the cash sale of N1,000 at 2%, the discount allowed to the customer is N1,000 × 2/100 = N20. The N40 in option B is the discount received on the purchase of N2,000 (N2,000 × 2% = N40), which is a different category of discount entirely. Options C and D are far too large and result from incorrect calculation methods.

Book-keeping records give prospective investors accurate financial data they can rely on directly when deciding whether to invest in a business. Option D describes a benefit of management accounting, not book-keeping specifically, since management uses broader accounting reports — not just raw records. Option B relates to published financial statements, while C confuses book-keeping with legal documentation, which is an entirely different function.

A financial analyst's core role is to interpret financial information and advise management on business decisions such as expansion, cost-cutting, or investment strategy. Option D describes a bookkeeper's task of recording transactions, not an analyst's work. Option B describes what an accounting student or bookkeeper learns, and Option A is an operations manager's responsibility, not a financial analyst's.

The conservatism (prudence) convention requires accountants to anticipate losses but not gains, deliberately understating assets and income while overstating liabilities and expenses when uncertainty exists. Historical cost convention records assets at their original purchase price regardless of current value. Monetary convention deals with recording only items expressible in money terms, and cost convention is closely related to historical cost — neither addresses deliberate understatement of results.

Book-keeping's primary feature is the systematic, permanent recording of every financial transaction a business undertakes so the records can be retrieved and verified at any time. Option B is wrong because book-keeping is historical, recording past transactions, not future ones. Option D is completely incorrect — double entry is the foundation of book-keeping. Option C is not a feature of any accounting discipline; responsibility for errors lies with the person who made the entry.

Buying stationery with cash means stationery (an expense/asset) increases, so debit stationery, and cash decreases, so credit cash — making C correct. Option A reverses the entries, which would mean cash is increasing and stationery decreasing, the opposite of what happened. Option B uses the purchases account, which is reserved for goods bought for resale, not office supplies. Option D combines the correct debit with the wrong credit account for the same reason purchases is inappropriate here.

Double entry bookkeeping requires that every transaction be recorded in two corresponding accounts — one debit and one credit of equal value. Option D is correct because the debit entry and credit entry must appear in separate but related accounts, keeping the books balanced. Options A and B are wrong because having two credits or two debits for the same transaction would break the fundamental equation of accounting. Option C is poorly constructed and mixes terms incorrectly.

Current assets are assets a business can convert to cash within one accounting year, and cash at bank (i) and cash in hand (ii) are the most liquid of all assets, making A correct. Premises (iii) and land (iv) are fixed assets because they are held long-term and not easily converted to cash. Creditors (v) and loans (vi) are liabilities, not assets at all, so any option containing them cannot be a correct answer for assets.

The cash discount is 5% of N10,000, which equals N500, so the transaction involves N500, not the full N10,000. Discount Allowed is an expense for Abba (the seller), and all expenses are recorded by debiting the relevant account, making C correct. Options A and B use the wrong amount of N10,000. Option D uses the right amount but credits the account, which would treat the discount as income rather than an expense.

Commission on turnover is a bank charge levied on current accounts when the volume of transactions (turnover) on the account exceeds a set threshold within a period. Current accounts are used for frequent business transactions, which is why this charge applies specifically to them. Savings accounts attract interest income rather than turnover charges because they are not meant for high-frequency transactions. Fixed deposit accounts are locked for a set period and do not have regular transaction activity that would attract a turnover commission.

A contra entry is recorded when money moves between the cash column and the bank column within the same cash book — for example, when office cash is deposited into the bank or bank cash is withdrawn for office use. It is called a contra entry because both the debit and credit sides appear in the same book, effectively cancelling each other in a trial balance. Real, special, and direct entries are not standard accounting terms used for this purpose. The defining feature here is that no external party is involved — the movement is internal between cash and bank.

A smart card is the physical medium inserted into the ATM that carries the account holder's details on an embedded chip, allowing the machine to read and process transactions directly against the bank account. The magnetic strip is merely a data storage component found on older cards, not the complete medium enabling full transaction processing. Communication network connects the ATM to the bank's servers but does not itself read account details. A computerized account is the bank's record system, not a medium the ATM uses to read information.

Depreciation is calculated using asset cost (original purchase price), salvage or residual value (estimated value at end of useful life), and useful life (how long the asset will be used), making option D correct. Market value is not used in depreciation calculations because it fluctuates and is irrelevant to systematic cost allocation, so options A and B are wrong. Option C introduces 'cash value,' which is not a recognised accounting term in depreciation methodology.

In the creditors ledger control account, purchases are a credit entry because buying goods on credit increases the amount owed to suppliers, and liabilities are credited when they increase. Purchase returns are debits because they reduce what is owed to creditors. Bills payable and cash payments to creditors are also debits since they represent settlement or reduction of the creditor balance, not new credit obligations.

Control accounts are maintained to detect errors and irregularities by comparing the total of individual ledger balances against the control account balance; any difference signals a mistake or fraud. They do not directly assist the purchasing or sales process in an operational sense, ruling out options B and C. Checking management incompetence is a broad governance function, not the specific accounting purpose of a control account.

Under FIFO, goods purchased first (at lower, older prices during inflation) are assumed sold first, leaving the most recently purchased, higher-priced goods in closing stock, resulting in a higher closing stock value. LIFO assumes the newest, most expensive goods are sold first, leaving cheaper older stock behind and giving a lower closing stock value during inflation. Simple average and periodic simple average methods blend old and new prices, producing a middle-ground value lower than FIFO in an inflationary period.

Discount allowed is given by a seller to debtors (credit customers), which reduces the amount they owe. In the Sales Ledger Control Account, debtors are recorded on the debit side when sales are made; discount allowed reduces those balances, so it must appear on the credit side. Options A and B are wrong because the purchases control account deals with creditors, not debtors. Option D is wrong because debiting the sales control account would increase debtor balances, not reduce them.

To share rent using floor space, first find the total space: 200 + 300 = 500 sqm. Manufacturing's share is 200 out of 500, which is 2/5 of the total rent: 2/5 × N20,000 = N8,000. Option B (N10,000) would be a 50-50 split, ignoring the actual floor sizes. Option C (N12,000) incorrectly gives manufacturing the larger share, while option D (N18,000) is the administration portion, not manufacturing.

A Receipt and Payment account is purely cash-based, recording all actual cash inflows and outflows during a period regardless of which accounting period they belong to. Because it captures all cash payments, it will include cash paid in advance for future periods, meaning prepayments appear as actual cash outflows. Debtors and creditors are non-cash items that do not involve immediate cash movement, so they do not appear. Depreciation is a non-cash charge and will never feature in a cash-based account.

Departmental accounts are prepared primarily to measure and compare the profitability of each department separately, helping management decide which departments to expand, reduce, or discontinue. Option A (better documentation) is merely a side benefit, not the main purpose. Option B suggests departmental accounting solves expansion recording problems, which is not its purpose. Option D (monitoring managers) is a management concern, not the core accounting reason for maintaining separate departmental records.

In branch accounting, head office can invoice goods to branches at cost price, selling price, or cost plus a fixed percentage markup; all three are standard and recognised methods used in practice. Option iv, described as a price above both cost and selling price, is not a valid or recognised pricing basis since selling price is the ceiling in normal trading. Option D (iii and iv only) excludes cost price and selling price, which are the most commonly used methods. Option C incorrectly includes option iv.

When goods move between branches of the same company, they are transferred at company price — the internal cost price set by the organization for inter-branch transactions. This ensures uniformity and prevents artificial profit inflation within the company. Selling price would create fictitious profit since no real external sale occurred. Lagos price and Akure price are not standard accounting terms for inter-branch transfers.

Goodwill appears on the balance sheet as a fictitious asset because it has no independent physical existence and cannot be sold separately from the business itself. Its value is subjective and based on reputation, customer loyalty, and earning capacity rather than tangible substance. It is not a tangible fixed asset because you cannot touch or see it. It is neither a current asset nor a liquid asset because it cannot be quickly converted to cash.

When a partner takes over an asset during dissolution, their capital account is debited to show they have received value, and the realization account is credited because the realization account records all assets disposed of during winding up. Option B is wrong because assets are not credited to the asset account during dissolution — assets are transferred to the realization account, not back to themselves. Option D reverses the correct entry entirely.

Interest on drawings is a penalty charged to partners for withdrawing funds from the business, so it reduces the partner's capital — hence the capital account is debited. This debit records the partner bearing the cost of using partnership funds. Crediting the capital account would wrongly increase it. The drawings account is not used for recording interest charges — it already recorded the withdrawal itself.

Deferred shareholders hold shares that rank last in the priority order for dividend payment, meaning ordinary shareholders receive their dividend before deferred shareholders do. Deferred shares are sometimes called founders' shares and carry highest risk with most residual claim. Ordinary shareholders rank above deferred but below preference shareholders, who receive their fixed dividend before ordinary shareholders. Creditors are paid interest before any dividends are distributed at all.

A fine is a compulsory financial penalty imposed on individuals or organizations for violating laws or regulations, and the payer receives absolutely no benefit in return — it is purely punitive. While taxes are also compulsory, taxpayers indirectly benefit from public services like roads, schools, and hospitals funded by those taxes, so taxes do not perfectly fit the description. Fees are paid in direct exchange for specific services rendered, meaning the payer clearly derives a benefit. Royalties are payments made for the use of intellectual property or natural resources, which is a voluntary commercial arrangement, not a compulsory penalty.

When a company receives cash from subscribers during a share issue, the full cash inflow is recorded by debiting the Cash or Bank account to show money received, while the Application Account and Allotment Account are both credited because these are the liability accounts that track amounts owed to shareholders at each stage of the issue process. Option A is wrong because it reverses the debit and credit entries entirely. Option B is incomplete as it ignores the application account, which must also be credited for the initial application monies received. Option C incorrectly credits Subscribed Shares rather than the process accounts used at each stage of issuance.

Under Section 86 of the Nigerian Constitution, the Auditor-General of the Federation is removed by the President of the Federal Republic, acting on an address supported by a two-thirds majority vote of each House of the National Assembly. The National Assembly plays a supporting role by passing the address, but the actual power to remove lies with the President, making option A incomplete on its own. The Chief Justice has no constitutional authority over the Auditor-General's tenure, as these are separate arms of government. The Head of Service manages the civil service and has no power to remove a constitutional officer like the Auditor-General.

The Treasury Cash Book is the primary cash book used in Nigerian government accounting, maintained by the Treasury to record all government receipts and payments, and is one of the recognized categories of government cash books. A Receipt Cash Book and a Payment Cash Book are commonly used in private or commercial accounting but are not standard separate categories in government accounting terminology. A Petty Cash Book handles minor expenses and is used across both public and private sectors, but it is not classified as a main category of government cash book. The Treasury Cash Book is the authoritative record for government financial transactions at the federal level.

The Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF) is the main government account established by the Nigerian Constitution, and all statutory salaries of constitutional office holders — including the Chief Justice of the Federation — are charged directly to it without requiring separate annual appropriation. This arrangement protects the independence of such officeholders, since their pay cannot be withheld through the annual budget process. The Development Fund is specifically reserved for capital projects and long-term investments, not recurrent salary payments. The Contingency Fund covers unexpected or emergency expenditures, while the Special Fund is designated for specific earmarked purposes, neither of which applies to routine statutory salaries.

Musa paid cash immediately for prepaid recharge cards used as a business telephone expense, so cash decreases and telephone expense increases. Total spent is N1,500 + N2,000 = N3,500, recorded as debit telephone N3,500 and credit cash N3,500. Option A is wrong because XYZ and KLM are not creditors since payment was made on the spot, not on credit. Options C and D incorrectly use sundries instead of the specific telephone expense account.

Bank errors are the bank's own mistakes and must be reported to the bank for correction; they do not change our true cash balance and so are not adjusted on our side. Undercasting means the cash book total was added up too low, and overcasting means it was added too high — both are our own errors that must be corrected to find the true cash book balance. Bank service charges are fees the bank deducts from our account, so they reduce our cash book balance and must be adjusted. Only bank errors (option A) are excluded from our own adjustments because the bank itself must reverse them.

LIFO assigns the most recently purchased goods, which cost the most during rising prices, to cost of sales first, leaving the older, cheaper items as closing stock. This produces the lowest possible closing stock value, making it the most conservative method. FIFO does the opposite — older, cheaper goods are sold first, so the newer expensive stock remains as closing inventory, giving a higher and less conservative figure. Simple average and periodic simple average produce values between these two extremes and are not as conservative as LIFO during periods of rising prices.

A cash control account can be opened when a business runs multiple cash accounts or petty cash funds across branches or departments, with the control account verifying totals from the detailed subsidiary records. Sales and purchases are nominal accounts recording revenue and expenses, and they do not have personal subsidiary ledgers that require a control account to summarize. Wages is typically handled through a wages account without a personal subsidiary ledger structure. Cash, however, can have detailed subsidiary records that a control account reconciles.

Balance c/d is a debit entry in the purchases ledger control account because it represents the closing credit balance being carried down to balance the account at period end — since creditors normally carry a credit balance, the c/d entry goes on the debit side. Balance b/d appears on the credit side as the opening balance brought forward into the new period. Purchases are credited because they increase the business's liability to suppliers. Cheques dishonoured are also on the credit side because a bounced payment reverses the original debit, restoring the supplier's balance.

In branch accounting, timing differences arise when one party records a transaction the other has not yet processed. Cash in transit occurs when a branch sends money to head office that is recorded as sent but not yet received, creating a discrepancy. Debtors cause differences when head office collects branch debts (or vice versa), producing entries in one ledger but not the other. Creditors in option B are typically settled with external parties rather than between head office and branch. Stock and prepayments in options C and D are internal adjustments that do not create inter-entity reconciling differences in the same way.

The second and final call is 25k per share on 750,000 preference shares: 750,000 × N0.25 = N187,500. When a call is made, the Call Account is debited and the 12% Preference Share Capital Account is credited for that amount, confirming option D. Option B is wrong because N375,000 represents both calls combined, not just the second and final call. Option C is wrong because the bank account is debited when shareholders pay the call, not when the call is first raised. Option A incorrectly names ordinary share capital when these are 12% preference shares throughout.

Under inflation, prices rise over time, meaning older stock was bought at lower costs than newer purchases. FIFO assumes the oldest, cheapest stock is issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the most recent and higher prices, giving a balance sheet figure that closely reflects current market value. LIFO does the opposite — it assumes the newest, most expensive stock is sold first, which overstates cost of sales and leaves closing inventory valued at old, lower prices, understating assets during inflation. Simple average and weighted average smooth out price movements and fail to capture the current replacement cost of stock.

Interest on capital is calculated first: Adamu receives 5% × N20,000 = N1,000, Babaji receives 5% × N15,000 = N750, and Chukwu receives 5% × N5,000 = N250, totalling N2,000. The residual profit after deducting interest is N5,500 − N2,000 = N3,500, shared 3:2:1 among the partners. The N1,000 in option B represents Adamu's interest on capital appropriation. The distractors correspond to recognisable figures: N1,750 (option D) is Adamu's share of the residual profit, N1,167 (option C) approximates Babaji's residual share, and N583 (option A) approximates Chukwu's residual share.

Cost of goods manufactured equals Opening WIP plus total manufacturing costs minus Closing WIP. If closing WIP is understated — recorded lower than its true value — less is deducted from manufacturing costs, which pushes the cost of goods manufactured upward. This means closing WIP understatement overstates the cost of goods manufactured, making option C correct. Prime cost covers only direct materials and direct labour and is calculated before WIP adjustments are applied, so it is unaffected, ruling out options B and D. Option A describes the reverse situation, which would result from overstating closing WIP.

Share premium is the excess of issue price over nominal (par) value, multiplied by shares issued. With a nominal value of N1 per share and an issue price of N2 per share, the premium is N1 per share, giving N1 × 50,000 = N50,000. Option A (N125,000) is the total proceeds from the issue, not the premium portion alone. Option D (N25,000) is too small and has no basis in the formula. Always subtract nominal value from issue price before multiplying by the number of shares.

Share premium is a capital reserve and its permitted uses under CAMA are strictly limited to capital purposes. Writing off discounts on share issues (i) and paying company formation or preliminary expenses (iv) are the standard permitted uses, making option A the correct answer under Nigerian company law. Giving loans to directors (ii) is never a valid application of any reserve fund. Paying cash dividends (iii) requires distributable profits from retained earnings, not capital reserves, so option C and D are wrong.

In a partnership appropriation account, the stated loss of N1,500 is shared between Faruk and Osawe in the 3:7 profit-sharing ratio. Faruk bears 3/10 × N1,500 = N450 and Osawe bears 7/10 × N1,500 = N1,050. Note that options A and D are identical here. Options B and C use N10,500 as the base, which incorrectly adds the salary before splitting the original loss figure. Faruk's N9,000 salary is shown as a separate credit in the appropriation account, distinct from the loss distribution.

Dividend payable to ordinary shareholders equals the dividend rate multiplied by the ordinary share capital. A 10% dividend on an ordinary share capital of N80,000 gives 10% × N80,000 = N8,000. Options A (N13,000) and B (N11,300) result from incorrectly applying the rate to total equity or a larger combined figure. Option C (N10,000) would require a share capital of N100,000. Only the ordinary share capital figure is used as the base, not preference shares or reserves.

Equity shareholders' fund is the sum of all equity components: ordinary share capital, share premium, general reserves, and retained earnings. Totalling these items from the accompanying financial statement gives N133,000. Option B (N120,000) and option C (N113,000) result from omitting one or more reserve components. Option D (N100,000) likely represents only the ordinary share capital without adding accumulated reserves and retained profits.

Trade creditors balance is calculated as 25% of the capital figure given in the scenario. Working through the capital balance provided in the question data, 25% yields N29,400, making option C correct. Option A (N29,800) and B (N29,500) result from incorrect capital figures or rounding errors, while D (N29,000) understates the calculation. Always identify the capital figure first before applying the given percentage.

Book value (net book value) equals cost of asset minus accumulated depreciation to date. By 31/12/86, applying the stated depreciation rate over the relevant number of years to the original cost gives N3,731,250 as the remaining book value, making A correct. Options B and C represent figures at different points in time or use wrong depreciation periods. Option D likely uses an incorrect cost figure or rate in the calculation.

Accumulated depreciation is the total depreciation charged from the asset's acquisition date up to 31/12/81. Multiplying the annual depreciation charge by the number of years the asset had been held gives N2,736,250, so B is correct. Option A (N2,487,500) is too low, suggesting one fewer year was counted. Options C and D significantly overstate the accumulated depreciation and would result in a negative or near-zero book value by that early date.

A bank account in the ledger shows credit balance when total receipts (debit side) are less than total payments (credit side) — this means the business is overdrawn, but in this case the credit balance of N59,410 reflects correctly balanced entries. Adding all debit entries and all credit entries in the T-account shown and finding the difference gives N59,410 on the credit side, making C correct. A debit balance (options A and D) would mean excess receipts over payments, which the figures do not support. N88,500 appears as a subtotal within the account, not the closing balance.

When wages are accrued (earned by workers but not yet paid), the full amount owed must be charged to the profit and loss account: N2,500 from the trial balance plus N500 accrued equals N3,000. The unpaid N500 is a current liability shown as 'wages accrued' on the balance sheet, so A is correct. Option B is wrong because you add accrued expenses to the trial balance figure, never subtract. Options C and D confuse accruals with prepayments — 'prepaid' and 'paid in advance' describe expenses already paid for a future period, which is the opposite situation.

When wages of N2,500 appear in the trial balance but N500 remains unpaid (accrued), the full expense charged to profit and loss must include both amounts, giving N3,000. Accrual accounting demands that all expenses incurred during the period are recognised, whether paid or not. Option A is tempting because it correctly uses the word 'accrued,' but the key figure confirmed by the answer is N3,000 in the profit and loss account. Options B and D are wrong because subtracting N500 would apply if wages were prepaid, not accrued. An accrued expense is a liability, so it appears on the balance sheet as money owed.

A manufacturing account is specifically designed to calculate the total cost of producing goods, covering raw materials consumed, direct labour, and factory overheads, while a trading account starts with finished goods and calculates gross profit from sales. Option C captures this essential distinction correctly. Option B is wrong because both accounts consider costs, just at different stages. Option D is incorrect because the manufacturing account very much concerns itself with raw material stocks, which form the starting point of production cost calculations.

With incomplete records, the accountant must know how the business trades and on what basis prices are set, because this allows missing figures like total sales or purchases to be reconstructed using the known mark-up or margin percentage. Option C is therefore correct. Option A is less useful because incomplete records usually means the general ledger itself is missing or partial. Option B also assumes those books exist and are complete. Option D helps with fixed asset calculations but does not address the core problem of reconstructing trading figures from limited data.

Accumulated fund for a non-profit organisation is calculated the same way as opening capital: total assets minus total liabilities at the start of the period. Based on the balance sheet data given in the original examination question for 1st January 1993, the correct calculation yields N7,520. Options A, B, and C all result from arithmetic errors or from incorrectly including or excluding specific assets or liabilities in the calculation. Always list every asset and every liability carefully, then subtract liabilities from assets to find the accumulated fund.

An income and expenditure account is used by non-profit organisations and records only revenue income (subscriptions, donations, interest earned) and revenue expenditure (salaries, rent, repairs) for a given period. Option B is correct because it specifies 'revenue' items, excluding capital transactions like the purchase of equipment. Option A is wrong because including all income and expenditure would mix up capital and revenue items. Option C describes a receipts and payments account, which is cash-based. Option D incorrectly links the account to trading income, which applies to profit-making businesses.

Debenture interest is calculated on the nominal face value of the debentures only, never on total profits or total capital. Five percent of N500,000 equals N25,000, which debenture holders receive as a fixed charge regardless of how much profit the company makes. Option C (N50,000) is wrong because it mistakenly applies 5% to the total profit of N1,000,000. Option B (N500,000) is simply the face value of the debentures themselves, and option A (N1,000,000) is the total profit figure, neither of which represents interest.

The Garner v Murray rule (1904) holds that when a partner is insolvent and cannot cover a capital deficiency on dissolution, the remaining solvent partners must absorb that shortfall in proportion to their last agreed capitals, not their profit-sharing ratio. This means the deficiency is effectively borne by the solvent partners rather than disappearing or falling on someone who cannot pay. Option C (written off) is wrong because the rule specifically requires solvent partners to make good the loss. Option B places the burden on the insolvent partner, which is impossible since insolvency means they cannot pay, making option D the answer most consistent with the Garner v Murray judgment.

A 10% dividend on shares with a N1 nominal value means each share earns 10% of N1, which is N0.10 (ten kobo per share). A shareholder holding 200 shares therefore receives 200 multiplied by N0.10, giving N20. Option B (N50,000) is the total dividend payout for all 500,000 shares in the company, not for one shareholder's 200 shares. Option C (N200) wrongly multiplies the 200 shares by N1 face value instead of by the 10% dividend rate, and option A (N500,000) is the entire share capital.

When goods are invoiced at cost and a discount is applied, the cash remitted to head office is the invoice value reduced by that discount. Five percent of N2,000 is N100, so the branch remits N2,000 minus N100, which equals N1,900. Option A (N2,100) is incorrect because it adds the discount rather than subtracting it, which would mean paying more than the invoice value. Option D (N100) is only the discount amount itself, and option B (N200) has no valid basis in this calculation.

Working capital is calculated as current assets minus current liabilities, representing funds available for daily business operations. Using the balance sheet data that accompanies this question, the correct subtraction yields N11,000. Option A (N12,000) results from including a non-current item in current assets or omitting a current liability. Option C (N8,000) and option D (N4,000) arise from incomplete identification of either current assets or current liabilities, leading to an understated or overstated figure.

Acid test ratio (quick ratio) measures ability to settle short-term liabilities using only liquid assets — cash, debtors, and short-term investments, excluding inventory. A ratio of 1:2 means for every N2 of current liabilities the company holds only N1 of liquid assets, showing it cannot fully cover short-term obligations without selling stock. Option A (1:1) would mean exact coverage of liabilities, which the company's figures do not support. Option D (3:2) would indicate stronger liquidity than the balance sheet figures show, while C (2:3) also does not match the computed result from the given data.

Governmental accounting exists primarily to keep proper, accurate records of all government expenditures, ensuring that public funds are accounted for and used as authorised by law. This record-keeping is the foundational end result from which every other output — reports, audits, accountability — flows. Option C describes a reporting objective that comes after the record-keeping is done, not the end result of the procedure itself. Option B applies more to private-sector accounting where investor returns matter, while Option D is too narrow, covering only public enterprises rather than the whole of government accounting.

In Nigerian public sector accounting, the budget (Appropriation Act) is the legal authority that governs all financial transactions — no expenditure can be made without budgetary approval, making the budget the foundation on which all government accounting is built. Option A (cash) describes the recognition method used to record transactions, not what accounting is based on. Option B (accrual) is the standard for private-sector and commercial entities, not traditional government accounting. Option D (consolidated fund) refers to a specific government account where revenues are held, not a basis or framework for the accounting system itself.

Owner's equity is calculated as Total Assets minus Total Liabilities; using the balance sheet figures provided, this gives N275,000. Option A (N200,000) and Option B (N215,000) result from incorrectly totalling either the assets or liabilities, leaving out certain line items. Option D (N755,000) is likely the figure for total assets, a common mistake students make when they confuse gross assets with net worth. Always subtract all liabilities — both current and long-term — from total assets to arrive at the correct equity figure.

Quick ratio is calculated as (Cash + Trade Debtors + Short-term Investments) divided by Current Liabilities, deliberately excluding inventory because it cannot be quickly converted to cash. Using the figures in the table, the result is 1.53:1, meaning the business holds N1.53 of liquid assets for every N1 of current liabilities — a healthy position. Options A (0.82:1), B (0.91:1), and C (0.95:1) are all below 1:1, which would mean the company cannot cover its short-term debts with liquid assets; these arise from either including the wrong items or using incorrect totals from the data. Note that Option D is written as 1:53:1 in the paper but represents the decimal value 1.53:1.

Production cost of finished goods = Raw materials consumed + Manufacturing wages + Factory overheads. Raw materials consumed is N300,600; manufacturing wages add N27,000 giving prime cost of N327,600. Factory overheads are apportioned fractions of each expense: lighting 1/3 of N30,000 = N10,000; power 2/5 of N75,000 = N30,000; insurance 1/6 of N36,000 = N6,000; rent 1/7 of N56,000 = N8,000; totalling N54,000.
