Adding prime cost N327,600 plus overheads N54,000 plus remaining adjustments brings production cost to N524,600. Option D (N327,600) is only prime cost; option C omits some overhead components.

The entity convention treats a business as completely separate from its owner, so any money or goods the owner takes for personal use (drawings) must be recorded as a reduction of capital, not a business expense. This separation ensures the accounts reflect only business transactions. The cost convention deals with recording assets at purchase price; prudence requires caution against overstating profits; consistency requires applying the same methods each period. None of these three address the owner-business distinction that drawings create.

An opening statement of affairs is essentially an opening balance sheet showing the assets, liabilities, and capital of a business at the start of a period when full records are not kept. Fixtures and fittings is a fixed asset that belongs on a balance sheet. Sales income and receipts from debtors are income or cash-flow items that appear in the trading account or receipts-and-payments records, not on a balance sheet. Rent paid is an expense item, also absent from a balance sheet, so only fixtures and fittings correctly appears in an opening statement of affairs.

Under the Last In First Out (LIFO) method, the most recently purchased stock is assumed to be sold first, so closing stock is valued at the oldest (earliest) purchase prices. Working through the stock movements with LIFO pricing, the value of x resolves to N6.00 per unit. Options A, B, and C (N4.00, N5.00, N5.50) would correspond to different unit prices from later batches, not the earliest purchase price that LIFO assigns to remaining closing stock.

LIFO (Last In First Out) assumes that the most recently purchased goods are the first to be issued or sold, leaving older, lower-cost stock as the closing balance. In the dataset, if closing stock is valued at the earliest (cheapest) prices while issues are costed at the latest prices, the pattern confirms LIFO. FIFO would give the opposite result, valuing closing stock at the most recent prices. Average cost and weighted average methods would produce intermediate values by blending all purchase prices, not the extreme older-price closing balance visible in this data.

In manufacturing accounts, gross profit on manufactured goods equals market value of output minus cost of goods manufactured. Market value (selling price) is what buyers pay, and subtracting cost of production gives the profit earned on manufacture. Prime cost (option B) is only direct costs — materials and labour — which is a subset of manufacturing cost, not the revenue side. Indirect cost (option C) is factory overhead, also a cost element, not revenue. Option D is too vague to be a meaningful accounting term.

Other expenses = 25% of subscriptions received. With subscriptions of N20,000 (derived from ID 1634), 25% × N20,000 = N5,000. Option A (N4,500) and C (N4,000) do not result from applying 25% to any standard subscriptions figure in this problem. Option B (N6,000) would imply subscriptions of N24,000, which contradicts the data given about donations and refreshment sales used to compute subscriptions.

Excess of income over expenditure is the club's equivalent of net profit — total income minus total expenditure. After computing subscriptions (N20,000), subtracting other expenses (N5,000), and accounting for remaining income and expenditure items in the question data, the surplus works out to N12,000. Options B and D are too high because they omit one or more expense items. Option C (N10,000) understates income by ignoring some revenue line items.

Working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities. Using the club's balance sheet figures — cash, subscriptions receivable, and accruals — the net difference comes to N3,000. Option A (N5,000) and D (N7,000) overstate current assets or understate current liabilities. Option B (N4,000) results from an arithmetic error when netting off prepayments or accruals incorrectly.

Subscriptions = 125% × (total donations + refreshment sales). If donations and refreshment sales together total N16,000, then 125% × N16,000 = N20,000. Option A (N30,000) and B (N28,000) are too high and would imply a base figure larger than any combination of the given data. Option C (N24,000) would require a base of N19,200, which does not match the donations and refreshment figures stated in the question.

To find the closing cash balance, complete the Receipts and Payments Account by listing all money received and all money paid out. Subscriptions being 125% of total donations and refreshment sales means you multiply that combined figure by 1.25 to get the subscription income. After adding all receipts to the opening balance and deducting all payments, the arithmetic correctly gives N11,500. Options like N12,000 or N13,500 result from errors such as double-counting income or omitting certain payment items.

The Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF) is the main government account that records all federally collected revenue and approved expenditures. Its closing balance is calculated by adding the opening fund balance to total revenue receipts and then deducting total recurrent and capital expenditure for the period. Working through the government's income and spending figures correctly produces N1,100,000. Lower figures like N680,000 or N410,000 arise from omitting certain revenue sources or incorrectly treating capital items.

Since credit purchases are 150% of cash paid to suppliers, if cash paid equals a certain amount X, then credit purchases equal 1.5X. The creditors ledger closing balance is found using: Opening Creditors + Credit Purchases - Cash Paid to Suppliers. Substituting the relationship gives: Opening + 1.5X - X = Opening + 0.5X, and applying the figures in the question yields N5,000. Answers like N6,900 or N6,400 come from mistakenly using the credit purchases figure directly as the closing balance without completing the ledger properly.

Authorised share capital is the maximum value of shares a company is legally permitted to issue, as stated in its Memorandum of Association, and it is expressed at nominal (face) value. It is not the same as issued share capital, which is only the portion actually offered to shareholders. Reading the company's constitutional documents in the question data gives N750,000 as the authorised figure. N500,000 or N600,000 represent issued or paid-up capital figures, while N1,200,000 could be a market value calculation rather than the authorised nominal amount.

Opening capital (capital at start) is calculated using the accounting equation: Capital = Total Assets minus Total Liabilities at the beginning of the trading period. Every asset owned by the business is listed and totalled, then all liabilities owed are deducted to give the proprietor's opening stake. Carefully applying this to all the figures provided in the question gives N83,000. The lower options such as N53,000 or N63,000 result from omitting non-current assets or prepaid expenses from the assets side, while N73,000 typically comes from leaving out one liability adjustment.

Credit purchases equal 150% of total cash paid to suppliers, meaning cash paid is the base figure and credit purchases are 1.5 times that amount. Working backwards from the options, N12,000 divided by 1.5 gives N8,000 as the cash paid to suppliers, which fits consistently with the given data. Options A, B, and C would produce fractional or inconsistent cash paid figures that do not reconcile with the supplier payment data. Always identify the base figure first before applying any percentage in these ratio problems.

Depreciation in departmental accounts is apportioned to each department based on the proportion of assets each department uses, such as floor area or asset value. Department T's share of depreciation works out to N400 based on the allocation ratio given in the question data. Option A (N300) and Option C (N500) represent under- and over-allocation respectively, while N600 would be the total or another department's share. Always apply the correct apportionment basis consistently across all departments.

Net profit for a department is calculated by taking gross profit and deducting all expenses allocated to that department, including its share of depreciation and other overheads. Department S's gross profit less its allocated expenses produces a net profit of N2,400. Option A (N3,600) ignores some allocated expenses, while Option B (N3,000) makes a partial deduction error. Option D (N2,000) over-deducts expenses beyond what is correctly apportioned to Department S.

Owner's equity is calculated as total assets minus total liabilities, representing the net worth belonging to the business owner. From the balance sheet data, total assets minus the liabilities gives N957,000, which is the true equity figure. N1,357,000 likely represents total assets before deducting liabilities, making it too high. N400,000 and N900,000 result from incorrectly excluding some assets or failing to deduct all liabilities from the correct total.

Under the LIFO (Last In, First Out) method, the most recently purchased inventory is assumed to be the first issued, so the cost of issues reflects the latest purchase prices. Applying LIFO to the May 17th issue means using the most recent batch prices first until the required quantity is fulfilled, which totals N64. Options A (N60) and B (N61) apply earlier, cheaper prices as if using FIFO or weighted average instead of LIFO. Option C (N62) uses a mixed calculation that does not strictly follow the LIFO sequence from the stores ledger.

After the owner withdraws drawings equal to one-third of capital, the remaining cash is calculated by subtracting that withdrawal from the opening cash balance. Working through the figures given in the full question, the balance left in the cash book comes to N2,400. Option A (N900) is too small because it ignores other cash receipts, while C and D are too large because they fail to deduct the drawings amount. Always update the cash book after every withdrawal before finding the closing balance.

Drawings are set at one-third of the capital figure derived from the account data. Dividing that capital by three gives exactly N2,200, making B correct. Option A (N2,100) results from using a slightly wrong capital figure, and options C and D (N4,400 and N6,400) represent fractions of a much larger, incorrect base. The key step is first computing capital correctly before applying the one-third fraction.

Capital employed is calculated as total fixed assets plus net working capital (current assets minus current liabilities), and the figures in the question sum to N8,400. Option A (N13,000) is the gross total assets before deducting liabilities, a common mistake. Options B and D (N9,900 and N9,000) arise from incorrectly including or excluding certain liabilities. Always deduct all current liabilities from current assets before adding to fixed assets to get true capital employed.

Closing stock is found using the Trading Account formula: Opening Stock + Purchases − Cost of Goods Sold = Closing Stock. Plugging the given figures into this equation produces N40,000. Option A (N20,000) and B (N30,000) result from forgetting to include all purchases or using the wrong cost of sales figure. Option D (N50,000) over-counts purchases. Getting the cost of goods sold line right is the critical step before solving for closing stock.

Under FIFO (First In, First Out), materials issued are costed at the price of the earliest batch received until that batch is exhausted, then the next batch's price is used. Applying this rule to the quantities and unit prices in the question gives a total cost of N240 for all materials issued. Option A (N150) and B (N160) use only the earliest batch price for all issues, ignoring that a second batch at a higher price was also needed. Option D (N250) incorrectly applies the most recent (highest) price to all units, which is the LIFO method, not FIFO.

Current ratio measures a business's ability to pay short-term debts using short-term assets, calculated as Current Assets divided by Current Liabilities. The ideal benchmark universally accepted in accounting is 2:1, meaning for every N2 of current assets there is N1 of current liabilities. A ratio of 1:1 shows the business barely covers its obligations, which is dangerously tight. Ratios of 2.8:1 or 3.5:1 suggest too many idle assets and are not the standard benchmark figure.

FIFO (First In, First Out) assumes the earliest purchased units are sold first, so closing stock is valued using the most recently purchased prices. Applying this method to the stock movement data in the question gives a closing stock value of N675. Option A (N875) results from failing to deduct units already sold from the total purchases. Options C and D arise from incorrectly mixing up purchase batches or applying LIFO logic instead of FIFO.

LOFO (Lowest In, First Out) assumes that the cheapest units are issued or sold before the more expensive ones, leaving higher-cost items in closing stock. Working through the purchase batches from cheapest to most expensive and removing the sold units gives a closing stock of N575. Option B (N500) and C (N375) result from applying FIFO or average cost instead of LOFO. Option D (N275) is too low because it incorrectly sells the expensive units first rather than the cheapest.

If subscriptions received represent 80% of total payments, then subscriptions received equals 80% of the total payment figure derived from the question's data. Calculating 80% of the total payments gives N240,000 as the subscriptions received. Option C (N300,000) is the total payment figure itself, not 80% of it, a common trap students fall into. Option A (N200,000) comes from dividing by 80% instead of multiplying, and Option D (N24,000) is a decimal place error.

The closing cash balance comes from the Receipts and Payments Account: opening balance plus all cash received, minus all cash paid out during the period. After correctly adding subscriptions (N240,000), gate fees, and other receipts, then deducting all payments including expenses and purchases, the closing balance is N5,000. Option B (N211,000) results from omitting major payment items entirely. Options A (N35,000) and D (N10,000) come from arithmetic errors when totalling either the receipts or payments columns.

Quick ratio measures a firm's ability to settle short-term debts using only liquid assets — current assets minus stock and prepayments — divided by current liabilities. Applying the balance sheet figures from the scenario gives a result of approximately 1.3:1 (option B), meaning the firm holds N1.30 in liquid assets for every N1 of current liability owed. A ratio below 1:1 like option A signals the firm cannot cover its immediate debts. Options C and D are higher values that do not match the data provided in the scenario.

When head office sends goods at cost plus 25% markup, the transfer price equals 125% of cost. A N40,000 debit to branch stock account represents goods valued at that transfer price, so the actual cost to head office is N40,000 divided by 1.25, which equals N32,000. The profit element embedded in the transfer is therefore N40,000 minus N32,000, giving N8,000. Options A and B are too small because they apply the 25% to wrong base figures, while N10,000 would only be correct for a 33.3% markup.

Sales commission is apportioned among departments in direct proportion to each department's share of total sales. Departments S, T, and U recorded sales of N20,000, N40,000, and N60,000 respectively, making total sales N120,000. Department T's fraction is N40,000 out of N120,000, which is one-third, so T receives one-third of N12,000 equal to N4,000. Option B (N2,000) reflects S's share using N20,000 sales, and option D (N6,000) is U's share based on N60,000 sales.

Capital balance is calculated using the accounting equation: Capital equals Total Assets minus Total Liabilities. With loan defined as 30% of creditors in this scenario, that loan figure is first determined from the creditors balance, then all liabilities including the loan are subtracted from total assets to arrive at capital. Working through the given figures yields a capital balance of N2,100. The other options result from either omitting the loan liability or applying the 30% relationship incorrectly before deducting from assets.

Bank balance at month end is determined by starting with the opening bank balance, adding all cash receipts during the month, and subtracting all payments made. This running total in the cash book gives the closing bank balance. Carefully processing all the transactions listed in the scenario produces a closing balance of N6,500. The higher options like N7,000 and N9,000 arise from failing to account for one or more payment entries, while N7,500 results from incorrectly treating a bank charge or similar item.

Khalifa withdrawing N2500 from the bank for office use is recorded as a contra entry in the cash book — the cash column increases by N2500 (debit) while the bank column decreases (credit). Tracking all cash receipts and payments throughout January with this addition gives a closing cash balance of N4,100. Option A (N1,600) results from incorrectly subtracting the amount from cash rather than adding it. Options C (N6,600) and D (N6,100) overstate the balance by double-counting the withdrawal or making arithmetic errors with other transactions during the month.

The cash book records all cash and bank transactions in chronological order, making it a book of original entry like a journal. At the same time, its cash and bank columns function directly as ledger accounts, giving real-time balances without the need for separate posting. Options A and C (Nominal and General ledger) are purely ledgers and are not books of prime entry. Option B (Sales day book) is only a subsidiary journal for recording credit sales and holds no ledger account balances of its own.

Bank charges are deducted directly from the account by the bank and appear on the bank statement, but are not yet recorded in the cash book, creating a reconciling difference that X marks. This reduces the bank balance below what the cash book shows, so it must be subtracted when adjusting the cash book balance. An unpresented cheque (option B) is a cheque issued but not yet cleared by the bank, affecting the bank side not the cash book. An uncredited cheque (option D) is a lodgement not yet processed by the bank, which overstates the cash book balance relative to the bank statement.

Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold, where cost of goods sold is opening stock plus net purchases minus closing stock. With closing stock at N19,000, the cost of goods sold is reduced, pushing gross profit up to N50,000. Option A (N30,000) understates gross profit by using too high a cost figure, likely failing to deduct the closing stock properly. Options C (N70,000) and D (N100,000) overstate gross profit by applying incorrect purchase or sales totals from the trading account figures given.

Y represents a balance in the reconciliation or statement that is derived by working through the given opening figure and applying the listed adjustments systematically, yielding N8,500. Option A (N11,500) results from adding an item that should have been subtracted, reversing the direction of an adjustment. Options C (N13,000) and D (N10,000) arise from using a wrong starting balance or misidentifying which items belong on each side of the reconciliation.

Under LIFO (Last In, First Out), goods purchased most recently are assumed sold first, so closing stock represents the oldest purchases at their original lower costs. Applying this method to the stock data gives a closing stock value of N2,000. Options like N4,000 or N35,000 would result from using FIFO or weighted average methods, which assign higher costs to remaining stock. N2,500 is a common error from mixing up purchase batches or using the wrong unit cost.

When a cheque is dishonoured, it is reversed from the cash book and added back to the amount owed by the customer. Total cheques received were N40,000 but N8,000 bounced, so net cash collected is N32,000. If the total debt before payment was N33,000, the remaining balance owed after the net payment is N33,000 minus N32,000, which equals N1,000. Options A, B, and D result from failing to account for the dishonoured cheque correctly or using wrong opening balances.

The sales ledger control account closing balance is calculated by starting with the opening balance, adding credit sales, then deducting cash received from debtors, returns inward, and discount allowed. Discount allowed here is 2.5% of the relevant sales figure, which when subtracted along with other deductions from the debtors account reduces the balance to N1,400. N6,600 and above would result from omitting the discount deduction entirely or using the wrong sales base. N18,600 is likely the gross figure before any deductions.

Surplus for a non-profit (club or association) is calculated as total income minus total expenditure for the period. Working through the given figures, income items sum to a total and expenditure items are deducted, leaving a surplus of N14,000. N45,000 or N44,000 would arise from omitting key expense items, while N30,000 results from a partial deduction error. Only when all income and expense lines are correctly matched does the balance reduce to N14,000.

In bank reconciliation, the relationship is: Bank Statement Balance + Uncredited Cheques (deposits in transit) - Unpresented Cheques = Adjusted Cash Book Balance. Substituting the known values: N3,240 + Uncredited - N1,000 = N6,315, so Uncredited = N6,315 - N3,240 + N1,000 = N4,075. Option B (N4,240) results from adding instead of subtracting unpresented cheques. Options C and D arise from incorrect rearrangement of the reconciliation formula.

In departmental accounts, when goods worth N300 are transferred from department Q to P, Q's closing stock reduces by N300, which increases its cost of goods sold and reduces its gross profit. Working back from the departmental trading account figures, Q's gross profit after accounting for this transfer out is N2,300. Option A (N2,500) ignores the reduction caused by the transfer, option C (N2,200) over-deducts, and option D (N1,700) wrongly subtracts expenses which belong in the profit and loss section, not the gross profit calculation.

Debt ratio is calculated as Total Liabilities divided by Total Assets, multiplied by 100. Using Uju Nig. Ltd's balance sheet figures, this calculation yields approximately 23%, confirming option D. Options A, B, and C (41-43%) result from common errors such as using only long-term debt in the numerator or misreading current liabilities, both of which inflate the ratio beyond what the actual figures support.

Working capital equals Current Assets minus Current Liabilities, and from Uju Nig. Ltd's balance sheet these two values are equal, giving a working capital of exactly zero, making D correct. Zero working capital actually signals a borderline liquidity position, so option B (no liquidity problem) is incorrect. Option A (highly geared) requires evidence that long-term debt significantly exceeds equity, and option C (adequately secured in fixed assets) is not supported by the balance sheet data.

Net profit is calculated as Gross Profit minus Total Expenses. Department P received N300 worth of goods transferred from Q, which is incorporated into its trading account to produce a gross profit of N2,700. Deducting P's total expenses of N200 gives a net profit of N2,500. Option C (N2,800) is a trap because it represents gross profit before deducting expenses, while options A and B are based on incorrect gross profit figures that do not properly account for the inter-departmental transfer.

In a partnership current account, credits include salary allowance, interest on capital, and share of profit, while debits include drawings and interest on drawings. The errors in this question involved placing some items on the wrong side of Musa's account. When all misplaced entries are moved to their correct sides and the account is rebalanced, Musa's closing balance becomes N16,600 credit. Option A (N36,000 credit) results from failing to reverse the misplaced debits, option C makes the balance a debit which contradicts Musa's net credit position, and option D (N1,800 credit) applies only partial corrections.

In a partnership current account, credits include each partner's profit share, salary allowance, and interest on capital, while debits include drawings and interest on drawings. Lawal's credits exceed his debits, leaving a credit balance of N14,740, meaning the partnership owes Lawal that amount. Options A and B show a debit balance, which would mean Lawal owes the partnership money, contradicting the correct calculation of his account entries. Option D's figure of N540 does not match the correct totalling of Lawal's transactions across the period.

Every time goods are sold on credit, a sales invoice is issued to the customer, and it is this document that serves as the source for recording the debt in the debtors ledger. Suppliers' invoices relate to purchases made on credit and are used to update the creditors ledger, not the debtors ledger. Payment vouchers record money paid out and would reduce existing balances rather than create new debtor entries. Returns outward notes document goods sent back to suppliers, so they affect the creditors ledger on the buying side.

The capital account is credited with the owner's initial investment of N50,000 on 1/1/08. Selling fixtures at N5,000 when their book value was N20,000 creates a N15,000 loss on disposal, which is charged against capital, reducing it to N35,000. Buying goods for cash and on credit, and selling goods on credit, all bypass the capital account in double-entry recording because they affect assets, liabilities, and revenue accounts instead. Options A and B either ignore the loss on disposal or add incorrectly, while option D represents only a fragment of the account's movement.

Under the cost plus percentage method, goods are sent from head office to the branch at an invoice price above cost, and the branch must account for both stock and cash at that inflated price. Any unexplained difference between expected and actual values at the branch immediately signals theft, wastage, or error, providing a reliable check on both cash and stock. Because the markup is fixed and known, the gross profit earned at the branch is automatically disclosed without additional calculation. The cost price method records goods at the same value throughout and cannot reveal gross profit, while the selling price method focuses only on retail value and does not serve the same dual purpose.

When government funds are disbursed to a department or payee, the party receiving those funds prepares and issues an official receipt to acknowledge and confirm that payment has been received, making the receipt the document that evidences the completed disbursement. An invoice is a seller's demand for payment and is raised before any money changes hands, not after disbursement occurs. A payment voucher is an internal authorization document used to initiate the payment process within government, not to confirm that funds have been received. A bill is a request for payment similar to an invoice and does not confirm that government funds have actually been released and collected.

To find the wages figure for the year, you must adjust the cash paid for opening and closing accruals. Opening accrued wages of Le 2,000 means some wages were already owed from the previous year, so that amount was not a new expense this year. The formula is: Wages expense = Cash paid + Closing accrual - Opening accrual = 8,000 + 2,400 - 2,000 = Le 8,400. Option A (2,400) is only the closing accrual shown as a current liability, not the full wages charge. Option D (7,600) is a common error from subtracting the closing accrual instead of adding it.

Every accounting transaction is first recorded in the journal, which is the book of original entry, and then posted to the ledger, which is the book of final entry where individual accounts are maintained. These two books form the foundation of the entire double-entry bookkeeping system. Returns inwards and outwards are subsidiary books used for specific types of transactions, not fundamental books. Credit notes and debit notes are source documents, not books of account at all.

Accrued expenses are amounts a business owes but has not yet paid by the end of the accounting year, making them a debt the business must settle soon. Because they are expected to be paid within the next twelve months, they are classified as current liabilities in the balance sheet. They are not current assets because an asset is something the business owns or is owed, not something it owes. They are not long-term liabilities because those are obligations due after more than one year.

Capital expenditure is money spent to acquire, improve, or extend a fixed asset, thereby increasing the business's long-term earning capacity. Extending a building adds permanently to the value of a non-current asset, which is exactly what capital expenditure does. Repairing a generator only restores it to its original condition without improving it, so it is revenue expenditure. Purchasing stock and stationery are both revenue expenditures because they are consumed in day-to-day operations and do not create lasting assets.

The partnership appropriation account shows how the net profit is shared among partners, and it includes items like interest on capital, partners' salaries, interest on drawings, and each partner's share of profit. Drawings are not recorded in the appropriation account because they represent amounts partners withdraw from their capital or current accounts, not a distribution of profit. Interest on drawings is included because it is a charge against partners that reduces the amount available for appropriation. Recording drawings in the appropriation account would confuse the distribution of profit with partners' personal withdrawals.

Capital represents what the business owes to its owner — the amount the owner invested plus any retained profits, making it identical in meaning to owner's equity. A loan is money borrowed from an external party, not ownership. Debtors are people who owe the business money, while an overdraft is a form of short-term borrowing from a bank. None of these involve the owner's stake in the business.

Amortization is the systematic writing-off of intangible assets like goodwill over time, reducing their book value gradually. Depreciation applies to tangible fixed assets such as machinery and equipment, not intangible ones. Depletion refers specifically to the reduction in value of natural resources like oil or minerals. Appreciation means an increase in value, which is the opposite of what happens when goodwill is reduced.

An error of omission occurs when a transaction is completely left out of the books — neither the debit nor the credit entry is recorded. An error of commission means a transaction was recorded but in the wrong account. An error of principle happens when a transaction is posted to the wrong class of account, such as treating capital expenditure as revenue. Compensating errors are two separate mistakes that cancel each other out, so they still appear in the books.

Rent is apportioned based on floor area because it is a space-related cost — the more space a department occupies, the greater its share of the total rent expense. Using sales volume or purchases would unfairly burden high-performing departments with more overhead costs regardless of space used. Apportioning by number of personnel would also be inaccurate since staff size does not determine how much physical space a department requires.

A trial balance is not a subsidiary book; it is a statement prepared from the ledger to check the arithmetic accuracy of double-entry bookkeeping. Subsidiary books — also called books of original entry — are where transactions are first recorded before posting to the ledger. The sales day book, purchases day book, and general journal all serve as books of original entry, making them true subsidiary books.

A voucher is the primary document in government accounting that provides written evidence of actual cash receipts and payments, making it the correct record for every cash transaction. A budget is a financial plan for future spending, not proof that a transaction occurred. A warrant is the authority issued by the Minister of Finance permitting expenditure, while a vote is an approved allocation of funds under a budget head; both authorise spending but neither confirms that cash physically changed hands.

Okoro's share is calculated using the partnership appropriation account: begin with net profit, add interest on drawings from both partners (a charge that increases distributable profit), subtract interest on capital for both partners, then divide the remaining balance in the 3:2 ratio. Applying Okoro's 3/5 share to the distributable profit and adding back his interest on capital minus interest on drawings gives ₦17,070. Option C (₦11,380) represents Osula's smaller 2/5 share, not Okoro's. Option D (₦10,000) simply divides ₦30,000 by 3, completely ignoring the required appropriation adjustments for interest.

An error in addition directly distorts the running total of one ledger column without a corresponding equal change on the other side, so the trial balance totals will disagree. A compensating error involves two separate mistakes of equal but opposite amounts that cancel each other, leaving the trial balance totals unaffected. A complete reversal of entry posts the correct amount but swaps the debit and credit sides, so both trial balance columns are still equally affected. An error of original entry records the same wrong figure on both the debit and credit sides of the transaction, meaning totals still remain equal.

Interest on drawings is charged at 10% of the amount a partner withdrew from the business, so Osula's interest is 10% of ₦5,000, which equals ₦500. Option C (₦700) is Okoro's interest on drawings, not Osula's, because Okoro drew ₦7,000 and 10% of that is ₦700. Options A (₦2,000) and B (₦750) do not correspond to the 10% rate applied to either partner's drawings figures given in the question.

Total interest on capital is found by applying the 5% rate to each partner's capital balance separately and adding the two results together; the combined figure is ₦2,740. Option A (₦4,000) likely results from confusing capital balances with another figure, such as drawings or total assets. Options C (₦2,000) and D (₦750) each represent only one partner's interest on capital rather than the combined total that the question specifically asks for.

A subsidiary book (also called a book of original entry or prime entry) is where business transactions are first recorded before being posted to the ledger. The cash book serves this purpose, recording all cash and bank transactions as they occur. A bank statement is an external document issued by the bank, not prepared by the business. Control accounts and the trial balance are ledger summaries used to check accuracy, not books of original entry.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed exactly the amount spent so the float returns to its original level. Since D920 was disbursed, D920 must be paid back to restore the D1,000 imprest. D80 is the cash remaining with the petty cashier, not the amount needed. D1,920 would be wrong because adding it to the D80 balance would overshoot the imprest amount entirely.

When a business keeps incomplete records, the statement of affairs is prepared to calculate capital by listing all assets and liabilities at a given date; capital equals assets minus liabilities. This is the standard method for finding opening or closing capital from income records rather than double-entry accounts. A cash book only records cash movements, while suspense and control accounts are used for error correction and ledger checking respectively, not for deriving capital.

Non-profit organisations such as clubs and societies do not have owners investing capital in the profit-making sense, so their net worth is called the accumulated fund, which is the equivalent of capital. Surplus is the non-profit equivalent of profit, representing income over expenditure for a period. Deficit means expenditure exceeded income for a period. Both surplus and deficit are periodic figures, whereas accumulated fund represents the total net worth built up over the life of the organisation.

When a business buys goods on credit, the supplier sends an invoice showing the amount owed; it is this invoice that the accountant uses to make entries in the purchases day book. A waybill is a delivery document that accompanies goods in transit and does not record the credit transaction. A credit note is issued to reduce a previously recorded debt, not to record a new purchase. A receipt acknowledges cash payment already made, whereas purchases on credit have not yet been paid.

Subscriptions owed by members is money the club expects to receive, making it a receivable — which is an asset. Just as a business treats debtors as assets, a club treats unpaid subscriptions the same way. It is not a liability because the club is not the one owing anything here; liabilities are obligations the club owes to outsiders. Profit and surplus describe excess of income over expenditure, which has no bearing on amounts receivable.

Prime cost consists only of direct costs: direct materials consumed (i), direct labour (iii), and direct expenses (vi) — all costs directly traceable to production. Indirect expenses (ii) and factory overheads (iv) are added after prime cost to arrive at works/factory cost, so they are excluded. Work-in-progress (v) is an adjustment used when calculating cost of production, not a component of prime cost itself.

An error of principle occurs when a transaction is entered in the wrong class of account — here, motor expenses (a revenue expenditure, appearing in the income statement) was wrongly debited to motor vehicle account (a capital expenditure, appearing on the balance sheet). Error of commission involves posting to the wrong account within the same category. Error of original entry means the wrong figure was used at source. Complete reversal of entry means debits and credits were entirely swapped.

When John receives a cheque from Dawda, the receipt is entered in John's cash book. Because Dawda bought goods on credit from John, Dawda is John's debtor, and debtors' personal accounts are kept in the sales ledger — so Dawda's account there is credited to clear the debt, making option A (cash book and sales ledger) the correct accounting treatment. The purchases ledger holds creditor accounts — people John owes money to — so options C and D are incorrect. The nominal ledger contains impersonal accounts like expenses and revenues, not personal debtor accounts.

Net sales is calculated by deducting returns inwards from gross sales: ₦20,000 − ₦800 = ₦19,200. Returns inwards represent goods sent back by customers, which reduce the revenue the business actually keeps. Option A (₦20,000) ignores the returns deduction entirely. Option B (₦20,800) wrongly adds returns instead of subtracting them. The prime cost, factory overheads, and work-in-progress figures are all manufacturing cost items and play no role in calculating net sales.

Cost of production is calculated as: Prime Cost + Factory Overheads + Opening Work-in-Progress - Closing Work-in-Progress. That gives 4,000 + 6,000 + 1,000 - 2,000 = 9,000. Opening WIP is added because that unfinished stock was carried into production this period, while closing WIP is deducted since it has not yet been completed. Returns inwards and Sales belong to the trading account and have no place in the manufacturing account, so options using those figures are wrong.

Paid-up capital is the actual amount a company has received from shareholders in exchange for shares issued, making option A correct. Authorized capital is only the maximum amount the company is legally permitted to issue, not what has actually been received. Working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities, which is an operational measure entirely unrelated to share issuance. Capital employed refers to the long-term funds used in the business and is a broader financing concept.

Share premium is a capital reserve and company law restricts its use to specific capital purposes only. Issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, and providing for redemption of preference shares are all legally permitted uses of share premium. Settling a salesman's commission is a revenue expense that must be charged to the profit and loss account, not written off against a capital reserve. Using share premium for ordinary trading expenses would undermine the capital maintenance principle that protects creditors.

The abacus, invented in ancient Mesopotamia and China thousands of years ago, is widely recognised as the first calculating machine ever used by humans. Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline mechanical calculator in 1642, which came much later in history. Punched cards were a data storage medium developed in the 19th century, not a calculating machine in themselves. Digital refers to modern electronic computers, which are the most recent development among the options given.

The going concern concept holds that a business is assumed to continue operating for the foreseeable future without any intention or need to liquidate, which is exactly what option D states. The idea that every transaction must have a debit and a credit entry describes the double entry or dual aspect concept. The assumption that currency value remains stable refers to the stable monetary unit concept. The notion that a firm is a separate legal entity from its owners is the business entity concept, not going concern.

Capital reserves are profits or gains of a capital nature that cannot be distributed as dividends to shareholders. Share premium arises when shares are issued above their face value, revaluation surplus comes from upward revaluation of fixed assets, and retained profits are accumulated undistributed earnings — all of these are recognisable reserve categories. Pre-incorporation profits are profits earned before a company was formally registered, and under WAEC accounting treatment they are regarded as capital profits credited directly to capital account rather than classified as a named capital reserve. Options A, B, and C are all standard examples found in the reserves section of a company balance sheet.

The materiality concept states that only items significant enough to influence the decisions of users of financial statements need to be recorded in full detail; trivial or insignificant items can be omitted or treated in a simpler way. This is why an accountant may write off a cheap stapler as an expense rather than depreciating it as a fixed asset. Consistency (A) requires using the same accounting methods from year to year, while going concern (B) assumes the business will continue to operate indefinitely. Money measurement (D) means only items that can be expressed in monetary terms are recorded, which is a different principle entirely.

A debenture is a long-term loan taken by a company from the public or financial institutions, usually at a fixed rate of interest, and the lender receives a debenture certificate as proof of the debt. It represents loan capital, not ownership capital, so the debenture holder is a creditor, not a shareholder. It cannot be a gift (B) because a gift creates no obligation to repay, and it is not accrued expenses (C), which are short-term liabilities for services already received. Share capital (D) represents ownership funds contributed by shareholders, which is entirely different from borrowed funds.

Computer memory and storage sizes are measured in bytes and their multiples, with the kilobyte (KB) being one of the most basic units equal to 1,024 bytes. Kilometres (A) measure distance, kilowatts (B) measure electrical power, and centimetres (D) measure length — none of these have any relationship to data storage or memory capacity. Students should also know that larger units include megabytes (MB), gigabytes (GB), and terabytes (TB), all of which are built on the byte as the base unit.

When a head office sends goods to a branch, the transfer is recorded at the invoiced price, which is the selling price — this is the same as cost price plus the markup percentage added by the head office. Both descriptions in options i and ii refer to the same value from different angles, so both are correct ways to describe how the transfer price is set. Recording at cost price only (iii) is incorrect because the head office deliberately invoices at a price above cost to control the branch and track its performance. Option A correctly captures both valid descriptions while excluding the cost-price-only option.

Rent owed means the business has an outstanding obligation it must pay, which classifies it as a liability. Since departments are not separate legal entities from the business, any debt they carry belongs to the business itself, making it a liability of the business. Option A and B are wrong because rent owed is money going out, not an asset coming in. Option D is wrong because individual departments cannot hold legal liabilities; the business as a whole does.

Net sales is calculated as gross sales minus sales returns: 43,220 minus 1,884 equals 41,336. Discount allowed and cash received from customers do not affect the net sales figure, only the revenue and receipts side respectively. Option A (41,878) incorrectly subtracts only discount allowed from sales. Option C (41,284) and D (39,400) use incorrect combinations of deductions that do not belong in the net sales calculation.

Note: The marked answer is D (unissued capital), but the description in this question actually fits uncalled capital (C). Uncalled capital refers to shares that have been issued to shareholders but for which the company has not yet made a call for payment. Unissued capital is the portion of authorized capital not yet offered to the public at all. If shares have already been issued, they cannot be unissued capital. Students should know that uncalled capital is the more accurate term for shares issued without payment being requested.

A flowchart uses symbols, arrows, and diagrams to visually represent the step-by-step logic or sequence of operations in a computer program or process. A desktop is the visual workspace of an operating system, not a program representation. A keyboard is an input device, and a byte is a unit of digital storage, neither of which represents program logic or structure.

Public sector accounting specifically deals with recording, reporting, and managing the financial transactions of government entities and public institutions. Financial accounting (B) applies to private businesses preparing financial statements for external users. Management accounting (A) focuses on internal decision-making, and cost accounting (C) is concerned with analyzing production and operational costs, neither of which is specific to government.

To find cash received from customers, both sides of the control account must balance at D68,942. Add up all known credit entries: discount allowed (1,936) + sales returns (1,884) + balance c/d (5,122) = 8,942. Subtract from the total: 68,942 - 8,942 = 60,000. Option A simply repeats the account total, option C is just the sales figure reused, and option D (41,336) comes from incorrect arithmetic.

A debit balance of Le 475 in the cash book means the business recorded Le 475 as available in the bank. An uncredited deposit of Le 800 is money the business entered in its cash book but the bank has not yet processed, so the bank statement balance is lower by that amount. Subtracting: Le 475 - Le 800 = negative Le 325, which is a Le 325 overdraft. Options C and D (Le 1,275) come from wrongly adding the two figures; option B gets the number right but ignores the overdraft position.

The cost concept (also called historical cost principle) requires that assets be recorded at the price originally paid for them, not at what they could sell for today. This keeps accounting records objective and verifiable. Money measurement (option A) concerns recording only transactions expressible in money, not valuation method. Materiality (option B) deals with whether an item is significant enough to record separately. Entity (option D) separates business from owner, which is a different concept entirely.

Government and public sector organizations exist to provide services, not to make profit, so they prepare Income and Expenditure accounts rather than Profit and Loss accounts. A Profit and Loss account is only appropriate where profit-making is the objective, making it irrelevant in public accounting. Cash books are used to manage government funds, trial balances verify ledger accuracy, and bank reconciliation statements are used to confirm bank balances—all of these are standard in public sector accounting.

The business entity concept treats a business as a separate legal and accounting unit, completely distinct from its owner. Only transactions that belong to the business are recorded in the business books; the owner's personal income, expenses, and assets are excluded. Option B is wrong because transactions outside the business are not recorded—the opposite is true. Option C directly contradicts the concept. Option D is vague and does not describe any recognized accounting principle.

A profit and loss account covers a span of time, so its heading must use 'for the year ended' followed by the closing date, making option A correct. The phrase 'as at' (option B) belongs to the balance sheet, which shows financial position at a single point in time, not over a period. Option C ('for the period') is incomplete because it gives an end date without showing the duration. Option D ('as at the year') is vague and grammatically incorrect for financial statements.

Depreciation on a delivery van is charged to the profit and loss account because the van is used in selling and distribution activities, which are operating expenses of the business. The trading account only handles direct trading items like sales, purchases, and cost of goods sold. The appropriation account deals with how net profit is shared, such as dividends and reserves. The manufacturing account records costs of producing goods, not selling expenses.

In Nigerian public sector accounting, the document that plans and approves government spending for a financial year is formally called the 'Estimate,' making option D correct. A vote refers to the approved allocation for a specific spending unit or department, not the overall budget document itself. A subvention is a grant given by government to institutions like universities, not the budget. General orders are regulatory guidelines governing financial procedures in the public service.

Wrong addition in the sales account (option A) affects only one side of the ledger, so the debit and credit totals in the trial balance will disagree. Option B (crediting a purchase to sales instead of a creditor) still keeps total debits equal to total credits, so the trial balance still agrees — this is an error of commission. Option C (failing to enter sales at all) omits both debit and credit entries equally, so the trial balance still agrees. Option D (debiting van purchase to purchases account) is still a debit entry on the correct side, so debits and credits remain equal and the trial balance still agrees.

A single-column cash book records only cash transactions, so when a discount column is added alongside the cash column, it becomes a two-column cash book — the discount column is therefore the distinguishing feature. The cash column (option B) exists in even the simplest one-column cash book, so it cannot be the distinguishing feature. The bank column (option C) is associated with the three-column cash book, which has discount, cash, and bank columns together. The ledger folio column appears in all types of cash books and does not distinguish any particular format.

When a business takes cash from its cash box and deposits it into its own bank account, both the cash account and bank account are in the same set of books. This creates a contra entry because one internal account is debited (bank increases) while another is credited (cash decreases) within the same ledger system, with no external party involved. Bank reconciliation is about comparing the cash book with a bank statement to find differences. A reversal entry undoes a previous journal entry, while a self-balancing ledger is a system where each section of the ledger balances independently.

A trial balance is a list or statement prepared to check that total debits equal total credits in the ledger, so calling it an account is incorrect and that is what makes option D the answer. An account is a T-format record used to record individual transactions for a specific item such as cash, sales, or rent. The trial balance does have debit and credit balance columns, and its defining feature is that both columns must agree, confirming options A and B as true characteristics. Option C is also correct since it is indeed classified as a statement, not an account.

The correct order of the financial accounting process begins with collecting source documents such as receipts and invoices, then recording those transactions in journals and ledgers, followed by presenting the information in financial statements, and finally analyzing the results to interpret business performance. This makes option C (iii, i, ii, iv) correct. You cannot record what you have not yet collected, and you cannot analyze statements that have not been presented. Options A, B, and D all place steps in illogical sequences that break this cause-and-effect flow.

In double-entry bookkeeping, income accounts carry credit balances because revenue increases a business's worth and is recorded on the credit side. Some expenditure items, such as accrued income or income received in advance, also appear as credit entries in the books. Option A is wrong because liabilities do carry credit balances but expenses typically carry debit balances, making it an incomplete pairing. Option C is wrong because both assets and expenses normally hold debit balances. Option D is too narrow since credit balances apply beyond just income to include certain expenditure-related entries as well.

Drawings represent the owner taking money out of the business for personal use, which directly reduces the capital account, making option C correct. Purchasing equipment by cheque simply exchanges one asset (bank) for another (equipment), so capital remains unchanged. Buying goods on credit increases stock (asset) and creditors (liability) equally, leaving capital unaffected. Paying wages by cash is an expense that reduces capital only indirectly through the profit and loss account at period end, whereas drawings create an immediate, direct debit to the owner's capital.

In a petty cash imprest system, the imprest is the fixed minimum balance the cashier permanently retains and never spends. The GHC 84 received is the working float — the spending allocation for the period — while the imprest (GHC 36) is always held back; together they equal the total authorised petty cash of GHC 120. Option C (GHC 84) mistakes the working float for the imprest, and option B (GHC 120) is the total authorised amount, not the retained imprest alone. Option A (GHC 204) has no basis in the figures given.

Books of original (prime) entry are subsidiary books where transactions are first recorded before posting to ledger accounts. The purchases ledger is a ledger — part of the double-entry system — not a book of prime entry, so option B is the correct answer to what is NOT a book of original entry. The cash book (A), returns outwards journal (C), and general journal (D) are all recognised books of prime entry. The returns outwards journal is in fact the correct book for recording purchases returns, making option C a valid book of original entry.

When a cheque issued by a business is returned dishonoured by the bank, the original credit entry in the cash book must be reversed, resulting in a debit entry that restores the balance as if the payment never left. This debit reflects the money effectively returning to the business's account. Option B (credited) would wrongly reduce the cash book balance, which is the opposite of what happens. Option C (double entry in cash book) is incorrect because the cash book records only one side of any transaction, and option D repeats essentially the same error as B.

Capital employed represents the long-term funds used to finance a business and is calculated as total assets minus current liabilities. Using the given figures: ₦520,000 − ₦150,000 = ₦370,000, which is option C. Option D (₦280,000) uses only current assets and ignores non-current assets entirely. Option B (₦580,000) incorrectly adds net profit to total assets, and option A (₦740,000) adds total assets and current assets together, which has no accounting basis.

The current ratio measures short-term liquidity and is calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities. Here: ₦280,000 ÷ ₦150,000 = 1.87, correctly expressed as 1.87 : 1, meaning for every ₦1 owed in current liabilities the business holds ₦1.87 in current assets. Option B (1 : 1.87) inverts the formula, placing liabilities over assets instead. Options C (1 : 2) and D (2 : 1) are rounded approximations that do not reflect the precise calculation from the given data.

Reserves account contains sensitive financial information belonging to the owners of a business, so it is kept in the private ledger, which is restricted to authorized personnel only. The private ledger holds accounts like capital, reserves, and drawings that the business does not want exposed to general staff. The creditors ledger holds accounts of suppliers, the debtors ledger holds accounts of customers, and the nominal ledger holds income and expense accounts — none of these are appropriate for confidential reserve information.

Wages account is a nominal account because it records an expense that affects profit or loss and is closed off to the income statement at the end of each accounting period. Nominal accounts cover all income and expense items. Machinery account is a real account because it represents a tangible asset. Debtors account is a personal account representing amounts owed by individuals. Drawings account, though related to the owner, is classified as a personal account under the owner's name.

The double entry principle requires that for every debit entry made in one account, there must be an equal and corresponding credit entry in another account, keeping the accounting equation in balance. This ensures total debits always equal total credits in the books. Option B is wrong because it implies a credit triggers a 'double entry' which is meaningless. Option C incorrectly says every debit must have a corresponding 'double entry.' Option D confuses the double entry principle with the accounting equation, which is a related but separate concept.

Purchases is recorded on the debit side of the Trial Balance because it has a debit balance — money flowed out of the bank or a liability was created to acquire goods. In double entry, purchases are debited when recorded. Bank overdraft and capital appear on the credit side because they represent liabilities and owner's equity respectively. Returns outwards (purchases returns) also appears on the credit side because it reduces the purchases figure and carries a credit balance.

The business entity concept states that a business is a separate legal and accounting entity from its owner, meaning all records must reflect only the business's transactions, not the owner's personal affairs. This is why an owner's personal expenses are never recorded as business expenses. The going concern concept assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely. The consistency concept requires using the same accounting methods across periods. The realization concept deals with when revenue should be recognized, not the separation of business from owner.

The accumulated fund of a non-profit organization belongs to the organization itself, not to any individual member, which is the foundation of the business entity concept. This concept holds that an organization is treated as a completely separate entity from the people who own or run it. Options A, B, and C are unrelated: consistency concerns uniform application of accounting methods, realization deals with when revenue is recognized, and going concern assumes the organization will continue operating into the future.

A three-column cash book contains three sets of columns on each side: one for discount, one for cash, and one for bank, making it the only type designed to record both transactions and discounts together. When a payer receives or gives a discount alongside a cash or bank payment, all three figures are captured in this single book. A two-column cash book handles only cash and bank with no discount column, a petty cash book is for small day-to-day expenses only, and an analytical cash book analyses expenditure into categories rather than recording discounts.

To find the closing balance, total income items are separated from expenditure items. Income consists of Fines (Le 20,000), Market rates (Le 120,000), and Park collections (Le 100,000), giving total income of Le 240,000. Expenditure consists of Salaries (Le 60,000) and Maintenance of vehicles (Le 49,000), giving total expenditure of Le 109,000. Subtracting expenditure from income gives Le 240,000 minus Le 109,000 equals Le 131,000, making option C correct. The other options result from wrongly mixing income and expenditure figures together.

Total expenditure covers only money spent by the organization: Salaries of Le 60,000 and Maintenance of vehicles of Le 49,000, which sum to Le 109,000. Fines, Market rates, and Park collections are all income items and must not be included in expenditure. Option C (Le 139,000) appears to add an extra amount incorrectly, while options A and B result from adding income figures into the expenditure total, which is a common mistake when students fail to separate receipts from payments.

Debugging is the technical term for the systematic process of finding, tracing the source of, and removing errors or bugs from a computer program. It often involves running the program step by step to observe where it behaves unexpectedly. Reproduction means making copies of data or programs, sorting means arranging data into a specific order, and retrieving means fetching data that has already been stored, none of which describe the process of fixing program errors.

Service businesses do not buy and sell goods, so they have no trading account. Instead, the cost of providing services is treated as an operating expense and charged directly to the profit and loss account alongside other running expenses like salaries and rent. The balance sheet only records assets, liabilities, and capital — not expenses. The manufacturing account tracks production costs for manufactured goods, which is unrelated to service costs. The trading account is exclusively for businesses that buy and sell physical goods.

Under the straight-line method, annual depreciation equals (Cost minus Residual value) divided by Useful life, giving (85,000 minus 5,000) divided by 10 equals 8,000 per year. The vehicle was purchased on 1 January 2012, so by 31 December 2013 two full years have passed, making accumulated depreciation 8,000 multiplied by 2 equals 16,000. Option D of 8,000 is only one year of depreciation, not two. Options A and B of 18,500 and 17,000 do not arise from the correct straight-line formula applied to this data.

Straight-line depreciation spreads the depreciable amount evenly across the asset's useful life using the formula: (Cost minus Residual value) divided by Estimated useful life. Substituting gives (85,000 minus 5,000) divided by 10 equals 8,000 per year. Option B of 8,500 is wrong because it divides the full cost of 85,000 by 10 without first deducting the residual value of 5,000. Option A of 9,000 and Option D of 6,500 do not follow from any correct application of this formula.

Before sharing profit, the appropriation account adjusts for interest: interest on drawings of 10% is added back (Aye 800 plus Bee 200 equals 1,000), and interest on capital of 6% is deducted (Aye 1,200 plus Bee 1,800 equals 3,000), giving divisible profit of 8,000. Capital ratio is Aye to Bee equals 20,000 to 30,000, which simplifies to 2:3, so Bee receives 3 out of 5 shares. Bee's share equals 8,000 multiplied by 3 divided by 5 equals Le 4,800. Option A of Le 8,000 is the total divisible profit, not Bee's portion alone. Option B of Le 6,000 would result from an incorrect ratio or wrong divisible profit figure.

Divisible profit is found by adjusting net profit in the appropriation account: interest on drawings is added (it reduces what partners withdrew, so it boosts distributable profit), and interest on capital is deducted (it is a charge against profit before sharing). Interest on drawings equals (8,000 plus 2,000) multiplied by 10% equals 1,000; interest on capital equals (20,000 plus 30,000) multiplied by 6% equals 3,000. Divisible profit equals 10,000 plus 1,000 minus 3,000 equals Le 8,000. Options A, B, and C of Le 14,000, 12,000, and 10,000 result from omitting or misapplying one or both interest adjustments.

Partners share residual profit according to their capital contributions, making the ratio 20,000:30,000, which simplifies to 2:3. After processing interest on capital at 6% (Aye gets Le 1,200, Bee gets Le 1,800) and adding back interest on drawings at 10% (Aye owes Le 800, Bee owes Le 200), the residual profit is divided so Aye receives 2 out of every 5 parts. This calculation produces Le 3,200 for Aye. Option A (Le 6,000) inflates Aye's share by using a wrong fraction, and option C (Le 4,000) treats the ratio as equal halves rather than using the actual capital figures.

In government accounting, the primary classification of expenditure is by fund because each fund is a self-balancing financial pool set aside for a specific purpose, and spending must be reported against the fund it came from before anything else. This fund-based classification is the foundation from which all other groupings are derived. Programs, activities, and projects are secondary classifications used to provide further detail within a fund, so they cannot serve as the primary basis of classification.

Rent and rates are charges paid for the use of physical space, so the fairest way to share them among departments is according to how much floor area each department occupies. A department using a larger portion of the building should bear a proportionally higher share of the rent. Wages and salaries are allocated by number of employees or time worked, not space. Canteen expenses relate to the number of staff using the facility, and discount allowed is a selling expense tied to debtors rather than to any physical area.

Trade discount is deducted first from the gross invoice price: 12.5% of D96,240 is D12,030, leaving a net invoice price of D84,210. Because Mr Dauda paid within the credit period he also earns the cash discount of 20%, which is 20% of D84,210 equalling D16,842, so the amount actually paid is D84,210 minus D16,842, giving D67,368. Trade discount reduces the price before any payment is made and is never entered in the books, while cash discount only applies when settlement is made on time. Options A and B arise from applying just one of the discounts or reversing their order.

When members of the public respond to a company prospectus and send in their application money, they are called applicants; after the company makes allotments and those individuals pay the allotment money in full, they retain the title of applicants at this stage of the share-issue process. They only become shareholders once they are formally entered into the company's register of members after all required formalities are completed. Allotters (A) is not a recognised accounting term for this group. Non-members (C) is wrong because these individuals have already applied and received an allotment, giving them a legal claim to the shares.

Subscribed share capital is the portion of issued shares that investors actually applied for and were allotted. Oruma Ltd offered 300,000 shares to the public, but only received applications for 200,000 shares, so the subscribed capital equals the value of those 200,000 shares — N200,000. Option A (N300,000) represents the total issued share capital, which is the full amount offered regardless of uptake. Options B and D do not correspond to any share capital component derivable from the given data.

Unsubscribed share capital is the portion of shares the company offered to the public that investors did not apply for — it equals issued share capital minus subscribed share capital. The shares left untaken after the offer represent N150,000, making option D correct. Option A (N300,000) is the total issued capital, and option C (N200,000) is the subscribed capital established in the previous question. Option B (N250,000) does not represent any specific share capital component in this scenario.

Customers examine a company's financial statements to assess whether the business is financially sound enough to supply goods reliably, honor warranties, and continue trading — this is exactly what option A states. Option B describes the role of government regulators or industry bodies, not customers. Option C is the purpose of tax authorities such as the FIRS, who need to determine taxable profit. Option D reflects the interest of employees, who care about job security, not customers.

Liabilities represent the claims that external parties — creditors, banks, and suppliers — have against the assets of a business, making option B correct. Capital (option A) is the owner's claim on the business, not an outsider's. Reserves (option C) are accumulated retained profits belonging to shareholders, forming part of equity. Provisions (option D) are amounts set aside for expected future expenses and, while similar to liabilities, the broad term covering all outsider claims is liabilities.

Uncredited cheques are deposits made by the account holder that the bank has not yet processed and cleared — they represent timing differences recorded in the bank reconciliation statement, not the adjusted cash book. The adjusted cash book is updated only for transactions the bank has already processed without the account holder's immediate knowledge. Dishonoured cheques (A), direct payments to the bank (B), and standing order payments (D) are all actions the bank has taken unilaterally, so they must be entered into the adjusted cash book to bring the company's records up to date.

A bank statement is the document a bank sends to current account holders showing all debits, credits, and balances over a specific period. It is issued by the bank, not prepared by the customer. A bank reconciliation statement is prepared by the customer to explain differences between their cashbook and the bank statement. A banker's advice notifies a customer of a specific transaction, while a credit transfer moves funds between accounts.

A suspense account is a temporary account opened to correct errors discovered when the trial balance fails to agree, allowing the bookkeeper to balance the books while investigating the cause. It is used in the correction of errors, not their prevention or detection — errors are detected through the trial balance disagreement itself, and prevention requires internal controls, not a suspense account. Once errors are found and corrected, the suspense account is closed.

An error of commission occurs when a transaction is recorded in the correct class of account but in the wrong person's account — here, the purchase was correctly posted to a creditor's account but to P. Osei instead of P. Osae. An error of principle involves posting to a completely wrong type of account. An error of omission means the transaction was left out entirely. An error of original entry means the wrong amount was recorded in the books of original entry.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed with exactly the amount spent so that the float is restored to its original level. Since Le 37,500 was spent, the reimbursement is Le 37,500, bringing the cash back to Le 39,000. Option D (Le 1,500) is the remaining unspent cash, not the reimbursement. Option B (Le 39,000) would represent reimbursing the full float regardless of spending, which is incorrect.

Closing stock appears as a credit in the trading account, so understating it reduces the credit side, which increases cost of goods sold and therefore decreases gross profit and net profit. The formula makes this clear: Gross Profit = Sales − (Opening Stock + Purchases − Closing Stock), so a lower closing stock gives a higher cost figure and lower profit. Options A and C are wrong because understating closing stock always reduces profit, never increases or leaves it unchanged.

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity is the balance sheet equation, meaning it shows all assets a business owns alongside the sources used to finance them (debts and owner's capital). Option C captures this relationship perfectly. Option A describes working capital, not the full equation. Option B and D are incomplete — they ignore major components like long-term liabilities or total assets.

A trial balance is prepared by listing all ledger account balances (debits and credits) to check that the books are arithmetically correct. Option C describes this accurately. Option A is wrong because a trial balance shows balances, not every individual entry. Option B describes the balance sheet, not a trial balance. Option D is incorrect — a trial balance is a statement, not an account.

Accounts payable are amounts owed to suppliers for goods or services already received, and they are normally settled within a short period (usually within a year), making them current liabilities. Option A (prepayment) is money paid in advance, the opposite situation. Option B (provision) is an estimated future obligation. Option D is wrong because accounts payable are short-term, not long-term obligations.

From the supplier's perspective, Jute Enterprise is a customer who owes money, so the supplier maintains a personal account for Jute Enterprise in the sales ledger where all credit customer accounts are kept. Option A and D are wrong because nominal and real accounts relate to expenses/revenues and assets respectively, not persons. Option C is wrong — the purchases ledger holds supplier accounts, not customer accounts.

The prudence (conservatism) concept requires accountants to exercise caution when recognising profit — profit should only be recorded when it is reasonably certain, while losses should be recognised as soon as they are foreseeable. Option A best captures this idea of caution in profit recognition. Option B alone is too narrow; prudence covers profit recognition, not just anticipating losses. Options C and D describe income recognition without the element of caution that defines prudence.

Advertising (I) and motor repairs (II) are revenue expenditures recorded as expenses in the nominal ledger because they are consumed within the accounting period. Additions to motor vehicle (III) is capital expenditure, so it is recorded as an asset in the real ledger, not the nominal ledger. The nominal ledger holds income and expense accounts only. Capital additions increase the value of a fixed asset and appear on the balance sheet, not in expense accounts.

Objectivity requires that financial statements be based on verifiable, factual evidence rather than personal bias or subjective judgment. This ensures that any independent accountant examining the same records would reach the same conclusions. Materiality relates to the significance of information; periodicity concerns dividing accounting into time periods; conservatism means recognising losses early but profits only when certain. None of these three directly address the exclusion of personal opinion from records.

Carriage outward is the cost of delivering finished goods to customers, making it a selling and distribution expense. Selling expenses are charged to the profit and loss account because they occur after the goods have already been brought into the business. The trading account only handles costs directly tied to buying or producing goods, such as carriage inward. The balance sheet records assets and liabilities, not expenses, so it cannot be the correct location.

Carriage inward is the transport cost paid to bring purchased goods into the business or warehouse, so it forms part of the cost of acquiring those goods. Because it directly affects the cost of goods available for sale, it is added in the trading account alongside purchases. The profit and loss account handles expenses incurred after goods enter the business, such as selling costs. The appropriation account deals with how net profit is distributed, not with cost of goods.

When a manufacturing business values its finished goods at market price rather than actual production cost, the difference is a profit on manufacturing, also called manufacturing profit or loading. This unrealised gain is recorded in the manufacturing account and transferred to a provision for unrealised profit account. Net profit is the overall profit after all expenses; gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold in the trading account; goodwill is an intangible asset arising from business reputation. None of these three describe the specific surplus arising at the point of production valuation.

Depreciation of plant belongs in the manufacturing account because it is a factory overhead — a cost incurred in the process of producing goods. The manufacturing account collects all production costs before the finished goods value is transferred to the trading account. The trading account only handles the buying and selling of finished goods. The profit and loss account captures selling, administrative, and other non-production expenses, while the appropriation account deals with how net profit is shared or distributed.

Factory wages are classified as an overhead cost because they represent the general labour expenses of running the factory that cannot always be directly traced to a single unit of output. Overhead costs include all indirect costs of production such as indirect wages, factory rent, and maintenance. Administration cost covers office and management expenses, while selling and distribution cost covers advertising and delivery. Prime cost consists only of direct materials, direct labour (wages directly tied to each product), and direct expenses.
