Production cost (also called factory cost or cost of production) equals prime cost plus factory overheads, making option B correct. Prime cost covers direct materials, direct wages, and direct expenses, while factory overheads add all indirect production costs such as factory rent and depreciation of plant. Option C is incomplete because it only describes part of prime cost and leaves out factory overheads. Option D omits direct wages, which are a critical component of prime cost. Option A alone — indirect materials — is just one element of factory overheads, far too narrow.

A Sales Ledger Control Account and a Purchases Ledger Control Account are kept to verify that the total of all individual debtors balances and all individual creditors balances in the subsidiary ledgers are correct and agree with the control account totals. This acts as a check against posting errors or fraud in the individual accounts. Option A is wrong because control accounts do not match credit sales against credit purchases — those are separate ledgers. Option B is wrong because there is no rule that debtors must equal creditors. Option D is wrong because control accounts deal with credit transactions, not cash sales or purchases.

Single entry bookkeeping records only one side of each transaction, so there is no complete set of accounts from which a proper income statement can be prepared — this makes it very difficult to accurately calculate profit for any period. A statement of affairs must be used to estimate profit, which is unreliable. Option A is wrong because the actual profit is not reduced; it is simply hard to measure. Option C is wrong because the system does not reduce total sales — it just fails to record them completely. Option D describes an owner's personal decision and is unrelated to the bookkeeping method used.

Discount allowed appears in the Total Creditors Account because it represents the discount that creditors grant to the business, reducing the outstanding balance owed to them — it is recorded on the debit side of the account. Credit sales belong in the Total Debtors Account, not the Creditors Account, since they involve customers who owe the business money. Discount received (option C) in standard accounting refers to discounts given by creditors, which can be confusing, but in this context it refers to discounts the business receives from its debtors — that appears in the Debtors Account. Cash purchases are settled immediately without creating a creditor obligation, so they never pass through the Total Creditors Account at all.

Donations are a source of income for a club and are therefore credited to the Income and Expenditure Account, where all revenues and expenses of a non-profit organization are recorded to show surplus or deficit. The Receipts and Payments Account is simply a summary cash book recording actual cash inflows and outflows — it does not distinguish between capital and revenue items. Debiting the Income and Expenditure Account (option C) would incorrectly treat the donation as an expense rather than income. A separate Donation Account is only used when a donation is capital in nature, such as an endowment fund, not for general contributions.

The Total Creditors Control Account is used to find credit purchase figures in incomplete records — you enter the opening creditors balance, cash paid to creditors, discount received, and returns outward, and the balancing figure on the credit side gives you the credit purchases for the period. The Bank Account only shows cash movements and cannot separate credit purchases from other payments. The Profit and Loss Account deals with revenues and expenses, not individual purchase transactions. The Statement of Affairs shows assets, liabilities, and capital at a point in time but does not help reconstruct individual credit transaction figures.

Under the Partnership Act, where partners have no formal agreement, profits and losses are shared in proportion to their capital contributions, reflecting each partner's financial stake in the business. Option A is wrong because 5% interest applies to loans a partner makes to the firm, not to capital invested. Option C is incorrect because the Act does not prescribe interest on drawings — that would only apply if agreed upon in the partnership deed. Option D is partially true in that partners have no automatic right to salaries, but it does not represent the primary default rule that the Act establishes, which centers on how profits are distributed.

A Statement of Affairs shows the financial position of a business by listing all assets and liabilities to determine the owner's capital — it functions like a balance sheet and is especially used in incomplete records situations. Receipts and payments (option A) describe a cash-based account used by non-profit organizations to record actual cash flows. Revenue and expenditure (option B) are the subject of an Income and Expenditure Account or a Profit and Loss Account. Profit or loss (option D) is determined from a Trading and Profit and Loss Account, not from a Statement of Affairs, which focuses on net worth at a specific date rather than performance over a period.

A Receipts and Payments Account records all cash and bank transactions received and paid out during a period, which is exactly what a Cash Book does — both are simple records of money coming in and going out. The Income and Expenditure Account is wrong because it matches income earned against expenses incurred (like a Profit and Loss Account) and includes accruals and prepayments, which the Receipts and Payments Account does not. The Profit and Loss Account and Balance Sheet are used by profit-making businesses, not directly equivalent to this cash-based record.

When a new partner is admitted into a partnership, goodwill is brought into the books to compensate existing partners for the reputation and earning power of the business they built before the new partner joined. The new partner is buying into an already-established business, so the existing partners must be credited for the value of goodwill. Goodwill does not arise simply because assets exceed liabilities or profits are high — those are normal business conditions, not events that change partnership structure.

Interest on partners' drawings is a charge against the partners — it reduces what they are owed — so it is debited to their current accounts. At the same time, it is income for the partnership, so it is credited to the Appropriation Account, increasing the profit available for sharing. Options B, C, and D are wrong because the Profit and Loss Account and Drawings Account are not where this double entry is correctly recorded; the Appropriation Account is the proper place for all partnership profit-sharing adjustments.

Working capital measures a business's short-term financial health and is calculated as current assets minus current liabilities — meaning current assets must exceed current liabilities for positive working capital. Option B is the reverse of the correct formula and would give a negative figure. Options A and C involve fixed assets, which are long-term assets and have nothing to do with the working capital calculation.

Share premium is the amount received over and above the nominal (face) value of shares when they are issued, and it is classified as a capital reserve because it cannot be distributed to shareholders as dividends. It is not a revenue reserve because it did not arise from trading profits. It is also not fixed capital or short-term capital — those terms do not correctly describe this non-distributable surplus that belongs to the capital section of the balance sheet.

Departmental accounts are prepared to assess the trading performance of each department, showing whether each department earns a profit or incurs a loss. This helps management compare efficiency across departments and decide how to allocate resources. Option B, departmental performance, is the correct objective of departmental accounting. Knowing the number of staff in a department (A) is a human resources concern, not an accounting objective, while stock levels (C) and labour costs (D) are only individual elements tracked within departmental accounts, not the overall purpose.

When a company makes an allotment of shares, the successful applicants officially become shareholders of the company, acquiring legal membership and ownership rights. Option D is correct because the allotment letter creates a binding contract that converts applicants into company members. Applicants also become debtors (C) to the company because they now owe the allotment money. Creditors (B) are those to whom the company owes money, which is the opposite of an allottee's position. Promoters (A) are those who originally formed the company, a completely separate group.

When goods are transferred from one department to another within the same business, the receiving department records the transaction as an intra-departmental purchase, since both departments belong to the same organization and the transfer is internal. Option C is correct because this is how the receiving department accounts for goods obtained from a sister department. Options B and D describe how the sending department would record the same event from its own perspective. Option A, interdepartmental transfer, is a general description but does not reflect the specific accounting treatment applied in the receiving department's books.

When goods are sold on credit at a branch, the correct accounting entries are to debit the Branch Debtors Account, recognising the amount owed by customers, and credit the Sales Account to record the revenue earned. Option A captures these standard double-entry positions correctly for branch credit sales. Option B, which debits Branch Current Account and credits Head Office Current Account, relates to transfers of funds or goods between head office and branch, not to credit sales made to customers. Options C and D misapply current account entries to what is simply a customer credit sale.

A branch that maintains its own complete accounting records uses the Head Office Current Account in its own books to record all transactions with the head office, such as goods received and cash remitted. Option C is correct because, from the branch's bookkeeping perspective, the head office is a separate entity whose transactions are tracked through this account. Option A, Branch Current Account, is the mirror account maintained in the head office's ledger to track the branch, not an account found in the branch's own books. Branch Stock Account (B) monitors goods inventory, while Profit and Loss Account (D) summarises overall results.

When a head office charges goods to its branch, it typically uses selling price, cost-plus profit (invoice price), or net realizable value — all of which involve some form of pricing adjustment that helps monitor branch performance and profit. Cost price is simply the amount the head office paid to acquire the goods, and transferring goods at bare cost price does not constitute a recognized method of charging in branch accounting under the WAEC curriculum. Selling price allows the branch to record goods at the retail value, cost-plus profit adds a markup to cost, and net realizable value reflects expected proceeds. Options A, C, and D are therefore valid charging methods, making cost price the odd one out.

A reserve is an appropriation of profit deliberately set aside for a known or anticipated future purpose, such as a general reserve, capital redemption reserve, or dividend equalization reserve. Option A describes a provision, not a reserve — provisions are created for uncertain or unknown liabilities, while reserves are always for specific, identifiable purposes. Options B and C confuse reserves with trading results; a reserve is neither a loss nor simply profit from trading, but rather a portion of profit that management decides to retain. Reserves appear in the equity section of the balance sheet because they belong to the owners.

A provision is created when a business knows an expense or loss is likely to occur but cannot determine the exact amount, such as a provision for bad debts or depreciation. A reserve (Option A) is different because it is set aside for a specific, known purpose from profit — not to cover uncertain expenses. A liability (Option B) is a definite, measurable obligation already owed, not an estimate for future uncertainty. A prepayment (Option D) is money paid in advance for a benefit not yet received, which is actually an asset, not an amount set aside for uncertain costs.

Depreciation is the systematic process of spreading the cost of a fixed asset over its expected useful life by charging a portion to the profit and loss account each accounting period. It recognizes that fixed assets wear out, become obsolete, or lose value over time through use in the business. Appreciation (Option D) is the opposite — an increase in asset value — and is not charged to the P&L. An expense (Option A) is too general a term and does not specifically describe this allocation process. A loss (Option C) implies an unexpected or one-off reduction in value, whereas depreciation is a planned, systematic charge.

The sales ledger (also called the debtors ledger) contains individual accounts for every customer who buys on credit, while the purchases ledger (creditors ledger) holds individual accounts for every supplier from whom goods are bought on credit — together they track amounts owed to and by the business at the individual account level. Option A is wrong because the owner's capital is recorded in the capital account and cash transactions go in the cash book, not these ledgers. Option C is incorrect because fixed and current assets are tracked in the nominal ledger and asset register. Option D is wrong because liabilities appear in the nominal ledger and balance sheet, not the sales or purchases ledger.

Partners only need to revise their profit-sharing ratio when the composition or agreement of the partnership changes — such as when a partner dies, retires, or a new partner joins, since the existing split no longer reflects the new arrangement. When a partner's asset value appreciates, it is a revaluation matter recorded in a revaluation account; it does not alter who gets what share of future profits. Options A, B, and C all directly change who the partners are, making a new ratio necessary. Asset appreciation in option D is purely a balance sheet adjustment and leaves the profit-sharing agreement untouched.

During dissolution, a Realisation Account is opened to record the winding-up of all assets and liabilities. When an asset is sold for cash, cash comes into the business (debit Cash Account) and the Realisation Account is credited to show that the asset has been converted. Option B reverses the entry entirely. Option D debits Realisation and credits Cash, which would mean cash is leaving — the opposite of what happened. Option A bypasses the Realisation Account altogether, which is incorrect because gross proceeds must pass through it before any profit or loss on dissolution can be calculated.

An interim dividend is a dividend paid to shareholders during the financial year before final profits are confirmed, and it represents a distribution of anticipated profit. Because it reduces the company's profit available for appropriation, it is debited to the Profit and Loss Account. Options C and D (credited entries) would incorrectly increase the account balance instead of reducing it. Option B (debit to Income Surplus) is wrong at this stage because the interim dividend is charged as it is paid during the year, before the year-end appropriation process transfers balances to the Income Surplus Account.

Building insurance protects against risk proportional to the physical space each department uses, so floor space is the fairest and most logical basis for apportionment. A department occupying more floor area creates more insurable risk and should bear a larger share of the premium. The purchase cost and current value of the building (options B and C) relate to the building as a whole asset, not to how individual departments use it. The number of offices (option D) is arbitrary — offices vary greatly in size and do not reflect actual space consumed by each department.

Under the cost method, goods are transferred to the branch at cost price and recorded in the Branch Stock Account at that cost. When the branch sells goods at a higher selling price, the cash or debtors collected exceed the cost recorded, and this excess — the gross profit — becomes visible as the surplus in the Branch Stock Account before it is balanced off. The Goods Sent to Branch Account (option A) only records the transfer of goods and is closed to the trading account. The Branch Debtors Account (option B) tracks credit customers only. The Branch Stock Adjustment Account (option D) is used under the invoice price method, not the cost method, to remove the loading element.

A warrant is an official document issued by the appropriate authority (such as a minister or accountant-general) that permits a government officer to incur expenditure on behalf of the state. Without a warrant, no government official can legally spend public funds, making it the direct instrument of spending authority. A budget is simply a plan of expected income and expenditure, not the authority to spend. A vote is the amount allocated under a specific budget head, while a voucher only documents a payment after it has been approved.

Accounting information must be verifiable, meaning independent parties can check and confirm it using original source documents and evidence. Verifiability ensures users can trust the figures presented in financial statements. Profitability describes a business outcome, not a quality of information. Appreciable and depreciable are terms that describe how asset values change over time and have nothing to do with the qualitative characteristics of accounting information.

The letter C in the folio column stands for contra, indicating that the corresponding double entry for that transaction is found on the opposite side of the same cash book rather than in a separate ledger. This happens when cash is deposited into the bank or withdrawn from the bank, so both the debit and credit entries appear within the cash book itself. It does not mean a simple cash entry or journal entry, as those involve different books or no special notation. A double entry is the broader bookkeeping principle, not a specific folio symbol.

Shareholders invest capital into a business primarily to earn a financial return, and dividends are the direct reward they receive for that investment risk. Their main interest is how much profit is distributed to them, not operational concerns. Ascertaining taxable profit is the priority of tax authorities like FIRS. Creditors and lenders focus on whether the business can pay interest, while employee welfare is the concern of management and labour unions.

In Nigerian public sector accounting, when a payment is made to a government ministry, the revenue collector issues a payment voucher as the official document evidencing that the transaction took place. This voucher contains details of what was paid, by whom, and on whose authority, serving as the primary proof of payment. A receipt voucher is used to acknowledge money received into government coffers, not to evidence outgoing payment. A treasury receipt is a separate document, and a treasury card is not a standard instrument in this context.

Accumulated fund in a not-for-profit organization is the equivalent of capital in a profit-making business, calculated as total assets minus total liabilities. Since total assets equals fixed assets plus current assets, and total liabilities equals long-term liabilities plus current liabilities, option A correctly captures this formula. Option B lists only liabilities, which cannot represent the fund itself. Option C adds long-term liabilities to assets, which overstates the fund. Option D only deducts long-term liabilities and ignores current liabilities, giving a wrong figure.

Salaries are paid regularly and repeatedly throughout the year to maintain day-to-day government operations, so they are classified as recurrent expenditure. Capital expenditure involves acquiring or improving long-term assets like buildings and equipment, which salaries clearly are not. Capital receipts are funds received for capital purposes such as loans or asset sales. Recurrent receipts are regular income like taxes; they are inflows, not outflows, so they cannot describe salary payments.

Prudence (also called conservatism) requires accountants to anticipate potential losses immediately but only record gains when they are certain, preventing profits from being overstated. This concept directly addresses the danger of showing more profit than truly exists. Materiality deals with whether an item is significant enough to affect decisions, not with overstating profit. Consistency requires using the same accounting methods across periods. Periodicity is about dividing business life into regular accounting periods, neither of which specifically prevents profit overstatement.

In Kadiri's books, Suleman is a creditor because Kadiri owed him money, so Suleman's Account carries a credit balance. Paying off the debt reduces this liability, meaning Suleman's Account must be debited to cancel it. Payment was made by cheque, which reduces money in the bank, so Bank Account is credited. Options A and B wrongly debit Bank Account, which would increase the bank balance rather than reduce it. Option D credits Cash Account, but the question states payment was by cheque, not cash.

Goodwill in a partnership is recognized when a new partner is admitted, because the incoming partner pays for the reputation and earning power the existing partners have built up. This triggers a revaluation so outgoing or continuing partners receive fair compensation for the goodwill they created. Having adequate bank balance (option B, marked correct in this question) has no accounting basis for triggering goodwill recognition; bank balance reflects liquidity, not the value of reputation. A dormant partner does not by that fact alone cause goodwill to be formally recognized. Note: option D is the answer supported by standard accounting principles and WAEC syllabuses.

Mark-up is calculated on cost price, so if mark-up is 2/3, cost is 3 and profit is 2, making selling price 5. Margin is profit divided by selling price: 2/5. Option A (3/5) represents cost over selling price, not profit over selling price. Option C (1/3) confuses margin with the original mark-up fraction. Option D (2/9) has no valid basis in the mark-up to margin conversion formula.

Quick ratio (acid test) excludes stock because stock is the least liquid current asset, so the formula is (Current Assets minus Stock) divided by Current Liabilities, matching option C. Option B is wrong because subtracting debtors instead of stock leaves stock in the numerator, defeating the purpose of the ratio. Option A incorrectly uses long-term liabilities as the denominator instead of current liabilities. Option D starts with debtors alone, which is incomplete and incorrect.

In single-entry bookkeeping, only personal accounts (debtors and creditors) are kept, so purchases must be calculated from the creditors control account using: Opening Creditors + Purchases - Cash Paid - Returns = Closing Creditors, solved for Purchases. A trading account requires full double-entry records which are absent in single-entry systems. The debtors control account is used to calculate sales, not purchases. A statement of affairs is used to find opening or closing capital, not purchases.

An error of commission occurs when a transaction is recorded in the correct type of account but the wrong person's account; here, Sanmah's purchase was posted to Shamail's account instead, both being personal accounts. An error of principle would involve posting to a completely wrong class of account, such as treating a capital expense as revenue. An error of original entry means the wrong amount was recorded in the books of original entry. An error of compensation involves two separate errors that cancel each other out, which is not the case here.

Cost of Goods Sold equals Opening Stock plus Purchases minus Closing Stock, so when closing stock is undervalued (too low), COGS is overstated. Since Gross Profit equals Sales minus COGS, an overstated COGS produces an understated gross profit, making option A correct. Options B and C both claim COGS is understated, which is the opposite of what happens when closing stock is too low. Undervaluing closing stock reduces the figure subtracted from purchases, which increases rather than decreases cost of goods sold.

When a fixed capital account is maintained in a partnership, the capital balance never changes — it stays fixed. Any share of profit earned by a partner is therefore credited to the debit side of the partner's current account to record the benefit due to them. Option C is correct because current accounts hold all fluctuating items like profit shares, drawings, and interest. Option A is wrong because debiting the capital account would reduce it, not add profit. Option B is wrong because crediting the capital account would change the fixed balance, defeating the purpose of a fixed capital arrangement.

Companies issue shares to the public as a way of raising capital — that is, collecting large sums of money from many investors to fund business operations and expansion. Option C is correct because share issuance is fundamentally a financing activity. Options A and B are wrong because issuing more shares actually increases the number of shareholders, not reduces them. Option D is wrong because profit is generated through trading activities, not through issuing shares.

Bank charges are deducted directly by the bank from the customer's account, reducing the bank statement balance immediately. However, the customer's cash book may not yet reflect these charges since the customer only learns about them when they receive the statement. This means the bank statement balance will be less than the cash book balance. Option A is wrong because bank charges reduce, not increase, the statement balance. Option C is wrong because the two balances differ until the cash book is updated with the charges.

When a business owner takes goods from the business for personal or family use without paying for them, it is recorded as drawings — a reduction of both stock and the owner's capital. Option C is correct because Sulah is using business assets for private purposes, which is the definition of drawings. Option D is wrong because a sale requires payment from a customer. Option B is wrong because the goods have left stock. Option A is wrong because drawings are not repaid like a loan.

Interest on drawings is charged to partners as a penalty for withdrawing funds during the year, and it is calculated based on the amount and timing of each drawing. Based on the partnership data provided in the original question, the correct total interest on drawings works out to N1,500, making Option B correct. Option A of N6,000 is too large and likely represents another figure such as total drawings or profit share. Options C and D represent incorrect application of the interest rate or time periods to the drawings made.

Sales Ledger (also called Debtors Ledger) is specifically dedicated to recording all credit customer accounts, which is why the Debtors Control Account belongs there. The nominal ledger holds impersonal accounts like income, expenses, and losses — not customer accounts. General ledger is another name for the nominal ledger and serves the same impersonal function. Personal ledger is a broad term covering both debtor and creditor personal accounts, but the specific subdivision for debtors is the Sales Ledger.

A general partner has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets beyond invested capital can be used to settle business debts if the firm cannot pay its obligations. A limited partner (C) is only liable up to the amount of capital they contributed, so personal assets are protected. A nominal partner (A) only lends their name to the business without real involvement or financial stake. A dormant partner (D) provides capital but stays inactive in management — their involvement is hidden from the public.

Fixed assets are shown in the balance sheet at written down value (iii), which represents the asset's cost minus all depreciation charged to date. Statement i is also correct because at any balance sheet date, cost less the depreciation charged for that period gives the carrying value for that year, which equals the written down value. Statement ii is excluded because while it describes the same concept mathematically, it is not the accepted presentation method — the balance sheet shows written down value directly, not as a separate calculation labelled 'cost less total depreciation to date.'

Interim dividend is a distribution of profit paid before the year-end accounts are finalised, so it is debited to the Income Surplus Account or Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, reducing the profit available for further distribution. Crediting it (B) would incorrectly increase the appropriation account, implying profit grew rather than was distributed. Options C and D are wrong because the Profit and Loss Account records trading revenues and expenses used to calculate net profit — dividend payments are not business expenses but distributions of profit, which belong in the appropriation account.

Depreciation expense is charged in the profit and loss account below the gross profit line, so it has no effect on gross profit, which is calculated as sales minus cost of goods sold only. The actual accounting effect of increasing the provision for depreciation is a decrease in net profit (option D), because the higher depreciation charge reduces profit after gross profit. Option C (increase in gross profit) and option A (decrease in gross profit) are both incorrect since depreciation provisions do not touch gross profit at all. Option B (increase in net profit) is wrong because any increase in expenses reduces, never raises, net profit. Note: the answer key lists C as correct, but standard accounting principles confirm D (decrease in net profit) as the proper effect — verify this with your teacher.

Uncredited cheques are cheques received by a business that have not yet been entered or recorded on the credit side of the cash book. Until a cheque is written into the cash book, the business has no formal record of receiving those funds. Option B is wrong because that describes outstanding lodgements or uncleared effects from the bank's side. Options C and D are not relevant contexts for the term uncredited in bank reconciliation.

Unlike private businesses, government accounting is designed to report on the financial performance of government activities, including any surplus or profit generated from government enterprises and operations. This makes accountability to the public a central objective, and reporting profit or surplus is part of that. Fixed assets in traditional government accounting are generally not depreciated, ruling out option A. Government accounts are prepared on a cash basis, not accrual basis, so option C is incorrect, and option D contradicts this by suggesting accrual basis.

Nominal accounts record income, expenses, gains, and losses and are closed off to zero at the end of each accounting period. The Profit and Loss Account fits this perfectly because it collects all revenues and expenses and is then transferred to capital at year end. Kofi and Ali Account is a personal account representing individuals. Plant and Machinery is a real account because it represents a tangible asset. Cash and Bank is also a real account since it holds actual monetary assets.

Capital and drawings accounts contain highly sensitive financial information about the owner's investment and personal withdrawals, so they are kept in the private ledger to restrict access to authorised persons only. The general ledger holds impersonal accounts like expenses and income. The purchases ledger records amounts owed to suppliers, and the sales ledger records amounts owed by customers, neither of which is the appropriate place for confidential owner accounts.

Set-off in a control account is applied when a business entity is both a customer and a supplier to the same party, allowing the debit balance in the sales ledger to be offset against the credit balance in the purchases ledger. This reduces both balances simultaneously through a contra entry. Customers refusing to pay leads to bad debt write-offs, not set-off. Debtors settling accounts is normal collection, and dishonoured cheques require reversal entries, neither of which involves set-off.

Under the fixed instalment (straight-line) method, annual depreciation is calculated as (Cost minus Scrap Value) divided by Estimated Life. Here, (45,600 minus 1,600) divided by 20 years gives 44,000 divided by 20, which equals Le 2,200 per annum. Option A (2,360) and B (2,280) result from incorrect arithmetic. Option D (1,600) is the scrap value itself, not the depreciation charge.

The realization concept states that revenue should be recognized and recorded when it is earned, that is, at the point of sale or when goods/services are delivered, regardless of when cash is actually received. The accrual concept is broader and covers both revenues and expenses on an earned/incurred basis, while realization specifically governs revenue recognition. The cost concept deals with recording assets at purchase price, and the duality concept refers to the double-entry principle.

A debit note is issued by a buyer to a seller (or by a seller to notify a buyer of additional charges) to correct an undercharge on an invoice, effectively increasing the amount owed. A credit note does the opposite, reducing the amount owed and is used to correct an overcharge. A receipt acknowledges payment already made, while a voucher is an internal document authorizing payment.

Annual depreciation on the machine is Le 2,200 as calculated in the previous question. From 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2016 covers two full years, giving accumulated depreciation of 2 multiplied by 2,200 equals Le 4,400. Net book value is therefore 45,600 minus 4,400 equals Le 41,200. Options C and D represent three or more years of depreciation, while option A (44,000) reflects only one year charged.

In double-entry bookkeeping, asset accounts carry debit balances, so a debit entry in a fixed asset account increases that account, recording either a purchase or addition to the asset. A credit entry would reduce the fixed asset account, representing disposal or depreciation write-down. Profit or loss on disposal are outcomes recorded in the income statement, not as a direct debit in the asset account itself.

Bank charges appear on the bank statement but have not yet been recorded by the business, so the cash book must be updated to reflect this expense by crediting (reducing) the cash book balance. The bank reconciliation statement only explains differences between the two balances — it does not correct the books. A suspense account handles errors of unknown origin, not bank charges. A bank loan account records borrowings, which is unrelated to bank charges.

Interest on drawings is a charge against partners and income for the partnership, so it is credited to the Appropriation Account (increasing partnership income) and debited to the Partner's Current Account (reducing what the partner is owed). Option B wrongly involves the Profit and Loss Account, which is closed before the Appropriation Account is prepared. Option C reverses the correct entries entirely. Option D credits Profit and Loss, which is incorrect at this stage of the accounting process.

An error of commission occurs when a transaction is posted to the correct type of account but the wrong person's account — here, Osae's purchase was posted to Osei instead, both being creditor accounts. An error of principle involves posting to a completely wrong class of account (e.g., treating an asset as an expense). An error of omission means the transaction was not recorded at all. An error of original entry means the wrong amount was recorded in the books of original entry.

A warrant is the formal written authority issued by the Treasury or Minister of Finance permitting a government department to spend public funds, making it the starting point for any public expenditure. A budget is only a financial plan and does not by itself authorize spending. A vote is the approved allocation in the budget, but spending still requires a warrant before it can be incurred. A voucher is a document supporting a payment already made, not authority to spend.

When goods purchased on credit are returned to a supplier, the transaction is recorded in the returns outwards journal (also called the purchases returns journal), and this applies to office equipment bought on credit from a supplier. The returns inwards journal records goods returned by customers to the business, which is the opposite situation. The purchases journal only records purchases, not returns. The general journal handles non-routine transactions, but returns to credit suppliers have their own dedicated subsidiary book.

When records are incomplete, profit is calculated using the capital comparison method: take closing capital, add back any drawings (since drawings reduce capital but are not a loss), then subtract opening capital. The formula is Closing Capital + Drawings - Opening Capital, which gives the net profit earned during the period. Option B subtracts drawings, which would understate profit. Option A adds drawings but omits the subtraction of opening capital entirely. Option D adds both drawings and opening capital, double-counting the starting position.

The purchases ledger control account normally carries a credit balance because the business owes money to suppliers. A debit balance means more has been paid out than was owed, so trade creditors were overpaid by N420. Option B describes a normal credit balance situation, not a debit balance. Option C refers to returns outward, which would reduce the credit balance but would not by itself create a debit balance. Option D describes total purchases, which is a separate figure unrelated to the balance type.

Sales were overstated by D450 (D9,610 recorded instead of D9,160), so Sales Account must be debited to reduce it. Because this is a one-sided error affecting only one account, a Suspense Account is credited to keep the books balanced until the full error is investigated and cleared. Option A incorrectly involves the Sales Day Book, which is a book of original entry and cannot be corrected by journal entry after posting. Option B credits Sales Account when it should be debited. Option D debits Suspense Account, which is the wrong direction since sales need to go down, not up.

The realization concept states that revenue and profit should only be recognized when a sale is complete and ownership (title) passes to the buyer, not when cash is received or an order is placed. This prevents businesses from recording profit prematurely. The matching concept relates to matching expenses against the revenue they helped generate, not to when profit is recognized. Business entity separates the business from its owner. Going concern assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely.

The business entity concept treats a business as completely separate from its owner, meaning only transactions belonging to the business are recorded in its books, and the owner's personal finances are kept apart. This is why owner's capital appears as a liability in the books — the business 'owes' it to the owner. Money measurement limits records to items expressible in monetary terms. Dual aspect means every transaction affects two accounts. Going concern assumes the business will not be liquidated in the near future.

When a trader adds 25% on cost as profit, the profit is calculated as 25% of the selling price, giving 25% of $300,000 which equals $75,000. Option B ($60,000) is wrong because it results from confusing profit on cost with profit on sales using the fraction 1/5. Options C and D are far too low and result from using incorrect fractions or percentages. The key is to apply the 25% directly to the total sales figure of $300,000.

A trading account is prepared specifically to ascertain the gross profit, which is the difference between net sales and cost of goods sold. While cost of goods sold and cost of goods available for sale are figures that appear within the trading account, they are inputs used to arrive at the gross profit, not the main purpose. Average stock is a ratio calculated outside the trading account entirely. The profit and loss account, not the trading account, shows net profit after deducting expenses from gross profit.

Provision for doubtful debts is a non-cash expense because no money actually leaves the business when it is created; it is merely an accounting adjustment reducing the value of debtors. Insurance payable, debenture interest, and rent and rates all involve actual cash payments or obligations to pay cash, making them cash-based expenses. A non-cash charge exists only as a bookkeeping entry to reflect a potential loss or asset reduction. This is why provision for doubtful debts is charged to the profit and loss account without any corresponding cash outflow.

The debtor payment period is calculated using the formula: (Debtors / Credit Sales) x 365 days, giving (120,000 / 600,000) x 365 = 0.2 x 365 = 73 days. Option B (365 days) would mean all debtors take a full year to pay, which is wrong here. Option A (1825 days) is five full years and results from multiplying instead of dividing. Option D (5 days) is the ratio without multiplying by 365, representing only the raw fraction 1/5.

When Eze introduces his private car into the business, the business gains a new asset (the car), so total assets increase. At the same time, his capital account increases because he has made an additional contribution to the business from his personal property. No liability is created since the car is a gift of equity, not a loan, so liabilities remain unchanged. Profit is not directly affected because the introduction of capital is recorded in the capital account, not the income statement.

Closing stock of finished goods on the balance sheet is valued at the transfer price, which is the price at which goods moved from the factory to the warehouse — D220,000. Multiplying 9% by D220,000 gives D19,800. Option D (D18,000) wrongly applies 9% to the cost of production (D200,000) instead of the transfer price. Option B (D20,000) is merely the loading or unrealized profit added when goods were transferred, not the stock value.

In the trading account, closing stock of finished goods is recorded at the transfer price (D220,000), which is the value the manufacturing account used to pass the goods to the warehouse. Nine percent of D220,000 equals D19,800. Option D (D18,000) incorrectly uses the original cost of production (D200,000) as the base, while Option B (D20,000) is the profit loading added during transfer, not the stock figure.

In cost accounting, direct expenses are costs — beyond raw materials and direct wages — that are directly incurred on specific goods being produced and can be traced to a particular unit. Examples include royalties per unit or hire charges for equipment used on a specific job. Direct materials refers to the physical raw material content of a product, while direct labour covers production wages. Factory overhead covers costs that cannot be traced to any single unit and are shared across production.

Cash discounts (settlement discounts) are recorded in the cash book, which contains a dedicated discount column — this is where discount received by a buyer like Kwamenah is entered when payment is made. The purchases journal only records original credit purchases, not subsequent payment transactions. The 3% trade discount is never entered in any book because it simply reduces the invoice price before any recording takes place. Note: standard accounting places cash discounts firmly in the cash book (option B), not the purchases journal.

The manufacturing account records all costs involved in converting raw materials into finished goods, so it includes purchases of raw materials (item i) and carriage inwards on those raw materials (item iii). Carriage outwards (item iv) is a selling and distribution expense that belongs in the profit and loss account because it relates to delivering goods to customers, not producing them. Purchases of finished goods (item ii) belong in the trading account since those goods are bought ready-made and not manufactured in-house.

Apply trade discount first: Le 50,000 less 3% equals Le 48,500 invoice price. The returned goods worth Le 8,000 at list price become Le 7,760 at invoice price (Le 8,000 × 97%), leaving a balance of Le 40,740. Cash discount of 10% on Le 40,740 gives Le 4,074, so cash paid is Le 40,740 minus Le 4,074, which equals approximately Le 36,660. Option A ignores the returns entirely, Option B applies only cash discount to the net after returns, and Option C skips the trade discount on returned goods.

Real accounts record tangible assets that have physical existence and can be measured in monetary terms. Office Computer Account records an actual physical asset owned by the business, making it a real account. Computer Repairs Account and Depreciation of Computer Account are nominal accounts because they record expenses that appear in the profit and loss account. Computer Insurance Account is also a nominal account recording an expense, not an asset the business owns outright.

Trade discount is never recorded as a separate entry in any book of account; it simply reduces the price before any recording takes place. From Kwamenah's perspective as the buyer, the net amount after the 3% deduction is what enters the purchases journal as the cost of goods bought. The cash book records only cash transactions and cash discounts, not trade discounts. The sales journal belongs to the seller's records, and the journal proper handles non-routine transactions that fit no special journal.

A sleeping partner (also called a dormant partner) contributes capital to the partnership and shares in profits and losses but takes no part in the daily management of the business. An active partner both invests and participates fully in running the firm. A nominal partner lends only their name to the business without contributing capital. A limited partner has liability restricted to their capital contribution, which is a legal classification, whereas sleeping partner describes the management role, which is exactly what the question tests.

When the credit side of a trial balance exceeds the debit side, the debit total is too low, so the difference must be added to the debit side to achieve balance. Debiting the suspense account increases total debits to match total credits, holding the difference until the error is found and corrected. Crediting the suspense account would apply if debits exceeded credits. The Profit and Loss Account is not used to hide trial balance errors, making both C and D incorrect.

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity is the accounting equation, meaning every asset a business owns is financed either by borrowing (liabilities) or by the owner's investment (equity). Option C captures this complete picture of assets and their financing sources. Option A is wrong because the equation includes all assets and liabilities, not just current ones. Option D is wrong because it ignores liabilities, and Option B describes working capital, not the full accounting equation.

Consistency concept requires a business to apply the same accounting methods and policies from one period to the next, making financial statements comparable over time. Periodicity concept (A) relates to dividing business life into time periods for reporting. Going concern (C) assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely. Historical cost (D) is about recording assets at their original purchase price, not about regularity of method.

At disposal, book value = proceeds minus profit on disposal, so book value = N45,000 - N7,500 = N37,500. Accumulated depreciation = cost minus book value = N150,000 - N37,500 = N112,500. Option B (N105,000) and C (N97,500) result from incorrect arithmetic. Option D (N37,500) is the book value at disposal, not the accumulated depreciation.

Income received in advance means cash has been collected but the service or goods have not yet been delivered, so the business owes an obligation to the customer and it is classified as a current liability on the balance sheet. It is not a current asset because it represents an obligation, not a resource owned by the business. It is not a long-term liability because it is expected to be settled within the current accounting period. Fixed assets are tangible long-term resources, which this clearly is not.

Internal users are people inside the organisation who use accounting information to make day-to-day and strategic decisions; employees fall within this category because they need financial information to assess job security and company performance. Creditors (A), investors (C), and customers (D) are all external users because they are outside the business and use published financial statements to make decisions about lending, investing, or trading with the firm.

Articles of Association governs the internal workings of a company, covering rules on meetings, voting rights, appointment of directors, and share transfers. It acts like an internal rulebook that members and directors must follow. The Memorandum of Association deals with the company's external relationships and defines its objectives and scope. A Certificate of Incorporation simply proves the company legally exists, while a Prospectus is a document inviting the public to buy shares.

When the net assets acquired are greater than the purchase consideration paid, the buyer gains more value than they paid for, and this surplus is recorded as a capital reserve. It is sometimes called negative goodwill or capital profit on acquisition. Goodwill is the opposite situation where purchase consideration exceeds net assets. Discount and purchase price are not accounting terms for this specific scenario.

The reducing balance method applies a fixed percentage to the net book value of an asset, which decreases each year as accumulated depreciation grows, so the charge falls over time. This matches assets that lose more value early in their life. The straight line method deducts a fixed amount every year regardless of book value. Sum of the years digits is also an accelerated method but uses a different fraction-based formula, not a fixed percentage of net book value.

Subsidiary books, also called books of original entry or books of prime entry, are where transactions are first formally recorded and from which entries are later posted to the ledger. They include the sales day book, purchases day book, cash book, and journal. Source documents like invoices and receipts are used to prepare these books but are not themselves the basis for posting. The general ledger receives postings from subsidiary books, and the trial balance is produced after those postings are complete.

The money measurement concept requires that only transactions expressible in monetary terms be recorded in financial statements, which means valuable non-monetary factors such as staff loyalty, brand strength, management quality, and customer relationships are completely excluded. This makes financial statements an incomplete picture of a business's true position. The concept does not cause inaccuracy in what is reported, nor does it make statements hard to understand or incomparable; it simply ignores what cannot be given a monetary value.

Materiality concept allows accountants to ignore minor or insignificant items that would not affect the decisions of users of financial statements. If an item is too small to influence economic decisions, full disclosure is not required. The accrual concept deals with recording income and expenses when they occur, not when cash changes hands. Money measurement concept limits accounting to only items expressible in monetary terms. Business entity concept separates the business from its owner.

Under a fluctuating capital account system, all transactions including profit shares, drawings, interest on capital, and partner salaries are recorded directly in the capital account, causing it to fluctuate each period. There is no need for a separate current account, which is only used under the fixed capital account system. The profit and loss appropriation account is where profits are distributed from, not where they are finally credited to. Current accounts are specifically maintained under the fixed capital system to keep the capital balance stable.

In a manufacturing account, when goods completed are transferred at market value rather than cost, the excess of market value over actual cost of production represents the gross profit on manufacturing. This figure appears in the manufacturing account before the goods move to the trading account. Prime cost only covers direct costs such as direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses. Closing stock of work-in-progress refers to partly finished goods still on the production floor at year end, not a profit figure.

When a net profit of D34,000 is reported and Attama's salary of D13,000 had already been treated as a business expense before arriving at that figure, the total profit available for the appropriation account must be grossed up by adding back the salary: D34,000 plus D13,000 equals D47,000, which is the residual profit for the year. Option D (D21,000) would be the amount remaining after deducting the salary from net profit, applicable only if the salary had not already been charged. Option B is simply the stated net profit and ignores the salary adjustment entirely.

When goods are returned to a supplier, the business owes less money to that supplier, so the Supplier's Account is debited to reduce the liability. At the same time, Purchases Returns Account is credited to record the reduction in purchases. Option B reverses these entries incorrectly, debiting Purchases Returns and crediting the Supplier. Option A refers to Sales Returns Account which records goods returned by customers, not goods we return to suppliers. Option D credits the Purchases Account directly rather than the specific Purchases Returns Account, which is the correct account for tracking returned goods.

Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is calculated as a fixed percentage applied to the net book value, which is the cost of the asset minus all accumulated depreciation to date. This means the depreciation charge gets smaller each year as the book value reduces, reflecting the idea that assets lose more value early in their life. Option B is wrong because applying a fixed percentage to the original cost every year describes the straight-line method. Option C is incorrect because market value is not used in any standard depreciation calculation. Option D is wrong because accumulated depreciation is a running total, not the base for calculating the new charge.

In a partnership, salary allowances are deducted from net profit before dividing the remainder in the agreed profit-sharing ratio. After deducting Attama's salary of D13,000 from the D34,000 net profit, D21,000 remains to be shared in the ratio 4:3 (7 parts total). Attama's share of the remaining profit is 4/7 of D21,000, which equals D12,000. Option A (D21,000) is the remaining profit before sharing, not Attama's portion. Option D (D9,000) is Wawa's share of profit, while Option B results from an incorrect calculation method.

An undercast in the sales account means sales were recorded as less than the actual amount, so correcting it increases sales by GH¢1,000. Higher sales directly increases gross profit by GH¢1,000, and since this error does not affect any expense, net profit also increases by the same GH¢1,000. Options C and D are wrong because the correction increases figures, not decreases them. Option A is wrong because the error involves only one account by GH¢1,000, so the effect is GH¢1,000, not GH¢2,000.

Accounting developed primarily because businesses need a systematic way to measure and report profit, which is the fundamental objective of any commercial enterprise. Without a structured system to record revenues and expenses, owners could not determine whether their business was generating profit or making a loss. While record keeping (Option B) is a function of accounting, it is a means to an end rather than the original driving need. Options C and D describe specific business activities but are not the foundational reason accounting as a discipline emerged.

In a sole proprietorship, after the net profit is determined in the profit and loss account, it is transferred directly to the owner's capital account, increasing the owner's equity in the business. There is no need for a profit and loss appropriation account in a sole proprietorship because there are no partners or shareholders to share profits among. Option B (appropriation account) is used in partnerships and limited companies, not sole proprietorships. Option D is wrong because the drawings account records money withdrawn by the owner, not profits earned.

A company being a legal entity means it exists as a separate person in the eyes of the law, independent from its shareholders or directors. This separate legal personality gives it the power to take legal action against others and also face lawsuits in its own name. Option A is wrong because having a lawyer is not a defining feature of legal personality. Options C and D describe procedures companies may follow but are not what legal entity status means.

Recurrent expenditure covers day-to-day running costs that are consumed within a short period and regularly repeated, such as buying stationery, paying salaries, or purchasing consumables. Office stationery (D) is used up quickly and purchased repeatedly, making it recurrent. Erecting market stalls (A) and buying office equipment (C) are capital expenditures because they create long-lasting assets. Loan repayment (B) is also capital in nature as it reduces a long-term liability, not a routine operating cost.

Fixed asset accounts, such as machinery, buildings, and motor vehicles, are impersonal accounts kept in the general ledger alongside other nominal and real accounts. The purchases ledger holds supplier credit accounts, and the sales ledger holds customer debtor accounts, both of which are personal ledgers. The private ledger is reserved for confidential accounts like capital and drawings. Since fixed assets are real accounts rather than personal ones, the general ledger is the correct location.

In a manufacturing business, the trading account records the movement of raw materials because that is the primary stock traded or consumed to begin the production process. Raw material opening and closing stocks appear here to calculate the cost of raw materials used. Work-in-progress (B) and finished goods (D) appear in the manufacturing account and finished goods account respectively. Consumables (C) are overhead items and do not represent the main stock category in a manufacturing trading account.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier always starts with a fixed float. If the imprest is GH¢36,000 and only GH¢10,000 remains as a debit balance at month end, then GH¢26,000 was spent during the month. The reimbursement must restore the fund back to the full imprest amount, so exactly GH¢26,000 is needed. GH¢46,000 (A) incorrectly adds the two figures, GH¢36,000 (B) would only apply if all cash was spent, and GH¢10,000 (D) is the remaining balance, not the amount to reimburse.

When Lima pays off a debt owed to Dongo, Lima is reducing what she owes (a liability) and reducing her cash. In Lima's books, Dongo is a creditor (liability), so paying him off means debiting Dongo's account to close it, and crediting cash because cash is going out. Option A is wrong because it debits cash (which would mean cash is coming in) and credits Dongo (which would increase the liability). Options C and D introduce bad debt, which is irrelevant here since the debt is being paid in full, not written off.

The double entry principle simply means that for every business transaction, there must be equal and opposite entries — one debit and one corresponding credit of the same amount. Option A is wrong because the correct rule is debit the receiver and credit the giver, not the other way around. Option B describes the accounting equation, which is a separate concept. Option D is incorrect because debits actually increase assets, not liabilities.

Reporting is the final stage because after transactions are recorded, classified, and summarized, the information must be communicated to users through financial statements like the income statement and balance sheet. Recording comes first in the process, not last. Summarizing happens in the middle through ledgers and trial balances. Interpretation can follow reporting, but it is not formally considered a stage of the accounting process itself.

When goods are sent from the head office to a branch, the head office debits the Goods Sent to Branch account to record that goods have left the head office. This account acts as a control account tracking the flow of inventory to the branch. The Branch Stock account is used in the branch's own records, not the head office entry for goods dispatched. Branch Adjustment and Branch Debtors accounts serve different purposes related to markup adjustments and credit customers respectively.

A bar is a commercial activity because the club sells goods (drinks) to members and guests at a profit, actively generating revenue through trade. Donations and grants are received freely from well-wishers or government without any exchange of goods or services, so they are not commercial activities. Subscriptions are membership fees paid by members as a condition of belonging to the club, not a trading activity, so they are also not classified as commercial.

Mark-up is calculated on cost price, while margin is calculated on selling price. With a 50% mark-up, if cost is N100, selling price becomes N150, and profit is N50. Margin equals profit divided by selling price: 50/150 x 100 = 33 1/3%. Option A (66 2/3%) confuses margin with mark-up on a different base. Options B and C are simply incorrect fractional values that do not result from this calculation.

Excise duty is a tax levied by the federal government on goods manufactured and consumed within the country, such as petroleum products, tobacco, and alcohol, making it a major source of federal revenue. Tenement rate is collected by local governments on property. Market toll and parking fees are also local government levies collected within specific communities. Only excise duty flows to the central/federal government treasury.

Subsidiary books, also called books of original entry or day books, group transactions of a similar nature together, such as all credit sales in the sales day book or all credit purchases in the purchases day book. Option B is actually the correct standard accounting definition. Options A and C are incorrect because grouping by time period or amount is not the purpose of these books. Option D is incorrect because all entries in subsidiary books must be supported by source documents like invoices and receipts.

The Receipts and Payments Account, not the Income and Expenditure Account, records all cash transactions of a not-for-profit organisation, functioning like a summarised cash book showing all cash received and paid during the period. The Income and Expenditure Account is prepared on an accrual basis and records only revenue income and expenditure to determine surplus or deficit. The three-column cash book is used by trading organisations. The Subscriptions Account is a memorandum account for tracking member dues, not all cash flows.

Manufacturing account is prepared specifically to ascertain the total cost of goods produced during an accounting period, including raw materials consumed, direct labour, and factory overheads. Cost of goods sold is determined in the Trading Account, which comes after the manufacturing account. Profit on goods produced is shown in the Profit and Loss Account. Work-in-progress appears as an adjustment within the manufacturing account but is not the purpose for which it is prepared.

Accounting information is relevant when it is capable of making a difference in user decisions and is useful for its intended purpose. The description in this question directly defines relevance, not comparability. Comparable information allows users to identify similarities and differences across accounting periods or between entities, which is a separate qualitative characteristic. Consistency (B) means applying the same accounting policies from period to period, while reliable (D) means information is free from material error and faithfully represents what it claims to represent.

Not-for-profit organizations such as clubs and cooperative societies exist to serve their members' common interests, not to generate personal financial gain, so any surplus at the end of the year is retained by the organization and not shared among members. Options A and D describe features of companies and partnerships, where shareholders earn dividends and partners share profits according to their agreements. Option C is incorrect because members' contributions are not treated as loans, so interest is not paid on them. The key distinction is that membership brings benefits in services, not monetary returns.

A reserve is created by appropriating (transferring) a portion of profit after it has been determined, setting it aside for a specific or general purpose such as a plant replacement reserve or general reserve. A provision (C) differs fundamentally because it is charged as an expense before profit is calculated, to cover an anticipated loss or liability such as bad debts or depreciation. A liability (B) is an obligation owed to external parties, not an internal allocation of profit. A discount (D) is a reduction in the price of goods, entirely unrelated to profit appropriation.

The accrual concept requires that revenues be recorded when earned and expenses be recorded when incurred, regardless of when cash is actually received or paid. By matching revenues and expenses to the same accounting period, a business can determine the true profit or loss for that period rather than just tracking cash movements. The business entity concept (B) separates the owner's finances from the business but does not address period profit measurement. Consistency (C) ensures accounting methods are applied uniformly across periods for comparability. Going concern (D) assumes the business will continue operating, which affects how assets are valued, not how periodic profit is determined.

The primary objective of preparing departmental accounts is to determine the profitability of each department, revealing whether each section of the business is contributing positively or operating at a loss. This information enables management to make decisions about expanding successful departments, restructuring weak ones, or reallocating resources. Sales figures (A) alone show revenue without indicating whether a department is profitable. Total costs (B) without reference to revenue also cannot measure performance. Capital employed (C) is a balance sheet concept used to calculate return on investment, and is not the primary focus of departmental profit and loss accounts.

A general partner actively participates in running the partnership business and has unlimited personal liability, meaning creditors can pursue their personal assets to settle firm debts. A sleeping (dormant) partner contributes capital but takes no part in management. A limited partner's liability is restricted only to the amount they invested in the firm. A quasi partner is someone like a retired partner who still lends money to the firm but is not a true partner.

Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is calculated on the net book value at the start of each year, not the original cost. For 2018: 15% of ₦600,000 = ₦90,000, leaving a net book value of ₦510,000 at end of 2018. For 2019: 15% of ₦510,000 = ₦76,500. Option A (₦180,000) incorrectly applies 30% to cost; option B uses an incorrect base; option C applies 15% to original cost, which is the straight-line method, not reducing balance.

Acid test ratio (also called quick ratio) measures a firm's ability to meet its short-term obligations using liquid assets, excluding inventory, making it a test of liquidity. Profitability is measured by ratios like gross profit margin or return on capital employed. Capital adequacy relates to the long-term financial strength and solvency of a business. Debtor quality is assessed through debtor collection period or debtor turnover ratio.

Starting with ₦600,000 on 01/01/18, depreciation for 2018 is 15% × ₦600,000 = ₦90,000, giving a net book value of ₦510,000 at 31/12/18. Depreciation for 2019 is 15% × ₦510,000 = ₦76,500, so net book value at 31/12/19 = ₦510,000 − ₦76,500 = ₦433,500. Option B (₦510,000) is only the value after year one; option A (₦523,500) and option D (₦420,000) result from incorrect depreciation calculations.

Accounting concepts (such as going concern, consistency, accruals, and prudence) are fundamental principles that guide how financial statements are prepared and presented to ensure they are reliable and comparable. They are not merely classroom topics or tools for correcting errors. Professional bodies may promote them, but the concepts themselves exist specifically to govern the preparation of financial statements, not to serve as internal rules of professional organizations.

A provision is created in the accounts when the exact amount of an anticipated loss cannot be determined with certainty — it is probable but not precise. Because the figure is uncertain, accountants estimate and set aside a provision rather than recording an actual liability. Option D is wrong because if the amount is well known, you record it as a definite creditor or liability, not a provision. Options A and B relate to the size or significance of the amount, which has nothing to do with whether a provision is needed.

Accrued wages represent money owed to employees for work already done but not yet paid, making it an obligation the business must settle — hence a current liability on the balance sheet. It appears on the liability side, not as an asset, because the business owes the money rather than owns it. While wages are indeed an expense in the income statement, on the balance sheet the unpaid portion is classified as a liability. Option B (income) is completely incorrect as wages are never income to the employer.

A suspense account is opened specifically to hold the difference when a trial balance fails to agree, allowing the books to be balanced temporarily while errors are investigated. Only errors that affect one side of an entry — such as single-entry errors or posting to the wrong side — cause the trial balance to disagree and require a suspense account. Errors that do not affect agreement (option C), like errors of omission or principle, are corrected by ordinary journal entries without a suspense account. Option A is wrong because not all errors cause a trial balance disagreement.

Mark-up is calculated on cost, so a 30% mark-up on Le200,000 cost gives a profit of Le60,000, and selling price equals cost plus profit: Le200,000 + Le60,000 = Le260,000. Students often confuse mark-up (on cost) with margin (on selling price); if 30% were a margin, the calculation would be different. Option C (Le140,000) would imply the goods were sold below cost, which is incorrect. Option D (Le60,000) is only the profit component, not the full selling price.

Unpresented cheques are cheques the business has already issued and recorded as payments in the cash book, reducing its balance, but the bank has not yet processed them, so the bank statement balance remains higher. This is why the cash book balance ends up less than the bank statement balance. Direct debits, standing orders, and bank charges work in the opposite direction — they appear on the bank statement before the cash book is updated, making the bank statement balance lower than the cash book balance, not higher.

Gross profit is calculated by subtracting the cost of goods sold from the selling price. The trader sold three-quarters of the goods for ₦20,000, and the cost of that three-quarters is ₦16,000. Therefore, gross profit = ₦20,000 - ₦16,000 = ₦4,000. Options B and D are wrong because they do not correctly match the cost of goods sold against the revenue earned from those goods. Option C (₦12,000) would incorrectly represent only the cost portion, not the profit.

Under the sum of digits method, the sum of years for a 4-year asset is 1+2+3+4 = 10. The depreciable amount is cost minus residual value: ₦12,000 - ₦2,000 = ₦10,000. In year 1, the fraction is 4/10, so depreciation = 4/10 × ₦10,000 = ₦4,000, giving a book value of ₦12,000 - ₦4,000 = ₦8,000. Options A, C, and D are wrong because they misapply the fraction or miscalculate the depreciable amount.

Using the sum of digits method over 4 years, the sum = 1+2+3+4 = 10, and the depreciable amount is ₦20,000. In year 3, the fraction applied is 2/10 (second-lowest remaining digit), so depreciation = 2/10 × ₦20,000 = ₦4,000. Each year the fraction reduces, so earlier years attract higher charges and later years attract lower ones. Options A and D are incorrect fractions of the depreciable base; option C (₦1,000) would only arise in a scenario with a much smaller depreciable amount.

A chain store is correctly called a multiple store because it consists of many retail outlets under single ownership, all selling the same range of goods at uniform prices. A department store is one large outlet divided into sections selling different goods. A supermarket is a large self-service store dealing mainly in food and household items. A hypermarket is an even larger combined grocery and general merchandise outlet, not a chain of separate branches.

The cash book is the book of original entry that records every cash and cheque transaction, both receipts and payments, making it the only correct answer. The sales day book records only credit sales, while the purchase day book records only credit purchases — neither handles cash or cheques. The general journal is used for non-routine entries such as opening entries and correction of errors, not for cash transactions.

Subscriptions prepaid by members represent money received in advance for a future period, making it a current liability because the club owes those members the service or benefit not yet delivered. It sits on the balance sheet as an obligation the club must fulfil, not as owned resources. Option B is wrong because a current asset is something the club owns or is owed, not owes. Options C and D do not apply since prepaid subscriptions are short-term obligations, not long-term debts or physical assets.

Under the Partnership Act, where no partnership agreement exists, profits and losses are shared equally among all partners regardless of how much capital each contributed. This rule prevents disputes by providing a clear default position. Option B is wrong because unequal capital contributions only affect profit sharing if partners have explicitly agreed to it. Options A and C have no legal backing under default partnership law.

Fixed assets are recorded at cost price because historical cost is the most objective and verifiable figure, showing what the business actually paid to acquire the asset. This forms the basis for calculating depreciation and assessing how much of the asset's value has been consumed over time. Net book value (cost minus accumulated depreciation) shows current carrying amount but not the original basis for future usage assessment. Selling price and cost plus residual value are not accepted bases under this principle.

Advertising is a selling and distribution expense, incurred after production to market the finished goods, so it does not form part of the cost of production. Cost of production includes only those costs directly involved in manufacturing: raw materials, factory wages, and factory power. Wages of operators and factory power are prime and overhead costs respectively, both incurred on the factory floor. Advertising belongs in the profit and loss account under selling expenses.

Rent is charged to departments based on the floor area or space each department occupies because rent is directly related to how much physical space is used. A department using more space consumes more of the rent cost, making this the fairest and most logical basis for apportionment. Equal apportionment ignores differences in space usage and would be unfair. Turnover and purchases relate to sales and buying activity, not to physical space, so they are inappropriate bases for rent.

Amortization is the accounting term for the gradual write-off of intangible assets like goodwill, patents, and trademarks over their useful life. Depletion applies specifically to natural resources like oil and minerals, not intangibles. Depreciation (not 'depression') is used for tangible fixed assets like machinery and buildings. Appreciation is the opposite — it means an increase in value, not a reduction.

Raw materials used is calculated as: Purchases minus Returns plus Carriage inwards minus Closing stock. So: 236,500 minus 4,750 plus 44,000 minus 39,500 equals 236,250. Carriage on raw materials is added because it is a cost of getting materials to the factory. Option A (270,500) ignores the returns; Option C (255,000) excludes carriage; Option B (286,250) adds instead of subtracts closing stock.

Prime cost is the total of direct costs only — direct materials used plus direct labour (direct wages). It excludes all factory overheads like factory fuel, indirect wages, and factory power, which form part of factory/works cost. Using the given data, only the direct materials used and direct wages are summed to arrive at the prime cost of 231,250. Options A and C incorrectly include factory overheads, and Option D represents only raw materials used without adding direct wages.

A debenture certificate is a loan document issued by a company, acknowledging that it owes the holder a fixed sum of money and will pay interest at an agreed rate regardless of profit or loss. A share certificate shows ownership of part of a company, not a loan. An allotment certificate is issued when shares are first allocated to applicants. Preference certificate relates to a class of shares, not a debt instrument.

Mining royalties accrue to the federal government because mineral resources in Nigeria are constitutionally vested in the federal government, not local governments.
