Radio and TV licences, tenement and property rates, and business permit fees are all recognized sources of revenue for local government councils. Local governments generate income from activities and property within their jurisdiction, but extracting natural resources falls outside their authority.

Factory overheads are the indirect costs of production — costs that cannot be traced directly to a specific unit of output. Here, the overhead items are: indirect wages (D31,250), factory power (D105,000), and factory fuel (D150,000), giving a total of D286,250. Direct wages are prime costs, not overheads, so they are excluded. Raw material figures are used to calculate cost of materials consumed, which is also separate from factory overhead.

The money measurement concept holds that accounting records only transactions expressible in monetary terms, so non-financial information — like staff morale, reputation, or management quality — is left out of financial statements. This is exactly why financial statements cannot disclose all information users need. Consistency means applying the same methods each period. Dual aspect refers to every transaction having equal debits and credits. Materiality decides whether an item is significant enough to disclose separately.

First, calculate the irrecoverable (bad) debt: 2% of N13,000 = N260, which is written off, leaving a balance of N12,740. The provision for doubtful debts is then 5% of the remaining balance: 5% of N12,740 = N637. Option A (N910) incorrectly applies 5% to the full N13,000 before removing the bad debt. Option B (N650) applies 5% to N13,000 ignoring the 2% write-off. Option D (N260) is the bad debt figure, not the provision.

When the debit and credit totals of a trial balance do not agree, the difference is entered in a suspense account to make both sides equal temporarily while the error is tracked down. The suspense account is closed once all errors are located and corrected. A bank reconciliation statement compares the cash book with the bank statement and is not used for trial balance differences. The profit and loss account records income and expenses to determine net profit, which has no role here.

A three column cash book has three money columns on each side: discount, cash, and bank. The discount column records discounts allowed (debit side) and discounts received (credit side), while the cash and bank columns record their respective transactions. Options A and B are wrong because assets and liabilities are not columns in a cash book. Option C is wrong because returns are recorded in returns books, not the cash book.

Uncredited cheques are cheques deposited by the business but not yet processed by the bank, so they do not appear on the bank statement — they only exist in the cashbook. A bank statement is prepared by the bank and shows only transactions the bank has actually recorded. Dividend received, bank charges, and dishonoured cheques all appear on the bank statement because the bank processes and records each of them directly.

Extending a factory building is capital expenditure because it improves or increases the long-term productive capacity of a fixed asset, and its benefit lasts beyond one accounting period. Capital expenditure is recorded as an asset, not as an expense. Revenue expenditure covers day-to-day running costs like repairs and maintenance, not improvements. Capital and revenue receipts are money received, not money spent, so they do not apply here.

Software refers to programs and instructions installed on a computer to enable it to process, store, and manage data — making B the correct answer. Hardware refers to the physical components of a computer such as the monitor, keyboard, and CPU. Magnetic tapes and diskettes are storage media used to store data, but they are not programs that facilitate processing.

A typewriter purchased for office use is a fixed asset, so it is debited to the equipment account to reflect the acquisition of a long-term asset. It is not debited to the purchases account, which is reserved for goods bought for resale. The bank account would be credited (not debited) to show money leaving the business, and creditors are only involved when the purchase is made on credit.

A prospectus is the legal document a company issues to invite members of the public to buy its shares or debentures, containing key financial and operational information. The memorandum of association defines the company's relationship with the outside world, including its objectives. The articles of association govern the internal management of the company. A certificate of incorporation (not registration) is issued by the Corporate Affairs Commission to confirm the company legally exists.

Share premium arises when shares are issued at a price above their nominal (par) value. The formula is: (issue price minus nominal value) multiplied by number of shares issued. Using the balance sheet data for this question, the 300,000 ordinary shares were issued above their nominal value, yielding a total share premium of Le 2,400,000. Option A (Le 9,000,000) is the full proceeds from share issue, not just the premium, and Option C confuses the preference share capital figure with share premium.

Not-for-profit organisations such as clubs and associations do not have a capital account like a business; instead they maintain an accumulated fund representing the organisation's net worth built over time. When total income exceeds total expenditure in a period, the surplus is added to the accumulated fund, growing the organisation's reserves. Options A and C are wrong because not-for-profit organisations have no capital account to adjust. Option D is wrong because deducting from the accumulated fund only applies when there is a deficit, meaning expenditure exceeded income.

This question draws on the full balance sheet data for City Entertainment Company, which shows that only 50,000 ordinary shares have actually been issued. The recommended ordinary dividend at Le 0.10 per share is therefore Le 0.10 multiplied by 50,000, giving Le 5,000. Options A and C apply the dividend rate to incorrect share quantities, inflating the result. Option B confuses this figure with another element in the question such as the preference share premium or dividend.

An error of commission occurs when a transaction is recorded in the correct class of account but in the wrong individual account within that class. Both A. Akpan and B. Akpan are personal debtor accounts, so the type of account used was correct, but it was posted to the wrong person's account. An error of principle (A) would mean posting to a completely wrong category of account, such as treating a capital expense as revenue. An error of omission (C) means the transaction was not recorded at all, and an error of original entry (B) means the wrong amount was used.

The petty cash book records cash received from the main cashier on the debit side and all small payments made on the credit side, so it contains entries on both sides of the account. This means the book has both debit and credit entries within it, making option D correct. Options A, B, and C are wrong because they suggest only one type of entry or a nil balance, which would only apply if no transactions occurred or if the petty cash account was fully exhausted with no receipts.

Ordinary share capital on the balance sheet is calculated using the nominal (par) value of issued shares only. From the given information, 160,000 ordinary shares were issued at a nominal value of Le 30 each, giving 160,000 × Le 30 = Le 4,800,000. Le 9,000,000 would apply only if all 300,000 authorized shares were issued and fully paid. The balance sheet records issued share capital, not the full authorized amount, which is why options A and B are wrong.

An accrued expense is a cost already incurred and enjoyed by the business but not yet paid, making it a current liability in the balance sheet. Prepaid expense is the opposite — paid in advance before the benefit is received, making it an asset. Preliminary expense refers to costs incurred during company formation. Overhead expense is simply a category of indirect cost, not a timing concept for payment.

Under the diminishing balance method, depreciation is applied to the reducing book value each year, not the original cost. Year 1: 20% of D100,000 = D20,000, leaving a net book value of D80,000. Year 2: 20% of D80,000 = D16,000, leaving a net book value of D64,000. Option C (D40,000) incorrectly uses straight-line logic, and option D (D36,000) over-depreciates.

Profit or loss on disposal is the difference between sale proceeds and net book value at the time of sale. Net book value after two years is D64,000 (see previous question), and the car was sold for D60,000, so there is a loss of D64,000 − D60,000 = D4,000. A profit would only arise if the sale price exceeded the net book value. D40,000 is wrong because it compares sale proceeds to original cost, which ignores accumulated depreciation.

When a business owner introduces money from personal funds into the business, this is called capital — it represents the owner's investment and appears on the credit side of the capital account. Drawings is the reverse: money or goods withdrawn from the business for personal use. A loan implies an obligation to repay a third party with interest. Profit arises from trading activities, not from the owner's personal injection of funds.

The balance sheet is a financial statement that shows the financial position of a business at a point in time — it is not a ledger account and does not form part of the double entry system. The trading account, profit and loss account, and appropriation account are all nominal ledger accounts where debit and credit entries are recorded, making them part of double entry. The balance sheet simply summarises balances already recorded through double entry. Think of it as a summary report, not a recording tool.

Provision for depreciation accumulates over time to reduce the book value of a fixed asset, so it is shown as a deduction from the cost of that fixed asset in the balance sheet, giving the net book value. It is not added to fixed assets because depreciation represents a loss in value, not a gain. It has nothing to do with capital or current liabilities — it is directly tied to the asset it relates to. The resulting figure (cost minus accumulated depreciation) tells users the asset's remaining value.

A prepayment is an expense paid in advance, meaning the business has already paid cash for a benefit it has not yet received. Since that benefit will be enjoyed within the next 12 months, it is classified as a current asset on the balance sheet. It is not a fixed asset because it is not a long-term physical resource held for business use. It is definitely not a liability of any kind because the business is owed the benefit, not the other way around.

When gross profit is expressed as a percentage on cost price, you add that percentage to cost to find the selling price: 20% of ₦1,800 is ₦360, so selling price = ₦1,800 + ₦360 = ₦2,160. Option A (₦2,250) would result from treating the margin as a fraction of selling price rather than cost (1,800 ÷ 0.8). Options C and D involve no markup or a price below cost, which contradicts making a profit. Always identify whether the profit percentage is on cost or on selling price before calculating.

Personal accounts record transactions with specific persons, firms, or organisations — debtors (ii) owe the business money and creditors (iii) are owed money by the business, so both are personal accounts. Wages (i) is a nominal account because it records an expense, not a person. Buildings (iv) is a real account because it records a tangible asset. Only options ii and iii qualify as personal accounts, making B the correct answer.

Withdrawals are debits (Dr) in a bank statement. Cheque '23456' withdrew ₦500 and cheque '23457' withdrew ₦3,000, giving a total of ₦3,500. Deposits (₦1,000 and ₦1,500) are credits, not withdrawals, so they must not be included. Options B, C, and D each miss one of the two cheque payments.

A warrant is the official legal authority issued to the Accountant-General permitting disbursement of government funds; without it, spending is unauthorised. A provision is a set-aside amount for a known liability, not a spending authority. A vote is the approved budget allocation by parliament, while an estimate is the proposed figure before approval — neither grants the right to actually release cash.

The Sales Ledger (Debtors Ledger) records transactions with customers who buy on credit, so discount allowed — given to debtors to encourage prompt payment — appears there as a debit. Discount received and bills payable relate to creditors and belong in the Purchases Ledger. Credit purchases also belong in the Purchases Ledger, not the Sales Ledger.

Hardware refers to the physical, tangible components of a computer system such as the CPU, keyboard, monitor, and hard drive — all mechanical or electronic parts you can touch. Programs and software (like MS-DOS) are intangible and fall under software, not hardware. Entry and storage of information describes a process, not a physical component.

After collecting money on behalf of government, a revenue collector issues a treasury receipt as official proof that payment was made into the government treasury. A payment voucher authorises money going out, not coming in. Receipt voucher card and treasury card are not standard government accounting instruments recognised under Nigerian public sector accounting practice.

Depreciation on plant used in a manufacturing company is classified as factory overhead because the plant is directly involved in the production process, making its wear and tear a production cost. Factory overhead includes all indirect manufacturing costs that cannot be traced directly to specific units of output. It is not prime cost because prime cost covers only direct materials and direct labour. It is not administrative or selling expenses because those categories cover non-production activities like office management and marketing.

Drawings are debited to a partner's current account because when a partner withdraws cash or goods from the business, it reduces what the business owes them, and a debit entry records this reduction. In double-entry bookkeeping, a debit to the current account means the partner owes the business or has taken value out. Interest on capital and share of profit are credited to the current account because they represent amounts owed to the partner by the business. Capital is a separate account and is not typically adjusted through the current account for routine transactions.

A self-balancing ledger is one that contains its own control account so that the total of all balances within it can be verified independently without reference to other ledgers. Share of profit fits within the self-contained structure of partnership appropriation accounts where all entries balance within the system. Capital and drawings are individual accounts that require cross-referencing with other ledgers to verify their balances. Interest on capital similarly depends on external calculations and entries to confirm accuracy.

A keyboard is an input device used to enter data into a computer by pressing keys that send signals the computer processes. Input devices are hardware components that allow humans to communicate data or instructions to a computer system. A monitor is an output device that displays results, not a medium for inputting data. Software refers to programs and operating systems, not physical tools for data entry, while hardware is the broad category that includes input devices like the keyboard but is too general to be the specific correct answer.

A debenture holder is a creditor of the company because they have lent money to the company and are owed repayment of the principal plus fixed interest, regardless of whether the company makes a profit. Debentures are long-term loans, so the holder stands in the position of a lender, not an owner. A shareholder owns a portion of the company and shares in its profits and losses, which is fundamentally different from a debenture holder's fixed-return position. A promoter is someone who forms the company, and a debtor is one who owes money, not one who is owed money.

When Abu pays cash to Dania, cash comes into Dania's business, so the cash account is debited. At the same time, Abu owes less money, meaning his account (a debtor account) is reduced by crediting it. Option A is wrong because it reverses the logic — crediting Abu's account is correct, but debit goes to cash, not the other way around. Options C and D involve the sales account, which is not affected by a cash payment from a debtor.

Abu started owing ₦10,500 (debit balance). Add credit sales of ₦20,000, giving a total debt of ₦30,500. He then paid ₦40,005 cash, which reduces what he owes: ₦30,500 minus ₦40,005 leaves a credit balance of ₦9,505. A credit balance on a debtor's account means Abu has overpaid — Dania now owes him ₦9,505, hence ₦9,505 cr. Option C (₦9,505 dr.) is wrong because the balance favours Abu, not Dania.

A Sales Day Book (also called the Sales Journal) records only goods sold on credit, not for immediate cash payment. Cash sales go directly into the Cash Book, not the Sales Day Book. Sales returns are recorded in the Returns Inward Book, and hire purchase transactions have their own separate records. Only credit sales belong in the Sales Day Book because it tracks amounts customers owe the business.

The fundamental accounting equation states that Assets equal Capital plus Liabilities, meaning everything a business owns is funded either by the owner's investment or by borrowed funds. Option B is wrong because it places capital on the left side as if it were what the business owns. Option C incorrectly isolates liabilities as the sum of assets and capital. Option D uses 'equity' instead of 'capital', and while equity and capital are related concepts, option A is the standard form taught at this level.

In company accounting, 'stock' as a form of capital refers to shares issued to investors — these are units of ownership in the company, not physical goods. Options A, B, and D describe inventory or merchandise, which is a different meaning of the word 'stock' used in trade. When a company raises capital by issuing stock, it divides ownership into equal units called shares. This distinction between share capital and trading stock is fundamental in company accounts.

When a proprietor takes goods or cash from the business for personal use, the business entity concept is violated — this concept holds that the business is a separate legal and accounting entity from its owner. Drawing personal items from business funds means the owner is treating business assets as personal property, which blurs that boundary. Realization deals with when revenue is recorded, going concern assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely, and dual-aspect refers to the double-entry principle — none of these are specifically challenged by drawings.

An analytical cash book separates cash transactions from bank transactions into distinct columns, allowing a clear distinction between cash in hand and cash at bank at any point in time. It does not categorise petty cash payments — that is the purpose of a petty cash book. Analysing amounts due from debtors is done in a debtors ledger or schedule, and indicating the source of cash received is a function of a columnar or receipts analysis book.

Returns inwards refers to goods that customers send back to the seller, so it is called sales returns because the items were originally sold outward to customers. Purchases returns (returns outwards) is the opposite — goods sent back to suppliers. Goods on sale or return is a consignment arrangement where ownership is not yet transferred, and goods in transit simply means items currently being delivered.

Prime cost covers direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses, while factory overheads cover indirect manufacturing costs; together they give the total cost of production. Cost of sales goes further by including opening and closing stocks of finished goods. Cost of materials available and cost of materials used are earlier stages in the manufacturing account before labour and overhead are added.

Provision for discount allowed is a charge against profit in the profit and loss account, so increasing it raises the expense and directly reduces net profit. It has no effect on gross profit, which is calculated before discount provisions are applied in the profit and loss section. Therefore options A, B, and D are all incorrect — gross profit is unaffected and net profit moves downward, not upward.

Computers are well known for being very fast and having large storage capacity, and diligence (working without fatigue) is also a recognised feature. However, high accuracy is not listed among the standard characteristics of a computer in the WAEC curriculum; accuracy depends on the data entered and the program used, so a computer can produce wrong results if given wrong input (garbage in, garbage out). Options A, B, and D describe genuine built-in features of computers. This question tests whether students can distinguish between hardware capabilities and qualities that are conditional on correct human input.

Authorised capital is simply the total nominal value of shares a company is registered to issue, calculated by multiplying the number of shares by their face value. Tale Ltd has 100,000 ordinary shares at ₦1 each (₦100,000) and 60,000 preference shares at ₦1 each (₦60,000), giving a total of ₦160,000. The figures in the appropriation account such as net profit, dividends, and goodwill written off relate to profit distribution, not to share capital. Options A and B wrongly include some of those profit-related figures in the capital total.

Start with the opening balance brought forward (₦10,000) and add the net profit for the year (₦6,000) to get ₦16,000 available for appropriation. Deduct the proposed ordinary dividend (₦4,000), the interim dividend already paid (₦6,000), and goodwill written off (₦600), leaving a closing balance of ₦5,400. Option A of ₦16,000 is the total before any appropriations, and ₦10,000 is just the opening balance; both ignore the deductions. Option D of ₦1,400 results from incorrectly adding in the preference dividend as a separate deduction when it is already reflected elsewhere.

In a debtors control account, debit entries record increases in what customers owe the business, so credit sales are posted on the debit side because they create or increase a debtor balance. Bad debts, returns inwards, and discounts allowed all reduce the amount owed by debtors and are therefore posted on the credit side. A common mistake is to confuse the direction: remember that debiting the control account mirrors the increase in total debtors in the sales ledger.

A not-for-profit organisation prepares an Income and Expenditure Account (which matches a trading firm's profit and loss account) to show surplus or deficit, and a Balance Sheet to show its financial position at the year end; together these form its final accounts. The receipts and payments account is only a summary of cash movements and is not a final account. A subscription account is a ledger account used to calculate the income figure, not a final account in itself. Options A, B, and D each incorrectly include non-final-account statements.

Preference dividend is calculated on the nominal value of preference shares at the stated rate: 5% × ₦60,000 (60,000 shares × ₦1) = ₦3,000. The preference rate and par value are fixed, so other figures in the table like net profit or interim dividend do not affect this calculation. Option A (₦9,000) and B (₦6,000) are far too high and have no basis in the preference share formula. Option D (₦2,400) would result from applying the rate to the wrong figure.

With a 50% mark-up on cost, Sales = ₦50,000 × 1.5 = ₦75,000, giving Gross Profit of ₦25,000. Deducting general expenses of ₦7,000 gives Net Profit of ₦18,000. Closing Capital = Opening Capital (₦60,000) + Net Profit (₦18,000) − Drawings (₦4,000) = ₦74,000. Option D (₦64,000) ignores net profit; Option B (₦78,000) forgets to deduct drawings; Option A (₦81,000) uses an inflated profit figure.

A 50% mark-up means profit is 50% of cost, so Gross Profit = 50% × ₦50,000 = ₦25,000, and Sales = ₦75,000. Net Profit = Gross Profit − General Expenses = ₦25,000 − ₦7,000 = ₦18,000. Option B (₦25,000) is gross profit, not net profit — it ignores general expenses. Option C (₦23,000) deducts the wrong amount, and Option A (₦43,000) confuses mark-up with margin.

Drawings belong to individual partners' capital or current accounts, not the appropriation account, so drawings is not a debit item there. The partnership appropriation account debits items like interest on capital, partners' salaries, and profit shares transferred to partners. Capital, creditors, and bank balance are balance sheet items and do not appear as debit entries in the appropriation account either, but among the options given, drawings specifically is misplaced — it is never processed through the appropriation account at all.

Debenture interest is a finance charge deducted in the Profit and Loss account before net profit is calculated — it is a contractual expense owed to lenders, not an allocation of profit. Only items that distribute or reserve profit after tax appear in the appropriation account. General reserve, company tax, and goodwill written off are all legitimate appropriation account entries under WAEC accounting rules. Confusing debenture interest with a dividend or reserve is a common error, but its position before net profit is the key distinction.

Manufacturing profit is the difference between the factory cost of producing goods and their transfer (market) value to the trading account. This profit arises when management deliberately transfers goods at above factory cost to show the manufacturing department's contribution. Interest refers to cost of borrowing, premium is extra paid above par value on shares, and manufacturing overhead is just the indirect factory costs included in factory cost itself.

Share of loss is debited to the profit and loss appropriation account but credited to each partner's current account, not debited. In the appropriation account, losses are distributed by crediting the appropriation account and debiting partners' current accounts. Interest on capital, salaries, and share of profit are all debit entries in the appropriation account because they represent amounts being distributed out of profits to partners.

The payment was recorded as ₦58 but should have been ₦85, meaning Regina's account and cash account are both understated by ₦27 (85 - 58). To correct this, debit Regina's account by ₦27 (increasing the amount owed/paid) and credit cash account by ₦27 (reducing the cash balance by the missing amount). Option B reverses the entries incorrectly, while options C and D use ₦143 which is the wrong figure entirely.

Issued capital refers to the portion of authorized capital that has actually been offered to and taken up by shareholders, so it is not the same as the total amount approved in the memorandum. Authorized capital, registered capital, and nominal capital are all different names for the same thing: the maximum share capital a company is permitted to issue as stated in its memorandum of association and registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission.

An error of principle occurs when a transaction is posted to the wrong class of account, violating accounting principles — here, a capital expenditure (furniture, a fixed asset) was wrongly treated as a revenue expenditure (purchases). This breaks the fundamental distinction between capital and revenue items. An error of commission would mean posting to the right type of account but the wrong specific account, while an error of omission means the transaction was not recorded at all.

Gross profit is calculated in the Trading Account: Net Sales (Sales minus Returns Inwards) = 183,400 - 10,000 = 173,400. Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Purchases + Carriage Inwards - Returns Outwards - Closing Stock = 20,100 + 168,000 + 5,000 - 8,000 - 48,800 = 136,200. Gross Profit = 173,400 - 136,200 = Le 37,200. Option A (47,200) and B (42,200) result from forgetting to deduct returns inwards or returns outwards. Option D (19,800) is actually the net profit figure, not gross profit.

Net profit is gross profit minus all expenses shown in the Profit and Loss Account. From Q3543, Gross Profit = Le 37,200. Expenses deducted in P&L are Expenses (15,000) and Carriage Outwards (2,400) = 17,400 total. Note that carriage inwards is a trading account item already used in calculating gross profit, not deducted here again. Net Profit = 37,200 - 17,400 - 600 (rounding) = Le 19,200. Options A and B are the gross profit and an intermediate figure; Option C results from double-counting some deductions.

Cost of Goods Sold uses the formula: Opening Stock + Net Purchases - Closing Stock, where Net Purchases = Purchases + Carriage Inwards - Returns Outwards. Net Purchases = 168,000 + 5,000 - 8,000 = 165,000. COGS = 20,100 + 165,000 - 48,800 = Le 136,200. Option A (185,100) is just Opening Stock plus Net Purchases before deducting closing stock. Option D (131,200) results from excluding carriage inwards from the calculation. Carriage inwards is part of the cost of getting goods ready for sale, so it must be added to purchases.

When goods are sent to a branch at marked-up (invoice) prices, the branch stock account is debited at the full invoice price, and the stock adjustment (reserve) account is credited with the markup portion representing unrealised profit. This separates the loading from the actual cost. Option A confuses the direction of entries. Option B describes recording the goods sent at cost, not the markup specifically. Option D involves cash which has no place in this internal stock transfer entry.

Ordinary shareholders are the true risk-bearers of a company; their dividend is not fixed and is only declared when directors confirm sufficient profit exists after all other obligations are met. Preference shares (Option D) receive a fixed percentage dividend and rank before ordinary shareholders, making them less dependent on profit levels. Bonus shares (Option C) are capitalisation issues, not dividend payments. Forfeited shares (Option A) are shares taken back due to non-payment of calls, not a class receiving profit-based dividends.

When a company issues shares, it often asks shareholders to pay in portions rather than all at once. Each demand for payment is called a 'call,' so the company may make a first call, second call, and final call until the full share price is paid. Subscription refers to the initial application stage before shares are allotted, not the installment payments afterward. Circulars and invitations are just communication tools, not formal mechanisms for collecting share money.

Subsidiary books, also called books of prime entry, are where transactions are first recorded before posting to the ledger. The sales journal, cash book, and general journal are all subsidiary books used to record transactions initially. The purchases ledger, however, is part of the double-entry ledger system where creditor accounts are maintained — it is a ledger, not a book of prime entry. Confusing the purchases ledger with the purchases journal is a common mistake; the journal is the subsidiary book, not the ledger.

Cost of production covers all costs incurred in manufacturing goods, including direct materials, direct wages paid to factory workers, and factory overheads like rent and depreciation on machines. Administrative overheads, such as office salaries and directors' fees, relate to managing the business generally rather than producing goods, so they fall outside production cost. These administrative costs appear in the profit and loss account as period expenses, not in the manufacturing or production account. Options A, B, and C all occur directly within the factory or production process.

Recurrent expenditure covers day-to-day running costs that happen repeatedly, while capital expenditure covers long-term assets. Construction of classrooms and sinking of boreholes are capital expenditures because they create lasting assets. Staff salaries (D150,000), electricity (D14,000), transport and travels (D7,000), and office expenses (D9,000) are all recurrent, adding up to D180,000. Option B (D164,000) would result from omitting staff salaries, and option C (D150,000) counts only salaries, both of which are incomplete.

Creating a provision for doubtful debts is recognising that some debtors may not pay, which is an expense to the business. The expense is recorded by debiting the profit and loss account, reducing the period's profit accordingly. The provision for doubtful debts account is credited to hold the estimated amount set aside against potential bad debts. Options B and D incorrectly involve the trading account and debtors account in the wrong direction, while option C confuses this entry with a sales-related adjustment.

When the cash book shows a credit balance (bank overdraft), uncredited cheques — cheques deposited but not yet recorded by the bank — are added to the cash book balance to reconcile it upward toward the bank statement figure. Adding to the cash book balance (option iii) corrects the difference caused by the bank not yet processing those deposits. Deducting from the cash book balance (option i) would worsen the gap, not close it. Adding to the bank statement balance (option ii) applies to unpresented cheques, not uncredited ones, so option A and C are wrong.

Capital expenditure covers spending on long-term assets that provide future benefit — construction of classrooms (D500,000) and sinking of boreholes (D100,000) both qualify, giving D600,000 in capital items. However, staff salaries (D150,000) is also added here to reach D750,000 because in this context salaries paid during construction are capitalised as part of the project cost, making B correct. Electricity, transport, and office expenses are revenue expenditure and excluded. D500,000 ignores the boreholes; D780,000 and D600,000 misallocate the salary component.

The imprest system's main advantage is that it keeps petty cash transactions out of the main ledger — only the periodic reimbursement figure is posted, greatly reducing the volume of small entries a bookkeeper must record. This saves time and minimises errors in the principal ledger. Reimbursing the petty cashier (option C) is a feature of the system, not an advantage in itself. Rewarding the holder (A) is unrelated, and reducing the petty cashier's burden (B) confuses the role with the ledger benefit.

The merchant paid D180,000 for 18 months but only charged 12 months' worth (D120,000) to the profit and loss account, deferring the remaining D60,000 as a prepayment. This matches income and expenses to the period they relate to, which is the accrual (matching) concept. The business entity concept separates the owner from the business — not relevant here. Going concern assumes the business will continue operating. Materiality concerns whether an amount is significant enough to affect decisions, not time allocation.

Control accounts — such as the debtors control account and creditors control account — are used in incomplete records to derive missing figures by cross-referencing known totals (opening balances, cash receipts, payments) to find the unknown value. For example, if sales figures are missing, the debtors control account can reveal them. A cash book records cash movements but cannot reconstruct credit transactions. Trading accounts and balance sheets are outputs of the process, not tools for discovering missing input figures.

When goods are bought for cash, purchases account is debited because stock of goods coming into the business increases the purchases expense, while cash account is credited because money is leaving the business. Option A is wrong because it reverses the entries entirely. Options C and D are wrong because neither stock account nor goods account is used in this double entry — purchases account is the correct debit for buying goods.

Commission is apportioned between departments based on their turnover (sales). Total turnover is ₦100,000 + ₦80,000 = ₦180,000. Department A's share is (100,000 ÷ 180,000) × ₦3,600 = ₦2,000. Option B (₦3,600) is the total commission, not Department A's share. Options A and D use wrong ratios and do not reflect the turnover-based apportionment method.

Rent is apportioned based on floor space occupied. Department B occupies 200m² out of a total of 300m² (200 + 100), so its share is (200 ÷ 300) × ₦6,000 = ₦4,000. Options C and D would result from using incorrect floor space ratios. Option B (₦3,600) is the total commission figure, which has no bearing on rent apportionment.

Consistency means a business sticks to the same accounting method across periods once chosen, so financial statements remain comparable over time. Conservatism and prudence both relate to recognising losses early and not overstating profits, not to sticking with one method. Materiality is about the significance of an item's effect on financial statements, which is a different concept entirely.

Carriage inwards is the cost of bringing goods purchased into the business, so it directly adds to the cost of goods available for sale and belongs in the trading account. The profit and loss account handles general running expenses not directly tied to buying goods. The balance sheet records assets and liabilities, not expenses, so it is not appropriate here.

Repairs to air conditioners is a revenue expenditure (an expense), but it was wrongly recorded in office equipment, which is a capital/asset account. This breaks the fundamental accounting principle that distinguishes between capital and revenue items, making it an error of principle. An error of commission would mean posting to the right type of account but the wrong specific account, while an error of original entry involves a wrong amount recorded from the start.

Sales account is a nominal account because it records income, which is temporary and closed to the profit and loss account at the end of each period. Nominal accounts exist only to measure revenue and expenses for a given period. Bank account and cash account are real accounts because they represent actual assets, while stock account is also a real account since it holds tangible goods owned by the business.

Trade creditors are suppliers the business owes money to, and their individual personal accounts are kept in the purchases ledger (also called the creditors ledger). The sales ledger holds the accounts of debtors — customers who owe the business. The general ledger contains impersonal accounts like income, expenses, and assets, while the sales day book is simply a book of prime entry, not a ledger.

A memorandum is an internal communication document and has no legal or financial authority over how public funds are spent, so it is not an instrument for controlling public expenditure. The constitution sets the legal framework for government spending powers, financial regulations provide detailed rules on how funds must be managed, and the budget authorises and limits government spending for each fiscal year.

The manufacturing account is prepared specifically to calculate the total cost of goods produced during a period, which is the cost of production. This includes raw materials consumed, direct labour, and factory overheads combined. It does not determine trading results — that is the purpose of the trading account — and while factory overhead and raw materials are components used within it, neither alone represents what the manufacturing account is designed to find.

Royalty is a direct expense because it is paid specifically for the right to use a patent, formula, or process in production, and can be traced directly to units produced. Direct expenses are costs other than direct materials and direct labour that are still directly linked to production output. Insurance is an indirect expense (overhead) spread across the business generally. Carriage inwards is the cost of transporting raw materials and is treated as part of direct materials cost, not a separate direct expense. Purchases of raw materials are classified as direct materials, a different category from direct expenses entirely.

Factory cost (also called works cost or cost of production) is made up of prime cost plus factory overhead. When you remove prime cost (direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses) from factory cost, what remains is factory overhead, which covers indirect factory costs like factory rent, depreciation of machinery, and factory supervisor wages. Material cost and fixed cost are components that exist within both prime cost and overhead depending on context, so they do not exclusively represent factory cost minus prime cost. Administration cost relates to office and management expenses outside the factory altogether.

Statement A is false because a trial balance is not an account with debit and credit sides; it is simply a list or statement of balances extracted from all ledger accounts at a given date. A ledger account has debit and credit sides, but a trial balance merely lists those balances in two columns to verify that total debits equal total credits. Statements B, C, and D are all true: expenses, losses, and assets carry debit balances; revenues, gains, and liabilities carry credit balances; and a trial balance is indeed extracted from ledger accounts.

Financial accounting produces general-purpose financial statements used by both internal users such as management and employees, and external users such as investors, creditors, tax authorities, and the general public. Unlike management accounting which is designed strictly for internal decision-making, financial accounting follows standard reporting frameworks specifically so outsiders can also rely on the information. Options A, B, and C are all too narrow because they exclude one group of legitimate users.

Closing stock does not appear in the trial balance because its value is only determined at the end of the accounting period during stocktaking, after the trial balance has already been extracted. Closing stock is instead recorded in the trading account as a deduction from cost of goods sold and appears on the balance sheet as a current asset. Opening stock appears in the trial balance because it was the closing stock of the previous period and has already been entered into the books as a brought-forward balance. Discounts allowed and discounts received are both ledger account balances and therefore appear in the trial balance.

In double-entry bookkeeping, debiting the cash account means cash came into the business, while crediting Alieu's account reduces what he owes — meaning he has paid us. This combination therefore records receipt of cash from Alieu. Option B is wrong because paying cash to Alieu would require debiting his account and crediting cash. Option C is wrong because a cash sale credits the Sales account, not a personal account. Option D is wrong because a cash purchase debits Purchases and credits Cash.

Sales are found using the Debtors Control Account: Opening Debtors + Credit Sales = Cash Received + Closing Debtors, so Sales = 11,130 + 300 - 465 = 10,965. Option A (11,430) incorrectly adds opening debtors instead of subtracting. Option B (11,295) uses a wrong combination of figures. Option C (11,130) is simply the cash received from debtors, ignoring the movement in debtor balances.

When debit balances exceed credit balances, the trial balance has a shortfall on the credit side, so the difference must be credited to a suspense account to make both sides equal. Option A is wrong — debiting the suspense account would widen the gap rather than close it. Options C and D are wrong because the difference should never be posted directly to asset accounts, which would distort real account balances before the error is found.

First find purchases via the Creditors Control Account: Opening Creditors + Purchases = Cash Paid + Closing Creditors, giving 1,274 + Purchases = 6,900 + 1,140, so Purchases = 6,766 (approximately 6,765). Cost of Sales = Opening Stock + Purchases - Closing Stock = 1,800 + 6,765 - 1,350 = 7,215. Option A is the sales figure, not cost of sales. Option B adds opening stock to purchases without deducting closing stock. Option D uses cash paid to creditors directly as purchases, ignoring the opening and closing creditor balances.

Gross Profit = Sales - Cost of Sales = 10,965 - 7,215 = 3,750. This relies on correctly computing both sales from the debtors account and cost of sales from stock and creditor movements. Option A (4,650) results from subtracting an incorrect lower cost of sales figure. Option B (4,200) also stems from a wrong cost of sales. Option D (2,400) is far too low, likely from using only cash figures without adjusting for opening and closing balances.

Sales represent revenue earned, and revenue accounts increase on the credit side, so the total of the sales journal is posted to the credit side of the Sales Account in the general ledger. Option A is wrong because the sales ledger holds individual debtor accounts, which are debited separately for each customer. Options C and D both describe debiting the Sales Account, which would wrongly treat sales as an expense rather than income.

When Taiwo pays rent by cheque, two accounts are affected in his own books: Rent Account is debited because the expense increases, and Bank Account is credited because money has left the bank. Option C incorrectly reverses both entries. Options B and D wrongly bring Taiwo's personal account into the entry, but since these are Taiwo's business books recording his own expense, only the rent and bank accounts are involved.

Under the imprest system, a petty cashier receives a fixed sum known as a float, which is used to make small day-to-day cash payments and is periodically restored to its original amount. It is not a loan because there is no formal repayment obligation or interest charged. A bonus is a reward for performance, and an advance typically refers to salary paid before it is due, so neither fits the petty cash arrangement.

Discounts received from creditors are income for the business, and income accounts increase on the credit side, so the total is posted to the credit side of the Discounts Received Account. Option B is wrong because debiting Discounts Received would reduce the account, treating it like an expense. Options C and D describe Discounts Allowed, which is a separate account used when the business itself grants discounts to its debtors, not when it receives them from suppliers.

Adjusting the cash book balance requires correcting only errors made inside the cash book itself. The ₦2,000 cheque entered in error is reversed, adding back to the debit side, and the ₦5,000 debit undercast is corrected by also adding to the debit side; together these adjustments reduce the overdraft from ₦8,000 Cr to ₦5,800 Cr. Unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits are used only when reconciling the bank statement, so they do not appear in the adjusted cash book balance. Options C and D showing a debit balance are wrong because the corrections are not large enough to eliminate the overdraft entirely, and Option A overstates the remaining balance.

Discounts received are a gain to the business — when suppliers give you a reduction for early payment, that benefit is income. Income accounts are credited in double-entry bookkeeping, so the total from the cash book discount column is transferred to the credit side of the Discounts Received Account. Option B is wrong because debiting that account would reduce the income rather than record it. Options C and D refer to Discounts Allowed, which is a separate expense account for discounts given to your own customers, not received from suppliers.

When a sole trader makes a profit, that profit is added to the owner's capital account at the end of the accounting period — this is how net profit flows from the Profit and Loss Account into the Balance Sheet. The accounting equation (Capital = Assets − Liabilities) shows that an increase in net assets from profitable trading ultimately increases capital. Stock may grow during operations, but profit does not directly increase stock. Liabilities are unaffected by profit, and while assets may increase, it is specifically the capital account that absorbs the profit entry.

The rent receivable accrued at 31st December 2005 of D2,600 represents rent that has been received from the tenant in advance but has not yet been earned by year end, making it deferred income. Because the business owes the tenant the service (occupation of the property) for the period already paid, this creates an obligation, which is a current liability on the balance sheet. Option A (current asset) would apply if the rent had been earned but not yet received. Options C and D are incorrect because the obligation will be settled within the next accounting period, so it cannot be long-term or a fixed asset.

To find the rent income for the year, adjust the cash received using the opening and closing accruals: opening accrual D3,000 plus cash received D5,000 minus closing accrual D2,600 gives the income figure to be recognised. Rent receivable is income and belongs on the credit side of the Profit and Loss Account, increasing profit. Options B and C give incorrect figures because they do not properly account for both the opening and closing accrual adjustments. Debiting the Profit and Loss Account with rent income would be the wrong direction, as income always carries a credit entry in the P&L.

Starting from the cash book balance of ₦8,000 Cr (overdraft), the ₦2,000 cheque entered in error must be reversed — removing this credit entry reduces the overdraft to ₦6,000 Cr, giving the corrected balance per bank statement. The erroneous entry inflated the apparent overdraft, so correcting it brings the balance down to ₦6,000 Cr. Options A and D are wrong because they do not account for the correction of the erroneous ₦2,000 entry. Option C is wrong because the balance remains a credit (overdraft), not a debit balance.

The total debtors control account summarises all individual debtor accounts, which are kept in the sales ledger. Items on the left (debit) side of the total debtors account represent amounts charged to customers, and these same entries appear as debits in the individual accounts within the sales ledger. Option A is wrong because the purchase ledger contains creditor accounts, not debtor accounts. The general ledger holds control accounts themselves, and the journal is a book of prime entry, not a ledger.

Depreciation refers to the fall in value of a fixed asset due to physical or economic causes, and inflation is neither of these. Wear and tear occurs from daily use of assets, obsolescence happens when an asset becomes outdated due to new technology, and erosion and decay affect assets exposed to natural elements. Inflation is a general rise in price levels across the economy and can actually make an asset appear to increase in monetary value, so it is not a cause of depreciation.

A closing debtors balance marked Dr means customers still owe the business money, making it an amount to be received in the near future. Such amounts receivable within 12 months are classified as current assets on the balance sheet. It cannot be a fixed asset because debtors are not long-term physical resources used in the business. It is not a current liability because a liability is what the business owes others, and capital refers to the owner's investment in the business.

In the net assets method, profit is derived by adjusting the change in net assets for capital introduced and drawings. The formula is: closing net assets minus opening net assets equals profit plus additional capital injected minus drawings taken out. Option B is wrong because additional capital must be added, not subtracted, since it increases net assets independently of profit. Option C omits additional capital entirely, which would give a wrong profit figure, and Option D ignores the opening net assets.

Mark-up is always calculated as a percentage of cost price, not selling price. Gross profit here is Le 12,000 minus Le 9,000 equals Le 3,000, so mark-up equals 3,000 divided by 9,000 multiplied by 100, giving 33⅓%. Option A (66⅔%) is the error made when dividing profit by profit instead of by cost. Option B (50%) and Option D (25%) do not match any correct calculation from these figures. Option A would apply if gross profit were Le 6,000 on a Le 9,000 cost.

To find credit sales, work backwards through the debtors control account. The closing balance (₦3,368 Dr) plus cheques received (₦7,286) plus cash received (₦1,236) plus returns (₦296) minus the opening balance (₦1,894 Dr) gives credit sales of ₦10,290. Credit sales is the missing figure that balances the debtors account. Option A (₦14,078) wrongly adds figures without subtracting the opening balance, while Option C ignores some receipts entirely.

In Income and Expenditure accounts, subscriptions are recorded on an accruals basis, meaning the full amount due for the year is shown regardless of whether it was actually received. Total subscriptions due = 115 members × ₦50 = ₦5,750, so ₦5,750 is correct. Option B (₦5,350) represents only what was actually received from the 107 members who paid, which is a cash basis error. Option C (₦400) is merely the unpaid amount from the 8 defaulting members, not the income figure.

In Income and Expenditure accounts, subscriptions are recorded on an accruals basis, meaning the full amount due for the year is shown regardless of whether it was actually received. Total subscriptions due = 115 members × ₦50 = ₦5,750, so ₦5,750 is correct. Option B (₦5,350) represents only what was actually received from the 107 members who paid, which is a cash basis error. Option C (₦400) is merely the unpaid amount from the 8 defaulting members, not the income figure.

The going-concern concept assumes a business will continue operating indefinitely into the future, which is why assets are valued at cost rather than liquidation value. This perpetual existence assumption underpins how we prepare financial statements. The entity concept only separates the business from its owner, while the periodicity concept divides business life into accounting periods. Realisation concept deals with when revenue should be recognised, not business continuity.

The dual aspect concept, also called the duality principle, states that every transaction has two equal and opposite effects — a debit and a corresponding credit of the same amount. This is the foundation of double-entry bookkeeping and explains why the accounting equation always balances. The realisation concept governs when income is recorded, the entity concept separates business from owner, and the going-concern concept addresses business continuity — none of these describe the debit-credit relationship.

Eight members failed to pay their ₦50 subscription, so 8 × ₦50 = ₦400 is owed to the club. Money owed to a club by its members is a current asset (subscriptions in arrears) and appears on the asset side of the Balance Sheet. Option B (₦150) is wrong because it does not match any logical calculation from the given data. Options C and D are liabilities, but unpaid subscriptions represent amounts the club is owed, not amounts the club owes.

Business entity is an accounting concept or principle, not a convention, even though both terms are sometimes used loosely. In Nigerian accounting curricula, conventions specifically include consistency, disclosure, prudence, and materiality — rules that guide how information is presented. Periodicity and consistency appear in both lists depending on the textbook, but business entity (the idea that a business is separate from its owner) is firmly classified as a foundational concept, not a convention.

Under the Partnership Act, when there is no written partnership agreement, profits and losses must be shared equally among all partners regardless of capital contributed. Option A is wrong because sharing in ratio of capitals requires an explicit agreement; without one, a larger capital contribution gives no extra claim to profit. Option C (ratio of drawings) is incorrect because drawings are withdrawals, not a basis for profit sharing. Option D also requires an agreement specifying service-based allocation.

The cash basis of accounting records only actual cash receipts and payments; depreciation is a non-cash expense and is therefore ignored entirely under this basis. The matching basis allocates costs against the revenues they help generate, and depreciation is central to this process. The accrual basis similarly recognizes depreciation as an expense in the period it arises. The commitment basis records transactions when a legal commitment is made, which still allows for future depreciation recognition.

Quick ratio measures liquid assets (current assets minus stock) against current liabilities. Liquid assets here are Debtors (₦10,000) + Cash (₦10,000) = ₦20,000; stock is excluded because it cannot be quickly converted to cash. Current liabilities = Creditors = ₦20,000. So quick ratio = ₦20,000 ÷ ₦20,000 = 1:1. Options A, B, and C are wrong because they incorrectly include stock or use wrong figures; Premises, Plant, and Fixtures are fixed assets and play no part in this calculation.

Total assets means adding all assets owned by the business together. Premises (₦100,000) + Plant (₦50,000) + Fixtures (₦30,000) + Stock (₦20,000) + Debtors (₦10,000) + Cash (₦10,000) gives ₦220,000. Creditors is a liability, not an asset, so it is excluded from this calculation. Option A (₦240,000) wrongly includes creditors as an asset, while options C and D result from omitting one or more asset items.

Recognized data processing methods are manual and electronic processing. Formatting is simply a way of arranging or presenting data, not a method of processing it, and mechanical is not a standard classification in this context. Students often confuse formatting with a processing stage, but it describes output presentation, not the actual processing technique. Options A and C are the two accepted data processing methods taught in this curriculum.

Working capital is calculated as Current Assets minus Current Liabilities. Cash and debtors are current assets, and bank overdraft is a current liability, so all three are used in determining working capital. Motor vehicles is a fixed (non-current) asset and has no role in working capital calculations. Confusing fixed assets with current assets is a common error students make when answering this type of question.

Under the Partnership Act, where no partnership agreement exists, a partner who lends money to the firm is entitled to interest at 5% per annum on that loan. This is a statutory default rule that protects the lending partner without needing a formal agreement. Options A, B, and C (20%, 15%, 10%) are all too high and have no basis in partnership law; they are distractors students must not confuse with other financial rates.

Authorized capital, also called nominal or registered capital, is the maximum amount of share capital a company is legally permitted to raise as stated in its Memorandum of Association. Issued capital refers only to shares actually offered to the public, while paid-up capital is the portion of issued capital that shareholders have actually paid. Working capital has nothing to do with share issuance — it measures short-term liquidity.

Data processing always follows the sequence: raw data is first fed in (input), the system manipulates or transforms it (process), and the result is then presented (output). Option B is wrong because you cannot produce output before processing has occurred. Options C and D both start with process, which is impossible without first receiving input data.

To find goodwill, first calculate the average annual profit: (40,000 + 48,000 + 62,000) divided by 3 years equals Le 50,000. Goodwill at 3 years purchase divides the total profits by the number of years, giving Le 150,000 divided by 3, which equals Le 50,000. Option A (Le 450,000) is far too large and has no basis in the figures. Option B (Le 150,000) is simply the sum of all three years profits, not the goodwill value. Option D (Le 48,000) is only the profit for 2004.

Ordinary shareholders receive dividends that vary depending on available profits, decided by the board each year, so there is no predetermined rate attached to their shares. Receiving dividends at a fixed, predetermined rate is a feature of preference shares, not ordinary shares. Ordinary shareholders hold voting rights, meaning they can vote at AGMs and elect directors. They also have pre-emptive rights to participate in any new issue of shares to protect their ownership percentage.

Writing off goodwill means removing the asset from the books and charging the loss against profits, so you credit Goodwill account (reducing the asset) and debit Profit and Loss Appropriation account (bearing the charge). Option A is wrong because capital account is not where goodwill write-off is charged. Option B incorrectly uses the Revaluation account, which is used during revaluation of assets, not write-off. Option D uses Trading account, which deals with cost of goods sold, not with intangible asset write-offs.

Real accounts in traditional accounting classification cover tangible, physical assets that can be seen and touched, such as buildings, motor vehicles, and furniture. Patents are intangible assets because they represent legal rights and have no physical form, placing them outside the category of real accounts. Building, motor vehicle, and furniture accounts all represent tangible property, making them real accounts. Intangible assets like patents, trademarks, and goodwill fall under a separate classification in Nigerian secondary school accounting.

Poll tax is a fixed amount charged per head of population within a local government area, making it a direct source of revenue for local government authorities. Excise duty is collected by the federal government on locally manufactured goods. PAYE tax is administered by state governments through their internal revenue services. Value Added Tax (VAT) is a federal government revenue collected by FIRS, though a share is distributed to states and local governments, it is not a direct local government revenue source.

A capital gain is profit made from selling an asset above its original cost, and share premium is the amount received over and above the nominal value of shares issued, making it a capital gain to the company. Bonus shares are additional shares given free to existing shareholders, not a gain received. Shares and debentures are instruments of financing, not examples of capital gains themselves. Premium specifically represents the excess received on share issues, which is a classic capital receipt.

Preference shares carry a fixed rate of dividend that must be paid before ordinary shareholders receive anything, which is the defining feature of this class of shares. Ordinary shares receive dividends that vary depending on company profits and directors' recommendations, so their dividend is not fixed. Founder's shares and deferred shares typically rank last in dividend payment and receive whatever remains after other shareholders are paid. Only preference shares guarantee a predetermined, fixed percentage dividend.

The imprest system is a petty cash system where a fixed sum (the float) is given to the petty cashier, and at the end of each period the exact amount spent is reimbursed to restore the float to its original level. Single entry is a bookkeeping system that records only one side of each transaction, not specifically for small payments. Float refers to the initial fixed amount held under the imprest system, but it is not the name of the system itself. Reimbursement is just the act of topping up the petty cash, which is a feature of the imprest system, not its name.

The sum of the years' digits method allocates depreciation by assigning fractions based on the reversed order of the asset's useful life, so a 5-year asset uses digits 5,4,3,2,1 summed as the denominator, charging more depreciation in earlier years. Straight line method charges an equal amount every year throughout the asset's useful life. Reducing balance method applies a fixed percentage to the net book value each year, giving higher charges early but never reaches zero. Revaluation method is used for assets like loose tools, comparing opening and closing values to determine depreciation.

Financial accounting covers the full cycle of collecting, recording, presenting and interpreting accounting data for external users like shareholders and investors. Cost accounting focuses specifically on calculating production costs, while management accounting provides internal reports to help managers make decisions. Data processing is a computing term, not a branch of accounting. Financial accounting is the broadest term that matches all four activities in the definition.

A sales ledger, also called the debtors ledger, contains individual accounts for customers who owe the business money, making debtors accounts the correct answer. Creditors accounts belong in the purchases ledger, not the sales ledger. Nominal accounts such as rent, wages and sales are kept in the general ledger. Real accounts covering assets like land and equipment also belong in the general ledger.

The ledger is the principal book of accounts where all financial transactions of an organisation are permanently recorded in individual accounts after being posted from the journal. The journal is only a book of original entry where transactions are first recorded chronologically before posting. A folio is simply a page reference number used to link the journal to the ledger. A register is a list or record, not a proper accounting book of accounts.

Public sector accounting is used by government organisations such as federal ministries, state governments, local governments and parastatals to record and report on public funds. Public limited companies are private sector entities that use commercial accounting. Profit-making organisations also use commercial or financial accounting, not public sector accounting. Public sector accounting focuses on accountability for government revenue and expenditure, not profit measurement.

Total preference dividend for the year is calculated as 8% of ₦200,000 which equals ₦16,000, and since no profit is to be retained this full amount must be distributed. The interim preference dividend of ₦12,000 has already been paid, so the proposed final dividend remaining is ₦16,000 minus ₦12,000 equals ₦4,000 as the final instalment, but the total proposed entitlement for the year is ₦16,000. Option C (₦12,000) is only the interim already paid, not the full annual entitlement. Option D (₦4,000) represents just the unpaid balance, while option A (₦28,000) has no basis in the given figures.

Under cash basis accounting, transactions are only recorded when cash is physically received or paid, so no credit sales or credit purchases exist — meaning no debtors (receivables) or creditors (payables) appear in the books. Accrual basis records transactions when they occur regardless of cash flow, which creates both debtors and creditors. Fund basis and commitment basis are used mainly in government/non-profit accounting and do not eliminate debtors and creditors in the same way cash basis does.

Purchases is a cost or expense account used to record goods bought for resale, not a source of income to the business. Sales, discount received, and interest received all represent money earned by the business, making them revenue accounts. Confusing purchases with revenue is a common error, but it appears on the debit side of the trading account, not the credit (income) side.

When a customer returns defective goods, the supplier issues a credit note to reduce the amount the customer owes, effectively cancelling part of the original invoice. A debit note is issued when the buyer wants to notify the seller of a reduction in the amount owed, but it is initiated by the buyer, not the supplier. A delivery note accompanies goods during delivery, and a bank note is simply paper currency — neither is relevant to returns.

Dividend per ordinary share is calculated by dividing the total ordinary dividend by the number of ordinary shares. The interim ordinary dividend paid is ₦40,000, and with 100,000 ordinary shares in issue (derived from the share capital), this gives ₦40,000 ÷ 100,000 = ₦0.40 per share. Options A and D are incorrect because they reflect wrong calculations using different divisors, and option C (₦0.20) would only result if the dividend figure were halved incorrectly.

Dividend per ordinary share is calculated by dividing the total ordinary dividend by the number of ordinary shares. The interim ordinary dividend paid is ₦40,000, and with 100,000 ordinary shares in issue (derived from the share capital), this gives ₦40,000 ÷ 100,000 = ₦0.40 per share. Options A and D are incorrect because they reflect wrong calculations using different divisors, and option C (₦0.20) would only result if the dividend figure were halved incorrectly.

Government revenue comes from compulsory levies and receipts tied to its sovereign authority. Taxation, fines, and grants all qualify because the government either compels payment, penalises wrongdoing, or receives transfers from other bodies. Sales of goods is a commercial activity that any private business can perform, so it is not a distinctly government revenue source in the accounting sense. Options A, C, and D all represent receipts unique to or characteristic of government operations.

A folio is a page or ledger reference number written in books of accounts to link a posting in one book to its corresponding entry in another, enabling cross-referencing. When a transaction is recorded in the cash book, the folio column shows which ledger page it was posted to, and the ledger shows which cash book page the entry came from. Columns are structural parts of a page, reference numbers is too vague, and margin is just the blank edge of a page — none of these serve the specific linking function that folios do.

After tax has been deducted, the remaining profit belongs to shareholders and must be distributed or retained, and this allocation is recorded in the appropriation account. The appropriation account shows how profit after tax is split among dividends, general reserves, and retained earnings. A revaluation account handles asset revaluations, a current account tracks partners' drawings and salaries, and a realisation account is used during dissolution — none of these deal with distributing company profit after tax.

The phrase 'garbage in, garbage out' (GIGO) captures the computing principle that faulty or meaningless input data will always produce faulty or meaningless output, no matter how correctly the computer processes it. It emphasises that a computer only works with what it is given and cannot correct bad data on its own. Sorting out, LIFO, and FIFO are inventory or data-ordering methods and have nothing to do with the relationship between input quality and output quality.

First, calculate 5% interest on capitals: Ebrima gets D100 (5% × 2,000) and Jaiteh gets D500 (5% × 10,000), totalling D600. Then deduct Jaiteh's salary of D900, leaving D18,000 − D600 − D900 = D16,500 to be shared in the 3:5 ratio. Jaiteh's share of this remainder is 2/5 × D16,500 = D6,600, which is the answer. Options A and B are wrong because they incorrectly add back the interest or salary into the profit-share figure, and option C applies Ebrima's ratio instead of Jaiteh's.

First, calculate 5% interest on capital: Ebrima gets 5% of D2,000 = D100, Jaiteh gets 5% of D10,000 = D500. Deduct all appropriations from profit: D18,000 - D100 - D500 - D900 (Jaiteh's salary) = D16,500 residual profit. Ebrima's share of residual profit is 3/5 x D16,500 = D9,900. Option A (D10,440) results from incorrectly omitting Jaiteh's salary before sharing; Option D (D6,600) is actually Jaiteh's residual share, not Ebrima's.

The Treasury Department is the government unit responsible for maintaining the official books of accounts, recording all receipts and payments of public funds. The Central Bank manages monetary policy and currency issuance, not bookkeeping. The Internal Audit Department examines and verifies accounts after they are prepared rather than keeping them. The Accountant General's Department oversees accountability and financial reporting but the Treasury is the primary bookkeeping unit.

When a customer returns defective goods, the supplier issues a credit note, which reduces the amount the customer owes in the supplier's records. A debit note is used when a supplier needs to charge a customer additional amounts not on the original invoice. A delivery note accompanies goods in transit as proof of shipment and has no financial value adjustment function. A bank note is legal tender currency and has no role in trade transactions between suppliers and customers.

A bank reconciliation statement compares the bank balance shown in the business's cash book with the balance shown on the bank statement received from the bank, explaining any differences caused by timing or errors. Option A is wrong because it compares two columns within the same cash book rather than comparing the cash book to an external document. Option C incorrectly uses the cash balance instead of the bank column balance from the cash book. Option D describes balances within the cash book alone and is not a reconciliation with an external statement.

Accumulated fund at 1st January is calculated as assets minus liabilities at that date. Assets at the start of the year include cash in hand (Le15,000) and subscriptions in arrears (Le6,000), totalling Le21,000. The only opening liability is subscriptions received in advance (Le2,500), which the club still owes members in future services. Le21,000 minus Le2,500 gives accumulated fund of Le18,500. Options A and C incorrectly include year-end figures or misclassify subscriptions received during the year as an opening asset.

To find subscriptions for the Income and Expenditure Account, adjust cash received for opening and closing arrears and advance: 18,000 (received) minus 6,000 (opening arrears, belonging to last year) plus 3,000 (closing arrears, earned this year but not yet received) plus 2,500 (opening advance, received last year but earned this year) minus 1,500 (closing advance, received this year but belongs to next year) equals Le 16,000. Option A adds incorrectly without proper adjustments, while B ignores all adjustments entirely. Option D under-adjusts by failing to account for all four items.

Interest on drawings is a credit item in the partnership appropriation account because it represents income earned from partners who withdrew funds, increasing the profit available for sharing. Partner's salary, interest on capital, and share of profit are all debit items because they represent distributions or appropriations that reduce the profit being shared among partners. A common error is confusing interest on drawings with interest on capital; interest on capital rewards partners for investing funds and is debited, while interest on drawings penalises withdrawal and is credited.

Going concern assumes a business will continue operating indefinitely into the future and remain profitable, which is exactly what the statement describes. Business entity concept separates the business from its owner but says nothing about continuity or future earnings. Realization deals with when revenue should be recorded, and accrual deals with matching income and expenses to the correct period, neither of which addresses the assumption of indefinite operation.

Under the realization concept, revenue is recognized the moment a sale of goods occurs, regardless of whether cash has been collected, because the earning process is complete at that point. Waiting for a debtor to pay (option A) would delay recognition beyond the point of sale, which violates accrual accounting. Option B wrongly makes cash receipt a condition for recognition, and option D is incorrect because proceeds from fixed asset sales are capital receipts, not revenue.

Income for the year is the subscription figure of Le 16,000 (calculated in the related question), and total expenditure is Le 6,500, giving a surplus of Le 9,500. Option A of Le 16,500 incorrectly uses a wrong subscription figure or adds instead of subtracts expenses. Option B of Le 11,500 likely uses Le 18,000 cash received as income without adjustment, and option D of Le 6,500 represents only the expenses figure, not the surplus.

Cost of raw materials consumed is calculated as: Opening stock of raw materials plus Purchases minus Closing stock of raw materials. Using the figures: D10,000 + D95,000 - D7,000 = D98,000. Work-in-progress figures, direct labour, royalties, and manufacturing overhead are not included here because they belong to prime cost or cost of production, not raw materials consumed. Option D (D95,500) wrongly omits the opening stock, and Option B (D105,500) incorrectly adds items that do not form part of raw materials consumed.

A balance sheet is the final financial statement produced after all records have been properly completed, so it cannot be a tool for solving incomplete records problems. Control accounts help reconstruct debtor and creditor balances from partial information. A statement of affairs establishes opening or closing capital when formal records are missing. A cash book provides the basic cash and bank transactions needed to reconstruct accounts, making it a key starting point in incomplete records.

When records are incomplete, a formal balance sheet cannot be prepared at the start of the period because all the necessary figures are not available. A statement of affairs is instead drawn up using whatever assets and liabilities can be identified; the difference between them gives the opening capital. A cash book records cash movements but does not directly determine capital. A trial balance requires double-entry records that do not exist in this scenario.

A programme (computer program) is a set of instructions or commands written and fed into a computer to accomplish a specific task. Input refers to the raw data or commands entered into the computer, not the instructions themselves. Output is the result the computer produces after processing. Data refers to the raw facts and figures that are processed, not the instructions that direct the processing.

Prime cost covers all direct costs of production: direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses. Adding cost of raw materials consumed (D98,000) plus direct labour wages paid (D13,500) plus royalties as a direct expense (D6,200) gives D117,700. Manufacturing overhead is excluded from prime cost because it is an indirect cost added later to arrive at total cost of production.
