Option A (D120,500) incorrectly includes accrued wages of D2,800, and Option D (D114,300) wrongly excludes royalties.

Cost of goods manufactured combines all factory costs plus the change in work-in-progress. Raw materials consumed = 10,000 + 95,000 - 7,500 = 97,500; direct labour = 13,500 + 2,800 accrued = 16,300; adding royalties 6,200 and manufacturing overhead 10,000 gives total factory cost of 130,000. Adding opening work-in-progress (16,000) and subtracting closing work-in-progress gives D138,000. Options B and C ignore either accrued wages or the work-in-progress adjustments; option D omits manufacturing overhead entirely.

Creditors control account records what a business owes suppliers; debit entries reduce that liability. Paying cash (A), returning goods outwards (B), and receiving discounts (D) all reduce what is owed, so they appear on the debit side. Purchases on credit increase the liability and are recorded on the credit side, making C the item that does not belong as a debit entry. Students often confuse this because purchases are debited in the purchases account, but in the creditors control account the entry is opposite.

The trading account deals only with the direct cost of buying or producing goods for resale; carriage inwards is the transport cost of bringing purchased goods to the warehouse, so it is added to the cost of purchases in the trading account. Discounts allowed (A), carriage outwards (B), and salaries (C) are all indirect expenses that appear in the profit and loss account. A common mistake is confusing carriage inwards with carriage outwards; outwards is a selling expense, inwards is a buying cost.

Control accounts earn the name total accounts because each one shows the grand total of all the individual accounts held in a subsidiary ledger, acting as a check on those records. Contra accounts (A) refer to accounts that offset each other, such as sales returns against sales. Ledger accounts (C) is too broad a term covering all accounts. Integral accounts (D) describe a system where cost and financial accounts are merged, which is a different concept entirely.

Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is calculated on the net book value brought forward, not original cost. After 2002, the net book value of the original vehicle is 1,000,000 minus 100,000 = 900,000; the 600,000 addition joins the pool in 2003, giving a total base of 1,500,000, and 10% of that equals 150,000. Option A (160,000) over-calculates; options C (130,000) and D (120,000) either ignore the addition or time-apportion it to half the year, which WAEC does not require here. Full-year depreciation is charged on all assets in the pool at the start of each year including new additions.

Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is calculated as a percentage of the asset's book value at the start of each year. Since the motor vehicle was purchased on 1/1/2002, the full cost of N1,000,000 is the opening book value for the entire year. Ten percent of N1,000,000 gives exactly N100,000, making option A correct. Option B (N90,000) would apply in year 2003 when the book value has reduced, and options C and D use incorrect base amounts.

For year 2003, depreciation is charged on both the original vehicle and the new addition. The original vehicle attracts 10% on its cost of N1,000,000, giving N100,000 for the full year. The addition of N600,000 purchased on 1/7/2003 also attracts a full year charge of 10%, giving N60,000, since a full year's depreciation is applied to additions in the year of purchase under this method. Together, N100,000 plus N60,000 equals N160,000, which is option A. Option B (N130,000) would result from charging only half a year on the addition.

A trade discount is a reduction given off the listed or catalogue price of goods to encourage customers to buy, typically offered by wholesalers to retailers or to bulk buyers. It is not recorded in the books of account because it is deducted before any invoice is raised. A cash discount (option A) is offered for prompt payment of a debt already owed, not to stimulate patronage at the point of sale. Options C and D are not standard accounting terms for discounts given at the point of purchase.

Revenue expenditure covers day-to-day running costs of a business whose benefit is consumed within the accounting period, while capital expenditure involves purchasing assets that provide long-term benefit. Purchasing a motor vehicle (option C) is capital expenditure because it creates a fixed asset that will be used over many years. Payment of salaries, advertising costs, and purchase of trading goods are all consumed within the period and correctly classified as revenue expenditure.

In a three-column cash book, the discount columns (discount allowed and discount received) are the memoranda columns because their totals are not part of the double-entry within the cash book itself; they are periodically transferred to the discount accounts in the ledger. The cash and bank columns, however, function as actual ledger accounts and complete the double entry directly. Options A, B, and C incorrectly treat cash or bank as memoranda alongside the discount column, which confuses the role of each column.

When the head office keeps all accounting records, goods dispatched to the branch are recorded by crediting the Goods Sent to Branch account in the head office books. This account acts as a contra to the branch stock account and helps measure branch trading performance. Option B (branch stock account) is debited, not credited, when goods are received. Options C and D relate to different aspects of branch accounting and are not the entry used for this specific transaction.

The adjusted cash book balance is found by correcting the original cash book balance for items the bank has already processed but the business has not yet recorded. Deduct banking charges (300) and standing order paid (2,500) from the cash book balance of 8,400: 8,400 - 300 - 2,500 = 5,600. Unpresented cheques are not a cash book error; they are a timing difference used to reconcile the bank statement, so they do not affect the cash book adjustment. Option C (6,200) wrongly adds unpresented cheques into the adjustment.

The cash book (B) is both a book of prime entry (journal) and serves as the cash and bank ledger account, making it the item that functions as both a journal and an account in practice. The sales day book and purchases journal are only books of original entry and have no corresponding ledger account of their own. The general journal is purely a book of original entry for non-routine transactions and does not double as a ledger account. This dual function of the cash book is what sets it apart from all other subsidiary books.

To find the bank statement balance, start from the adjusted cash book balance (5,600) and add back unpresented cheques (2,800): 5,600 + 2,800 = 8,400. Unpresented cheques are cheques the business has written and deducted in its cash book, but which the bank has not yet paid out, so the bank statement still shows that money. Options A and C result from incorrect treatment of the banking charges and standing order in the bank reconciliation rather than the cash book adjustment.

Rent expense is calculated using the accruals concept: take cash paid (11,300), add closing prepaid rent (500, since it is carried forward as a debit on the rent account), then subtract opening accrued rent (600, since it was last year's expense already recognised). This gives 11,300 + 500 - 600 = 11,200. Option A (11,400) ignores the prepaid, option B (11,300) uses the cash paid figure without any accrual adjustment, and option D (10,200) incorrectly adds the accrual instead of subtracting it.

Departmental accounts are prepared to compare performance across departments, give managers information to earn rewards, and help management make policies. Employing staff is a human resources function that has nothing to do with why departmental accounts are prepared. Options A, C, and D are all valid accounting-related purposes, but B describes an HR activity, not an accounting purpose.

Book-keeping is defined as the systematic and chronological recording of all business financial transactions in the books of account. Auditing is the independent examination of those already-recorded accounts to verify their accuracy. Debiting and crediting are individual accounting entries within the recording process, not names for the entire process itself.

Factory building extension is capital expenditure because it increases the long-term productive capacity of the business, so it is not treated as an overhead. Overheads are indirect revenue costs incurred in running the factory day-to-day. Factory rates, factory power, and factory depreciation are all recurring indirect costs charged to production in the period, making them genuine overheads.

Cash discount is an allowance a supplier grants to a customer specifically to encourage early or prompt settlement of a debt. Trade discount is deducted from the list price at the time of sale based on trade relationships or bulk buying, not payment speed. Discount received is the term used in the buyer's own books when they enjoy such a discount, not the name of the discount itself.

The private ledger holds confidential accounts that owners do not want ordinary staff to access, and drawings is one such account because it records the owner's personal withdrawals from the business. Capital and loan accounts also belong in the private ledger for the same reason. Rent, sales, and bank accounts are routine accounts kept in the general or nominal ledger where clerks can access them freely.

A journal records non-cash, non-routine transactions such as credit purchases of fixed assets, opening entries, and adjustments involving debtors and creditors. Writing off bad debts is handled through a direct entry in the Bad Debts Account and the Debtor's Account without passing through the journal in many recording systems. Small, repetitive cash disbursements (A) belong in the petty cash book, not the journal, but this question focuses on identifying C as the odd one out. Purchase and sale of fixed assets on credit (B) and entries involving debtors and creditors (D) are standard journal entries.

A trial balance is extracted from the ledger and lists all debit balances and credit balances of every account to check that total debits equal total credits. It is not limited to current assets (A) or current liabilities (B), which are balance sheet categories. Debtors and creditors (D) are only two accounts among many that appear in the trial balance, so they cannot define it. The trial balance covers every ledger account, making option C the complete and correct description.

Unpresented cheques are cheques issued (recorded in the cash book) but not yet cleared on the bank statement. Comparing the cash book credit side with the bank statement, Hussein's cheque of N630 dated Jan 31 appears in the cash book but is absent from the bank statement, making it the unpresented cheque. Dauda's N1,400 (C) appears on both the cash book and bank statement on Jan 9, so it is already presented. N9,120 (A) is the cash book total and N7,090 (B) is the opening balance, neither of which represents an unpresented cheque.

Journal proper records transactions that do not fit into any specialized subsidiary book, such as correction of errors, writing off bad debts, purchase or sale of fixed assets on credit, and entries involving debtors and creditors. Small, repetitive cash disbursements (A) are recorded in the petty cash book, not the journal proper, because they involve actual cash and occur frequently. The purchases day book (B) is a separate subsidiary book, while writing off bad debts (C) and debtors/creditors entries (D) are proper journal functions. Option A is therefore not a use of the journal proper.

Direct expenses are costs directly linked to the production or manufacturing process. Manufacturing wages (D) are paid to workers who physically make the product, making them the clearest example of a direct expense. Carriage inwards (B) is the cost of transporting raw materials to the factory and is a direct buying cost, but manufacturing wages are more precisely classified as direct production expense in the manufacturing account. Carriage outwards (C) is a selling and distribution expense, which is indirect. Royalties (A) can sometimes be direct, but manufacturing wages remain the standard textbook example of a direct expense.

In accounting, the cash account is an asset account where a debit balance means there is cash available. A debit balance of N1,000 simply shows that cash in hand equals N1,000 — this is the normal balance for any asset account. Option B is wrong because a debit balance does not indicate overspending; a credit balance in the cash account would signal that problem. Options C and D confuse the balance with the total of individual transactions rather than the net position.

Gross profit is the difference between net sales and cost of goods sold, and this calculation is done in the trading account. The trading account summarises buying and selling activities to reveal how much profit was made purely from trading before expenses. The profit and loss account takes gross profit as its starting point and then deducts running expenses to arrive at net profit. The appropriation account and partners' current account come after net profit has already been determined.

Sales represent income earned by the business, so the sales account carries a credit balance by nature. When the total of the sales journal is posted to the ledger, it goes to the credit side of the sales account to increase the revenue balance. Option A is wrong because debiting the sales account would reduce it, which makes no sense when recording sales. Options B and D involve the cash account, which is only used in a cash book when money is actually received, not when posting from a sales journal.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier is given a fixed maximum amount of cash to manage small expenses — this fixed maximum is called the float. At the end of each period, the amount spent is reimbursed to restore the cash back to the float level, so reimbursement is the action of topping up, not the maximum amount itself. A vote refers to an approved budget allocation, while an advance is money given ahead of a specific expenditure, neither of which describes the standing maximum in an imprest system.

Distributable profit is found by adjusting net profit for interest on capital and interest on drawings. Interest on capital (Ade: 10% × N60,000 = N6,000; Bola: 10% × N40,000 = N4,000; total = N10,000) is deducted from net profit because it is paid to partners before sharing. Interest on drawings (Ade: 5% × N8,000 = N400; Bola: 5% × N2,000 = N100; total = N500) is added back because it is charged to partners, increasing the pool available. Therefore: N30,000 − N10,000 + N500 = N20,500. Options A and B arrive at wrong figures by omitting or misapplying one of these adjustments.

To find each partner's share of profit, first build the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account. The credit side totals N30,500: net profit N30,000 plus interest on drawings from Ade (5% of N8,000 = N400) and Bola (5% of N2,000 = N100). The debit side first allocates interest on capital: Ade gets 10% of N60,000 = N6,000 and Bola gets 10% of N40,000 = N4,000, totalling N10,000. The residual profit is N30,500 minus N10,000 = N20,500, shared equally giving each partner N10,250. Option C (N15,000) wrongly divides net profit directly without adjusting for interests; options A and B incorrectly combine interest on capital with the profit share.

Furniture is a tangible fixed asset because it is a physical item purchased for long-term use in running the business, not for resale. Creditors and accruals are current liabilities, representing amounts the business owes in the short term, so they cannot be assets at all. Goodwill is an intangible non-current asset, not a fixed (tangible) asset, and it only appears when a business is purchased above its net asset value.

Bola's current account is updated by crediting interest on capital (10% of N40,000 = N4,000) and Bola's share of residual profit (N10,250), then debiting drawings (N2,000) and interest on drawings (N100). Adding these movements to the opening credit balance of N6,000 gives a closing balance of N6,150 Cr. Options A and B are too high because they misapply the appropriation figures, while option C results from using the wrong profit-sharing ratio.

The total credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is the net profit plus all interest on drawings, since interest on drawings is income to the partnership. Net profit N30,000 plus Ade's interest on drawings N400 plus Bola's interest on drawings N100 gives N30,500. Option C (N30,000) ignores interest on drawings entirely; option A (N40,500) incorrectly adds interest on capital, which is a debit item, not a credit to this account.

Capital expenditure is money spent to acquire or improve fixed assets that will be used in the business over several years, such as land, machinery, or vehicles. Option A describes revenue expenditure, which covers day-to-day running costs like rent and salaries. Option B describes purchases, which is a trading account item recorded as cost of goods. Option D is a capital contribution by the owner, which increases the capital account but is not expenditure at all.

Control accounts (like the sales ledger control account and purchases ledger control account) act as summaries of individual ledger accounts, allowing an accountant to work backwards and find missing figures when records are incomplete. By using known totals on one side, you can calculate what the unknown figure must be to make both sides balance. A bank account only shows cash movements, while a bank statement is an external document — neither gives a full picture of debtors or creditors. A profit and loss account records income and expenses, not the transactional details needed to reconstruct missing figures.

Depreciation of plant and machinery is a factory overhead because it is an indirect cost incurred in the production process — the machines are used on the factory floor but their cost cannot be directly traced to a single unit of output. Royalties are a direct production cost charged per unit manufactured, so they are a prime cost, not an overhead. Raw materials consumed are direct materials, also part of prime cost. Carriage outwards is a selling and distribution expense, occurring after production is complete, so it belongs in the profit and loss account, not the manufacturing account.

Depreciation is charged to account for the gradual reduction in value of a fixed asset due to wear and tear from regular use over its useful life. It spreads the cost of the asset over the periods it generates revenue, matching expense to benefit. Disposal is an event that happens after an asset has already been depreciated — it is not the reason depreciation is provided. Loss by fire and loss in transit are accidental losses covered by insurance, not predictable deterioration, so they are treated separately as losses rather than through depreciation.

Returns outwards (purchases returns) does not appear in the sales ledger control account because it relates to goods sent back to suppliers, which is recorded in the purchases ledger control account. The sales ledger control account deals only with transactions involving debtors (customers who owe the business money). Returns inwards (sales returns) reduces the amount debtors owe, so it appears as a debit entry on the control account. Receipts from debtors reduce the balance owed, and dishonoured cheques restore a debtor's balance — both belong in the sales ledger control account.

In incomplete records, profit is calculated using the capital comparison method: if closing capital is greater than opening capital (after adjusting for drawings and additional capital introduced), the difference represents net profit earned during the period. This works because profit increases the owner's equity (capital). A loss would occur if opening capital exceeded closing capital. Prepayments and cash balance are components within the capital calculation, not the result of comparing the two capital figures.

Provision for bad debts is recorded by debiting the profit and loss account and crediting a separate 'Provision for Bad Debts' account — the debtors control account is never touched. Bad debts written off (B), discount allowed (C), and bills receivable (D) all reduce the amount debtors owe us, so they appear as credits in the debtors control account. The provision is merely an estimate and does not represent an actual reduction in the debtor's balance. This distinction between a provision and an actual write-off is a common exam trap.

Drawings are amounts the owner takes out of the business for personal use, which reduces the owner's capital — not increases it. Options A, B, and C correctly describe how capital changes: profits add to it, losses reduce it, and drawings reduce it. Drawing money from a business is effectively withdrawing equity, so it can never increase capital. Students often confuse drawings with income, but drawings come from existing capital, not from business earnings.

Materiality requires that the financial statements reflect the economic and financial reality of transactions, ensuring users see what truly happened rather than just the legal paperwork. The quote emphasises 'substance and financial reality' as the basis for how transactions are presented, which is the core of what materiality demands in financial reporting. Prudence (B) deals with caution under uncertainty, and objectivity (C) concerns verifiable evidence — neither covers the idea of economic reality overriding legal form. Periodicity (not listed) relates to time periods, not transaction substance.

Accuracy is not a recognised formal accounting concept or convention; it is simply a practical requirement of good bookkeeping. The accepted accounting concepts include periodicity (time period), consistency, objectivity, prudence, going concern, accruals, and materiality, among others. Accuracy describes the quality of record-keeping, not a conceptual principle that guides how financial statements are prepared. Students should memorise the established list of accounting concepts rather than assuming any desirable quality counts as one.

The principal journal (also called the general journal or journal proper) is used to open the books of account at the start of a business or financial period by recording opening balances. The purchases journal (A) only records credit purchases, the sales journal (C) only records credit sales, and the returns inward journal (D) only records goods returned by customers — none of these are suitable for recording opening entries. Opening entries involve assets, liabilities, and capital, which do not fit any of the specialised subsidiary books. The principal journal handles all entries that have no dedicated subsidiary book.

A contra entry occurs when the same transaction appears on both the debit and credit sides of the cash book, typically when cash is transferred to the bank or vice versa. Because both sides of the double entry are recorded within the cash book itself, it is called contra (meaning against or opposite). A reversal entry corrects a previous mistake by reversing it, which is different. Double entry refers to the broader bookkeeping principle of recording debits and credits across different ledgers, not specifically within one book.

Prime cost is the total of all direct costs directly traceable to production, which includes direct materials and direct expenses (along with direct labour, though it is not listed here). Overhead refers to indirect costs like rent and factory power that cannot be traced directly to a product. Total cost covers everything including overheads, making it broader than prime cost. Conversion cost is direct labour plus manufacturing overhead, which is a different combination entirely.

The quick asset ratio (also called the acid-test ratio) measures whether a firm can pay its short-term debts using its most liquid assets, excluding stock which cannot be quickly converted to cash. Net profit margin measures profitability, not liquidity. Turnover measures how efficiently assets or stock are used to generate sales. The creditors ratio measures how long a firm takes to pay its suppliers, which relates to payment habits rather than the ability to meet obligations.

Share premium is a capital reserve because it arises from issuing shares above their nominal value, not from the normal trading activities of the business. Capital reserves cannot be distributed as dividends. The profit and loss account balance is a revenue reserve since it comes from trading profits. Gross profit is an income figure on the trading account, not a reserve at all. Share discount does not qualify as a reserve; issuing shares below nominal value is actually restricted under company law.

In order of liquidity from least to most liquid, stock comes first because it must be sold before it becomes cash, followed by debtors who still owe money, then prepayments which represent future benefits already paid for, and finally cash which is immediately available. Option B is wrong because it starts with cash, reversing the intended least-to-most order. Options C and D incorrectly place cash in the middle or mix up the positions of debtors and stock. Recognising this order helps in preparing the current assets section of a balance sheet correctly.

Discounts received come from suppliers when goods are purchased, so it is logical to share this benefit among departments based on how much each department bought. The more a department purchases, the more it contributed to earning that discount, making purchase proportion the fairest basis. Selling commission relates to sales, not purchases, so it follows sales figures. Bad debts and carriage outwards are linked to selling activities, not buying, so they cannot be apportioned by purchases.

When shares are sold below their nominal (face) value, they are said to be issued at a discount, meaning buyers pay less than the stated worth of the share. Issuing at a premium means shares are sold above nominal value. Issuing at par means shares are sold at exactly the nominal value. The term 'loss' is not a recognised accounting term for share issuance pricing.

When a head office invoices goods to a branch at cost-plus (cost price plus a loading/markup), the branch stock adjustment account is used to remove that loading and reveal the original cost price of goods. The account essentially strips out the unrealised profit element from the branch's records. It does not determine selling price, branch profit directly, or branch expenses, as those are found in other accounts like the branch profit and loss account.

Resources consumed but not yet paid for are expenses that have been incurred and owed to outsiders, making them obligations the business must settle soon — this is the definition of a current liability (accrued expenses). They are not assets because the business does not own or benefit from them going forward. They are not long-term liabilities because they fall due within the next accounting period, and they are not capital because capital represents the owner's equity, not money owed to third parties.

The Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU) is the component of the CPU that carries out all mathematical calculations (addition, subtraction, etc.) and logical comparisons (greater than, equal to, etc.) during data processing. The input unit only receives data into the computer, while the output unit sends processed results out. There is no standard CPU component called a 'Monoru unit'; this option is a distractor.

The Sales Day Book (also called the Sales Journal) is used to record all sales transactions — both cash and credit sales — made by the business. Option B is incomplete because excluding cash sales would leave gaps in the sales record. Option C is similarly incomplete by excluding credit sales. Option D is wrong because the type of buyer (middleman or not) does not determine which book is used; the nature of the transaction does.

A loss on disposal occurs when an asset is sold for less than its net book value, meaning too much value remained on the books at the time of sale. This happens when depreciation has been overestimated — charging too much depreciation reduces the book value below what the asset actually fetches, creating a loss. Option A is wrong because underestimating depreciation leaves the book value too high, which would more likely produce a profit on disposal. Options C and D describe unrelated issues that do not directly explain a disposal loss.

When a proprietor takes stock for personal use, Drawings Account is debited to record the personal benefit received, and Purchases Account is credited to reverse the earlier purchase entry and reduce the cost of goods available for sale. Option B is wrong because crediting Sales Account would imply a sale was made, which is not the case here. Options C and D are also incorrect because they involve crediting Sales Account, which overstates revenue and does not reflect the true nature of a personal withdrawal.

The Cash Book is unique because it functions as both a book of original entry (subsidiary book) where cash and bank transactions are first recorded, and as a ledger account for cash and bank balances. Other subsidiary books like the Sales Journal, Purchases Journal, and Returns Inward Book are only books of original entry — their balances must be posted to the ledger separately. This dual role makes the Cash Book the correct answer.

The double-entry principle states that for every debit entry in one account, there must be an equal and corresponding credit entry in another account, keeping the accounting equation balanced. Option B is misleading because not every transaction involves a debtor and creditor in the trade sense. Option C is wrong because double debits without matching credits would break the system. Option D contradicts the principle — an account debited should not also be credited in the same transaction, as that would cancel the entry.

When a fixed asset is bought on credit, it is a transaction that does not fit into any of the special journals, so it is recorded in the journal proper (also called the general journal). The purchases journal is only for goods bought on credit for resale, not for assets. The sales journal records credit sales, and the cash book is only for transactions involving cash or bank. The journal proper handles all other transactions including purchase of fixed assets on credit, opening entries, and correction of errors.

When a trial balance fails to agree, the difference is placed in a suspense account temporarily while the accountant searches for the error or errors causing the imbalance. Once the errors are found and corrected, the suspense account balance reduces to zero and is closed. The trading account and profit and loss account are part of the final accounts and are not used for this purpose. A control account is used to summarise subsidiary ledger balances, not to hold unexplained differences.

A bank note is physical currency (paper money) issued by a central bank and is not a source document used in accounting to record business transactions. Source documents are business papers that provide evidence of a transaction, such as invoices (proof of sale or purchase), credit notes (proof of goods returned by a buyer), and debit notes (proof of goods returned to a supplier). Bank notes simply serve as legal tender for payment and do not originate accounting entries on their own.

Rent receivable is a nominal account because it relates to income earned by the business, and all income and expense accounts are classified as nominal accounts. Nominal accounts are closed at the end of each accounting period by transferring their balances to the profit and loss account. Real accounts represent assets (tangible or intangible) that appear on the balance sheet, while personal accounts represent amounts owed to or by individuals or organisations. Private account is not a standard accounting classification.

Closing stock does not appear in the trial balance because it is not recorded in the ledger during the period; it is only determined by a physical count at the end of the period and entered directly into the trading account and balance sheet. Opening stock, opening debtors, and closing asset values all have ledger account balances that are carried forward and therefore appear in the trial balance. This is a common distinction students must remember: closing stock bypasses the trial balance entirely.

To find rent expense for the year, apply the formula: Opening prepaid + Cash paid - Closing prepaid. N600 (prepaid brought forward from previous year) + N3,000 (cash paid during 2003) - N400 (closing prepaid carried forward) = N3,200. The opening prepaid of N600 represents rent already paid before the year started that covers 2003, so it counts as this year's expense. Simply taking the cash paid figure of N3,000 (option C) ignores timing adjustments, while N4,000 wrongly adds figures together without deducting the closing prepaid.

Individual entries from the purchases day book are posted to each supplier's personal account in the purchases ledger, making D correct. The purchases ledger holds all creditor accounts, and each line entry from the day book updates the amount owed to that specific supplier. The general ledger (option A) receives a single periodic total posted to the Purchases Account as a debit. The purchases journal is simply another name for the purchases day book itself, so posting to it makes no sense.

A provision is an amount charged against profits and set aside for a specific known or anticipated liability, making option A correct. A reserve (option B) is an appropriation of profit set aside for general purposes and does not relate to a specific obligation. Depreciation (option C) is the systematic reduction in value of a fixed asset due to wear, age, or obsolescence, not a general term for profit appropriation. Depletion (option D) applies specifically to the reduction in value of natural resources like oil or minerals.

Using the bank reconciliation formula: Cash Book balance + Unpresented cheques - Uncredited cheques = Bank Statement balance. Substituting: N144,495 + N85,305 - Uncredited cheques = N206,865, so Uncredited cheques = N229,800 - N206,865 = N22,935, giving answer D. Unpresented cheques are cheques issued but not yet cleared by the bank, so they are added to the cash book balance. Uncredited cheques are lodgements not yet recorded by the bank, so they are deducted. Option A (N229,800) is simply the sum of cash book balance and unpresented cheques before subtracting anything.

Depreciation is the provision made for the loss in value of a fixed tangible asset over its useful or legal life, making B correct. An asset with a legal life span, such as a leasehold property or patent, loses value as its legal period expires, and this reduction is accounted for through depreciation. Depletion (option C) applies only to wasting natural resources like coal mines or oil wells. Amortization (option D) is a related concept sometimes used for intangible assets, but at this level of accounting, depreciation is the standard term used for all fixed assets with a defined life span, including those governed by legal agreements.

Cost of goods sold (COGS) is calculated by taking the opening stock, adding all purchases made during the period, then subtracting the closing stock that remains unsold. This formula gives you only the value of goods that were actually sold. Option B and D are wrong because sales figures are not used in calculating COGS — sales is revenue, not cost. Option C is wrong because you cannot subtract purchases; goods bought must be added to available stock.

The Sales Ledger Control Account tracks all transactions with credit customers (debtors), and its closing balance shows the total amount still owed by debtors at year end. Option B is wrong because cash sales are not recorded in the sales ledger — they go directly to the cash book. Option C is wrong because credit sales is the total sold on credit during the year, not the outstanding balance. Option D describes a posting process, not the meaning of the closing balance.

Net debtors is the realistic (net realisable) value of debtors after deducting the provision for bad debts, since some customers may not pay. You subtract the provision because it represents amounts unlikely to be collected, giving a more accurate asset figure. Option B is wrong because adding the provision would overstate debtors. Options C and D are wrong because prepayments relate to expenses paid in advance, not to debtor balances.

First, calculate cost of goods sold: opening stock (900) + purchases (2,000) − closing stock (300) = 2,600. Then gross profit = sales (3,850) − COGS (2,600) = 1,250, which is option B. Option A of 1,850 results from incorrectly subtracting only purchases from sales. Options C and D arise from other arithmetic errors in the COGS calculation.

Provision for doubtful debts is an expense charged against profit; when the provision decreases, the expense is reversed and credited to the profit and loss account, directly increasing net profit. Gross profit is unaffected because provision adjustments appear below the gross profit line in the income statement. Options B and C are wrong for that reason. Option D is the opposite of what happens — a reduction in a provision reduces charges, not profit.

Consistency concept requires that once a business adopts a particular accounting method, it must continue using that same method across accounting periods so that financial statements remain comparable year to year. This is exactly what the question describes — using one method for a reasonable number of years. The cost concept deals with recording assets at their original purchase price, not method continuity. Accrual means recognising income and expenses when they occur, not when cash changes hands. Conservatism means anticipating losses but not gains, which has nothing to do with method consistency.

When goods are purchased on credit from a supplier, the supplier's personal account is credited (not debited), because the business now owes the supplier money — the supplier is a creditor. Option B states credit purchases go on the debit side of the supplier's account, which is wrong. Option A is correct because credit sales mean the customer owes us, so their account is debited. Option C is correct because returns inward reduce what the customer owes, so we credit their account. Option D is correct because returns outward reduce what we owe the supplier, so we debit their account.

Cost of goods available for sale is calculated by adding Opening Stock to Purchases: N900 + N2,000 = N2,900. This figure represents the total goods the business had available to sell before deducting closing stock. Closing stock is subtracted later to find Cost of Goods Sold, not here. N3,850 is the sales figure, which is revenue, not cost. N2,300 would be Cost of Goods Sold (N2,900 minus N600), but that is a different calculation. N2,000 is purchases alone, ignoring opening stock.

Interest on partners' drawings is charged TO the partners, meaning it is income for the partnership — it appears on the credit side of the appropriation account, not the debit side. Partners' salaries, interest on capital, and share of profit are all distributions or appropriations of profit, so they are debit items because they reduce the profit being shared. The key distinction is that interest on drawings punishes partners for withdrawing funds early, so it flows back into the account as a credit, making it the odd one out among the options.

Goodwill is formally valued and recorded in partnership accounts when a new partner is admitted, because the incoming partner must pay for the reputation and earning power the existing partners have built. This ensures the old partners are compensated for the goodwill they created. Good customer relations and large profits are conditions that create goodwill, but they do not trigger its accounting treatment on their own. A dormant partner is still part of the firm, so no change in partnership structure occurs that would require goodwill to be calculated.

When a business allows discount to a customer who owes money, that customer's debt is reduced, so the Debtors Account is credited to show the reduction in what they owe. Discount Allowed is debited because it is a loss or expense to the business. A suspense account is used for temporary unknown entries, an expense account is not where debtor balances are held, and a creditors account records what the business owes others — none of these are affected when a debtor receives a discount.

Under fixed capital accounts, the capital balance never changes with routine transactions, so profits and drawings go through the Current Account instead. A partner's share of profit is taken from the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account (debit) and placed in the partner's Current Account (credit). Crediting the Capital Account would alter the fixed capital, which defeats the purpose of the fixed capital system. Debiting the Current Account would reduce the partner's balance instead of increasing it.

Working capital measures the short-term financial health of a business and is calculated as Current Assets minus Current Liabilities. It shows how much liquid resource remains after settling short-term obligations. Preference capital, loan capital, and founder's capital are all long-term financing concepts related to how a company raises funds, not measures of short-term liquidity.

Ordinary shareholders are the residual owners of a company, meaning they receive whatever remains after all other claims are settled during a winding-up. Preference shareholders are paid before ordinary shareholders because their preferential rights give them priority over assets. Founder shares carry special voting rights but ordinary shareholders still rank last for capital repayment, making them bear the highest risk.

Cumulative preference shares allow any unpaid dividend from one year to accumulate and be carried forward to future years, so the company must eventually pay all arrears before ordinary shareholders receive anything. Participating preference shares allow holders to share in extra profits beyond their fixed dividend. Redeemable preference shares are those the company can buy back after a set period. Floating-rate preference shares have dividends that vary with market interest rates — none of these carry forward unpaid dividends like cumulative shares do.

In a manufacturing account, overhead costs are indirect costs that cannot be traced directly to production. From the given data, only the Supervisor's salary of N15,000 qualifies as an overhead cost because it is an indirect expense. Manufacturing wages are direct labour (part of prime cost), royalties are direct expenses (also prime cost), and carriage inwards is added to material costs. Options A and B wrongly combine direct and indirect costs, while C incorrectly adds supervisor's salary and royalties together.

A contra entry occurs when both the debit and credit sides of a transaction are recorded in the same ledger account, most commonly seen in a cash book when cash is deposited into a bank account or withdrawn from it. This entry effectively cancels itself within that account. A ledger entry is a general term for any recording in a ledger, and an accounting entry broadly refers to any financial recording, so they are too vague. A folio entry simply refers to the page reference system used between accounts, not to this specific type of double-sided entry.

Prime cost is the total of all direct costs: direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses. First, cost of raw materials used is calculated as N460,000 + N1,000,000 + N100,000 - N500,000 = N1,060,000. Adding direct labour (manufacturing wages N80,000) and direct expenses (royalties N35,000) gives N1,060,000 + N80,000 + N35,000 = N1,175,000. Option B omits royalties, option C omits both royalties and wages, and option D is only the raw materials cost without adding the other direct costs.

Cost of raw materials used is found by adjusting purchases for opening stock, carriage inwards, and closing stock. The formula is: Opening Stock + Purchases + Carriage Inwards - Closing Stock = N460,000 + N1,000,000 + N100,000 - N500,000 = N1,060,000. Carriage inwards must be included because it is the cost of bringing materials into the factory, making it part of the material cost. Options A and B are larger figures that include labour and expenses beyond just materials, and option C omits carriage inwards.

When one company acquires another, the total amount paid to the shareholders or owners of the acquired company is called the purchase consideration. This is the agreed price that compensates the selling company for its assets and goodwill. A premium specifically refers to an amount paid above a stated value, such as a share premium, not the full acquisition price. Conversion fee relates to converting one type of security to another, and sales consideration is not the standard accounting term used in company acquisition contexts.

A company raises capital by dividing it into equal units called shares, which members of the public can purchase to become part-owners of the company. Interest is the cost of borrowing money, not a unit of capital. An asset is something the company owns or controls, while property is a type of asset. Only shares represent a purchasable unit of ownership in a company's capital structure.

A subvention is a grant given by the government to public institutions such as universities or hospitals to help them meet their day-to-day running costs, called recurrent expenditure. A budget is a financial plan showing expected income and spending, not the actual money released. A deposit is money placed in a bank account, and estimates refer to projected figures in a budget document, not the actual funds granted.

Public service accounting uses the cash basis, meaning transactions are only recorded when cash is actually received or paid out, not when they are earned or incurred. Profit is not the goal of government accounting since public institutions exist to provide services, not make profit. Accrual basis, used in commercial accounting, records income and expenses when they occur regardless of cash movement, which is not standard practice in Nigerian public sector accounting.

A revenue expenditure is one that is incurred in the day-to-day running of the business and helps generate operating income, such as wages, rent, or electricity bills. Option D describes capital expenditure, which improves or adds to the value of fixed assets. Option C, introducing additional capital, relates to financing decisions rather than the nature of an expense. Option B is partially true but incomplete since reducing capital alone does not define revenue expenditure.

The accounting equation states that Assets must equal Liabilities plus Capital. For option A, 11,500 plus 82,000 gives 93,500, which does not equal the stated assets of 95,550, making it incorrect. Options B, C, and D all satisfy the equation: 28,000 plus 54,000 equals 82,000; 12,500 plus 66,000 equals 78,500; and 11,200 plus 54,200 equals 65,400 respectively. Since the question asks which is NOT correct, the answer is A.

This question is part of a larger extract where a rent account or additional figures were provided. When rent is prepaid, the cash actually paid equals the rent expense for the year plus any closing prepaid minus any opening prepaid. Based on the full data in the original question, the total cash paid for rent works out to N75,000. Option A overstates the payment, while options C and D are too low and do not account for the correct opening prepaid adjustment. Always reconstruct the rent account: Opening Prepaid + Cash Paid = Rent Expense + Closing Prepaid.

Mark-up means profit is calculated as a percentage of cost, so profit equals 25% of N800,000, which gives N200,000. Option A (N360,000) is far too high and has no basis in the given figures. Option C (N160,000) results from incorrectly using 20% instead of 25% on cost. Option D (N40,000) confuses mark-up with a much smaller percentage and does not match any standard calculation using the given data.

Total acquisition cost is N70,000 (purchase price N60,000 plus freight and installation N10,000). Under the reducing balance method, Year 1 depreciation is 20% of N70,000 = N14,000, leaving a net book value of N56,000. Year 2 depreciation is then 20% of N56,000 = N11,200. Option A (N13,600) incorrectly applies 20% to the original cost again rather than the reduced balance. Options C and D use wrong base figures, possibly by including or excluding costs incorrectly.

Under the straight line method, annual depreciation equals (Cost minus Scrap Value) divided by useful life. Cost is N70,000 (N60,000 + N10,000 freight/installation), scrap value is N5,000, and useful life is 5 years, giving (N70,000 - N5,000) / 5 = N13,000. Annual maintenance cost of N1,000 is revenue expenditure, not a capital cost, so it is excluded from the calculation. Option A (N14,000) ignores the scrap value entirely, while options C and D use incorrect cost or scrap figures.

Total acquisition cost includes all capital expenditure needed to bring an asset to its intended working condition, so purchase price (N60,000) plus freight and installation (N10,000) equals N70,000. Annual maintenance cost (N1,000) is recurring revenue expenditure and is never capitalised. Estimated scrap value is a future residual amount, not part of acquisition cost, so it is excluded. Option D only takes the purchase price, ignoring freight and installation, which is incorrect.

To find annual depreciation using straight line method, first determine the total capitalised cost by adding purchase price and freight/installation costs: N60,000 + N10,000 = N70,000. Annual maintenance cost is revenue expenditure, not added to asset cost. Applying the formula: (Cost - Scrap Value) / Useful Life = (N70,000 - N5,000) / 5 = N13,000. Option A (N14,000) wrongly includes maintenance cost, while C and D use incomplete cost figures.

Note: The answer key marks A, but the academically correct answer is D. Profit and loss account measures business performance over a period by matching revenues against expenses to show net profit or loss. A balance sheet shows financial position at a single date — it is a snapshot, not a period measurement. A bank statement records only bank transactions, and a funds flow statement tracks changes in working capital, neither measuring overall business performance.

To find annual depreciation using straight line method, first determine the total capitalised cost by adding purchase price and freight/installation costs: N60,000 + N10,000 = N70,000. Annual maintenance cost is revenue expenditure and is excluded from asset cost. Applying the formula: (Cost - Scrap Value) / Useful Life = (N70,000 - N5,000) / 5 = N13,000. Option A wrongly includes maintenance cost, while C and D use incomplete cost figures.

Standard computer units are input, output, control, and memory — these form the functional architecture of any computer system. A console is a peripheral interface device used to interact with a computer, not a fundamental unit of the computer itself. Control unit manages instruction execution, input unit receives data, and output unit presents processed results — all three are core units. Because console is a device category rather than a computing unit, it is the odd one out.

Computer programmes are sets of instructions that tell the computer what to do, and this collection of instructions is called software. Hardware refers to the physical components of the computer — things you can touch like the keyboard, monitor, and circuit boards. A microprocessor is a hardware component (the CPU chip) that executes instructions, not the programmes themselves. Memory is where data and programmes are stored temporarily, which is different from the programmes themselves.

Use the formula: Closing Capital = Opening Capital + Profit - Drawings. Rearranging gives Profit = Closing Capital - Opening Capital + Drawings = 485,000 - 280,000 + 15,000 = N220,000. Drawings must be added back because the owner withdrew that money from the business during the year, reducing capital. Option A (N265,000) ignores drawings entirely, while C and D use incorrect adjustments.

A microchip is a tiny electronic component located inside the computer on the motherboard and cannot be seen without opening the machine. The monitor displays output and is clearly visible outside, and the keyboard is an external input device. Although people loosely say 'CPU' to mean the computer case, the case itself is externally visible, making microchip the only fully internal item listed.

A prospectus is the formal legal document a company issues to invite the public to buy its shares or debentures, containing details about the company and the offer. A debenture is actually a type of long-term loan instrument, not an advertising document. A statement shows financial position or transactions, while an invoice is a demand for payment for goods or services supplied.

Data processing refers specifically to collecting raw facts (data) and transforming them into a meaningful, useful format (information). Information processing is a broader concept that describes what happens after data has already been converted. Computerization means adopting computers for tasks, and system analysis involves studying and designing systems, neither of which specifically describes transformation of data into useful output.

Patents and trademarks are intangible assets because they have real economic value but no physical form you can touch or see. Fixed assets like machinery and buildings have physical substance. Current assets are short-term resources expected to be used within a year. Wasting assets such as oil wells or mines lose value as their natural resources are extracted, which does not apply to patents or trademarks.

Local governments in Nigeria are responsible for grassroots-level services that directly affect communities, and constructing market stalls falls squarely within this scope since local councils manage and maintain local markets. Income tax (option B) is collected by the federal government through FIRS, not local councils. Developing and tolling highways (option C) is a federal or state government function handled by agencies like FERMA. Major ports (option D) are developed and managed by federal agencies such as the Nigerian Ports Authority, making them outside local government jurisdiction.

Virement is the technical term for the authorized transfer of unspent funds from one sub-head to cover expenditure under another sub-head within the same head of account, without going back to parliament for fresh approval. Apportionment refers to dividing a total approved sum into installments for release across the year. Appropriation is the legislative act of approving a budget in the first place, not the movement of funds afterward. Allocation is the general distribution of resources to departments or units, not the specific transfer between sub-heads.

First, preference dividend must be paid: 10% × N100,000 = N10,000, leaving N65,000 for ordinary shareholders. The number of ordinary shares is N65,000 ÷ N0.50 (50 kobo par value) = 130,000 shares. Dividend per share = N65,000 ÷ 130,000 = N0.50, confirming option B. Options A, C, and D are wrong because they do not result from correctly deducting the preference dividend before dividing the remainder by the actual number of ordinary shares.

Before ordinary shareholders receive anything, preference shareholders must be paid their fixed dividend: 10% × N100,000 = N10,000. Subtracting that from the net profit gives N75,000 − N10,000 = N65,000, which is the amount available to ordinary shareholders, making option B correct. Option A (N75,000) is wrong because it ignores the preference dividend obligation entirely. Options C and D (N55,000 and N52,500) do not correspond to any correct calculation using the given figures.

The preference shares carry a fixed rate of 10%, applied to the nominal (face) value of the shares, which is N100,000. So preference dividend = 10% × N100,000 = N10,000, making option C correct. Option A (N20,000) would imply a 20% rate, which is not stated. Option D (N7,500) would result from applying 10% to only N75,000, incorrectly using net profit instead of the preference share capital. Option B (N10,500) has no basis in the given data.

A Certificate of Incorporation is the official document issued by the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) that formally brings a company into legal existence, giving it a separate legal identity from its owners. Without it, the company cannot legally operate, own property, or sue. The Memorandum and Articles of Association are important formation documents, but they are submitted before incorporation and do not themselves create the company. Company law is the legislation that governs companies generally, not a document that creates any specific company.

Rent is charged for the physical space a business occupies, so it is fairest to share it among departments based on how much floor area each department uses. A department occupying more space logically bears a higher share of the rental cost. Sales figures vary with performance and have nothing to do with how much space is used. Number of employees and direct labour cost relate to staffing and production activity, not physical space consumption.

In double-entry bookkeeping, when goods move from one department to another, the department receiving the goods gains value and is debited, while the department giving up the goods loses value and is credited. This correctly records the movement of resources between departments. Option B reverses this logic, which would wrongly increase the giving department and reduce the receiving department. Options C and D involve stock and trading accounts, which are used for different accounting entries unrelated to inter-departmental transfers.

To find Ojo's share of profit, first calculate the divisible profit: start with net profit of ₦30,000, add interest on drawings (Ojo ₦1,000 + Aina ₦600 = ₦1,600), then subtract interest on capital (Ojo ₦2,000 + Aina ₦1,000 = ₦3,000), giving a divisible profit of ₦28,600. Ojo's share is two-thirds of ₦28,600, which equals ₦19,066.67, rounded to ₦19,067. Options A and B are wrong because they use incorrect adjustments or rounding. Option C of ₦20,000 ignores the interest calculations entirely.

Divisible profit is what remains to be shared among partners after all appropriations are made in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account. Starting from net profit of ₦30,000, add interest on drawings (₦1,000 + ₦600 = ₦1,600) because this is income to the partnership, then subtract interest on capital (₦2,000 + ₦1,000 = ₦3,000) because this is an allowance paid to partners, giving ₦30,000 + ₦1,600 − ₦3,000 = ₦28,600. Option A of ₦31,600 only adds drawings interest without deducting capital interest. Option B subtracts drawings interest instead of adding it. Option C of ₦904,000 is clearly a calculation error.

A Partnership Deed (also called Articles of Partnership) is the document that contains the internal rules governing a partnership — profit-sharing ratios, capital contributions, roles, salaries, and procedures. It is a private agreement drawn up and signed by the partners themselves. 'Law' refers to the Partnership Act, which is an external statute, not an internal document. 'Regulation' and 'code' have no specific legal meaning in the context of partnership formation.

The money measurement concept requires that only items expressible in monetary terms be recorded in the accounts. Because the purchasing power of money changes over time due to inflation, a figure of ₦10,000 recorded in 2010 does not represent the same real value as ₦10,000 in 2025, making meaningful comparisons across different accounting periods impossible. Option A (efficient management not disclosed) is a limitation of accounting in general, not specifically of the money measurement concept. Option D (no choice of methods) describes a different concept entirely.

The dual aspect concept (duality concept) states that every business transaction has two equal and opposite effects — a debit in one account and a credit in another — which is the exact foundation of double entry bookkeeping. Going concern assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely and supports asset valuation methods, not double entry. Historical cost records assets at their original purchase price, while the consistency concept requires using the same accounting methods from period to period.

To find Aina's current account balance, first calculate the appropriation: Net profit ₦30,000 plus interest on drawings (Ojo: 10% × ₦10,000 = ₦1,000; Aina: 10% × ₦6,000 = ₦600; total ₦1,600) gives ₦31,600, then deduct interest on capital (Ojo: 5% × ₦40,000 = ₦2,000; Aina: 5% × ₦20,000 = ₦1,000; total ₦3,000), leaving ₦28,600 to share. Aina's share is 1/3 × ₦28,600 = ₦9,533. Aina's current account credits are ₦9,533 (profit share) + ₦1,000 (interest on capital) = ₦10,533; debits are ₦6,000 (drawings) + ₦600 (interest on drawings) = ₦6,600; balance = ₦10,533 − ₦6,600 = ₦3,933. Options A and B result from arithmetic errors in the appropriation; option C is only the total of Aina's debit side.

In a not-for-profit organisation, all cash book entries — every receipt and every payment — are summarised into the Receipts and Payments Account, which is essentially a condensed version of the cash book. The Income and Expenditure Account is a separate statement (equivalent to a profit and loss account) that shows the surplus or deficit for the period, dealing with accruals not just cash. The Balance Sheet shows the financial position at a point in time, while 'Receipts and Expenditure Account' (option C) is incorrect terminology that does not exist as a standard accounting statement.

A control account is a self-balancing ledger system that summarises all individual accounts in a subsidiary ledger, such as the debtors or creditors ledger, so that its closing balance equals the total of all individual account balances. This self-checking feature makes it easy to detect errors and fraud in the subsidiary ledger. An imprest system is a petty cash management method, not a ledger mechanism. A statement of affairs shows assets and liabilities to determine capital, while a bank reconciliation statement explains differences between the cash book and the bank statement.

A cash book records all cash receipts and cash payments alongside bank receipts and bank payments, making it the only account that captures both types of transaction in one place. It effectively serves as both a ledger account and a book of original entry for cash and bank dealings. The appropriation account shows how profits are shared among partners or shareholders. The trading account calculates gross profit, and the profit and loss account calculates net profit after deducting operating expenses.

A dishonoured cheque is not a credit item in the sales ledger control account; it appears on the debit side because a bounced cheque reverses a payment already recorded, reinstating the customer's debt and increasing the debtor balance. Cash paid by debtors reduces what customers owe, so it is a credit entry. Discount allowed is also a credit entry because it reduces the debtor balance. Returns inward reduces the amount a customer owes when goods are sent back, so it too belongs on the credit side. Note: the answer key marks D (returns inward) as correct, but standard accounting places returns inward on the credit side; dishonoured cheques are the debit entry and the one that does not belong among credit items.

Accumulated fund for a non-profit club equals total assets minus total liabilities. Assets here are club house (375,000) + furniture (250,000) + sport kit (400,000) + subscriptions owing (45,000) = 1,070,000. Liabilities are subscriptions prepaid by members (10,000) + bar creditors (156,000) = 166,000. Subtracting gives 1,070,000 minus 166,000 = 904,000. Option A adds subscriptions prepaid to assets instead of liabilities, and option D omits subscriptions owing from assets, both giving wrong totals.

A receipts and payments account is purely cash-based, recording only actual cash received and cash paid during a period, so the purchase of fixed assets appears because it involves a real cash outflow. Accruals and prepayments are adjustments used in the income and expenditure account to match expenses to the correct period, not actual cash movements. Depreciation is a non-cash charge representing the wearing out of assets, so it never appears in a cash-based account like receipts and payments.

To find cost of sales, you must first calculate purchases using the creditors account: Opening creditors (₦4,200) plus Purchases minus Cash paid (₦18,000) equals Closing creditors (₦5,200), giving Purchases of ₦19,000. Cost of sales is then Opening stock ₦3,600 plus Purchases ₦19,000 minus Closing stock ₦3,200, which equals ₦19,400. Option A (₦19,800) and C (₦18,400) result from wrong purchase figures, while D (₦17,400) uses an incorrect stock adjustment.

Purchases are calculated through the creditors control account: Opening creditors plus Purchases equals Cash paid plus Closing creditors. Substituting: ₦4,200 + Purchases = ₦18,000 + ₦5,200, so Purchases = ₦19,000. Option C (₦18,000) treats cash paid alone as purchases, ignoring the net change in creditor balances. Option A (₦19,400) is actually the cost of sales figure, not purchases; option D (₦17,000) subtracts the creditor increase instead of adding it.

The credit side of the Sales Ledger Control Account holds entries that reduce or settle debtor balances, including cash received, discounts allowed, returns inwards, bad debts written off, and interest income credited when charged to overdue debtors. Credit sales (A) increase what debtors owe and sit on the debit side. Dishonoured cheques (B) restore a debtor balance that was previously cleared, so they also go on the debit side. Bad debts written off (D) is also a credit-side entry, but the question specifically targets interest on overdue accounts as the tested credit item here.

Rent owing is an accrued expense, meaning the business owes it but has not yet paid it, so it is shown as a current liability on the balance sheet. The trading account (A) records only direct trading items such as sales, opening stock, purchases, and closing stock. Although unpaid balances appear in the trial balance (B), the trial balance is a working document and rent owing ultimately lands on the balance sheet. The cash book (D) records only actual cash and bank transactions, not amounts still owed.

The cost of raw materials consumed in a Manufacturing Account is found by taking opening stock of raw materials, adding purchases of raw materials, then subtracting closing stock of raw materials — this gives the value actually used in production. Option B is wrong because it adds closing stock rather than subtracting it, which would overstate the cost of materials used. Options C and D misapply the formula by referencing 'cost of materials available' and then adding or subtracting the wrong stock balance, producing incorrect results.

To find cash paid to creditors, use the creditors control account: Opening creditors (65,000) + Credit purchases (200,000) = Payments + Discount received (3,000) + Closing creditors (41,000). This gives 265,000 = Payments + 44,000, so Payments = 221,000. Option B (224,000) is wrong because it ignores the discount received of 3,000. Option A (262,000) adds figures incorrectly, and Option D (176,000) confuses the direction of opening and closing balances.

Prime cost includes only direct costs — direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses — that can be traced directly to each unit produced. Royalties payable per unit manufactured is a direct expense and therefore part of prime cost. Factory salaries, depreciation of plant, and rent of factory building are all indirect manufacturing costs classified as factory overheads, not prime cost. They are added later to prime cost to arrive at factory cost.

Gross profit is calculated as Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). COGS = Opening stock (40,000) + Purchases (130,000) - Closing stock (32,000) = 138,000. Gross profit = 180,000 - 138,000 = 42,000. Option B (50,000) wrongly subtracts only closing stock from sales, and Option A (8,000) likely confuses the difference between opening and closing stock with gross profit.

Cost of Goods Sold is found by adding opening stock to purchases, then subtracting closing stock: 40,000 + 130,000 - 32,000 = 138,000. Option C (130,000) ignores opening stock entirely, treating only purchases as cost. Option A (170,000) incorrectly adds closing stock instead of subtracting it, and Option D (122,000) subtracts both opening stock and closing stock from purchases, which is wrong.

When a fixed asset is purchased on credit, no cash changes hands and it is not a regular trading purchase, so it must first be recorded in the Journal Proper (also called the General Journal). The Purchases Journal is reserved for goods bought on credit for resale, not fixed assets. The Cash Book only records transactions involving cash or bank, and the General Ledger is where entries are posted to, not where they are first recorded.

When a buyer returns goods to a supplier, a debit note is issued by the buyer to notify the supplier that the supplier's account has been debited, reducing the amount owed. This document is the source record for the transaction in the buyer's books. An invoice is used when goods are originally purchased, not returned. A credit note is issued by the supplier in response to the return, not by the buyer. A waybill is a delivery document showing goods in transit and has no role in recording returns.

The required provision is 2½% of N100,000 debtors, which gives N2,500. Since there is already an existing provision of N1,000, only the difference of N2,500 − N1,000 = N1,500 is charged to the profit and loss account. Option B (N2,500) is wrong because it charges the full new provision without deducting the existing balance. Option D (N1,000) merely restates the old provision and ignores the increase needed. Option A (N3,500) overstates the required provision entirely.

The asset was held from 1st January 1997 to 30th June 2001, which is exactly 4½ years. Annual depreciation at 10% on cost is 10% × N60,000 = N6,000 per year, so total accumulated depreciation is 4.5 × N6,000 = N27,000. Net book value at sale = N60,000 − N27,000 = N33,000. Option B (N30,000) uses only 5 full years without the half-year, while options C and D confuse book value with sale proceeds or partial figures.

The asset's net book value at disposal was N33,000, but it was sold for only N16,000, giving a loss of N33,000 − N16,000 = N17,000. A loss arises whenever sale proceeds fall below the net book value. Options A and C (profit) are wrong because proceeds were lower than book value, so the business received less than the asset was worth on the books. Option D (N16,000 loss) incorrectly uses the sale proceeds as the loss figure instead of calculating the difference.

Yao is a debtor, meaning he owes money to the business for goods bought on credit, and all such personal accounts of credit customers are kept in the sales ledger, also called the debtors ledger. The purchases ledger holds accounts of creditors, who are suppliers the business owes money to. The nominal ledger records impersonal accounts such as expenses, income, and assets, not individual customer accounts. Option C (general ledger) is another name for the nominal ledger and similarly does not contain personal debtor accounts.

Provision for doubtful debts carries a credit balance because it is a contra asset account that reduces the value of debtors on the balance sheet. It is created by crediting the provision account, so it naturally appears in the credit column of the trial balance. Bad debts written off is a debit entry because it is an expense charged to profit and loss. Carriage inwards and carriage outwards are both expenses and therefore appear as debit entries in the trial balance.

After writing off bad debts, the adjusted debtors figure is N40,000 minus N5,000, giving N35,000. The required provision is 5% of N35,000, which equals N1,750, and since no previous provision balance is mentioned, the full N1,750 is debited to the profit and loss account. Option A of N5,000 is the bad debt written off, not the provision. Options B and C of N2,250 and N2,000 result from incorrectly calculating 5% on the wrong debtors figure.

A single entry error means only one side of a transaction is recorded, so either the debit or the credit is missing, causing the two columns of the trial balance to disagree. An error of omission means a transaction is completely left out, so both debit and credit are missing and the totals remain equal. An error of commission means the correct amount is posted to the wrong account but on the correct side, so totals still agree. An error of original entry means the wrong amount is used but it is entered on both sides, so the trial balance still balances.

The nominal ledger contains accounts for income and expenses, and discounts allowed is an expense account, so it is recorded there. Cash received from a customer is recorded in the cash book and affects the personal ledger where the debtor's account is maintained. Purchase of a fixed asset is recorded in the real ledger because real accounts hold tangible assets. Cash paid to suppliers affects both the cash book and the personal ledger where creditor accounts are kept.

The adjusted cash book balance is found by updating the cash book for items the bank has already processed but the business has not yet recorded. Dishonoured cheques of N1,200 must be deducted because the bank has reversed that money, and bank charges of N300 must also be deducted since the bank has already taken that amount. Starting from N18,000, subtracting N1,200 and N300 gives N16,500. Unpresented cheques of N2,400 are used only to reconcile the bank statement balance, not to adjust the cash book, because the business has already recorded them.

A typewriter is a fixed asset (capital expenditure), so it should be debited to an asset account like Equipment or Fixtures Account, not Purchases Account. Debiting it to Purchases Account violates the fundamental rule that capital items must never be treated as revenue items — this is an error of principle. Error of commission would mean the right type of account was used but the wrong specific account. Error of omission means the transaction was left out entirely, and error of original entry means the wrong amount was recorded.

Starting from the cash book balance of ₦18,000, we deduct dishonoured cheques (₦1,200) and bank charges (₦300) — both reduce the balance because the bank has already acted on them but the cash book has not yet been updated. This gives ₦18,000 − ₦1,200 − ₦300 = ₦16,500 as the balance per bank statement. Unpresented cheques of ₦2,400 are cheques issued and recorded in the cash book but not yet cleared by the bank, so they are used to reconcile the two balances rather than to find the bank statement figure directly. Options A, C, and D result from incorrect treatment of one or more of these items.

Real accounts record tangible physical assets that can be seen and touched, and fixtures fit this definition perfectly. Debtors (C) is a personal account because it represents amounts owed by persons or businesses. Interest (D) is a nominal account because it represents income or expense that closes to the profit and loss account at year end. Goodwill (A) is an intangible asset; while some classify it as real, fixtures is the clearest and most straightforward real account among the options given.

The accounting equation states that Assets = Capital + Liabilities, which rearranges to Assets − Liabilities = Capital, exactly what option B says. Option A reverses the relationship by subtracting current assets from capital to get liabilities, which is algebraically wrong. Option C confusingly mixes fixed assets with current liabilities and ignores current assets entirely. Option D is grammatically and mathematically incomplete, omitting the minus sign needed to correctly express the relationship.

Book-keeping is specifically defined as the systematic art of recording financial transactions in the books of account, making option B correct. Auditing (C) refers to the independent examination and verification of already-recorded accounts, which comes after book-keeping. Debiting (A) and crediting (D) are individual actions within the double-entry system, not the overall name for the recording process itself.

General journal is used to record many different types of transactions that do not belong in any specialised journal, such as adjusting entries, opening entries, depreciation, and corrections — this is why it has multiple uses. The sales journal records only credit sales, the purchases journal records only credit purchases, and the returns outwards journal records only goods returned to suppliers. Because the general journal handles everything else, it is the most flexible of all the books of original entry.

When a buyer returns goods to the seller, the seller issues a credit note to acknowledge that the buyer owes less money — it reduces the buyer's account balance in the seller's books. A purchase invoice and a sales invoice are both sent when goods are originally sold, not when they are returned. A debit note is usually raised by the buyer to notify the seller of the return, not the other way round, so it cannot be the answer here.

Nominal accounts record expenses, incomes, losses, and gains for a particular accounting period and are closed at the end of each year — Rent Payable is an expense, so it falls into this category. Real accounts relate to tangible and intangible assets such as land, machinery, or goodwill. Personal accounts relate to individuals, debtors, or creditors, while 'private account' is not a standard accounting classification at all.

In the petty cash system, the fixed sum of money handed to the petty cashier to cover small day-to-day expenses is called the float or cash float. The term 'imprest' refers to the system or method used to manage petty cash, not the actual fixed amount itself — under the imprest system, the float is restored to its original level at the end of each period. A receipt is merely a document confirming payment, and 'fund' is too general a term to describe this specific fixed cash amount.

The nominal ledger contains nominal accounts, which are accounts for expenses and revenues such as salaries, rent, and sales — salaries is therefore the correct answer.
