Fixtures is a real (asset) account. Stock is also a real account representing goods held for resale. Debtors account is a personal account and belongs in the sales ledger (debtors ledger), not the nominal ledger.

Discounts allowed are reductions given to customers who pay their debts early, making it a business expense that reduces profit. Because it is an expense, it is recorded on the debit side of the Profit and Loss account alongside other overhead costs. The Trading account only handles items directly related to buying and selling goods, such as purchases and sales. The Balance sheet records assets and liabilities, not expenses, and a current account is used in partnership accounts to record each partner's transactions.

A prepayment occurs when a business pays for something in advance, meaning the benefit is yet to be received, so it is a current asset on the balance sheet, not a liability. Accrued wages, rent arrears, and insurance due but unpaid are all amounts owed by the business that have not yet been paid, which makes each of them a liability. Liabilities represent obligations the business must settle in the future. Prepayment, by contrast, represents a resource the business is owed, classifying it firmly as an asset.

Factory overhead includes all indirect manufacturing costs, which are indirect wages plus factory expenses (rent and insurance): N10,800 + N18,000 + N3,000 = N31,800. Direct wages are excluded because they are a prime cost, not an overhead. Option A (N42,300) incorrectly adds direct wages into the overhead figure. Option C (N28,800) omits the indirect wages, and Option D (N21,000) only includes the two factory expense items without indirect wages.

Prime cost is the total of direct materials consumed plus direct labour (direct wages). Raw materials consumed = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock = N4,500 + N30,000 - N6,000 = N28,500; adding direct wages of N34,200 gives N62,700. Option A (N68,700) wrongly includes indirect wages, and Option B (N65,700) likely includes some overhead item. Option D (N58,800) understates either the materials or wages figure used in the calculation.

Raw materials consumed is calculated as Opening stock plus Purchases minus Closing stock: N4,500 + N30,000 - N6,000 = N28,500. The opening stock represents materials already on hand at the start of the year, purchases add to what is available, and closing stock is what remains unused at year-end. Option A (N34,500) forgets to deduct closing stock, and Option B (N31,500) uses incorrect figures. Work-in-progress balances are not part of this calculation as they relate to the cost of production, not raw materials consumed.

Bad debt refers specifically to a debt that has been written off because all reasonable efforts to collect it have failed and recovery is impossible. The key word is 'cannot' — it is not merely late or difficult, it is permanently unrecoverable. Option B is wrong because an overdue debt may still be collected; being late does not make it bad. Options C and D are unrelated — an overcharge is a billing error, and the employment status of a debtor has nothing to do with classifying a debt as bad.

A provision is an amount deliberately set aside from profits to cover an anticipated future expense or loss, such as provision for bad debts or depreciation. It is a charge against profit made before that loss actually occurs, based on reasonable estimation. Option B is wrong because a trading loss is an actual result, not a set-aside amount. Option C describes a cash expense or accrual, and Option D describes depreciation specifically — both are narrower than the general definition of a provision.

Carriage inwards is the cost of transporting purchased goods into the business, so it is directly related to the cost of obtaining stock and belongs in the Trading Account alongside purchases. It increases the cost of goods available for sale and reduces gross profit. Carriage outwards — the cost of delivering goods to customers — goes in the Profit and Loss Account, so students must not confuse the two. Options B and C (balance sheet and appropriation account) deal with assets/liabilities and profit distribution respectively, neither of which applies here.

Depreciation at 20% on cost means N60,000 × 20% = N12,000 per year. Since depreciation is charged fully in the year of disposal, four full years are charged: 1995, 1996, 1997, and 1998, giving total depreciation of N48,000. Net book value at disposal = N60,000 − N48,000 = N12,000, which is Option D. Option A (N39,000) suggests only one year was depreciated, Option B and C result from miscounting the years or applying a wrong rate — all stem from not carefully counting each calendar year including the year of sale.

When applicants send money to apply for shares, the company debits Bank and credits Application for Shares Account (a liability). When applications are unsuccessful and money must be refunded, this entry is reversed: Application for Shares Account is debited to cancel the liability, and Bank Account is credited because cash is leaving the business. Option A correctly states this. Option B reverses the entry wrongly, which would mean money is coming in rather than going out. Options C and D involve the wrong accounts — allotment and cash accounts are not relevant to refunding application monies.

In non-profit organisations like clubs and societies, there is no owner's capital or retained profit. Instead, the excess of assets over liabilities is called the accumulated fund, representing the net worth built up over time from surpluses. Working capital refers to the difference between current assets and current liabilities, not total net worth. Consolidated fund is a government treasury concept, and reserved capital applies to limited liability companies, not clubs.

Annual depreciation is 20% of N60,000 = N12,000 per year. Since depreciation is charged fully in the year of disposal (1998), four full years apply: 1995, 1996, 1997, and 1998, giving accumulated depreciation of N48,000. Net book value at disposal is N60,000 minus N48,000 = N12,000. Selling price N21,000 minus book value N12,000 gives a profit of N9,000. Option A (N24,000) would result from using only two years, and options B and C reflect arithmetic errors.

Depreciation is calculated at 20% on cost: 20% of N60,000 = N12,000 per year. Since depreciation is charged fully in the year of disposal, four complete years are counted: 1995, 1996, 1997, and 1998. Total accumulated depreciation is 4 multiplied by N12,000 = N48,000. Options B and C (N39,000 and N36,000) wrongly use fewer than four years, while option D (N21,000) is merely the sale price and has no bearing on accumulated depreciation.

When a company receives more applications than available shares, it is oversubscribed, and must allocate shares fairly by reducing each applicant's allotment in proportion to their application — this is called pro-rata allotment. Issuing at a discount means selling below face value, which is generally prohibited under company law. Issuing at par means selling at face value, and at premium means above face value — neither describes the method of scaling down allocations among applicants.

In government accounting, a warrant is the formal written authority issued to a spending officer, permitting expenditure up to a specified amount from an approved vote. A budget is the overall financial plan showing expected revenue and expenditure, not an authorisation document for a specific officer. Virement is the approved transfer of funds from one budget head to another, while a vote is the approved sum allocated for a particular purpose — neither directly authorises an officer to spend.

When the purchases day book is totalled, that total is posted to the debit side of the Purchases Account, which lives in the General Ledger. The General Ledger holds all nominal and real accounts that are not personal accounts of individual suppliers or customers. The Purchases Ledger (option A) contains individual creditor accounts, not the purchases account itself. The Private Ledger holds confidential accounts like capital and drawings, while the term General Ledger and Nominal Ledger are sometimes used interchangeably, but in standard WAEC usage, General Ledger is the correct and complete term for where the purchases account is kept.

Current liabilities are debts a business must pay within one year or the operating cycle. From the data, these are Creditors (N11,000), Rent Owing (N400), and Bank Overdraft (N8,750), which together total N20,150. Option D (N11,000) only counts creditors and ignores the rent owing and bank overdraft. Option A (N32,750) incorrectly adds long-term or non-liability items. Profit and Loss b/f is part of the owner's equity section, not a liability, so it is excluded from this calculation.

Purchase consideration is the agreed total price paid by the buyer when acquiring an entire business, covering all its assets. Goodwill (option D) is not the sale price itself but rather the excess amount paid above the fair value of the net identifiable assets. A premium (option B) refers to amounts paid above a base value in contexts like share issues or insurance. Capital reserve (option C) is a reserve created from capital profits and has nothing to do with the agreed sale price of a business.

General purpose computers are classified into three types based on the nature of data they process: analog computers, digital computers, and hybrid computers. Analog computers process continuous data, digital computers process discrete data represented as binary digits, and hybrid computers combine features of both. Options B, C, and D suggesting four, five, or six types are incorrect because this three-part classification is the standard accepted grouping for general purpose computers in secondary school ICT and accounts curricula.

Fixed assets are long-term tangible assets used in running the business and not intended for resale. From the balance sheet data, the fixed assets are Land and Building (N20,000), Furniture and Fittings (N7,500), and Motor Vehicle (N12,000), giving a total of N40,000. Stock, cash in hand, and debtors are current assets because they are expected to be converted to cash within one year and so must not be included. Option B (N47,500) and Option A (N57,300) incorrectly add current assets to the fixed asset total, while Option D (N37,500) omits one of the three fixed asset items.

Opening capital is found using a Statement of Affairs: Capital equals total assets minus total liabilities. Assets here include Land and Building, Stock, Cash in hand, Furniture and Fittings, Motor Vehicle, and Debtors, while liabilities include Profit and Loss b/f (an accumulated loss that reduces capital), Rent Owing, Creditors, and Bank Overdraft. Subtracting total liabilities (N34,150) from total assets gives N25,600. Option A (N32,000) omits some liabilities in the calculation, and Option D (N14,000) is merely the Profit and Loss b/f figure on its own, not the full opening capital.

Current assets are resources expected to be converted to cash within one year. From the table, these are Stock (N5,000), Cash in hand (N1,000), and Debtors (N13,750), which total N19,750. Land and buildings, motor vehicles, and furniture and fittings are fixed assets used long-term in the business, so they are excluded. Option B (N20,150) is actually the sum of current liabilities — Rent Owing, Creditors, and Bank Overdraft — a very common mix-up. Option A (N28,500) incorrectly includes a fixed asset alongside the current assets.

The materiality concept requires that every item of financial significance to an accounting period must be properly identified and recognised in that period alone. The trader paid N15,000 for 15 months, which works out to N1,000 per month; only N12,000 — the amount material to the current 12-month trading year — is charged to the Profit and Loss Account, while N3,000 is carried forward as prepaid rent. The accrual concept (Option A) deals with recognising income and expenses when they are earned or incurred rather than when cash moves; prudence (Option C) involves providing for expected losses without anticipating gains; going concern (Option D) is the assumption that the business will continue operating into the foreseeable future.

When the purchase price of a business is paid to the seller, cash leaves the business so the Cash Account is credited, and the Vendor's Account is debited to record that the seller has been fully paid and their account is now closed. Option B is wrong because debiting the Cash Account would mean cash is coming in, which is the opposite of making a payment. Option C incorrectly credits the Asset Account, which would reduce assets rather than record them. Option D could apply to buying individual assets for cash, but it does not correctly capture the two-stage process — first crediting the vendor, then settling by paying cash — used when purchasing an entire business.

A budget is the formal annual financial plan of the government, detailing estimated revenues and approved expenditures for the coming fiscal year, making it the primary tool for government financial planning and control. A gazette is an official government journal used to publish laws, regulations, and public notices — it records decisions already made, not financial plans. A vote refers to a specific amount of money approved and allocated to a particular ministry or spending head within the budget, so it is a component of the budget rather than the budget document itself. An analysis book is an accounting record used to classify transactions and has no role in government financial planning.

Rent of N15,000 covers 15 months, meaning N1,000 per month. Only 12 months belong to the current accounting year, so N12,000 is correctly charged to Profit and Loss. The accrual (matching) concept requires that expenses be recorded in the period they are incurred, not when cash changes hands. Materiality deals with the significance of an item, prudence involves caution in estimating values, and going-concern assumes the business will continue operating — none of these explain the time-period adjustment made here.

Cash discount is a reduction in price offered to encourage a buyer to settle their debt quickly, within a stated time period such as 7 or 14 days. Trade discount is deducted at the point of sale based on the buyer's relationship with the seller or their status as a wholesaler or retailer, and is not linked to payment timing. Quantity discount is granted for buying in large volumes. A rebate is a partial refund given after payment has already been made, often for meeting a sales target.

Interest on capital is recorded in the Profit and Loss Account because it represents a cost charged against the business before the net profit is determined. It compensates partners for the funds they have invested in the firm, treating that cost similarly to an interest expense owed to an outside lender. The Trading Account only handles cost of goods sold and gross profit calculations. The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account distributes the net profit that has already been calculated, while partners' fixed capital accounts record only the original capital contributions.

From the net profit of N40,000, first deduct salaries: Baba N5,000 + Tude N5,000 = N10,000. Then deduct interest on capital: Baba 10% of N40,000 = N4,000, Tude 10% of N50,000 = N5,000, totalling N9,000. Residual profit = N40,000 - N10,000 - N9,000 = N21,000, shared equally giving each partner N10,500. The other options confuse the total appropriations with individual profit shares, or calculate only one component such as interest on capital.

Tude's capital account on 1 January 2000 stands at N50,000, and interest on capital is agreed at 10% per annum. Multiplying N50,000 by 10% gives exactly N5,000 as Tude's interest on capital for the year. N10,000 would be 10% of N100,000, which is Baba's capital, not Tude's. N4,000 is the interest on Baba's capital of N40,000, and N1,500 has no basis in any figure given in the question.

Interest on capital is an appropriation of profit, meaning it is a way of distributing the firm's profit to reward partners for investing their capital. It is recorded in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account because that account handles all profit distributions among partners. The Profit and Loss Account (A) is for business operating expenses, not partner distributions. The Fixed Capital Account (B) records only the amount a partner contributed as capital, not returns earned on it. The Trading Account (D) is strictly for calculating gross profit from buying and selling goods.

When a business receives a cash discount from a supplier for early payment, all three accounts are affected. The Cash Book (i) records the actual amount paid and captures the discount in its discount column. The Discount Received Account (ii) is credited because the discount is a gain for the business. The Supplier's Account (iii) is debited with the full invoice value to completely clear the debt owed. Leaving out any one account means the double entry is incomplete, which is why options A, B, and C are all wrong.

Baba's current account is built up step by step: start with the opening credit balance of N20,000, then add salary N5,000, then add interest on capital which is 10% of N40,000 giving N4,000. The residual profit available for sharing is N40,000 minus total salaries N10,000 minus total interest on capital N9,000, leaving N21,000 shared equally, so Baba gets N10,500. Total credits are N39,500; deduct drawings of N4,000 to get the closing balance of N35,500. The wrong options arise from common errors like omitting the opening balance, miscalculating interest, or forgetting to add the profit share.

Tude's current account for the year is calculated by taking the opening credit balance of N15,000, adding salary of N5,000, and adding interest on capital which is 10% of N50,000 giving N5,000. Total credits come to N25,000, and after deducting drawings of N15,000, the closing balance is N10,000. Option C of N25,000 is wrong because it ignores the drawings deduction. Options A and B of N30,000 and N25,500 result from incorrectly inflating the credits by adding figures that do not belong to Tude's account.

Depreciation is the process of spreading the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life to account for the gradual loss of value through continuous use, ageing, and wear. Option B captures this precisely with the phrase 'wear and tear of fixed assets.' Cost of repairs (A) is a separate revenue expense incurred to maintain an asset and keep it working; it does not reduce the asset's book value the same way. Replacing an asset (C) is capital expenditure, a completely different transaction. Provision for loss (D) confuses depreciation with accidental or unexpected losses, which are accounted for differently.

Divide the total premium by the number of months to find the monthly rate: N45,000 divided by 15 months equals N3,000 per month. Since the policy covers a period that includes all 12 months of the year 2000 (January to December), only those 12 months belong to year 2000's Profit and Loss account: 12 × N3,000 = N36,000. The remaining 3 months of the policy fall into the next year and are carried as a prepayment on the Balance Sheet, not charged to P&L. Option A (N45,000) wrongly charges the full premium to one year, while Option B (N42,000) and Option D (N33,000) use incorrect month counts of 14 and 11 respectively.

A printer produces output from the computer to paper or screen, making it an output device, not an input device. Input devices are hardware used to send data into the computer for processing. A keyboard sends typed characters into the computer, a diskette (floppy disk) can be used to load data into the computer, and a punched card feeds coded data into the system — all are input devices. Only the printer sits on the output side of the data flow, so it is the correct answer here.

Prepaid insurance is insurance already paid for but not yet used — it represents a future economic benefit that the business is still owed. Because this benefit will be consumed within the next 12 months, it is classified as a current asset on the Balance Sheet. It is not a liability of any kind because the business does not owe anyone money; rather, money has already been paid in advance. Capital refers to the owner's equity, which is entirely separate from short-term operational prepayments like this one.

In government accounting, a fund is the total sum of money specifically set aside and earmarked for a defined purpose, such as education or health. A vote is a specific line-item allocation approved within the budget for a department or programme, which is narrower than a fund. Virement is the authorized transfer of money between different budget heads when one head has a surplus and another a deficit. A budget is the government's financial plan and estimate of revenue and expenditure, not the actual money set aside.

At 31st December 2000, the unused portion of the insurance policy — covering the 3 months from January to March of the following year — remains unexpired and must appear on the Balance Sheet as a prepaid expense. That figure is 3 months × N3,000 per month = N9,000. Option A (N45,000) is the total cost paid, not the unexpired portion. Option B (N12,000) would represent 4 months, which does not correspond to any valid unexpired period in this scenario. Option D (N4,500) equals only 1.5 months and has no basis in the calculation.

A suspense account is a temporary account opened when the trial balance fails to agree, allowing the bookkeeper to still prepare financial statements while errors are investigated and corrected. It holds the difference between the two sides of the trial balance until the mistakes are found. Recording sales and purchases have their own dedicated accounts (Sales Account and Purchases Account respectively), so those options are wrong. The balance sheet is prepared after the trial balance agrees, not what a suspense account helps with.

The realisation concept states that revenue should only be recognised when it has actually been earned and received or is legally due, not before. The phrase 'do not count chickens before they are hatched' perfectly captures this idea of not recording income that has not yet been realised. Accrual means recognising income and expenses when they occur, not when cash changes hands. Going concern assumes the business will continue operating, and materiality relates to whether an item is significant enough to affect decisions.

Subscriptions in arrears means members owe money to the club that has not yet been paid, making it money owed to the club and therefore a current asset on the balance sheet. It is expected to be collected within the short term, which is why it sits under current assets alongside debtors. It is not a liability because the club is owed money, not owing it. It is not an intangible or fictitious asset since those relate to non-physical items like goodwill or preliminary expenses.

A reserve represents the surplus or excess of assets over specific liabilities, and it belongs to the owners of the business as part of equity. In companies, reserves are set aside from profits for future use or as a cushion against losses. A provision is created for a known liability or expense whose amount is uncertain, not an excess of assets. Premium refers to the extra amount received above the nominal value of shares, and a bonus is an additional payment, neither of which describes this surplus concept.

Debenture holders are creditors who lend money to a company and in return receive a fixed periodic payment called interest, regardless of whether the company makes a profit. Dividends are paid to shareholders, not debenture holders, because shareholders are owners while debenture holders are lenders. Net profit belongs to the company and its shareholders after all expenses are deducted. Shares represent ownership in a company, which is completely different from debentures, which are loan instruments.

The sales ledger, also called the debtors ledger, contains accounts for customers who owe money to the business, making Debtors Account the correct answer. It is a subsidiary ledger that records all credit sales transactions with individual customers. Bank Account belongs to the nominal or general ledger, Motor Van Disposal Account is a nominal account also in the general ledger, and Rent and Rates Account is a nominal account recording expenses — none of these relate to customers owing money.

Prime cost is the total of all direct costs incurred in manufacturing a product, which includes direct material, direct labour, and direct expenses. Direct expenses are costs that can be specifically traced to a unit of production, such as royalties or special hire costs. Option A is incomplete because it omits direct expenses. Option C is wrong because overheads are indirect costs added later to get works cost or total cost of production, not prime cost. Option D omits direct labour, which is always a core component.

Fictitious assets are not real assets but are shown on the balance sheet because they represent expenditure not yet fully written off, or a debit balance with no tangible value. Raw materials stock is a genuine, tangible current asset that physically exists in a warehouse, so it is not fictitious. The debit balance of a profit and loss account, preliminary expenses, and incorporation costs are all fictitious because they represent losses or costs carried forward that have no physical form or realisable value.

Rates prepaid is a prepayment, which is a current asset representing money paid in advance for a future period, and all assets carry debit balances. A bank loan is a liability and therefore has a credit balance. Income received in advance is also a liability because the business owes a service yet to be delivered, so it carries a credit balance. Ordinary share capital represents money owed to shareholders and is part of equity, which always has a credit balance.

Under the imprest system, the amount reimbursed at the end of the month equals the total of all payments made during that month, restoring the float back to N4,000. Adding all payments: 328 + 914 + 375 + 536 + 928 + 437 + 210 = N3,728, which is the reimbursement needed. Option A (N4,000) would be wrong because that is the full imprest amount, not the reimbursement. Option C (N3,483) was the reimbursement made at the start of the month to top up from N517, not the end-of-month figure. Option D (N1,842) has no basis in the figures given.

Stationery includes items like notebooks (N328) and envelopes (N437), giving a total of N765. Postage stamps, though bought from petty cash, fall under a separate 'postage' column, not stationery. Option D (N437) only counts envelopes and ignores notebooks. Option B and C do not correspond to any correct grouping of stationery items in the petty cash book.

The personal ledger records transactions involving named individuals — debtors and creditors. The only payment made to a named person is N536 paid to J. Thomas, a creditor, so that amount is posted to the personal ledger. Option D (N517) is merely the opening cash balance, not a payment to any person. Option A (N765) is total stationery expenditure, which belongs in the impersonal or nominal ledger.

Preliminary expenses are costs incurred in forming a company (legal fees, registration costs) before trading begins. They appear on the balance sheet as an asset but have no physical existence or realisable value, making them fictitious. Overdraft is a liability. Cash in hand is a real, tangible asset. Reserves are part of a company's equity and represent retained earnings or provisions.

A subsidiary book — also called a book of original (prime) entry — is where transactions are first recorded before being posted to the ledger. Examples include the sales day book, purchases day book, returns books, and the journal. It is not the ledger itself (option B), nor is it found inside the journal (option C). The balance sheet (option D) is a financial statement, not a book of entry.

The acid test ratio (quick ratio) measures whether a company can pay its short-term liabilities using its most liquid assets — cash, receivables, and short-term investments — excluding inventory. This makes it the standard test of short-term solvency. Debt-to-equity ratio measures long-term financial leverage. Net profit margin and gross profit margin both measure profitability, not the ability to meet immediate obligations.

Commission paid to a sales representative should be recorded in the commission account, not the salaries account. Debiting the wrong class of account — treating commission as salaries — is an error of principle because these two expenses are fundamentally different in nature. An error of principle occurs when a transaction is posted to an account of the wrong type, even though the arithmetic may be correct. Reversal of entries means debiting what should be credited and vice versa, which is not the case here. Compensation errors cancel each other out across two mistakes, which also does not apply.

Control accounts (debtors control and creditors control) are prepared in the general ledger, which serves as the main ledger summarising all transactions. The general ledger contains both personal and impersonal accounts including the control accounts that check the accuracy of subsidiary ledgers. The sales ledger and purchases ledger are subsidiary ledgers that contain individual customer and supplier accounts respectively, not control accounts. The nominal ledger is sometimes used interchangeably with general ledger, but in this context the correct specific answer is the general ledger.

Suppliers are creditors of the business, and their individual personal accounts are maintained in the purchases ledger, also called the creditors ledger. Each supplier has their own account in this subsidiary ledger showing amounts owed to them. The sales ledger holds customer (debtor) accounts, not supplier accounts. The purchases account and sales account are impersonal nominal accounts in the general ledger that record the total value of purchases and sales, not individual supplier details.

Labour costs incurred in installing machinery are capital expenditure because they form part of the total cost of bringing the asset into working condition. Such costs must be added to the machinery account, increasing the value of the fixed asset on the balance sheet. Treating it as salaries would incorrectly record a capital cost as a revenue expense, reducing profit unfairly and understating the asset value. Debtors and creditors accounts are irrelevant here as no sale or credit purchase is involved.

Option D is incorrect because decreases in liability accounts are entered on the debit side, not the credit side. When you reduce a liability such as paying off a creditor, you debit the liability account. Options A, B, and C correctly follow the double-entry rules: assets increase on the debit side and decrease on the credit side, while liabilities increase on the credit side. Confusing the side used to decrease liabilities is a common mistake, but the debit entry is always what reduces a liability balance.

Recording a purchase in the sales day book means the transaction was classified under the wrong category entirely — purchases represent expenses or stock inflows, while sales represent revenue. This fundamental misclassification of transaction type is what defines an error of principle. Error of reversal would mean the correct accounts were used but debited when they should have been credited; error of omission means the transaction was never recorded at all; error of original entries means a wrong amount was entered in a subsidiary book.

When a firm pays N10,000 to a creditor, it debits the creditor account (reducing the liability) and credits cash or bank (reducing the asset). Both liabilities and assets therefore decrease, making option A the correct answer. Option D, stating that liabilities and assets both increase, actually describes what happens when goods are purchased on credit — not when an existing creditor is paid. The answer key indicating D appears to be incorrect; standard double-entry rules confirm that settling a creditor reduces both sides of the accounting equation.

The only external obligation the business owes is the N20,000 borrowed from a friend, and that alone constitutes the firm's liability. The remaining N40,000 of the cash balance is the owner's own money and forms part of capital, not a liability. Total assets equal N520,000, and with liabilities of N20,000, capital works out to N500,000 — consistent with question 3890. Option D (N20,000) is the correct liability amount; the answer key showing B (N60,000) appears to be a printing error.

Capital equals Total Assets minus Total Liabilities. Adding up all assets gives N520,000 (Motor Van N120,000 + Buildings N300,000 + Stock N40,000 + Cash N60,000), and the only liability is the N20,000 borrowed from a friend, so capital equals N500,000. Option B is therefore the correct answer. Option A (N520,000) would only hold if there were zero liabilities, which contradicts the information given; the answer key showing A appears to be a marking error.

The Purchases Ledger holds individual accounts for every supplier (creditor) who sold goods on credit, so the control account that consolidates all those balances into one total is rightly called the Total Creditors Account. It lets management confirm the total owed to suppliers without checking each personal account individually. Option B (Total Debtors Account) refers to the Sales Ledger Control Account, which is a completely different ledger; Cash Account records cash and bank movements; Personal Account is a general description of any individual debtor or creditor account, not the control account itself.

Start with the total invoice value: 5 items at N40,000 each gives N200,000. Trade discount of 25% is deducted first (N200,000 x 25% = N50,000), reducing the amount to N150,000. The cash discount of 10% is then applied to this reduced figure (N150,000 x 10% = N15,000), leaving N135,000 to be paid within the credit period. Option A ignores both discounts entirely, while Option B only deducts the trade discount and misses the cash discount calculation.

The diminishing balance method applies a fixed percentage to the reducing book value of an asset each year, meaning the depreciation charge is largest in the first year and decreases over time. This reflects the reality that assets are often most useful and productive in their early years. The straight line and fixed instalment methods charge equal amounts every year, making no distinction between early and later years. The revaluation method is based on changes in the asset's market value and is typically used for assets like livestock or loose tools.

Cost of raw materials consumed is calculated as: Opening stock (N8,000) plus Purchases (N45,000), which gives N53,000, then subtract Closing stock (N9,500), arriving at N43,500. Option A of N53,000 is the mistake of forgetting to deduct closing stock. Options B and C are incorrect because they mishandle either the opening or closing stock figures. Direct wages, indirect wages, and other factory overheads are not part of raw material cost but are added later when calculating prime cost or factory cost.

The debtors ledger records amounts owed to the business by customers who bought goods on credit, so entries originate from sales invoices issued to those customers. A sales invoice creates the debt and serves as the primary source document for updating the debtor's account. Suppliers invoices are source documents for the creditors ledger, not the debtors ledger, because they record what the business owes its suppliers. Returns outward notes reduce amounts owed to suppliers, and payment vouchers record cash paid out, neither of which creates entries in the debtors ledger.

The debtors ledger records amounts owed to the business by customers who bought goods on credit, so entries originate from sales invoices issued to those customers. A sales invoice creates the debt and serves as the primary source document for updating the debtor's account. Suppliers invoices are source documents for the creditors ledger, not the debtors ledger, because they record what the business owes its suppliers. Returns outward notes reduce amounts owed to suppliers, and payment vouchers record cash paid out, neither of which creates entries in the debtors ledger.

Production cost is calculated by taking the factory cost and adjusting for work-in-progress. Raw materials consumed = 8,000 + 45,000 - 9,500 = 43,500; add direct wages 6,450 to get prime cost of 49,950; add factory overheads (indirect wages 2,800 + depreciation 3,200 + factory rent 350 = 6,350) to get factory cost of 56,300; then add opening WIP 3,250 and subtract closing WIP 3,750, giving 56,300 + 3,250 - 3,750 = N55,800. Option A (57,300) and B (56,300) ignore or misapply the WIP adjustment, while D (53,000) omits factory overheads entirely.

Factory cost of production is the total cost incurred in the factory before adjusting for work-in-progress. Raw materials consumed (8,000 + 45,000 - 9,500) = 43,500, plus direct wages 6,450 gives prime cost 49,950; adding all factory overheads (indirect wages 2,800 + depreciation 3,200 + factory rent 350 = 6,350) gives 49,950 + 6,350 = N56,300. Unlike production cost, factory cost does not adjust for opening or closing WIP, which is why C (52,750), which subtracts WIP incorrectly, and D (45,500), which omits wages, are wrong.

Prime cost covers only direct costs: raw materials consumed plus direct wages, with no factory overhead included. Raw materials consumed = 8,000 + 45,000 - 9,500 = 43,500; adding direct wages of 6,450 gives 43,500 + 6,450 = N49,950. Option A (53,000) incorrectly adds indirect wages, B (52,750) uses a wrong combination, and D (46,300) understates raw materials consumption by forgetting to add opening stock properly.

Government accounting is cash-based and not profit-oriented, so a Profit and Loss Account is irrelevant and never prepared in government financial statements. A vote is an approved spending limit unique to government budgeting, a consolidated fund is the main government treasury account, and a trial balance is a universal bookkeeping tool used in government accounts too. Since the government aims to provide services rather than make profit, income and expenditure statements replace profit and loss accounts in public sector accounting.

Head offices issue goods to branches at cost price so that branch accounts reflect the actual cost of inventory, making it easier to calculate the true gross profit earned at the branch level. Issuing at prime cost (A) would exclude some overheads and understate the value, while production cost (B) and net realisable value (C) are less commonly used for this purpose in standard branch accounting practice. Using cost price keeps the accounting straightforward and allows the head office to monitor branch performance accurately.

When a proprietor withdraws cash for personal use, the Drawings account is debited because drawings represent money taken out of the business by the owner, reducing capital. The Cash account is credited because the business is giving out cash, reducing this asset. Option A is wrong because purchases has nothing to do with personal withdrawals. Options B and C wrongly involve the Purchases account, which records goods bought for resale, not personal withdrawals.

From 1996 to 1999 is 3 years of depreciation. At 20% straight-line on N10,000, annual depreciation is N2,000, so total accumulated depreciation is N6,000, leaving a book value of N4,000. The asset was sold for only N2,000, which is N2,000 less than the book value, giving a loss of N2,000. Option A suggests a profit, which is impossible since the sale price is below book value. Option B incorrectly implies the sale price equals book value with no loss.

When disposing an asset, the net book value at disposal (N4,000) is transferred from the Fixed Asset Account to the Disposal of Asset Account. This means Disposal of Asset Account is debited N4,000 and Fixed Asset Account is credited N4,000, which is Option B. Option A reverses the debit and credit entries. Options C and D use N2,000, which is the sale proceeds, not the book value that must be transferred out of the fixed asset account.

The asset cost N10,000 in 1996 and was sold in 1999, giving exactly 3 years of depreciation. At 20% per annum using straight-line method, annual depreciation is N2,000 (20% of N10,000). Over 3 years, total depreciation is N6,000, so book value at disposal is N10,000 minus N6,000, which equals N4,000. Option A (N8,000) reflects only one year of depreciation, Option B (N6,000) reflects two years, and Option D (N2,000) is the sale proceeds, not the book value.

To find Baba's share of profit, first deduct all appropriations from net profit. Interest on capital: Ali gets 5% of N5,000,000 = N250,000 and Baba gets 5% of N4,000,000 = N200,000. Partner salaries are N500,000 for Ali and N300,000 for Baba, totalling N800,000. Total appropriations = N450,000 + N800,000 = N1,250,000. Residual profit = N4,000,000 minus N1,250,000 = N2,750,000. Baba's share is 2/5 of N2,750,000 = N1,100,000. Option B (N1,600,000) would be Baba's total earnings including salary and interest, not just the profit share.

Realization concept states that profit is only recognised when a sale actually occurs, not when goods are produced or an order is received. This means revenue is earned at the point of sale or transfer of ownership. Matching concept is about linking expenses to the revenues they generate in the same period, not about when profit is recognised. Periodicity divides business activities into accounting periods, while going concern assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely.

The money measurement concept requires that only items which can be expressed in objective, verifiable monetary terms are recorded in the accounts. When an accountant merely 'thinks' an investment is worthless without objective evidence, that subjective opinion does not constitute a measurable monetary fact. Objectivity concept is related but focuses on using verifiable evidence rather than the monetary unit itself. Conservatism would actually support writing the investment down, and consistency refers to applying the same accounting methods from period to period.

A Partnership Deed (also called Articles of Partnership) is the formal written agreement between partners that sets out how the business will be run, including profit-sharing ratios, salaries, interest on capital, and other rules. The Partnership Act is a piece of legislation passed by government, not an agreement made by the partners themselves. A Memorandum of Association is a formation document used by registered companies, not partnerships. There is no recognised document called a partnership code.

Ali's current account is built up by crediting his opening balance (N400,000), interest on capital (5% of N5,000,000 = N250,000), salary (N500,000), and share of residual profit (3/5 of N2,750,000 = N1,650,000), giving total credits of N2,800,000. Drawings of N2,300,000 are debited, leaving a closing credit balance of N500,000. A debit balance would only arise if drawings exceeded all credits, which is not the case here. The N1,600,000 figures refer to Baba's closing current account, not Ali's.

To find Ali's share of profit, first deduct all prior-charge appropriations from net profit: interest on capital (N250,000 + N200,000 = N450,000) and partner salaries (N500,000 + N300,000 = N800,000) total N1,250,000, leaving residual profit of N2,750,000. Ali's share at 3/5 is N1,650,000. Option C (N1,280,000) and option D (N1,100,000) apply incorrect ratios or wrong residual figures; N1,100,000 is actually Baba's residual profit share at 2/5.

When goods are stolen, the business suffers a loss, so the profit and loss account must be debited to record that loss. The purchases account is credited to remove the cost of stolen goods from the trading account, since those goods never generated sales revenue. Option A is wrong because debiting purchases and crediting trading reverses the logic entirely. Option E involving capital account is incorrect because theft is an operational loss, not a capital matter.

To realize an asset means to convert it into cash or its cash equivalent, which is what happens when a business sells a fixed asset or collects money from a debtor. Closing an account in the ledger (A) is just a bookkeeping entry and does not bring in cash. Giving an asset as collateral (B) or mortgaging it (E) still leaves the business with a debt, so no true conversion to cash has occurred. Opening an account in the ledger (D) is simply recording, not converting anything.

Goodwill is an intangible asset representing the reputation, brand, and customer loyalty of a business, and it has no independent existence apart from the business itself — it cannot be sold separately for cash. Debtors (A) can pay their debts in cash, fixtures (C) and motor vehicles (E) can be physically sold to third parties, so all of these can be realized. Creditors (B) are liabilities the business owes, not assets, so the question of realizing them does not apply. Goodwill uniquely has no standalone realizable value, making it the correct answer.

When a shareholder pays more money than the company has actually called or demanded for shares, that excess is recorded as a call-in-advance, because the company holds money it has not yet requested. Call-in-arrears (E) is the exact opposite situation — money that has been demanded by the company but not yet paid by the shareholder. A dividend warrant (A) is a document that authorizes dividend payment to shareholders and has nothing to do with share application. Capital reserve (C) and revenue reserve (B) are retained earnings classifications, not accounts for excess share payments.

A provision for discount on debtors is created to account for the discount the business anticipates giving to customers who pay their debts early, and since this reduces business income, it is debited to the profit and loss account. The corresponding credit entry goes to the provision for discount on debtors account, not to the debtors account itself (C), because the debtors still owe the full amount until they actually pay. Option B is wrong because crediting profit and loss would incorrectly increase profit rather than reduce it. Option D confuses this provision with provision for bad debts, which are two separate accounts for two different purposes.

Recurrent expenditure refers to day-to-day spending on items that are consumed or used up within a short period and must be repeatedly purchased. Drugs are consumable — once administered to patients they are gone, and the council must keep buying them, making it a recurrent expense. Building classrooms (A), sinking wells (B), constructing markets (D), and purchasing hospital beds (E) all create durable physical structures or assets that serve the community for many years, classifying them as capital expenditure. Capital expenditure provides long-term benefit, recurrent expenditure does not.

Recurrent expenditure covers costs that are regular, recurring, and do not create long-lasting physical assets. From the table, annual inter-house sports competition (N20,000) and payment of teachers' salaries (N80,000) qualify as recurrent because they happen repeatedly and produce no permanent asset. Construction of classrooms, purchase of tablets and chairs, and purchase of textbooks for the library all create lasting assets and are therefore capital expenditure. Adding the two recurrent items: N20,000 + N80,000 = N100,000.

Capital expenditure is spending that creates long-lasting assets benefiting the organization over several years. Construction of classrooms (N500,000), purchase of tablets and chairs (N50,000), and purchase of textbooks for the library (N40,000) all produce durable assets, so they are capital expenditure. Teachers' salaries and the sports competition are recurrent and must be excluded from the capital total. Adding the three capital items: N500,000 + N50,000 + N40,000 = N590,000.

This question tests the concept of prepaid expenses, where part of the cash paid in one period actually covers the next period. If N2,000 was paid during 1995 but N200 of that amount was a prepayment covering 1996, then the actual rent expense for 1995 is N2,000 minus N200, giving N1,800. Options A and B (N2,400 and N2,200) would only apply if there were additional accrued rent owed but not yet paid, making the expense higher than cash paid. Option C (N2,000) would mean the full cash paid equals the expense with no prepayment involved.

When a company refunds unsuccessful share applicants, cash leaves the bank so the bank account is credited, and the application for shares account is debited to close and reverse the original liability recorded when application money was received. Option B reverses the entries completely — crediting the application account would increase the liability instead of cancelling it. Options C and D bring in the allotment account, which is only used when shares are actually allotted to successful applicants, not for refunds. Option E incorrectly uses a cash account instead of bank account for the refund.

Factory rent is paid to maintain the production facility, making it an indirect manufacturing cost — a production overhead. Discount allowed is a financial/selling expense, carriage inwards is part of the cost of purchasing raw materials, carriage outwards is a selling and distribution expense, and depreciation of office equipment is an administrative overhead because the office is outside the production floor.

Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is calculated on the opening book value each year. Year 1 depreciation = 10% × N600,000 = N60,000, leaving NBV of N540,000. Year 2 depreciation = 10% × N540,000 = N54,000, so NBV at end of Year 2 = N540,000 − N54,000 = N486,000. Options A, B, and C result from using the wrong base or ignoring the reducing effect, while option E understates the accumulated charge.

When shares are issued at below their nominal (face) value, the shortfall represents a share discount, and accounting rules require it to be debited to the share discount account. Share premium account is used only when shares are sold above nominal value, not below. The profit and loss account handles revenue income and expenses, not capital transactions, and reserves are appropriations of profit — none of them absorb a share issue discount.

Under the reducing balance method, Year 1 depreciation = 10% × N600,000 = N60,000, and Year 2 depreciation = 10% × N540,000 = N54,000. The accumulated (total) depreciation charged by the end of Year 2 is N60,000 + N54,000 = N114,000. Option D (N54,000) represents only the Year 2 annual charge and ignores Year 1; the other options use incorrect bases or rates.

Cost of raw materials used = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock = N5,800 + N19,000 − N4,500 = N20,300. Carriage outwards (N1,300) is excluded because it is a selling and distribution expense, not a cost of obtaining raw materials — carriage inwards would be added instead. Options with higher figures mistakenly include carriage outwards or other non-material costs in the calculation.

Under the straight-line method, annual depreciation = (Cost − Scrap Value) × Rate = (N600,000 − N60,000) × 10% = N54,000 per year. After two full years, accumulated depreciation = N108,000, so NBV at the beginning of Year 3 (same as end of Year 2) = N600,000 − N108,000 = N492,000. Option A ignores scrap value; options C and D reflect wrong periods or miscalculations.

Under straight-line depreciation at 10% of cost, annual depreciation = 10% × N600,000 = N60,000. Cumulative depreciation at the end of Year 3 = 3 × N60,000 = N180,000. Option A (N216,000) represents four years; options D and E (around N162,000) result from applying the rate to the depreciable amount after deducting scrap value rather than to the full cost.

Factory overhead comprises all indirect production costs: Factory electricity N2,500 + Supervisor's salary N5,500 + Depreciation of Plant N1,500 = N9,500. Direct labour (N4,000) is a direct cost forming part of prime cost, not overhead. Administrative expenses and selling/distribution expenses are period costs that never enter factory overhead.

Prime cost = Cost of Raw Materials Used + Direct Labour = N20,300 + N4,000 = N24,300. Only direct inputs enter prime cost; indirect factory costs such as electricity, supervisor's salary, and plant depreciation are factory overheads added at the next stage. Options A and B are too high because they include overhead items, while option D understates the materials figure.

Production cost (factory cost) = Prime Cost + Factory Overhead = N24,300 + N9,500 = N33,800. Selling and distribution expenses (N3,000) and administrative expenses (N5,500) are period costs excluded from production cost because they are not incurred on the factory floor. Options B through E omit either components of prime cost or factory overhead items, producing understated totals.

Carriage outwards refers to the cost of transporting goods to customers after a sale has been made, so it relates to goods sold. Carriage inwards, by contrast, is the cost of bringing purchased goods into the business. Options B, C, D, and E all relate to goods coming into or remaining within the business, not goods being delivered to buyers.

Interest on partners' drawings is treated as income to the partnership because it penalises partners for withdrawing funds early, increasing the profit available for sharing. This income is credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, which is the 'appropriate account' referred to in option E. The current account (C) is debited for the charge against each partner, not credited. The profit and loss account (D) handles general business expenses and income, not partnership-specific appropriations.

To find gross profit, first calculate cost of production: opening raw materials (5,800) + purchases (19,000) minus closing raw materials (4,500) = 20,300, then add direct labour (4,000), factory electricity (2,500), supervisor salary (5,500), and plant depreciation (1,500) to get 33,800. Carriage outwards is excluded because it is a selling expense, not a manufacturing cost. Gross profit equals sales (58,000) minus cost of goods sold (33,800 minus closing finished goods 4,500 = 29,300), giving N28,700.

Traditional public sector accounting operates on a cash basis, meaning expenditure is recognised when cash is paid rather than when assets are acquired and used over time. As a result, the full cost of an asset is expensed in the year it is purchased instead of being capitalised and depreciated. Options A and B describe depreciation methods used in private sector accounting, which do not apply under traditional government accounting rules.

Discount allowed is a reduction granted to customers who pay their debts promptly; it is an expense incurred after the sale and therefore belongs in the Profit and Loss account alongside other operating expenses. It does not appear in the Trading account (C), which only includes the direct cost of buying and selling goods to arrive at gross profit. The Appropriation account (A) deals with how net profit is shared among owners, not with general business expenses.

Non-profit organisations do not use the terms profit or loss; when their expenditure exceeds their income they record a deficit, and when income exceeds expenditure they record a surplus. Deficit correctly describes the shortfall, making C the right answer. Surplus (A) is the opposite situation where income is greater. Drawing (B) refers to money taken by an owner of a business, which is irrelevant to non-profit organisations.

Subscription in advance is money paid by members for a future period, meaning the organisation has received cash it has not yet earned and still owes the benefit to those members. This obligation makes it a current liability on the balance sheet, as it must be settled within the next accounting period. Subscription in arrears, by contrast, would be a current asset because money is owed to the organisation, not by it.

Undercasting of purchases means the purchases column in the books was added up to a total that was too low, so the purchases account balance was understated. To correct this, purchases must be increased by debiting the purchases account, and the suspense account is credited to remove the compensating difference that was placed there when the trial balance failed to agree. Overcasting (B) would require the opposite correction — a credit to purchases to reduce an overstated balance.

When a trial balance fails to agree, the difference between the debit and credit totals is placed in a suspense account so that the trial balance can be made to agree temporarily while the bookkeeper locates the underlying errors. The suspense account is not a permanent ledger for sales (B) or purchases (C); it is a temporary holding account. Once all errors are found and corrected, the suspense account balance reduces to zero.

A Receipts and Payments Account is simply a summarised cash book showing all money received and all money paid out during a period, and its closing balance represents cash in hand or at bank. It is not an income statement, so it reveals neither profit, loss, surplus, nor deficit — those figures come from the Income and Expenditure Account. Options A, B, D, and E all relate to profitability measures that require accrual-based calculations, not a cash summary.

When goods are sent to branch at invoice price (cost plus loading), the seller records the full invoice price by debiting Branch Stock Account and crediting Goods Sent to Branch Account. The loading portion is then separated by debiting Goods Sent to Branch Account and crediting Branch Stock Adjustment Account, which is what option B describes. This adjustment ensures the Goods Sent to Branch Account reflects only cost price, while the Branch Stock Adjustment Account holds the unrealised profit. Option A wrongly debits Branch Stock Account for the loading, which would double-count it. Options C and D reverse the correct entries entirely.

XYZ issues 30,000 shares of N1 each at a 5% discount, so each share is worth N0.95, giving a purchase consideration of N28,500. The total net assets taken over from ABC are Stock N18,000 plus Debtors N11,000, totalling N29,000. Capital Reserve arises when net assets acquired exceed the purchase consideration: N29,000 minus N28,500 equals N500. Options A and B suggest higher reserves that do not match the correct calculation, and option D (N150) has no basis in the figures given.

When a buyer is undercharged, they owe more money than what was originally invoiced, so the seller must increase the amount the buyer owes by sending a debit note. A debit note increases the buyer's liability in the seller's records, correcting the shortfall. A credit note (option B) does the opposite — it reduces what the buyer owes and is used when the buyer was overcharged. Options C and D do not represent valid source documents used to correct billing errors in accounting.

An error of original entry occurs when a transaction is recorded with the wrong amount from the very beginning, affecting both sides of the entry equally. Here, N650 was written as N560 in the books, so both the debit and credit sides carry the same wrong figure of N560. An error of commission means posting to the correct type but wrong account; an error of principle means using the wrong account category entirely. An error of compensation involves two separate errors that cancel each other out, which is not the case here.

Gross Profit is calculated in the Trading Account as Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold (Opening Stock plus Purchases minus Closing Stock). Option C captures this correctly because Cost of Goods Sold accounts for stock movements, not just purchases. Option A is wrong because gross profit does not deduct all trading expenses — only the cost of goods sold is deducted at the gross level; expenses like wages and rent are deducted later to arrive at net profit. Option B is too simplistic because ignoring opening and closing stock gives an inaccurate cost figure.

External storage devices like hard drives, USB drives, and CDs are called backing storage because they back up or supplement the computer's main memory by storing data permanently outside the CPU. Primary storage refers to RAM, which is internal and temporary. Options like logging storage and extra storage are not recognised computing terms, making them incorrect.

Rent owing at 31st December 1998 (N800) is rent accrued, meaning the business has used the space but not yet paid for it, making it a debt owed within the short term. This classifies it as a current liability on the balance sheet. It is not a current asset because assets represent what the business owns or is owed, not what it owes. Long-term liabilities are debts payable beyond one year, and fixed assets are physical resources like buildings or equipment.

Rent charged to the Profit and Loss account is calculated as: cash paid plus closing accrual minus opening accrual, which gives N1,700 + N800 - N500 = N2,000. The opening accrual (N500) is subtracted because it was already charged in the previous year's accounts. Simply using the cash paid figure of N1,700 ignores the accrual adjustments, which is why options B, C, and D are all wrong.

Petty cash is used to pay for small, routine daily expenses that are too minor for formal payment processes. Machinery is capital expenditure, meaning it is a large-value asset purchased for long-term use and must go through the main cashbook or bank, never petty cash. Stationery, postage stamps, and a cutlass for gardeners are all low-cost operational expenses that correctly belong in a petty cash book.

ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit, which is the component inside a computer's processor responsible for performing mathematical calculations and logical comparisons. Accounting Logic Unit and Additional Liability Unit are not computing terms at all. Access Logic Unit is also fabricated and has no meaning in computer architecture.

Margin is profit calculated as a fraction (or percentage) of the selling price, which is why B is correct. For example, if a good sells for N100 and profit is N20, the margin is 20%. Mark-up (option A) is different — it expresses profit as a fraction of the cost price, not the selling price. Gross profit (C) and net profit (D) are amounts of money, not ratios, so they do not fit the definition given.

Prime cost covers only direct costs: direct materials and direct labour. Raw materials consumed equals opening stock (N6,500) plus purchases (N12,500) minus closing stock (N4,000) = N15,000. Adding manufacturing wages (N2,000) gives prime cost of N17,000. Factory rent is an overhead, not a prime cost, so it is excluded — including it would wrongly give N17,500 (option C).

Cost of production adds factory overheads and adjusts for work-in-progress to the prime cost. Starting from prime cost N17,000, add factory rent N500, then add opening WIP N2,500 and subtract closing WIP N1,000: N17,000 + N500 + N2,500 - N1,000 = N19,000. Option B (N18,500) forgets to add opening WIP, while option C omits the WIP adjustment entirely.

Cost of raw materials consumed is calculated using the standard formula: opening stock of raw materials plus purchases minus closing stock of raw materials. That gives N6,500 + N12,500 - N4,000 = N15,000. Option B (N16,000) uses wrong figures, option A (N18,500) incorrectly includes other costs, and option D (N12,500) is just the purchases figure without any stock adjustment.

A debit balance exists when the total monetary value of all debit entries exceeds the total monetary value of all credit entries — that is why C is correct. Option B is wrong because the number of entries does not matter; one large credit could outweigh many small debits. Option A is incorrect because the first entry recorded has no bearing on the final balance, and option D is the opposite of a debit balance situation.

When depreciation is recorded each year using the provision method, the provision for depreciation account is debited to recognize the reduction in asset value, while the asset account (machinery) is credited to reduce its carrying value on the books. This keeps the original cost visible in the asset account while the provision account tracks accumulated depreciation separately. Option B is wrong because debiting the provision account and crediting P&L reverses the normal flow of the transaction. Options C and D are wrong because trading and manufacturing accounts deal with buying and producing goods, not with fixed asset depreciation entries.

In Public Sector Accounting, the vote book records the amount of money allocated (voted) by government for each expenditure head and tracks spending against those allocations to prevent overspending. It is essentially a spending control tool that ensures ministries do not spend beyond their approved budget limits. Option A is wrong because voter registration belongs to electoral bodies, not accounting departments. Option C is wrong because government policy is set by lawmakers and executives, not accounting records. Option D is wrong because revenue is recorded in separate revenue ledgers or cash books, not the vote book.

Annual depreciation using straight-line method is (N16,000 minus N2,000) divided by 4 years, which equals N3,500 per year. After three years, total depreciation is N10,500, so net book value at end of year three is N16,000 minus N10,500, giving N5,500. The vehicle was sold for N6,000, and since the sale price exceeds net book value by N500, there is a profit of N500. Options A and D suggesting N1,000 profit or loss are wrong because they miscalculate either the depreciation or the net book value. Option C suggests a loss, but since N6,000 exceeds N5,500, a profit results, not a loss.

Straight-line depreciation divides the depreciable amount evenly over the asset's useful life. The formula is: (Cost minus Scrap Value) divided by Useful Life, which gives (N16,000 minus N2,000) divided by 4 equals N14,000 divided by 4 equals N3,500 per year. Option C of N4,000 is wrong because it ignores the scrap value and simply divides N16,000 by 4. Option B of N5,500 confuses the annual charge with the net book value at year three. Option A of N9,000 has no valid basis under this calculation.

Net book value at the end of year three equals the original cost minus total accumulated depreciation for three years. Annual depreciation is N3,500, so three years gives N10,500. Net book value equals N16,000 minus N10,500, which is N5,500. Option A of N9,000 is actually the net book value at the end of year two, not year three. Option C of N3,500 is the annual depreciation charge, not the net book value. Option D of N2,000 is the estimated scrap value, which would only be the book value after all four years of depreciation are complete.

Bills receivable are written promises from customers to pay a specific amount on a future date, making them assets the business expects to receive. Because they are expected to be converted to cash within one year, they are classified as current assets. A current liability is money the business owes others, so option A is wrong. A fictitious asset has no real value and only appears due to accounting treatment, which does not apply here.

When provision for bad debt increases, the business recognises an additional expense, so the Profit and Loss account is debited to record that expense. The Provision for Bad Debt account is credited because the provision (a liability-like contra asset) is growing. Option A wrongly involves the debtor's account, which is only adjusted when a debt is actually written off, not when provision is merely increased. Option B credits the debtor's account, which is incorrect at this stage.

The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the brain of the computer that processes instructions; it neither receives data from the user nor sends output, so it is not an input device. Input devices are hardware used to feed data into a computer. A keyboard and card reader both send data into the computer, making them input devices. A Visual Display Unit (VDU) is an output device, but the question asks what is NOT an input device, and the CPU fits best since it is a processing unit, not input or output.

A trial balance is prepared by listing all debit and credit balances extracted from every ledger account to check that total debits equal total credits. It is the direct product of the ledger and serves as a check on arithmetic accuracy. A profit and loss statement shows only income and expenses to determine net profit or loss. A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities, and capital at a point in time, while a statement of affairs is used mainly for non-trading or insolvency purposes.

Share discount (also called discount on issue of shares) arises when shares are issued below their nominal value, representing a loss or cost to the company, and therefore carries a debit balance. Capital reserve, revenue reserve, and share premium all represent gains or surpluses for the company and normally carry credit balances. Share premium specifically arises when shares are issued above nominal value, giving the company extra funds, so it is a credit balance account.

When a trader sells at a margin of 20% on selling price in this context, it means profit equals 20% of the cost price. Profit = 20% × N1,000 = N200, so selling price = N1,000 + N200 = N1,200. Option A (N1,250) would only be correct if margin were strictly calculated on the final selling price using the formula Cost ÷ 0.8. Option D (N250) is just the profit figure, not the selling price, and Option C (N1,000) is the cost price with no profit added.

Gross profit is calculated as Net Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold. Net Sales = N14,600 − N150 (return inward) = N14,450; Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Purchases − Closing Stock = N100 + N5,500 − N250 = N5,350; Gross Profit = N14,450 − N5,350 = N9,100. Options A and B are wrong because they ignore return inward or misapply closing/opening stock. Rent, salaries, and discount received belong to the profit and loss account, not the trading account, so they do not affect gross profit.

Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) uses the formula: Opening Stock + Purchases − Closing Stock = N100 + N5,500 − N250 = N5,350. Option B (N5,150) incorrectly deducts return inward from purchases before calculating COGS; return inward reduces net sales, not cost of goods sold. Options C and D result from wrong combinations of the stock and purchase figures. Return inward, rent, salaries, and discount received are not part of the COGS calculation.

A control account (such as a sales ledger control account or purchases ledger control account) is specifically designed to detect and locate errors in the individual ledger accounts by providing a summary total that must agree with the total of all personal accounts. A trial balance can reveal errors that affect the balance of accounts but cannot pinpoint which ledger contains the mistake. A trading account shows profitability, and a journal proper records non-routine transactions; neither is designed for error location in the ledger.

In a not-for-profit organisation such as a club or association, the equivalent of capital is called the accumulated fund, which represents the excess of assets over liabilities built up over time from surpluses of income over expenditure. A capital reserve fund is specific to limited companies and arises from capital profits, not from operational surpluses. An endowment fund is a specific donation given for a stated purpose, and a development fund is set aside for expansion projects; neither represents the general capital of the organisation.

Net sales is calculated by subtracting Returns Inward (goods returned by customers) from gross Sales: N14,600 minus N150 gives N14,450. Returns Inward reduce revenue because those goods came back unsold, so they cannot count as income. Option C (N14,600) is wrong because it ignores the returns. Options A and B use figures that do not correspond to any valid net sales formula using the given data.

The journal proper (general journal) is the correct book for correcting ledger errors because it allows a narration explaining the nature of the correction, providing an audit trail. Specialized day books like the sales day book and purchases day book are only designed to record specific types of original transactions, not corrections. A control account is used to verify the accuracy of totals in a ledger, not to correct individual errors within it.

A warrant is the official document that gives legal authority for the release of government funds for approved expenditure, making it the instrument that controls public spending. A bank cheque is a private-sector payment instrument and is not used to authorize government fund releases. An order is too informal and carries no specific legal authority in government accounting. A vote book records and monitors how much of an approved budget has been spent, but does not authorize the release of funds.

A reserve is an appropriation of profits set aside for a specific or general future purpose, such as replacing assets or covering contingencies, rather than distributing it as dividend. Amounts owed to creditors are liabilities, not reserves. A provision for dividends is distinct from a general reserve because it is set up for a specific and immediate obligation. Bad debts recovered are income credited to the profit and loss account, not a reserve.

Note: The marked answer (A) appears to contain an error. Carriage outwards is the cost a business pays to deliver goods to customers and is a selling expense. Standard accounting treatment is to debit it to the Profit and Loss account (option B), since it is an expense incurred after the point of sale and does not form part of the cost of goods sold in the Trading account. Carriage inwards, not carriage outwards, appears in the Trading account. Option B is the correct treatment you should apply in your examination.

Discount received is money saved when a business pays its creditors early and gets a price reduction, so it is income for the business. Income is credited to the Profit and Loss Account, which is where all incomes and expenses below the gross profit line are recorded to arrive at net profit. It does not go into the Trading Account because that account only deals with buying and selling goods to find gross profit. The Appropriation Account is only used by partnerships and companies to share out net profit, so it has no place there either.

When preparing a bank reconciliation, items in the bank statement but not in the Cash Book are those the bank acted on without the business recording them first, such as bank charges, standing orders, and interest on overdraft. A presented cheque is one the business already wrote out and recorded as a payment in its own Cash Book, so it exists in both records and does not belong to this category. Bank charges, standing orders, and interest on overdraft are all initiated by the bank, which is why the business finds them in the statement before updating the Cash Book. Since a presented cheque was recorded by the business when it was issued, it is not an item unique to the bank statement.

Net profit is found by adjusting gross profit with the remaining incomes and expenses in the Profit and Loss Account. Discount allowed (N500) and bad debts written off (N750) are expenses that reduce profit, while discount received (N125) is income that increases profit. Starting from gross profit of N3,000, subtract N500 and N750, then add N125, giving N3,000 minus N1,250 plus N125 equals N1,875. Options A and B are wrong because they either add expenses or subtract income incorrectly, and option C ignores discount received entirely.

Sales for the year are found by reconstructing the Debtors Control Account. The debit side has opening debtors (N2,000) plus credit sales, and the credit side has cash received from debtors (N6,000), bad debts written off (N750), discount allowed (N500), and closing debtors (N1,250). The credit side totals N8,500, so sales must be N8,500 minus N2,000 equals N6,500. Option A of N8,500 is the total of the credit side before subtracting opening debtors, which is a common mistake if you forget to balance the account properly.

A contra entry is a transaction that affects both the cash column and the bank column of the Cash Book at the same time, appearing on the debit side of one and the credit side of the other. Lodging cash in hand into the bank means cash physically leaves the till (credited in the cash column) and enters the bank account (debited in the bank column), so both columns of the same Cash Book are touched. Lodging cheques received from customers is not a contra entry because the cheque is recorded straight into the bank column only when first received. Withdrawing cash for private use is drawings and only affects one column, and discount received is recorded in the discount column, not as a contra entry.

Mark-up is profit calculated as a fraction of the cost price, which makes option B correct. This is a key distinction in trading accounts: when profit is expressed over cost, it is called mark-up. Margin (option C) is different because it expresses profit as a proportion of the selling price, not the cost price. Gross profit (option A) is the actual naira amount of profit before deducting expenses, not a ratio. Profit percentage (option D) is a general term and does not specifically describe profit over cost price the way mark-up does.

The balance sheet shows the closing debtors figure, which is the amount owed to the business at the end of the period, given directly as N1,250 at 31st December 1998. This figure already reflects all adjustments: cash collected, bad debts written off, and discounts allowed have all reduced the debtors balance from the opening N2,000. The N6,000 (option A) is the cash received from debtors during the year, not a balance. The N2,000 (option C) is the opening balance at 1st January 1998, which is outdated. The N3,250 (option B) has no basis in the given data.

In government accounting, a vote book is maintained to monitor and control government expenditure so that spending does not exceed the approved budget allocation for each vote head. It records every commitment and payment against the budgeted amount, acting as an internal check on overspending. It has nothing to do with registering voters (option A), which belongs to electoral administration. Recording government revenue (option C) is done through revenue accounts, not the vote book. Taxes paid (option D) are handled through separate revenue records.

Deferred charges are payments made in advance for expenses that will benefit a future accounting period, which is exactly what a prepayment is, making option A correct.
