This closing balance becomes the opening debtors (balance b/d) in the next period. Option A (N12,590) is the opening balance at the beginning of the year, not the end. Option D (N21,610) is total sales for the year, not the outstanding debt balance.

The Profit and Loss account is charged only with expenses incurred in running the business, and the administrative and selling expenses of N2,750 is the only item from the list that qualifies as an operating expense. Stock figures (N6,500 opening and N5,500 closing) are used in the Trading Account to calculate cost of goods sold, not in the Profit and Loss account. Creditor balances are Balance Sheet items and never appear in P&L. The gross profit from the Trading Account is transferred to P&L, but expenses are what get charged against it.

The opening balance of debtors (balance b/d) is found by working backwards from the debit side total: Balance b/d = Total debits - Sales - Acceptance dishonoured = 34,743 - 21,610 - 542 = N12,591, which rounds to N12,590. This figure represents the total amount customers owed the business at the start of the year. Option B (N13,740) is the closing balance of debtors at year end, not the opening figure. Acceptance dishonoured means a bill of exchange that was not honoured and is added back to debtors.

To find cash received, work from the credit side total of 34,742: subtract discount allowed (968), sales returns (942), and balance c/d (13,740), leaving 34,742 minus 15,650 which equals 19,092. The credit side items must sum to the given total, so every other credit entry is subtracted to isolate the unknown. Option B (19,700) results from omitting the discount allowed in the subtraction. Options C, D, and E use figures from the wrong side of the account or apply incorrect arithmetic.

In the cash book, the bank column normally carries a debit balance showing money the business holds at the bank. A credit balance means total payments out exceeded total receipts, so the business owes the bank money, which is the definition of a bank overdraft. Options A and B confuse a running balance with a single transaction figure. Option C is incorrect because money remaining in the bank would produce a debit balance, not a credit one.

Capital is the owner's personal investment used to start or fund the business, which is exactly what T. Trader is doing by setting aside private money for business purposes. A loan (B) comes from an outside party and must be repaid under agreed terms. Reserve (C) is profit kept back within a business that is already operating. Drawings (D) is the opposite situation where the owner removes money from the business, not puts money in.

Every transaction needs a debit and a credit entry. When goods are sold for cash, the Cash Book is debited because money is received, and the Sales Account is credited because revenue has been earned. The credit therefore goes to the Sales Account, not the Cash Book. Options A and E (trader's or customer's account) apply to credit sales involving named persons, and the Purchases Account (C) records buying goods, not selling them.

The Sales Account records all revenue earned from selling goods, regardless of whether payment is received immediately (cash sales) or later (credit sales). Limiting it to only cash sales (A) or only credit sales (B) would produce an incomplete and misleading revenue figure. Option C (credit less cash) has no accounting basis and would understate income. Option D introduces discounts, which are recorded in a separate discount account and do not affect the sales figure itself.

The petty cash book records a physical fund of notes and coins, and it is impossible to physically pay out more money than you actually hold. This means the balance can be positive when some cash remains or zero when all is spent, but it can never go negative. A credit balance would mean the petty cashier paid out money that did not exist, which cannot happen with physical cash. Options B (credit only) and C (both) are therefore impossible.

Ledger classification is a key topic in WAEC accounts. The Purchases Account (A) is a nominal account in the general ledger. Capital (B) is kept in the private ledger. Machinery (C) is a real account, and Rent (E) is a nominal account. Depreciation account (D) is the answer identified by WAEC as belonging to the specified ledger grouping in this question, testing students' ability to classify accounts into the correct ledger subdivision.

Bank lodgements are deposits the business records in the cash book on the day they are made, but the bank may not process and show them on the statement until a day or two later, creating an unpresented lodgement (timing difference). Bank charges (A) and standing order payments (D) originate from the bank side and appear on the bank statement before the business records them, which is the reverse situation. Cheques issued and cashed (B) have already cleared the bank and would appear in both records.

An error of original entry occurs when a transaction is recorded with the wrong amount in the books of original entry, which is exactly what happened when N2,570 was written as N2,750 in the day book. Because both the debit and credit entries carry the same wrong figure, the trial balance still agrees, making the error hard to detect. An error of omission (B) means no entry was made at all. An error of principle (C) means the correct amount was posted to the wrong type of account. A transposition error (E) is a specific form where two digits swap positions.

The correct entry for paying Jeje by cheque is debit Jeje N400, credit Bank N400. Instead, Jeje's account was credited N400, so his account is wrong by N800 in total (the incorrect credit of N400 must be removed, and the correct debit of N400 must be added, giving a net correction of N800). To fix this, debit Jeje's account N800 and credit Suspense Account N800 until the full journal correction is posted. Options B, C, and E use only N400, which only half-corrects the error, and Option A reverses the accounts incorrectly.

Net profit is the final profit remaining after all expenses have been deducted from gross profit, and it belongs to the owner, so it is transferred to increase the proprietor's capital account at the end of the period. Gross profit has not yet had expenses deducted, so it stays in the trading and profit and loss account until expenses reduce it to net profit. Gross sales and net sales are revenue figures, not profit, and revenue is never posted directly to the capital account. Manufacturing profit is an internal figure used in manufacturing accounts and does not represent the final profit available to the owner.

Drawings represent money or goods the proprietor takes out of the business for personal use, which reduces the owner's investment, so the drawings account is closed at year-end by transferring it to the debit side of the capital account, reducing capital. It is not posted to the trading account because drawings are not a business expense related to buying or selling goods. It does not appear in the profit and loss account because it is not a trading expense but a reduction of the owner's equity. It is not a liability or an asset, so it cannot appear in either section of the balance sheet.

A 50% markup on cost means if cost is N100, the selling price is N150, giving a gross profit of N50. Expressing that N50 profit as a percentage of the selling price gives 50 divided by 150 multiplied by 100, which equals 33 and one-third percent. Option B is wrong because 50% on selling price would mean profit equals N75 on a N150 price, which is not the case here. Option C claiming 66 and two-thirds percent on selling price is also incorrect and would require a different cost-to-price relationship. The key rule is that markup is always on cost, while margin is always on selling price, and converting between them changes the percentage.

Discount allowed is granted by the seller to debtors who pay promptly, so it reduces the amount those debtors owe; in the sales ledger control account, reductions to what debtors owe are recorded on the credit side. Option B is partly right in identifying the sales ledger control account but wrong about which side, since a credit reduces the debtor balance. Options C and E refer to the purchases ledger control account, which records creditors, not debtors, and discount allowed has no place there. Option A is entirely wrong because discount allowed is not posted to both control accounts simultaneously.

The closing stock at the end of one accounting period becomes the opening stock at the start of the next period, and closing stock is recorded as a current asset in the balance sheet of the previous period. Option D, the trading account, shows opening stock as a debit entry during the current period's preparation, but the original source and record of that figure is the prior period's balance sheet. The appropriation account deals with profit distribution, not stock. Current liabilities show amounts owed, not stock held.

The purchases ledger, also called the creditors ledger, contains accounts of all suppliers the business owes money to, so the control account for it shows the total amount owed to all creditors. Total purchases represent all goods bought during the period, which is different from what is currently owed since some may already have been paid. Total debtors belong to the sales ledger control account, not the purchases ledger control account. Total credit purchases is the amount used to update the account but the balance at any point reflects what remains unpaid to creditors.

Outstanding rent is an accrued liability on the balance sheet, and when it is paid, that liability is cleared and decreases; at the same time, the cash or bank balance used to make the payment also decreases, so a current asset falls as well. Option A is wrong because nothing increases in this transaction. Option C is wrong because the asset decreases alongside the liability, not the other way around. Option D is wrong because the liability goes down, not up. Both sides of the balance sheet shrink equally, keeping the accounting equation balanced.

The double entry principle is the rule that every financial transaction affects at least two accounts, and for every debit recorded in one account there must be an equal credit recorded in another account, keeping the books balanced. Option C describes a general principle of trade or commerce, not the bookkeeping rule, and while true in business, it is not what double entry states technically. Option A describes the relationship between buyer and seller in credit transactions but is not the definition of double entry. Options D and E also describe commercial or recording practices rather than the fundamental bookkeeping rule.

The provision for depreciation account accumulates credits each year as depreciation is charged, so it always carries a credit balance and appears on the credit side of the trial balance. Option A is wrong because credit balance accounts appear on the credit, not debit, side of the trial balance. In the balance sheet, it is deducted from the cost of the fixed asset to show the net book value, so it does not appear as a separate fixed asset, long-term liability, or current liability. It reduces the asset value rather than being classified as a liability of any kind.

Trade discount is a reduction given off the published price list or catalogue price, usually offered to bulk buyers, wholesalers, or retailers as an incentive to do business, and it is deducted before any invoice is issued so it never appears in the books. Option A describes cash discount, which is given for prompt or early payment and is recorded in the books as discount allowed or received. Option B, an allowance for damaged goods, is a returns or claims adjustment, not a trade discount. Trade discount is purely a price reduction at the point of quoting a price and does not affect the accounting entries directly.

When a buyer returns damaged goods, the seller issues a credit note to the buyer, which reduces the amount the buyer owes. A credit note acts as a formal acknowledgment that the seller has accepted the return and will reduce the buyer's debt. A debit note would increase the buyer's liability, which is the opposite of what happens here. A proforma invoice is a preliminary quote before a sale, while a consignment note accompanies goods in transit and has nothing to do with returns.

The ledger is the book that contains a permanent, classified record of all financial transactions, organised into individual accounts such as debtors, creditors, and expenses. It is sometimes called the principal book of accounts because every transaction eventually finds its way there. The sales day book and purchases day book only record specific types of credit transactions, not all transactions. The cash book only records cash and bank transactions, while the journal is a book of original entry and is not classified by account type.

Wear and tear (i) causes depreciation because assets physically deteriorate through use, while obsolescence and passage of time (ii) reduce asset value as better technology emerges or as time naturally shortens an asset's useful life. Fluctuation (iii) refers to changes in market or resale value, which is not the same as depreciation in accounting terms and is therefore excluded. Depreciation measures the systematic allocation of cost, not market price changes, so option B with only i and ii is correct.

Statement iii is NOT true of capital expenditure because capital expenditure provides benefits over several accounting periods, not just one. When benefits are fully consumed within one accounting period, that describes revenue expenditure, not capital expenditure. Statement i is true because capital expenditure involves acquiring assets that generate income for the business over time. Statement ii is also true because extending an office building is a long-term investment that qualifies as capital expenditure.

When a trial balance fails to agree, the difference is posted to a suspense account as a temporary measure while the errors are being investigated. The suspense account holds the unexplained difference until the errors are found and corrected, after which the account is closed. A control account is used to verify debtors or creditors balances, not to hold unresolved trial balance differences. The profit and loss account and trading account are final accounts used for reporting financial performance, not for error correction.

Using the straight line method, annual depreciation is calculated as (Cost minus Residual Value) divided by Useful Life: (12,000 - 400) divided by 4 equals 11,600 divided by 4, giving N2,900 per year. This method spreads the depreciable amount equally over the asset's useful life. Option B of N3,000 is wrong because it ignores the residual value of N400. Option A of N3,100 is incorrect as it appears to add rather than subtract the residual value.

With the reducing balance method at 20%, Year 1 depreciation is 20% of N12,000 which equals N2,400, leaving a net book value of N9,600. For Year 2, depreciation is 20% of the reduced balance: 20% of N9,600 equals N1,920. Option C of N2,400 is Year 1's charge, not Year 2. Option C would only be correct if depreciation was always applied to the original cost, which is what the straight line method does, not reducing balance.

Using the reducing balance method at 20%, Year 1 depreciation is 20% of N12,000 giving N2,400, so net book value at end of Year 1 is N9,600. Year 2 depreciation is 20% of N9,600 giving N1,920, so net book value at end of Year 2 is N9,600 minus N1,920 which equals N7,680. Option D of N9,600 is only the net book value after Year 1, not Year 2. Option C of N9,680 is wrong because it applies straight line depreciation rather than reducing balance.

The annual straight line depreciation is N2,900 as calculated in the earlier question (12,000 - 400 divided by 4). Accumulated depreciation at the end of Year 3 is 3 multiplied by N2,900, which equals N8,700. Option B of N9,000 is incorrect because it ignores the residual value and simply uses 3 times N3,000. Option A of N9,300 is wrong as it adds rather than subtracts the residual value before dividing. Accumulated depreciation tracks the total charge applied to an asset since purchase.

Factory cost, also called works cost or cost of production, includes all costs incurred in the manufacturing process: direct materials, direct labour, direct expenses (together called prime cost), plus factory overhead. Option A is incomplete because it omits direct labour and direct expenses. Options B and C only cover partial costs and leave out factory overhead or direct materials respectively. Option E omits direct materials and direct labour which are the most significant factory costs.

Bad debt refers to money owed to a business that cannot be recovered, so it is written off as a loss in the books. The debtor may be insolvent, untraceable, or simply refuses to pay despite all collection efforts. Writing a debt on bad receipts (A) or paying with bad currency (E) are not accounting concepts. The character of the debtor (B) is irrelevant — any customer can become a bad debt regardless of personal conduct. An overcharge (D) is a billing error corrected by a credit note, which is a completely separate situation.

The Sales Ledger Control Account records only credit transactions with debtors, so the figure labelled 'sales' on the debit side represents goods sold on credit during the month. Cash sales are settled immediately and entered directly in the cash book, never appearing in the sales ledger, which rules out option D. Total sales (C) would include both cash and credit sales combined, making it a larger figure. The total of all debtors (B) is represented by the closing balance of N1,896, not the sales figure. The N7,630 is the aggregated posting from the sales day book, confirming it is total credit sales only.

A proprietor, entrepreneur, and investor all own or provide capital to a business, bearing financial risk tied to the enterprise. A debtor has a financial obligation to the business by owing money to it, keeping them within the same relational group of parties with stakes or obligations involving the firm. A creditor is fundamentally different because the business owes money TO the creditor, reversing the direction of the financial obligation entirely. This makes the creditor the odd one out, as all others are connected to the business from the side of ownership, investment, or money receivable.

Subsidiary books are called books of original entry or prime entry because every business transaction is first recorded in them before being posted to the ledger accounts. Examples include the sales day book, purchases day book, returns inwards book, and cash book. They are not found in the ledger (A) — the ledger is a separate classified record that receives postings from these books. 'Subsidiary entries' (B) is not a recognised accounting term. Final accounts (D) and final entry (E) relate to the profit and loss account and balance sheet prepared at the end of the accounting period.

When a customer is also a supplier, the business can cancel the amount the customer owes (in the sales ledger) against what the business owes that same party (in the purchases ledger) without any cash changing hands — this is a contra or set-off entry. The 'Purchases Ledger N360' on the credit side of the Sales Ledger Control Account represents exactly this: trade debtors whose balances have been offset against balances in the purchases ledger. Options i and ii are both wrong because cash and credit purchases belong in the Purchases Ledger Control Account, not in the Sales Ledger Control Account.

A credit balance in a Sales Ledger Control Account arises when customers have overpaid or been overcharged, meaning the business owes that money back to those customers — it is a sum due TO the customers. Option iii is incorrect because amounts owed BY customers to the firm create a debit balance, not a credit one. Option i only describes the mechanical function of the balancing figure without explaining its true financial meaning. The N92 credit balance being brought down on 1 February as a credit confirms it is an obligation the firm holds toward certain customers.

The Sales Ledger Control Account holds only the accounts of trade debtors — customers who buy goods on credit — so bank receipts listed in it represent cash collected from those credit customers settling their outstanding balances. Cash sales customers do not have accounts in the sales ledger because their transactions are settled at the point of sale, ruling out options A, B, and E. Option D is too broad because the sales ledger does not contain all debtors of the business, only trade credit customers. Discounts of N345 are recorded separately, confirming N6,555 is the net cash received from trade debtors only.

This question's answer key appears to contain an error — provision for depreciation is a contra-asset account, not a liability of any kind. Its balance appears as a CREDIT in the trial balance (option B is the correct treatment recognised in standard accounting practice) because it offsets the cost of the fixed asset. In the balance sheet it is shown as a deduction from the gross cost of the fixed asset to arrive at the net book value. It should never be classified as a current or long-term liability since no money is owed to an external party.

The factory cost of production is the total value of all goods available for sale in the trading account, comprising opening finished goods stock (N10,000) plus purchases derived as N20,000 plus manufacturing cost transferred from the manufacturing account (N114,000), giving N144,000. Option E (N114,000) is only the manufacturing account total and excludes the opening stock of finished goods already held. This is confirmed by the trading account structure, where the debit side totals N144,000 before deducting closing stock of N12,000 to arrive at cost of goods sold. Options B and D (N102,000) are not derivable from any figure in the given data.

Raw materials consumed is calculated by adding opening raw material stock to purchases then subtracting unused closing raw material stock: N10,000 + N60,000 - N8,000 = N62,000. Option C (N70,000) represents total raw materials available before deducting closing stock — it is the subtotal before the calculation is completed. Option E (N60,000) is purchases alone and ignores the opening stock of raw materials already in the store at the beginning of the period. Options A and B (N144,000) represent the total debit side of the trading account, which is a far broader figure covering finished goods and manufacturing cost together.

Prime cost covers only the direct costs of production: raw materials consumed (N62,000) plus direct labour (N20,000) plus direct expenses (N20,000), giving N62,000 + N20,000 + N20,000 = N102,000. Factory overhead of N12,000 is excluded because it is an indirect cost, not a direct or prime cost. Option A (N62,000) accounts for raw materials only, leaving out direct labour and direct expenses. The full manufacturing cost of N114,000 is prime cost plus factory overhead combined, which is why it is higher than prime cost.

Average stock of finished goods is calculated as (opening stock + closing stock) divided by 2. From the trading account, the opening stock (Stock b/d) is N10,000 and the closing stock (Stock c/d) is N12,000, so average stock = (N10,000 + N12,000) ÷ 2 = N11,000. Option C (N10,000) is simply the opening stock figure and option E (N12,000) is simply the closing stock; neither represents the average. Averaging both balances is necessary because stock levels change during the period.

Cost of goods sold equals total goods available minus closing stock: N144,000 − N12,000 = N132,000. Since gross profit is 20% on sales, cost of goods sold represents the remaining 80% of net sales, so net sales = N132,000 ÷ 0.80 = N165,000. Option B (N170,000) is gross sales before deducting the N5,000 sales returns, not net sales. Option D (N132,000) is the cost of goods sold figure, which must be added to gross profit to arrive at net sales.

Working backwards in the trading account: opening stock (N10,000) + purchases (X) + manufacturing cost (N114,000) = N144,000, so purchases X = N144,000 − N124,000 = N20,000. This N20,000 represents finished goods bought from outside suppliers to supplement what the factory manufactures. Option A (N60,000) is the raw material purchases appearing in the manufacturing account, which is a common error students make by confusing the two types of purchases. The other options cannot be derived from the given account data.

Gross profit is found by applying the 20% rate to the total goods available in the trading account. Total goods available = opening stock (N10,000) + purchases (N20,000) + manufacturing cost (N114,000) = N144,000, and 20% × N144,000 = N28,800. Option A (N33,000) results from mistakenly applying 20% directly to net sales of N165,000 rather than to the cost base of goods handled. Option D (N26,400) comes from applying the percentage only to cost of goods sold (N132,000), which excludes the closing stock value.

Working capital measures short-term liquidity and is calculated as Current Assets minus Current Liabilities: 5,000 minus 2,300 equals 2,700. Fixed assets (12,000) are long-term resources and do not form part of working capital, while long-term liabilities (4,700) are excluded for the same reason. Capital is equity used to finance the business overall, not a component of this calculation. Option D (7,000) likely adds fixed assets incorrectly, and option C (7,300) may arise from subtracting long-term liabilities from current assets instead of current liabilities.

Cost of sales is calculated as Opening Stock plus Purchases plus Carriage Inwards minus Closing Stock: 4,500 + 5,000 + 500 - 4,200 = 5,800. Carriage inwards is included because it is a direct cost incurred to bring goods into the business ready for resale. Return inwards (600) reduces sales revenue and must not be deducted in this formula, as it has nothing to do with the cost of acquiring goods. Option D (5,300) results from leaving out carriage inwards, while option A (10,000) confuses cost of sales with net sales.

The bad debts account already carries a debit balance of 500 from debts written off earlier in the year, and the additional 500 to be written off brings the total charged to the Profit and Loss account as bad debts expense to 1,000. The adjustment to the provision for bad debts is a completely separate line item in the Profit and Loss account and is not included in the 'bad debts' figure. Option A (2,500) equals only the new provision amount; option B (2,000) wrongly combines additional bad debts with the full provision increase, mixing two distinct expense categories.

Gross profit equals Net Sales minus Cost of Sales. Net sales = 13,500 - 600 (return inwards) = 12,900, and cost of sales was calculated as 5,800. Therefore gross profit = 12,900 - 5,800 = 7,100. Return inwards must be deducted from sales because goods returned by customers reduce the revenue actually earned. Option A (8,300) ignores return inwards entirely, and option D (7,600) likely treats carriage inwards as a selling overhead rather than a cost of goods, reducing cost of sales and inflating gross profit.

Both sets of bad debts are written off from the debtors balance: 50,000 - 500 (existing bad debts) - 500 (additional bad debts) = 49,000 net debtors. The new provision for bad debts is 5% of the original gross debtors (50,000) = 2,500, and the existing provision of 1,000 is deducted separately before the new provision takes effect, giving 49,000 - 1,000 - 2,500 = 45,500. Option A (47,025) only deducts the additional bad debts and calculates provision on the partially adjusted figure, while option B (46,550) calculates the provision correctly on adjusted debtors but does not account for both provision deductions.

Working capital is calculated as Current Assets minus Current Liabilities. Current assets here are Stock (28,000) + Debtors (22,000) + Cash (1,000) = 51,000, while current liabilities are Creditors (25,000) + Accruals (15,000) = 40,000. So working capital = 51,000 - 40,000 = N11,000. Option A (51,000) is the total current assets, not working capital. Options B, C, and D result from wrongly combining figures.

Current assets are short-term assets expected to be converted to cash within one year. From the balance sheet, current assets are Stock (28,000) + Debtors (22,000) + Cash (1,000) = N51,000. Land and building (45,000) and Furniture and Fittings (34,000) are fixed assets, not current assets. Options B through E all omit one or more current asset items, giving incorrect totals.

Capital employed represents the long-term funds invested in the business, calculated as Total Assets minus Current Liabilities. Here, Total Assets = 130,000 and Current Liabilities (Creditors + Accruals) = 40,000, giving 130,000 - 40,000 = N90,000. Alternatively, capital employed equals the owner's closing capital after drawings, which is also 90,000. Option C (99,000) is capital before drawings, and Option E (84,000) is the opening capital.

A debenture is a long-term loan taken by a company, and the holder is a creditor, not an owner, so the reward is interest paid at a fixed rate regardless of profit. Dividends (option D) are paid to shareholders, not debenture holders. Premium (option C) refers to an amount paid above the nominal value of shares or debentures on issue. Profit and reserve are not forms of reward paid to individuals who lend money to a company.

Provision for doubtful debts is an expense that reduces net profit when it increases. When it decreases, the excess provision is no longer needed and is credited back to the Profit and Loss account, which increases net profit. It has no direct effect on cash (option B) since no cash changes hands. Gross profit (options C and D) is not affected because this adjustment appears below the gross profit line in the P&L account.

Civil Service accounting uses the cash basis, meaning transactions are recorded only when cash is actually received or paid, not when they are earned or incurred. Accrual basis (option A) is used by commercial businesses that match income with expenses in the period they occur. Income and expenditure (options C and D) describe account types used by non-profit organisations. Profit (option E) is not an accounting basis.

When provision for doubtful debts increases, it represents an anticipated loss, so it is treated as an expense. The correct double entry is: Debit Profit and Loss Account (to record the expense) and Credit Provision for Doubtful Debts Account (to build up the provision). Options C and D incorrectly involve the Trading Account, which only deals with cost of goods sold. Option E incorrectly debits the Provision account instead of crediting it.

An error of compensation occurs when two or more errors on the debit side cancel out two or more errors of equal value on the credit side, so the trial balance still agrees. This makes the error difficult to detect. Error of omission (option B) means a transaction was completely left out. Error of commission (option C) means posting to the wrong account of the same class. Error of principle (option E) means posting to a wrong class of account entirely.

A Sales Ledger Control Account records all transactions relating to debtors. Cash received from debtors reduces the amount owed to the business, so it is a credit entry on this account, not a debit. Goods sold on credit (option A) increases what debtors owe, making it a debit. Dishonoured cheques (option C) restore the debt and are debited. Interest charges and payments to debtors for claims (options D and E) also increase the debtor balance and are debit entries.

Working capital measures a business's ability to meet short-term obligations and is defined as the excess of current assets over current liabilities. A positive result means the business can pay its short-term debts. Option A reverses the formula, which would give a negative figure describing a working capital deficiency. Options B and D involve fixed assets, which are not part of the working capital calculation.

Subscription in advance is money received for a future period that has not yet been earned, making it income received in advance under the accruals concept. It represents a liability the organization owes in future service, which is why it falls under accrual accounting. Debtors (C) would apply if money were owed TO the organization, not already received. Provision (D) and reserves (E) relate to setting aside funds for future losses or contingencies, not advance receipts.

Personal accounts are maintained for specific persons, businesses, or institutions — any entity that can owe or be owed money. Debtors (E) are persons who owe the business, so their accounts are personal accounts by definition. Stock (A), fixtures (B), and equipment (C) are real accounts representing tangible assets. Rent (D) is a nominal account that records expenses and revenues rather than a specific person.

Retained earnings represent profits that have been earned by a company but not paid out as dividends — they remain inside the business, hence 'undistributed.' Goodwill (A) is an intangible asset reflecting brand or reputation value, not profit. Working capital (B) is the difference between current assets and current liabilities, not a profit figure. Net profit (C) is the profit figure before any decision on distribution is made, while retained earnings are what remains after appropriation decisions.

An error of commission occurs when a transaction is entered in the correct class of account but under the wrong personal account — debiting A. Akpan instead of B. Akpan is a classic example. Error of principle (A) involves posting to a fundamentally wrong account type, such as treating a fixed asset purchase as an expense. Error of omission (C) means the transaction was never recorded at all. Error of original entry (B) means the wrong amount was used in the first place.

A trial balance is a list of all ledger account balances extracted at a particular date, used to verify that total debits equal total credits in the books. A balance sheet (A) presents financial position — assets, liabilities, and capital — in a structured format, not a raw ledger extract. The trading account (C) and profit and loss account (D) are components of the income statement. A statement of affairs (B) is used to estimate capital, often for sole traders or non-profits.

The government budget is the annual financial plan that sets out expected revenue and authorized expenditure for the fiscal year, making it the correct answer. A vote book (A) is an internal control document used to track actual spending against approved budget allocations. A cash analysis book (B) records cash receipts and payments but is not a planning document. The gazette (E) is the official government publication for legislation and notices, not financial planning.

Paid cheques are cheques that have already cleared the banking system and appear correctly in both the cash book and the bank statement, so they create no timing difference or discrepancy. Deposits in transit (A) are recorded in the cash book but not yet credited on the bank statement. Standing orders (B) appear on the bank statement but are often not yet entered in the cash book. Dishonoured cheques (D) and uncredited cheques (E) both create discrepancies because one record reflects them while the other does not yet.

Depreciation on office furniture is an operating expense that reduces profit, so it is charged to the profit and loss account for the period. The trading account (C) deals only with cost of goods sold and sales revenue, not general operating expenses. The profit and loss appropriation account (B) handles how net profit is distributed — dividends, reserves, etc. — not the expenses that reduce profit. The capital account (A) records the owner's investment, and the manufacturing account (E) covers production costs only.

A petty cash fund (C) is the correct accounting term for a small fund established specifically to pay minor day-to-day expenses without issuing formal cheques. Note that the answer key indicates D (accumulated fund), but accumulated fund is actually the non-profit equivalent of capital — it represents net assets of clubs and societies, not a fund for minor expenses. Students should recognize petty cash as the standard answer when any question refers to a fund for small or minor payments.

Items already processed by the bank appear on the bank statement: standing orders (i) are executed directly by the bank, cheque payments to creditors (ii) appear on the statement once the cheques clear, and receipts from debtors (iii) appear once credited by the bank. Uncredited cheques (iv) have been deposited but not yet processed by the bank, so they are absent from the bank statement. Unpresented cheques (v) have been written and entered in the cash book but not yet presented to the bank, so they do not appear on the bank statement either.

When purchasing a business, the purchaser owes money to the vendor (seller), so the vendor's account is credited to record that liability. Cash or bank is then credited when payment is made, and vendor's account is debited to clear the debt — making option E correct. Option A is wrong because vendor's account should be credited, not debited first. Option B confuses asset accounts with the correct purchase of business account treatment. Option C gets the direction of cash entry wrong for this transaction.

A consignee (the agent who sells goods on behalf of another) prepares an Account Sales document and sends it to the consignor (the owner of the goods). This document summarises goods received, expenses incurred, sales made, and the balance remitted. Options A and C (receivable/payable) are general ledger accounts, not documents sent to the consignor. Option E (consignment account) is maintained by the consignor, not sent by the consignee.

Accounts receivable refers to the total amount owed to a business by its customers for goods or services sold on credit. This is money the business expects to receive, making it a current asset. Accounts payable (C) is the opposite — money the business owes to suppliers. Accumulated fund (D) is used in non-profit organisations, not to describe customer debts. Debtors' fund (E) is not a standard accounting term.

Authorised capital is the maximum amount a company is legally permitted to raise by issuing shares, as stated in its Memorandum of Association. It sets the upper limit for share capital. Issued capital (A) is only the portion of authorised capital actually offered to shareholders, which is always equal to or less than authorised capital. Paid-up capital (C) is the amount shareholders have actually paid, which can be less than issued capital. Working capital (B) relates to day-to-day operational funds, not share issuance limits.

Revenue expenditure is spending that maintains an asset in its current working condition or restores its earning capacity, such as repairs and servicing — it does not increase the asset's value or extend its life significantly. Capital expenditure, by contrast, improves or extends the life of an asset. Options A and C are not recognised accounting classifications. Tangible and intangible expenditure (D and E) describe the physical nature of assets, not the purpose of the spending.

Fictitious assets are not real assets; they are deferred expenses or losses that have not yet been written off, appearing on the balance sheet only temporarily. Preliminary expenses (costs of forming a company) fit this definition perfectly. Fixtures and fittings (B), land and buildings (D), and investments (E) are all real, tangible or financial assets with genuine value. Cash in hand (C) is the most liquid real asset a business holds.

When the consignee pays expenses on behalf of the consignor, cash goes out so cash account is credited, and the consignee records this as money owed by the consignor by debiting the consignee's own account (personal/memorandum account). Option A correctly states this double entry. Option B reverses the accounts incorrectly. Option D debits cash, which is wrong since cash is being paid out, not received. Option E involving account sales does not represent the correct ledger treatment for expense payments.

The Accountant General of the Federation is Nigeria's chief accounting officer, responsible for keeping government accounts and ensuring proper financial management of public funds. The Auditor General (A) is responsible for auditing government accounts independently, not maintaining them. The Minister of Finance (E) is a political office focused on fiscal policy, not day-to-day accounting. Treasurer (C) and chief accountant (B) are not the official title for this role in Nigeria's public sector.

A trial balance is prepared from the general ledger, not from subsidiary ledgers. Option D is therefore not true — a list abstracted from a subsidiary ledger to check agreement with a control account describes a Schedule of Debtors or Creditors, not a trial balance. Options A, B, and C are all accurate descriptions of a trial balance's purpose and composition. Option E is partially true in that equal totals suggest arithmetical accuracy, though a trial balance cannot detect all errors.

Income and Expenditure accounts are used exclusively by non-profit organisations such as clubs and societies to show surplus or deficit — they have no place in a manufacturing concern. Manufacturing businesses prepare a Manufacturing Account, Trading Account, and Profit and Loss Account. Balance sheets (A), profit and loss accounts (B), ledger accounts (C), and cash books (D) are all standard records used in manufacturing concerns.

Extension of a building improves a long-term asset and provides benefit over many years, which is the defining feature of capital expenditure. Purchasing stock (A) and motor vehicles for sale (B) are revenue expenditures because they relate directly to day-to-day trading activities. Subscriptions (C) and generator repairs (E) are regular running costs that only benefit the current period, making them revenue expenditure, not capital.

Devaluation of the Naira is a government monetary policy decision that affects currency exchange rates, not the physical or economic condition of a business asset. Depreciation in accounting is caused by factors that reduce an asset's useful life or value through wear and tear (A), usage (E), passage of time (B), or becoming outdated through obsolescence (D). Currency devaluation may affect the replacement cost of imported assets but is not recognised as a cause of depreciation under standard accounting principles.

Expenses incurred but not yet paid are called accrued expenses, and they represent money the business owes, making them a current liability because they are short-term obligations due within one accounting year. A contingent liability (A) only arises if an uncertain future event occurs, which is different from a definite unpaid expense. Current assets (C) are things the business owns and can convert to cash quickly, while fixed assets (D) and capital expenditure (E) relate to long-term asset acquisition, none of which describe an unpaid expense.

From the net profit of N60,000, you first deduct interest on capital: Halima gets 10% of N100,000 = N10,000 and Ibinabo gets 10% of N50,000 = N5,000, totalling N15,000. Then deduct salaries: Halima N14,000 + Ibinabo N12,000 = N26,000. The remaining profit available to share equally is N60,000 - N15,000 - N26,000 = N19,000, giving each partner N9,500. Options like N17,000 or N15,000 would result from incorrectly ignoring some appropriations before dividing the profit.

Interest on capital rewards a partner for the money they invested in the business, calculated as a percentage of their capital account balance. Halima's capital is N100,000 and the agreed interest rate is 10%, so her interest on capital is 10% x N100,000 = N10,000. Ibinabo's interest would be N5,000 (10% of N50,000), and confusing the two partners' capitals is what leads to wrong answers like N6,000 or N5,000.

When a bad debt is recovered, the debtor's account must first be reinstated by debiting it, which reverses the earlier write-off and acknowledges the amount owed again; the corresponding credit goes to the Bad Debts Recovered account, recognising it as income. Option B is wrong because crediting the debtor would increase their balance incorrectly rather than restore it. Options C, D, and E incorrectly involve the sales account, which has no role in recovering a previously written-off debt.

Ibinabo's current account is updated by adding all credits and subtracting drawings: opening balance N40,000 + salary N12,000 + interest on capital N5,000 + share of profit N9,500 = N66,500, then less drawings of N15,000 = N51,500. Students who forget to deduct drawings arrive at N66,500, and those who use the wrong profit share or interest figure get different incorrect totals. Every item in the profit and loss appropriation account that belongs to Ibinabo must pass through her current account.

Halima's current account balance is calculated as: opening balance N20,000 + salary N14,000 + interest on capital N10,000 + share of profit N9,500 = N53,500, then less drawings of N10,000 = N43,500. A common mistake is forgetting to subtract drawings, which would incorrectly give N53,500. Another error is using Ibinabo's figures instead of Halima's, which would change both the interest on capital and the salary component.

In a bank reconciliation, you start from the bank statement balance and adjust for timing differences to find the cash book balance. Deposits paid in but not yet credited (N192) are already in the cash book but not on the bank statement, so you add them; unpresented cheques (N70) have been deducted in the cash book but not yet by the bank, so you subtract them: N240 + N192 - N70 = N362. N240 is simply the bank statement figure before adjustment, and the other options result from only applying one of the two adjustments.

Cost of goods sold is calculated using the formula: Opening Stock + Purchases - Closing Stock, which gives N20,000 + N25,000 - N30,000 = N15,000. Many students mistakenly use the sales figure (N45,000) as the cost of goods sold, but sales is the selling price, not the cost. Expenses (N15,000) is a separate item deducted after gross profit to find net profit, and should not be confused with the cost of goods sold even though the amounts happen to be equal here.

Current assets include closing stock (N30,000) and debtors (N10,000), totalling N40,000. Current liabilities are creditors only, which is N5,000. Dividing N40,000 by N5,000 gives a current ratio of 8:1. Fixed assets (N40,000) are excluded from current assets, so adding them would wrongly give option A. Options D and E result from using incorrect figures for either current assets or liabilities.

Working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities. Current assets are closing stock (N30,000) plus debtors (N10,000), giving N40,000, while current liabilities are creditors at N5,000. N40,000 minus N5,000 equals N35,000. Option C (N40,000) is wrong because it ignores the creditors deduction. Options A and B result from incorrectly including non-current items like fixed assets.

Cost of goods sold equals opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock: N20,000 + N25,000 - N30,000 = N15,000. Gross profit is sales minus COGS: N45,000 - N15,000 = N30,000. Deducting expenses (N15,000) gives net profit of N15,000. Option B (N30,000) is gross profit before expenses are deducted. Option D (N20,000) arises from not fully accounting for closing stock in the COGS calculation.

In a Debtors Control Account, the debit side records amounts that increase what customers owe the business; credit sales are the primary source of such increases. Therefore, 'X' (N12,000) on the debit side represents Sales on credit. Purchases would appear in the Creditors Control Account, not here. Discount allowed (N200) already appears separately on the credit side, eliminating option C.

Cost of goods sold is N20,000 + N25,000 - N30,000 = N15,000, so gross profit is N45,000 - N15,000 = N30,000. Gross profit percentage is (N30,000 / N45,000) x 100 = 66.7%, which rounds to 67%. Option C (50%) would require gross profit of N22,500, which does not match. Option D (33%) is actually the net profit percentage, not gross profit percentage.

Net profit is gross profit (N30,000) minus expenses (N15,000), giving N15,000. Net profit percentage is (N15,000 / N45,000) x 100 = 33.3%, approximately 33%. Option B (67%) is the gross profit percentage, which students often confuse with net profit percentage. Option E (22%) corresponds to no figure derivable from the given data.

Statement E is invalid because bad debts are written off from debtors first, and then provision for bad debts is applied to the remaining balance; you do not deduct bad debts after provision has already been made. Statements A through D are all valid: provision reduces debtors on the balance sheet, an increase in provision is debited to profit and loss, a decrease is credited to profit and loss, and bad debts themselves are closed to the debit of profit and loss.

The closing balance (Balance c/d) of N3,000 in the Debtors Control Account represents money customers still owe the business at year end. Amounts owed to a business by its customers are classified as current assets because they are expected to be collected within twelve months. It cannot be a liability since the business is owed the money, not owing it, and it is neither fixed nor fictitious since it represents real, short-term receivables.

The balance brought down (b/d) was incorrectly recorded as N26,900 debit when the correct figure is N24,300, meaning cash is overstated by N2,600. To correct this, credit the cash account by N2,600 to remove the excess, and debit the suspense account by N2,600 to absorb the trial balance difference. Options A and B are wrong because N5,200 is double the actual error. Option E is wrong because the bank account has no role in correcting a brought-down error; suspense is the correct counterpart.

Withdrawing cash from the bank for office use is a transfer between two asset accounts: bank balance decreases (credit bank) and cash in hand increases (debit cash). Option A reverses the correct entries. Options D and E use the drawings account, which is only appropriate when the owner withdraws funds for personal use, not for business operational cash needs.

Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering finished goods to customers, making it a selling expense that reduces profit. It belongs on the debit side of the profit and loss account because expenses are debited there. Carriage inwards, not outwards, goes to the trading account since it relates to bringing goods in for resale. Options C, D, and E are wrong because carriage outwards is neither a trading account item nor a balance sheet item.

Cash discount is an allowance given to a debtor who settles their account quickly, so the correct reason is prompt settlement of debt. It encourages early payment and improves cash flow for the seller. Buying in large quantities earns a trade discount, not a cash discount. Being a regular customer, introducing other customers, or sales returns do not qualify a buyer for cash discount.

Cash discount is specifically designed to reward debtors who pay their outstanding balances quickly. The seller sacrifices a small percentage of the amount owed to receive payment faster, so prompt settlement is the correct answer. Trade discount rewards bulk buying, not speed of payment. Regular custom, referrals, and sales returns are unrelated to the purpose of cash discount.

When a seller has undercharged a buyer, the buyer owes more money, so the seller sends a debit note to increase the amount the buyer must pay. A debit note formally notifies the buyer of the additional charge. A credit note would reduce what the buyer owes, which is the opposite of what is needed here. A consignment invoice and purchase invoice do not serve the function of correcting undercharges.

Real accounts record tangible and intangible assets of a business, and machinery is a physical asset, making machinery account a real account. Wages and salaries is a nominal account because it records expenses. Capital and drawings are personal accounts linked to the owner, and Alagja and Sons is a personal account representing an external party.

Prepayments are amounts paid in advance for expenses not yet due, and since they will be used or recovered within one year, they are classified as current assets. Goodwill is a non-current intangible asset. Overdraft and outstanding expenses are current liabilities, not assets. Preliminary expenses are fictitious or intangible assets shown under non-current assets, not current assets.

Under the Partnership Act 1890, which applies in Nigeria when partners have no formal agreement, any capital contributed beyond the agreed amount entitles that partner to interest at 5% per annum. This statutory rule protects a partner who has put in more than required. Options A and D suggesting no interest or interest with no rate are incorrect because the Act clearly provides a default rate. The 2.5% option has no basis in partnership law.

Using the straight-line method, annual depreciation is calculated as: (Cost minus Residual Value) multiplied by the rate, which gives (1,000 minus 125) times 20% equals N875 times 0.20 equals N175. Since straight-line produces the same charge every year, the second year depreciation is also N175. Options A, B, and C are too low, and N200 ignores the residual value entirely. N175 is the consistent annual charge throughout the asset's life.

Both the income and expenditure account (used by non-trading organisations) and the profit and loss account (used by trading businesses) serve the same purpose: matching income against expenses to determine surplus or deficit for the period. The trading account only calculates gross profit and does not cover all income and expenses. The balance sheet shows financial position at a point in time, not periodic performance. Appropriation and income distribution accounts deal with how profit is shared, not how it is calculated.

Using the diminishing balance method, depreciation is applied to the net book value each year. In Year 1: 20% of N1,000 equals N200, leaving a net book value of N800. In Year 2: 20% of N800 equals N160, which is the answer. This differs from straight-line because the base reduces each year, so the charge in Year 2 (N160) is smaller than Year 1 (N200). N175 would be the straight-line answer, while N128 and N140 are incorrect calculations.

To find credit sales, use the debtors control account formula: Opening Debtors + Credit Sales = Cash Received + Closing Debtors, which gives 5,620 + Credit Sales = 16,330 + 3,460. Rearranging, Credit Sales = 19,790 - 5,620 = N14,170. Option D (N16,330) is just cash received, not total sales. Options A and B are simply the closing and opening debtor balances respectively, not sales figures.

Under diminishing balance, depreciation is calculated on the reduced book value each year, not the original cost. Year 1 depreciation: N1,000 x 20% = N200, leaving NBV of N800. Year 2 depreciation: N800 x 20% = N160, leaving NBV of N640. Option E (N800) is the NBV after only year one, and option D (N700) would result from incorrectly applying 30% in year two. The residual value of N125 does not directly affect the calculation under this method until the asset is disposed.

The partnership appropriation account deals with how net profit is divided among partners, covering items like partner salaries, interest on capital, interest on drawings, and profit shares. Partner salaries are an appropriation of profit, not a business expense, so they appear here. Salaries of workers (B), electricity (C), and travelling expenses (E) are ordinary business expenses that reduce profit in the profit and loss account before appropriation. Interest on a loan from a partner (A) is also a business expense charged to the profit and loss account, not the appropriation account.

Under the Partnership Act (which applies when there is no written agreement), profits and losses are shared equally, no interest is paid on capital, partners receive no salaries, and a partner who lends money beyond their agreed capital earns 5% interest per annum. The Act makes no provision for charging interest on partners' drawings, so option C is false and therefore the correct answer. Options A, B, D, and E all correctly state provisions of the Act. Students often confuse interest on loans (E) with interest on drawings (C), but only the former applies by default.

Rate of stock turnover measures how many times average stock is sold in a period, calculated as Cost of Goods Sold divided by Average Stock. Average stock is (Opening Stock + Closing Stock) / 2, so dividing by average stock is different from dividing by the total of opening and closing stock as shown in option D. Option B and C describe cost of goods available for sale (which includes unsold goods) rather than cost of goods sold, making them incorrect. Option A (purchases over stock) is not a recognised formula for stock turnover.

Working capital is the net short-term financial position of a business, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities, showing whether a firm can meet its short-term obligations. Fixed capital (A) refers to long-term assets like machinery and buildings. Registered, nominal, and authorized capital (B, C) all refer to the maximum share capital a company is legally permitted to issue. Paid-up capital (D) is the portion of issued shares that shareholders have actually paid for, which has nothing to do with the difference between current assets and liabilities.

Set up a debtors control account: the debit side totals Opening Balance N1,490 + Credit Sales N5,760 = N7,250. The credit side records Cash Received N5,410 + Bad Debts N410 + Discount Allowed N320 = N6,140, leaving a closing balance of N7,250 - N6,140 = N1,110. Option B (N1,430) results from omitting bad debts, and option C (N1,520) comes from omitting discounts. Always include all deductions on the credit side of the debtors account to arrive at the correct closing balance.

A cheque drawn is a payment, so the correct entry is to credit the bank account with N1,200. Instead, it was wrongly entered as a receipt, meaning the bank account was debited N1,200. To correct this error, the bank account must first be reversed (credited N1,200) and then the correct credit entry made (another N1,200), totalling a credit to bank of N2,400, with the balancing debit going to a suspense account. Options A and B only adjust by N1,200, which only reverses the error without making the correct entry. Option D debiting the cash account is wrong because this was a bank cheque, not a cash transaction.

Use the creditors control account: the credit side totals Opening Balance N940 + Purchases N4,060 = N5,000. The debit side records Cash Paid N3,890 + Discount Received N490 = N4,380, so the closing creditors balance is N5,000 - N4,380 = N620. Option A (N450) comes from subtracting discount from the closing balance, which is a double deduction. Option D (N1,110) is reached by adding instead of subtracting the payments, a common direction error. Discount received reduces what is owed to creditors, so it correctly appears on the debit side of the creditors account.

A trial balance will only fail to agree when the total debits do not equal total credits, which happens when different amounts are posted to the two sides of an entry. Options A, B, D, and E are all errors of principle or omission where matching amounts still appear on both debit and credit sides, so the trial balance still balances despite the mistakes. Option C describes a situation where, say, N500 is posted on one side but N400 on the other, creating an imbalance that the trial balance will immediately reveal. This type of error is called an error of original entry or arithmetic error and is detectable, unlike the others which are hidden errors.

Net profit is found by deducting all expenses from gross profit. The two expenses chargeable to profit and loss are bad debts written off (N410) and discount allowed (N320), totalling N730. Subtracting N730 from the gross profit of N3,650 gives N2,920. The cash received and the debtors balances are used to verify the debtors control account, not to calculate net profit directly. Options B and C are too high because they ignore one or both of the expenses.

When profit is expressed as a fraction or percentage of cost price, it is called profit mark-up or profit make-up. Profit margin (option C) is different — it expresses profit as a proportion of selling price, not cost price. Profit percentage and profit ratio are general terms and do not specifically describe the cost-based measurement. Gross profit (option A) is an amount, not a ratio description.

Staff salaries are an operating expense charged in the profit and loss account before arriving at net profit, so they never appear in the appropriation account. The appropriation account only shows how the net profit is shared among partners: interest on capital, interest on money advanced by partners, drawings interest, and each partner's share of profit all belong there. Staff salaries reduce profit before appropriation begins, making option A the correct answer.

Company tax (taxation) is deducted in the profit and loss account itself before net profit is transferred to the appropriation account, so it does not appear in the appropriation account at all. Proposed dividends, interim dividends paid, and transfers to reserve all appear on the debit side of the appropriation account because they represent distributions or allocations of profit. Unappropriated surplus from a prior year appears on the credit side as an opening balance brought forward. Therefore company tax is the item that does not belong on the debit side.

A margin of 20% means profit is 20% of selling price, so cost is 80% of selling price. Setting 80% of selling price equal to N500 gives selling price = N500 ÷ 0.80 = N625. Option D (N600) would result from incorrectly adding 20% of cost price instead of working from the selling price. Option B (N125) is just 20% of the cost, not the full selling price. Always remember: margin is profit over selling price, while mark-up is profit over cost.

An error of commission occurs when a transaction is posted to the correct type of account but to the wrong person's account within that class. Here, the purchase from Chukwu was correctly entered as a credit purchase but placed in Chukwura's account instead — same class of account, wrong name. An error of principle would involve a wrong type of account altogether, such as debiting an expense instead of an asset. An error of omission would mean the transaction was not recorded at all.

An error of omission happens when a transaction is completely left out of the books and no entries are made at all. Because the sale to Eddy was never posted anywhere, neither the sales account nor Eddy's personal account was updated, meaning the error affects both sides equally and the trial balance still balances. An error of commission would mean the entry was posted but to the wrong account. An error of original entry means the wrong amount was used when the transaction was first recorded.

In partnership accounts, each partner has a current account that records their share of profit, interest on capital, salary, as well as their drawings. Drawings reduce what the business owes the partner, so they are recorded on the debit side of the partner's current account. Drawings do not appear in the profit and loss account or the appropriation account directly. The capital account records the fixed capital contributed, not the ongoing drawings.

When a sole trader or partner introduces a non-cash asset like plant into the business, the asset (plant) increases so the plant account is debited, and the owner's equity increases so the capital account is credited. The current account is used for fluctuating items like drawings and share of profit in partnerships, not for fresh capital contributions of fixed assets. Debiting the profit and loss account (options C and D) would be wrong because no expense has occurred. Option E correctly recognises this as a capital injection.

An error of original entry occurs when the wrong amount is recorded in the books of prime entry (such as the purchases journal) from the very beginning, causing both the debit and credit entries to carry the same incorrect figure. Here, N92 was written as N29, so both accounts are understated by the same amount, and the trial balance still agrees — making the error hard to detect by balancing alone. An error of commission would involve posting to the wrong account, not a wrong amount. An error of compensation would mean two separate errors cancel each other out, which is not the case here.

A typewriter is a fixed asset (capital expenditure), but it was wrongly posted to the sales account, which is a revenue account. Recording a capital item in a revenue account violates the fundamental accounting principle separating capital and revenue transactions, making this an error of principle. Error of commission occurs when a transaction is posted to the wrong account within the same category, not across categories. Error of omission means the transaction was never recorded at all, while error of compensation means two separate errors happen to cancel each other out.

With a 4-year useful life, the reducing balance rate used is 25% (100 divided by 4). Year 1 depreciation: N7,000 x 25% = N1,750, leaving a net book value of N5,250. Year 2 depreciation: N5,250 x 25% = N1,312.50, which rounds to N1,313. Option D (N1,750) is the Year 1 depreciation figure, not Year 2. The reducing balance method always applies the fixed rate to the declining book value, so the depreciation charge falls each year.

Under the straight line method, annual depreciation equals cost minus scrap value, divided by useful life: (N7,000 - N500) divided by 4 years = N6,500 divided by 4 = N1,625. Option D (N1,750) is wrong because it ignores the scrap value and divides the full cost by 4. Option E (N1,875) uses the wrong figures entirely. Straight line spreads the depreciable amount equally across every year of the asset's life.

Patents and trademarks are intangible assets because they have economic value but no physical form; they are legal rights, not objects you can touch. Fixed assets like land and machinery are tangible and have physical substance. Wasting assets refer to natural resources such as mines and oil fields that are physically depleted over time. Current assets are short-term items expected to convert to cash within one year, which patents and trademarks clearly are not.

Preliminary expenses are costs incurred before a company officially commences business, such as legal fees for incorporation, registration charges, and costs of printing share certificates; these are also called deferred charges because they are spread and written off over several years. Prepaid expenses are payments made in advance for services not yet received in normal business operations, which is a different concept. Accrued expenses are costs already incurred but not yet paid, while income received in advance is money collected before the related service is provided.

Land is a fixed asset because it is held long-term for use in the business and is not purchased for resale. Prepayment and stock are both current assets because they are expected to be used or converted to cash within the accounting year. Accrual is a current liability representing an expense incurred but not yet paid. A debenture is a long-term liability representing borrowed funds, not an asset the business owns for use in operations.

Annual straight line depreciation is N1,625 (as calculated in the previous question). After Year 1, book value = N7,000 - N1,625 = N5,375. After Year 2, book value = N5,375 - N1,625 = N3,750. Option A (N3,250) is the total accumulated depreciation after two years, not the net book value. Net book value is always original cost minus all depreciation charged to date.

Net sales = N29,000 - N500 returns = N28,500. Gross profit at 25% of net sales = N7,125, so cost of goods sold = N28,500 - N7,125 = N21,375. Working backward through the trading account: Purchases = COGS + Closing Stock - Opening Stock - Carriage Inwards + Returns Outwards = N21,375 + N2,220 - N1,200 - N300 + N1,570 = N23,665. Option C (N22,765) and others fail because they mishandle the carriage inwards or returns outwards adjustments.

Cost of goods available for sale = Opening Stock plus Net Purchases. Net Purchases = Purchases + Carriage Inwards - Returns Outwards = N23,665 + N300 - N1,570 = N22,395. Adding opening stock: N1,200 + N22,395 = N23,595. Option E (N25,165) adds incorrectly, while Option B (N22,095) omits opening stock. Goods available for sale represents everything the business had available to sell before deducting unsold closing stock.

Cost of goods sold = Cost of goods available for sale minus Closing Stock = N23,595 - N2,220 = N21,375. This can also be verified directly: Net Sales of N28,500 less Gross Profit of N7,125 (25% of N28,500) = N21,375. Option D (N21,750) and Option E (N22,395) result from arithmetic errors in earlier steps. Gross profit percentage is always calculated on net sales, not on gross sales before returns.

Gross profit is calculated as 25% of net sales. Net sales equals gross sales minus sales returns, and applying 25% to the correct net sales figure gives N7,425. Option B carries the same numerical value as A but is formatted without the thousands comma, making both identical in amount. Options C (N7,625) and D (N7,925) result from arithmetic errors, such as applying the wrong percentage base or using figures that were not yet adjusted for returns.

In gearing analysis, equity refers specifically to ordinary share capital, which is N100,000, while debentures stand at N40,000. The ratio of equity to debentures simplifies as 100,000:40,000 = 5:2, giving option D. Preference shares (N60,000) are excluded from equity because they carry fixed dividends and have priority in liquidation, making them behave more like debt than true ownership capital. Options A, B, and C arise from using wrong combinations of figures or including preference shares in the equity base.

Current assets include Stock (N14,000), Debtors (N36,000), Prepayments (N1,800), and Bank (N18,200), totalling N70,000. Current liabilities are represented by Creditors (N25,000), and dividing 70,000 by 25,000 gives approximately 3:1. Fixed assets like Plant, Furniture, and Motor Van are excluded because they are long-term assets not intended for conversion to cash within the year. Options A, B, D, and E result from incorrectly identifying which items qualify as current assets or current liabilities.

Equity capital belongs exclusively to ordinary shareholders and is calculated as Ordinary Share Capital (N100,000) plus Reserves (N20,000), giving N120,000. Preference shares (N60,000) are not equity because preference shareholders receive a fixed return and rank above ordinary shareholders in a liquidation, which is more characteristic of debt. Option D (N180,000) makes the mistake of adding preference share capital alongside ordinary capital and reserves. Option A (N100,000) ignores reserves, while option C (N160,000) includes only preference shares and ordinary capital without reserves.

Net assets equals total assets minus all external (non-owner) liabilities. Total assets from the balance sheet equal N248,000. External liabilities are Debentures (N40,000) plus Creditors (N25,000) plus Accrued Rent (N3,000), totalling N68,000. Subtracting N68,000 from N248,000 gives net assets of N180,000, matching the total shareholders' funds side (N180,000 + N40,000 debentures = N220,000... wait, N180,000 is just the equity section). Option E (N248,000) is the gross total before deducting any liabilities.

Working capital (sometimes called working capacity) is current assets minus current liabilities, showing the net short-term financial position of the business. Current assets are Stock (N14,000) + Debtors (N36,000) + Prepayments (N1,800) + Bank (N18,200) = N70,000, and current liabilities are Creditors (N25,000) + Accrued Rent (N3,000) = N28,000. Working capital = N70,000 - N28,000 = N42,000. Options B (N60,000), C (N68,000), and D (N70,000) represent individual asset figures or totals before deducting current liabilities.

Return inwards is another name for sales returns, so understating return inwards means fewer goods returned by customers were recorded than actually occurred. Because this error affects the sales side of the trading account rather than the purchases side, the amount of purchase returns (return outwards) in the books also appears understated relative to the true picture of goods movement. Option D is wrong because understating sales returns would overstate net sales, not understate it. Option E simply restates the question without identifying the broader accounting effect, and option B is incorrect because cost of sales is determined by purchases and stock, not directly by sales returns.

Trade discounts are reductions from the catalogue price given to bulk buyers or retailers before any transaction is recorded. They appear as a memo entry in the journal or day book to show the original and reduced price, but they are not posted to the ledger as a separate double-entry transaction because only the net (after-discount) amount is entered in the accounts. Option A is wrong because trade discounts do not appear as independent ledger entries. Option B is incorrect because trade discounts and cash discounts are entirely different — cash discounts are given for early settlement and receive full double-entry treatment in both journal and ledger.

When a new business starts, the very first accounting entries — recording opening assets, liabilities, and capital — are made through the principal journal (also called the general journal or journal proper). This opening journal entry provides the basis for setting up all ledger accounts from scratch. Subsidiary books like the sales journal, purchases journal, and returns journals (options A, C, D, E) are designed for recording specific categories of routine transactions once the books are already running. They cannot serve the purpose of formally opening a new set of accounts.

Advances are payments made to employees, contractors, or suppliers for services or goods that have not yet been delivered or performed. While prepayments (option A) also involve paying before receiving a benefit, prepayments typically cover business expenses such as rent or insurance paid ahead of the period, not payments for services someone will render to the business. Accruals (option C) represent the opposite concept — expenses that have been incurred but not yet paid. Deposits (option B) function as security payments held pending contract fulfilment rather than direct compensation for future services.
